stories.Headline: Amazon withdraws Ashburn data center plan and will convey 25 acres to Loudoun County
stories.Summary:
On November 17, Loudoun County, Virginia, is set to take a final vote on pausing new legislative data center applications for up to 12 months. The vote comes four weeks after Amazon agreed on October 20 to drop its plans to build four data centers on its 122-acre Ashburn campus. Amazon had purchased the campus for around $427 million. The site is the former George Washington University campus. Under the October 20 deal with the county, Amazon agreed to withdraw its plan for four data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 sq ft.

Under the county's terms, Amazon cannot construct data centers or host their supporting infrastructure on the Ashburn campus. Amazon will convey about 25 acres to the county and seek to rezone the rest for housing. The pause would cover rezonings and special exceptions, the maximum Virginia law allows. The county hosts about 233 data center buildings, which generated $1.2 billion in tax revenue in FY2026, 39% of its budget. For fiscal 2027, estimated budget projects hold around 40%, at $1.3 billion.

Board Chair Phyllis Randall announced the agreement, called "Project Potomac Promise," on October 20. Randall said the campus was "just the wrong location for a data center," owing to the infrastructure it would need and residents' opposition. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company had "heard the community's pointed concerns" and "took them seriously." Weissman added that while Amazon and the county have differing views on the site's legal potential, it chose "a shared vision" over "costly litigation." Neither Amazon nor Randall cited power supply as the reason for calling off the planned data center construction.

Supervisor Juli Briskman vowed on July 30 to "fight it every step of the way." In early October, county staff told supervisors that Amazon would need additional county approval before building, citing a zoning determination that data centers were not a permitted primary use on the property. On September 15, Loudoun County supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause Board consideration of certain legislative applications for data centers and electrical substations. The written resolution got deferred from October 20 to November 17 to give staff more time to gather additional information before the final vote. According to the county attorney, a moratorium on data center approvals would not be legal, so the county is considering a pause of up to 12 months.

Amazon originally purchased the Ashburn campus for around $427.3 million in March 2026. Four months later in July the company filed a site plan called Bridgefield Tech Center, which included four two-story data center buildings spanning over 800,000 square feet in total alongside three parking garages. Amazon sought a "by-right" approval for this plan, an administrative process with no Planning Commission, public hearing or Board vote. Part of the reason behind the county's data center concentration is a 2000 zoning ruling that assigned data centers as office buildings, letting companies build them by right in office-zoned areas. Since March 2025, new data centers have required a special exception approved by a Board vote, though projects grandfathered under the old rules can still proceed administratively.

The pause does not cover administrative applications, including at least 17 grandfathered applications totaling over 11 million square feet. Despite the final decision, the Board can continue to consider "grid reliability" substations during the period. According to Governor Abigail Spanberger, the decision on approving or blocking data center projects should rest with the community and not the state. State Senator Russet Perry has separately drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals. According to Loudoun County, it has the highest concentration of data centers worldwide, home to around 233 data center buildings and 56.5 million square feet built or under construction as of March 1, 2026, plus 35.7 million square feet approved but not yet built.

stories.Headline: Riham Hashi launches Novara Strategies to help companies navigate AI governance and regulation
stories.Summary:
Riham Hashi, a 2026 graduate of Penn Carey Law’s Master in Law program, launched Novara Strategies in April 2025, a boutique consulting firm that helps companies navigate regulation, technology policy and artificial intelligence governance. She had worked in state policy and management roles focused on community-based initiatives and public policy implementation, and she noticed gaps between policy intent and real-world execution. She also worked on the Postsecondary Student Basic Needs Act, which passed in Washington State in May 2023. Soon after launching her firm, she entered the Master in Law program to build the legal expertise her clients needed. Hashi said the program was a deliberate step to strengthen the legal and regulatory foundation she was already building, and that she wanted a stronger framework in regulatory law and to think more precisely about legal structure and compliance, especially in artificial intelligence.

Through the curriculum she gained skills in legal reasoning, building compliance programs and regulatory interpretation. She first noticed a change in her U.S. Law and Legal Methods course, which she called foundational to how she analyzes legal issues for clients, and she said it changed how she reads and structures information and helped her approach statutes and case law with greater discipline and clarity. She also found immediate professional relevance in her Corporate Governance and Compliance and Intellectual Property Law for Strategists, Innovators, and Owners of IP Assets courses, and she said it was easy to connect classroom learning to real-life work. Hashi valued learning from faculty who are actively practicing in the fields they teach, and she pointed to her Corporate Governance and Compliance professor, Andrew Kandel, as an example of that practitioner-driven perspective. She said he is actively doing the work and that it is helpful to learn from someone directly in the field.

She also credited the program’s flexibility as a major advantage for professionals whose work intersects with the law, saying students can come from any field and mold the program to fit what they think is important to their work. She encouraged prospective students to take advantage of the larger Penn ecosystem and to enter the program with a clear sense of how they want to use the degree. For Hashi, the degree provided more than legal literacy, offering a structured framework for understanding governance, compliance and organizational decision-making at a deeper level. That framework now informs the work she is building through Novara Strategies and her broader approach to AI governance and regulatory strategy.

stories.Headline: Penn State researchers build AI that explains manufacturing fixes to engineers
stories.Summary:
A team led by Penn State researchers, funded by the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, is building a neurosymbolic intelligent system that pairs a neural network learning from industrial data with knowledge graphs of engineering rules. The work was published on November 16, 2026, by Tucker Leighty-Phillips of Penn State University. The system is meant to flag manufacturing problems and explain its recommendations to plant engineers. The Genesis Mission is a national effort led by the U.S. Department of Energy to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery and innovation. The team's aim is to combine data-driven learning with human-like reasoning.

The system will identify manufacturing issues through pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning, and use engineering and physics knowledge to understand and resolve problems. Operators will see what the neural system flags and decide whether to agree or override it with symbolic knowledge and reasoning assistance. The system will talk with engineers, draw out hidden constraints and work with the optimization models plants already use, updating recommendations as floor conditions change. A knowledge graph stores expert knowledge as a web of connected facts, linking items such as a weld defect, a machine setting or an assembly line step to the others they affect. Porosity in a weld can be caused by a travel speed that is too fast, and engineers can add new rules to the graph as they learn them.

Soundar Kumara, Allen E. Pearce and Allen M. Pearce Professor of Industrial Engineering and principal investigator, said the team is building a neurosymbolic intelligence with an explanation capability that will make the future of the global manufacturing landscape different and truly useful. He said neurosymbolic manufacturing intelligence will open new avenues and revitalize manufacturing by providing better explanations for the inferences made. He said the major focus is building neurosymbolic architecture that integrates neural inference with symbolic reasoning. He said the team is building neural reasoning connected with knowledge graphs for two case studies, one from General Motors and another from a small and medium-sized manufacturer in Pennsylvania. He said the architecture will be adaptable enough for other manufacturing applications.

Anirudh Subramanyam, Charles and Enid Schneider Early Career Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering, said optimization models are very good at finding the best plan under the rules you give them. He said the trouble on a real assembly line is that many of the most important rules have never been written down, as they only live in the heads of the engineers who run it. He said the team wants a system that learns those rules from engineers' feedback and can tell them not just what to change, but which constraint forced its hand. Rebecca Napolitano, co-principal investigator, associate professor of architectural engineering and associate director of the Digital Twin Hub, said the physics and engineering knowledge built into the symbolic side gives a way to test the AI, not just train it. She said that when the system makes a recommendation, the operator can see what it is based on and how confident it is.

The team includes collaborators from multiple Penn State units, industry, a national lab and commonwealth groups, including the Pennsylvania Technical Assistance Program (PennTAP) and Team Pennsylvania Foundation. Los Alamos National Laboratory will provide foundational expertise on neurosymbolic intelligence. Kumara said PennTAP and Team Pennsylvania Foundation work directly with manufacturers across the state, which gives a practical path into the shops that need this most. He said PennTAP offers no-cost energy assessments for companies, so they will measure energy usage at the shop before and after the tools are brought in. He said Team Pennsylvania Foundation will support the project by finding other in-state manufacturers and connecting them.

The researchers are building and testing their approach in two real-world case studies: welding quality inspection at a Pennsylvania manufacturer and assembly line rebalancing with General Motors. The researchers intentionally selected both a small and large manufacturer to test their approach, stating that if the model works at both scales, it should work for all enterprises of different scales. Currently, weld inspection relies on a person looking at the weld, which is getting harder as experienced welders retire, the researchers said. Penn State students are training neural models to spot defects like cracks, porosity and undercut, and are building knowledge graphs from real-world welding rules and standards. For example, if the system spots porosity in a weld image, it can use its welding rules to trace the likely cause to a setting such as electrode travel speed or voltage and suggest an adjustment for the welder to check.

For the General Motors case study, the researchers are applying neurosymbolic intelligence to rebalance assembly lines, where work is split into small tasks across a sequence of workstations. When the product mix shifts or the line must speed up, those tasks must be redistributed, and because tasks depend on one another, moving them can set off a chain of further moves down the line. Plants plan these changes with optimization models, but those models are limited by their hardcoded rules, and their recommendations can be hard for line engineers to interpret. In the team's approach, an optimization model proposes each plan while a neural layer learns from engineers' feedback, and when an engineer rejects a plan, for example because a needed tool sits at only one station, the system automatically infers the unwritten rule, adds it to the optimization model and proposes a new plan. Anirudh Subramanyam is leading the optimization effort with Seog-Chan Oh of General Motors, while Kamesh Madduri, associate professor of computer science and engineering, is leading development of the dynamic knowledge graph.

The researchers are also exploring federated learning, where models improve by learning across several companies without any of them having to share their data. Kumara said small manufacturers usually don't have enough data on their own to train a good AI model, and they also really don't want to hand their production data to a big company or a competitor. Federated learning lets each shop's model learn on its own data and only share what the model learned, not the raw data itself, allowing them to build a better model while ensuring their data stays in-house, the researchers explained. The project also draws on the interdisciplinary research community fostered by Penn State's Digital Twin Hub, a joint initiative of the Cocoziello Institute for Real Estate Innovation and the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences (ICDS). Jessica Menold, co-principal investigator and associate professor of mechanical engineering and industrial engineering, directs the Hub, which connects researchers working across manufacturing, infrastructure, healthcare and other domains to advance digital twin research and applications.

Menold said the challenges of developing digital twins often transcend individual disciplines and industries. She said the project demonstrates the value of bringing together expertise in AI, engineering, advanced manufacturing and human-centered design to advance digital twin research and address real-world manufacturing challenges. She said that by integrating deep learning, engineering knowledge and human expertise, we can move beyond simply modeling physical systems to understanding, predicting and improving their behavior. The researchers said it is equally important to ensure that these increasingly sophisticated systems remain transparent, allowing engineers to understand and critically evaluate the reasoning behind AI-generated recommendations. Other Penn State personnel on the project are Paul Griffin, Lucas Professor in Industrial Engineering; Guha Manogharan, professor of mechanical engineering; Ilya Kovalenko, assistant professor of mechanical engineering; and Tanna Pugh, director of PennTAP.

In addition to Seog-Chan Oh, other external co-principal investigators are Abby Smith of Team Pennsylvania Foundation and William Peck of Los Alamos National Laboratory. Graduate students include Vinay Saji Mathew, Chen Zhou and Xiaowen You, all from industrial engineering. Xiaowen You, doctoral student in industrial engineering, is advised by Soundar Kumara. The article was last updated November 16, 2026, and contact is the College of Engineering Media Relations at communications@engr.psu.edu. The article carries tags including Research, Science and Technology, University Park, Engineering, architectural engineering, industrial and manufacturing engineering, mechanical engineering and Artificial Intelligence.

stories.Headline: O'Fallon dispatchers use AI to transcribe 911 calls and suggest questions while a person always answers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of crime fighting and is being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country, according to articles published on November 17, 2026. The police dispatch in O'Fallon, Missouri, is using artificial intelligence-based technology to assist dispatchers who answer 911 calls. Dispatchers there said a person will always answer the call. The articles were published by kttc.com, wdtv.com, wndu.com and wect.com, and the wdtv.com article was written by Lauren Trager. The wdtv.com article was published at 12:47 PM EST and updated 18 minutes later.

Based on the call, the technology displays a specific list of questions for the dispatcher to ask. It also listens in, transcribes the call in real time and suggests information the dispatcher might have missed. In Fairfax, Virginia, AI translates calls into more than 170 languages instantly. In New Orleans, AI automatically answers calls about accidents officials already know about, and the system will inform the caller about the incident. If the caller is involved in any way, the person can stay on line to talk to a dispatcher.

Paul Jokerst, emergency communications administrator for O'Fallon Police, said the technology is there to assist dispatchers. He said it is clearly here to assist, and it is just to assist them. He said the technology is not intended to replace dispatchers. He said it is not here to replace anybody, not here to take a job away or hamper somebody's job. O'Fallon police dispatcher Mike Conte said he supports the use of AI.

Conte said the technology helps when dispatchers are trying to pick out information they cannot understand from a caller. He said it is very helpful when they are trying to pick out pieces of information they cannot understand the caller. He said he supports the technology as long as he is also on the line. He said you will always talk to a human, one of them is always there, and they are always ready to answer your call. Experts say AI would not replace dispatchers at the moment because humans are better at compassion, processing emotion and keeping people calm.

The articles state that artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of crime fighting and being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country. The use of AI in 911 is expanding rapidly, the wdtv.com article states. AI in law enforcement continues to evolve, the same article states. The kttc.com article carries the same statement that artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of crime fighting and being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country. The wdtc.com article was published at 12:36 PM EST and updated 29 minutes later.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond stating that AI in law enforcement continues to evolve. The articles leave open which other dispatch centers use the technology and how many calls it has handled. The articles leave open what the technology costs and how it was procured. The articles leave open what experts were consulted and what data supports the claim about compassion and emotion. The articles leave open whether the Fairfax and New Orleans systems are connected to the O'Fallon system.

stories.Headline: Fraud experts say AI makes impersonation scams more believable and harder to detect
stories.Summary:
Scammers are finding new ways to impersonate people and organizations you trust, fraud experts warn, and scams can start across multiple channels including phone calls, texts, email, messaging apps and social media. New technology such as artificial intelligence is making these tactics more believable and harder to detect, according to the articles. Impersonation scams happen when someone pretends to be a trusted person or organization, such as a government agency, law enforcement, a bank, a tech support provider, or even a family member. These scams are effective because they create a sense of urgency and rely on trust to push people to act quickly. In some cases, criminals now use AI to generate realistic messages, real-time videos or even mimic a person's voice, which can make a scam feel more urgent and personal.

The articles describe the anatomy of a scam in five steps: contact from someone claiming to be a trusted source, trust built by a message that sounds believable, familiar or authoritative, urgency created by a claimed problem or emergency needing immediate action, a request to send money or share information, and extraction of money or sensitive information often before the request can be verified. Scammers may pose as familiar or authoritative sources, with common examples including calls claiming to be from a bank, a government agency or a relative in distress. Contact can happen in multiple ways, with calls, texts, email and social media messages all used together. Messages may be more polished and personalized and timed to feel legitimate. People impersonating law enforcement or bank employees often tell people to mention nothing to the bank employees during a withdrawal transaction because they are "compromised."

Joshua Del Valle, executive director of enterprise fraud at PNC Bank, said the technology may be new but the strategy behind these scams is not. He said fraudsters want to build trust, create pressure, and keep you from pausing long enough to question the request. He said that instead of relying on how convincing a message, voice or video appears, people should verify the request through a contact method they already know and trust. The articles attribute these remarks to Del Valle and give his title at PNC Bank. The articles also state that pressure is a key tactic, with scammers often pushing for immediate action or asking people not to involve others.

The articles list five ways to protect yourself: verify the request using a trusted contact method such as a known phone number or official website rather than the information provided in the message, do not rely on caller ID or voice alone because phone numbers and messages can be altered, faked or manipulated and sometimes show the name of the institution even when it is not real, slow down and ask questions because a person or organization with a legitimate request will not rush you into immediate action, be cautious about sharing personal information and avoid providing sensitive data in response to unexpected requests, and talk to someone you trust before acting because a second opinion can help spot red flags. The articles say impersonation scams continue to evolve but the underlying tactics remain the same: gaining your trust and pushing you to act quickly. They say slowing down and verifying before you respond can help you avoid making a payment or sharing information based on a false request. The articles direct readers to PNC's Security and Privacy Center for more information on best practices to help prevent fraud. The articles were published on 2026-11-16, one at 12:15:00Z by the Mesabi Tribune and one at 11:15:00Z by the Watauga Democrat.

The Mesabi Tribune is published in Virginia, Minnesota, at 704 7th Avenue, and the Watauga Democrat is a Mountain Times Publications outlet whose articles describe 8 full-time reporters and editors providing journalism in the High Country. The Mesabi Tribune page lists sister publications including the Grand Rapids Herald-Review and the Walker Pilot Independent. The Watauga Democrat page lists publications including the Blowing Rocket, Mountain Times, Avery Journal and Ashe Post & Times. Both articles carry a StatePoint byline and are filed under Tech Talk and Innovation. Both pages offer a Day Pass for only $1.99 and newsletters sign-up.

The articles say to visit PNC's Security and Privacy Center for more information on best practices to help prevent fraud. They leave open who exactly is behind any particular scam, beyond saying criminals use AI in some cases. They give no figures on how many people are affected or how much money is lost. They do not name any specific victim, company or case. They do not say what PNC or law enforcement will do next beyond the verification steps and the Security and Privacy Center resource.

stories.Headline: Google blocks K-12 search access unless districts opt into its AI version
stories.Summary:
Google announced that starting in January it plans to block K-12 students from using its search engine unless districts opt into the company’s AI-generated version of it, EdSource reported on November 14, 2026. Google automatically activated its Gemini chatbot in August for millions of young users enrolled in Google Classroom, a platform previously restricted to users 18 and older. Google’s announcement comes as districts across California debate restrictions on artificial intelligence and technology use in the classroom. Los Angeles Unified, the state’s largest district, has already placed restrictions on generative AI. Google’s decision could complicate such efforts, particularly because schools rely on the company’s digital workspace for daily lessons and its search engine for research and assignments.

Under the revised framework, products such as Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will remain inactive by default for K-12 student accounts. School administrators retain the authority to toggle individual applications on or off. Google will block both its integrated AI tool and Google search for K-12 students unless a district decides to turn either feature on, with no option for a search engine without AI integration. The company said in a blog post on Tuesday that it will update its search function for schools by making its “Guided Learning” AI product the default. The company also clarified in a post on X on Tuesday that schools can turn off its separate AI products, Gemini and Gemini Notebook, and use search, but AI Mode and AI Overview will remain integrated into Google search.

Google’s Vice President and General Manager of Education Chris Phillips said in a blog post that the company believes schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach. Phillips said on Monday during a virtual briefing that if a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have Search on at all. The company said in its post on X that it knows there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork and that schools have told the company they want control. The post said that is exactly why the company is making these changes today to address the feedback it has heard from educators in recent months. The post said the company will continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure it is giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.

Lila Byock, founder of parent advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, described Google’s decision as an act of “bullying” and said in a statement that educational value, not shareholder value, must determine the technology used by students. Byock said Google forced its AI products into classrooms and parents fought back, and that the company’s hostile ultimatum is a desperate attempt to maintain its stranglehold on public education. Rory Mir, director of community tech engagement at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said the tricky thing with schools is that they enter into long contracts, and that there is a lot of training that goes into making sure educators know how to use these different tools. Mir said the switch comes with real monetary costs as well as labor costs and disruption. Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense Media, said students use Google search and it helps with media literacy, understanding, evaluating, and analyzing resources, which are so crucial to learning.

About three-quarters of American teens and tweens use or interact with the AI summaries in search results, according to a recent report by Common Sense Media. In a series of 180 tests, Common Sense Media researchers found that Google’s AI Mode completed students’ homework assignments for them every time. The AI feature also invented fake answers to questions, returned different answers to the same questions and cited unreliable sources such as Reddit, Facebook and YouTube. Common Sense Media researchers have not reviewed Google’s Guided Learning mode. Google Classroom is used by over 100 million students and teachers in addition to school-provided Chromebook computers.

Many school districts will have to decide to opt into Google’s AI-integrated search or find a new search alternative in the middle of the school year. L.A. Unified uses a statewide purchasing arrangement for Google Workspace for Education, which includes Google Docs and Slides, and it also has a new Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee. A district spokesperson told EdSource that the district is reviewing Google’s announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students. Some parents of Long Beach Unified students, who are part of a new tech policy group that also includes teachers, students, administrators and industry experts, will have an opportunity to provide input into the district’s options, a district spokesperson said. The district is also in the middle of a student survey about AI use in school.

stories.Headline: Global shares decline as AI stocks tumble following new US chip restrictions and Nvidia leadership turmoil
stories.Summary:
Global shares traded broadly lower on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, as markets remained under pressure from artificial intelligence stocks. Wall Street saw these industry stocks tumble, which caused U.S. futures to edge lower and oil prices to fall. European shares declined and most Asian markets fell, although India advanced during this period of global financial instability. Regional leaders are gathering at summits in Asia this week, while investors watch for signs of cross-border cooperation. Nvidia is set to announce its quarterly earnings results on Tuesday amid this widespread decline in global stock values.

The DAX fell 0.8% to 26,387.92 in Germany, the CAC 40 dropped 0.5% to 8,307.83 in Paris, and the FTSE 100 slid 0.7% to 10,805.92. South Korea's Kospi declined 2.6% to 4,968.48, Samsung Electronics fell 3.1%, SK Hynix dropped 1.8%, and the Nikkei 225 lost 1.3% to 58,860.43. SoftBank Group tumbled 3.9%, Advantest slumped 4.4%, the Hang Seng sank 1% to 23,508.17, and the Shanghai Composite was 0.5% lower at 3,584.58. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.8% to 8,883.20, Taiwan's Taiex plunged 2.3%, and India's Sensex edged 0.6% higher during the trading day. The S&P 500 future fell 0.2%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average future dropped 0.4%, and the Sensex rose slightly.

Zhiwei Zhang, the president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, stated that the market was already worried about risk. He noted in a commentary that the current situation at Nvidia has made these existing market risks even more serious. The Trump administration is responsible for issuing new rules on Monday to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips. These new government rules also restrict access to servers, increasing the level of scrutiny facing the artificial intelligence sector. Interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street when Nvidia reports its latest quarterly results on Tuesday.

Other chip companies fell after previously climbing on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage over the struggling Nvidia. Investors are affected by the volatility, as they are used to Nvidia reporting results and revenue forecasts above expectations. The Bank of England may raise interest rates further depending on October inflation data that Britain will release on Wednesday. Japan's economy contracted in the July-September quarter, ending three consecutive quarters of growth, which affects the upcoming October trade data. Geopolitical tensions are high as leaders meet for the ASEAN summit in Manila and the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

Nvidia sank 4.1% after a leadership crisis involving CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned following disclosures of extramarital affairs and spy ties. The company lost 735 billion dollars in market value, while the S&P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq lost 2.5% Monday. The Dow fell 1.4% as losses broadened, and the AI industry faced criticism that its stock prices were in a bubble. Democrats may favor restrictions on AI data center construction following their victories in the U.S. midterm elections this year. Treasury yields eased back after a jump caused by a worse than expected report on U.S. inflation last week.

President Donald Trump will land in the Philippines on Tuesday and arrive in Shenzhen, China, late on Wednesday for summits. Brent crude edged 0.7% lower to 91.80 dollars, U.S. crude slid 0.6% to 85.20 dollars, and the dollar fell to 159.24 yen. The euro rose to 1.1004 dollars, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late on Friday. Investors will watch for progress on trade agreements and signs of cooperation between regional leaders during the upcoming Asian summits. The articles leave open whether the Bank of England will raise rates and how the AI sector will respond.

stories.Headline: Google warns AI agents accelerate cyberattacks in third quarter analysis
stories.Summary:
Google warned that artificial intelligence is now doing more heavy lifting in hacking during a third quarter analysis of attacks. Russian speaking hackers carried out the first fully automated cyberattack without any human in the loop at any stage. This operation targeted French websites in the media, entertainment, and education sectors using a system called exploit agent. Google first noted an increase in LLMJacking, where hackers hijack AI model systems, earlier in November of 2026. These automated intrusions allow hackers to scale their operations significantly by chaining together complex attack paths at machine speed.

The shift requires using autonomous workflow multi agent frameworks including Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi stage intrusions. A Chinese speaking threat actor used the open source Cairn attack on more than a dozen different organizations. Google researchers observed a threat actor using that same framework to breach companies within the United States aerospace sector. Between August and October, hackers used a customized platform based on PentAGI to scan for vulnerabilities in Asian organizations. These frameworks allow attackers to automate the reverse engineering of patches to weaponize n day vulnerabilities more quickly.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant are responsible for the report and found a critical inflection point in hacking. They stated that the speed and scale of these frameworks introduce a new defensive challenge for security teams. Researchers believe threat actors will continue using these frameworks because of the low barrier to entry and scaling potential. They noted that unrestricted autonomous execution currently generates forensic traffic and leaves behind distinct code level traces for defenders. However, they warned that attackers will likely become stealthier and more sophisticated as agentic pen testing frameworks improve.

The report echoes findings from Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 regarding the use of the open source Cairn framework. Organizations in the aerospace sector and various Asian entities were affected by these automated vulnerability scanning and breach attempts. Financially motivated threat actors are also affecting companies by using LLMJacking to resell access to hijacked AI models. Defenders are also burdened by a wave of LLM generated exploits that are claimed to work but actually do not. This creates additional verification work for those defending networks against these new, automated, and often fake AI threats.

The background shows that attackers still use compromised credentials and target unpatched systems, though the execution speed has increased. The first fully automated attack was identified by Russian language comments in the code and specific configuration file instructions. This code instructed the user to enter API keys for auto exploitation rather than using a standard chat interface. The exploit agent system compares software code before and after patches to infer changes and draft automatic exploits. Other discovered scripts handled internal reconnaissance, password guessing, and the installation of webshells to maintain access to systems.

Next, researchers expect that more attacks will become autonomous because this capability can compress the timelines for successful intrusions. Attackers may eventually stop trading stealth for speed as the underlying AI models and agentic frameworks continue to evolve. Google's report leaves open the specific identity of the Russian speaking group or state responsible for the automated attack. It remains unclear how many other organizations have been breached by these specific autonomous frameworks without being detected yet. The articles do not state when the next quarterly analysis will be released to track these evolving AI trends.

stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
Negotiations on possible rules for lethal autonomous weapons, also called killer robots, are underway at the United Nations in Geneva. This week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, or CCW, meets just once every five years. Supporters of controls say it is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late. Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, and some experts warn the world is months away from weapons that choose targets and decide to kill autonomously. In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, though these are still controlled remotely by humans.

At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree binding rules governing autonomous weapons. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules. Washington proposes a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead. U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus, which was achieved in 1995 when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers. This week there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period for rules individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be crossing a moral red line. Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, said the risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, autonomous weapons cannot understand contextual signals the way a human does. She said the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target. U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk called on states to urgently agree on binding international rules to regulate autonomous weapons and protect human lives before it is too late. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society this weekend, warned against quoting laws to men with swords.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill, and responsibility for that choice, must stay in human hands. The United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules ahead of this week's meeting. The Red Cross is especially worried that the Geneva Conventions cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons, under which soldiers who are wounded or surrendering can no longer be targeted. Human rights groups warn the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use, with greater danger of proliferation and use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or everyone speaking a certain language.

Ukrainian civilians have reported being hunted by drones as they shop or go to school. The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties and did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, although it over time stopped deploying them and reduced its stockpiles. Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown, and Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention. An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies was demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29.

No treaty or laws will be enacted after this week's conference, but it could lay the groundwork for future legislation. Nicole van Rooijen, part of the campaign group Stop Killer Robots, told Newsweek that the majority of states worldwide want a legally binding treaty. She says failing to act could allow technology to further shape the rules surrounding killer robots in warfare. For diplomats supporting a compromise, it is a way to ensure at least some progress, while for campaigners it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road. Last month, Anthropic, operator of Claude, said in its latest threat intelligence report that Russian-based cybercriminals and Iranian propaganda actors tried to use the AI model for malicious reasons, including attempts to develop software for conventional weapons, firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions, as well as targeting and control systems.

stories.Headline: China integrates artificial intelligence into national education to create an AI-native generation
stories.Summary:
Beijing is currently pushing to integrate artificial intelligence into its national education system to create an AI-native generation of students. This state-led effort involves nearly 200 million primary and secondary students across the country in a massive learning experiment. The government wants universal AI literacy for all school children by the year 2030 to ensure economic success. This initiative aims to nurture homegrown innovation to help China win its technological rivalry against the United States. President Xi Jinping has declared that AI education is fundamental to the reform of the national schooling system.

The Beijing New Talent Academy costs 39,000 dollars annually and serves over 2,000 students on a 12 hectare boarding campus. Shanghai mandates 30 hours of annual AI teaching per grade, while Beijing plans 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Ningxia and Gansu plan to include AI literacy in high-stakes entrance exams by 2027, and Yunnan will record 14,000 classrooms. Guizhou uses AI facial recognition and behavioural analysis, while Shanghai deploys systems for monitoring the mental and physical health of students. The education ministry has encouraged AI courses, teacher training, and pilot programmes since the start of 2024.

President Xi Jinping vowed to make AI for all during his debut at the top tech summit in China. Headmaster Liu Wei stated that AI should be an everyday tool for most students rather than just for future scientists. Headmaster Yang Tianliang said AI agents do not suffer from fatigue and never make students feel stupid for asking questions. An Alibaba spokesperson noted that the Cloud for Youth Programme gives students direct access to AI tools and education. Ted Mo Chen of ClassIn said implementation is all over the place and few schools integrate AI effectively.

Parents like Rita Luan worry that AI might shortcut learning and require close supervision to ensure children digest the solutions. Students using AI three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical, and creative skills than those who used it less. A study of 27,000 teenagers found an 18 per cent homework score increase but a 20 per cent exam score decline. Rural students may be more vulnerable to device addiction and cognitive outsourcing, where they delegate mental tasks to the technology. Many educators are grappling with how to deploy AI without reinforcing the rote-learning habits that policymakers want to move beyond.

The US relies on non-binding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to the 2026 Stanford AI Index. Government procurement records show at least 31 million dollars spent last year on AI classroom equipment, training, and teaching platforms. iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under 83 billion dollars, with generative AI taking 46 per cent. Funan County Qinqing High School in Anhui uses AI to solve teacher shortages for 4,000 pupils who are migrant children. This school uses AI models from Z.AI, ByteDance, and Alibaba's Qwen to generate interactive lessons, text, images, and videos.

China has not yet established a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment without a clear scorecard. Selena Guo of China Policy noted that mature assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built now. The education ministry did not respond to requests for comment, and ByteDance and Z.AI also did not respond to inquiries. It remains unclear if the short-term gains in homework scores will lead to long-term intellectual development or cognitive decline. The articles leave open whether the government can successfully balance AI efficiency with the need for independent and critical thinking.

stories.Headline: Australia circulates first draft decision as COP31 ministers arrive to seek compromises
stories.Summary:
The COP31 climate conference entered its second and final week on Monday, November 16, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, with ministers arriving for talks. Negotiators remained deadlocked on fossil fuels, adaptation, and finance, while new initiatives on green industrialization and artificial intelligence were showcased during the event. Australia, acting as the lead negotiator and co-host, circulated a first draft of an overarching decision late Monday to start negotiations. Ministers will gather in a Divan, an Ottoman term for an imperial assembly, to seek political compromises on the most contentious issues. The first seven days of the conference were dominated by various speeches, technical negotiations, and announcements before the high-level segment began.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge attracted 80 endorsements and 271 commitments to make technology more sustainable through cleaner energy and better emissions tracking. Governments launched the Antalya Green Industrialization Compact to accelerate investment in cleaner cement, steel, and other industrial products for developing countries. Vulnerable nations are pushing for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to publish its next major assessment by a 2028 deadline. The Climate Club Secretariat, a coalition of 53 countries, is working to cut industrial emissions using technologies that exist today. The Solomon Islands became the first country at COP31 to announce a contribution to the Green Climate Fund for climate action.

Soenke Kreft of the United Nations University said the slow first half of negotiations now requires a momentum swing for the second week. Laurence Tubiana, CEO of the European Climate Foundation, stated that the world must defend science and the scientists during these critical talks. Mary Robinson, the former President of Ireland, urged countries to resolve differences so the next IPCC assessment is delivered on time. ITU Deputy Secretary-General Tomas Lamanauskas warned that data centre energy consumption for AI is expected to double by the year 2030. Ciyong Zou of UNIDO said green industrialization turns renewable energy momentum into industrial opportunity that creates jobs and strengthens energy security.

Climate activists warned that cover decisions could become a distraction from concrete action and criticized just transition mechanisms that lack necessary resources. A representative noted that coal miners in Australia and steel workers in Germany, India, and the UK cannot afford more dialogues. Scientists warned about the risks of overshoot, which is temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C warming threshold, and called for evidence to guide decisions. Álvaro Rojas of the United Nations University used AI to analyze 1,600 disaster risk management documents to identify where countries need support. Michael Apicelli stated that investments in steel and cement production are critical because they lock in technologies for 30 to 40 years.

AI can predict extreme weather and improve energy efficiency, but powerful models require vast amounts of water and electricity to function properly. A UNESCO and University College London study found that chatbots sometimes abandon established climate facts when challenged and vary across different languages. Brigitte Perrin is developing Beluga, an AI platform by Earth Info Hub, to create a safe place for reliable environmental research. Peter Schniering of Future Cleantech Architects suggested using electric furnaces and smarter building designs to reduce emissions from steel and concrete. He noted that decarbonizing aviation, shipping, and steel production depends on the availability of more clean electricity and green hydrogen.

Ministers must now decide if they will agree on a cover text that addresses the transition away from fossil fuels and energy. Negotiators need to bridge disagreements over public funding obligations and financial support for developing economies to help them adapt to climate change. The final outcome must address the issue of overshoot and reinforce the 1.5°C temperature goal to protect the global environment. It remains open whether ministers can agree on a mechanism to support workers and communities during the transition to green energy. The articles leave open if countries will reach a consensus on the scientific timetable for the next major IPCC climate assessment.

stories.Headline: Asian investors sell off AI stocks ahead of Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO
stories.Summary:
Asian investors sold off artificial intelligence stocks on Sunday, November 15, 2026, as they reduced their exposure to the volatile tech sector. This market movement occurred because investors are cautious ahead of a crucial week for the boom in artificial intelligence technology. The selloff caused benchmark stock indexes in Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan to slump, with the Taiex plunging more than 4 percent. US Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.5 percent after the cash index dropped 1.2 percent on the previous Friday. These actions reflect a fragile market sentiment as traders await several major corporate and economic events scheduled for the coming days.

Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, while Claude chatbot maker Anthropic prices its initial public offering on Wednesday and debuts on Nasdaq Thursday. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the former chief financial officer, must now shore up investor confidence following the resignation of Jensen Huang. Huang left the company last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, leaving a leadership void at the signature AI bull market stock. LSEG data shows Nvidia lost 1.9 trillion dollars in market capitalisation since early October due to concerns over debt-fuelled AI buildouts. Additionally, Democrats won the US midterm elections earlier this month, which threatens to bring more stringent regulations on data-centre expansion.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is responsible for managing the company, but media speculation suggests Jensen Huang might discuss a possible comeback. The Financial Times reports that Nvidia has approached Rene Haas, the CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, for the leadership role. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the company needs to find a leader outside the firm. Elon Musk stated on X on Saturday that Nvidia would lose critical deals if Huang is not at the helm. These figures believe the leadership crisis is a primary driver of the current pressure on the artificial intelligence trade.

Investors in Asia are the most affected by the current slump, though European markets have remained more resilient during this volatility. The lower concentration of AI shares in Europe has bolstered the continent's appeal as a haven, with futures rising in Germany. US consumers are also in focus as earnings from Home Depot, Lowe's, Target, and Walmart provide insight into their resilience. Retail sales data on Tuesday will further clarify the economic state of the consumer during this period of tech market instability. Market participants are now watching to see if the AI trade can recover from this recent series of shocks.

The AI boom has been led by a four-year tech-led bull market, but sustainability concerns have grown since early October 2026. Inflationary pressures have raised market bets to about 8 percent for a supersized half-point interest rate hike in December. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will speak in San Francisco on Monday about how AI will reshape the entire US economy. The Federal Reserve is also under scrutiny following hawkish comments from officials regarding the current state of national inflationary pressures. These background factors have created a tense environment for investors who are weighing tech growth against broader economic risks.

Markets will monitor the retail sales data and the specific earnings results from Nvidia to determine the next direction for stocks. stories.Headline: HPE and AMD debut Lux AI cluster at No 14 on TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops
stories.Summary:
At SC26 in Chicago, HPE announced that Lux, an AI cluster built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, debuted at No. 14 on the TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops of measured HPL performance. HPE said the system, purpose-built for AI training and inference, placed ahead of machines designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. HPE and AMD co-designed and co-constructed the cluster, which gives researchers across the U.S. multi-tenant, cloud-like access. The debut was announced on November 16, 2026, according to the articles.

Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 systems with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and AMD Pensando DPUs. The network uses HPE Juniper Networking QFX switches running 800G Ethernet, with load balancing and congestion management that HPE says reduce bottlenecks and improve GPU utilization. HPE Networking Data Center Director handles intent-based deployment, management, and lifecycle automation. Half of Lux’s 3.5 million annual node-hours are dedicated to the Genesis Mission, and the other half are available for proprietary use, a total equivalent to about 400 nodes running around the clock for a year. HPE has made a $37 million in-kind investment in the program to support research projects.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company, with ORNL and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation and was furthering what it can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership. She said HPE was proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems. Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said she was excited for the debut and the opportunities it creates to expand access to advanced computing resources. She said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility to advance innovative SI approaches in Earth system prediction, materials development, biology, and fusion energy. Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president of global public sector and strategic partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together.

AMD said the cluster runs its ROCm software stack, and neither company has published a node or GPU count for the system. AMD said Lux is now open to scientific users. HPE describes Lux as the first deployment of HPE Networking products at a DOE national laboratory, bringing scalable, high-performance, open Ethernet to AI-driven science. The Genesis Mission is a DOE program that applies AI to energy research, scientific discovery, and national security on a platform combining AI, supercomputing, quantum systems, and scientific instruments. Zacharia tied Lux to an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that researchers across the country can use.

HPE announced Lux about a year ago as part of its broader collaboration with ORNL and AMD. The partnership also includes Discovery, a forthcoming next-generation supercomputer developed as the successor to Frontier, which first broke the exascale speed barrier. ORNL has said Discovery will pair AMD EPYC Venice CPUs with AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs on an HPE Cray Supercomputing platform, with delivery expected in 2028. Lux carries the integrated management and Silicon Root of Trust protection found across HPE ProLiant servers. The configuration equips Lux with the performance necessary for large model AI training and deep learning.

The articles do not say when Lux began operating beyond its debut at SC26. They leave open how many nodes or GPUs the system contains. They do not state which proprietary users will take the half of node-hours not dedicated to the Genesis Mission. They do not give a date for Discovery’s delivery beyond 2028. They do not say what the $37 million in-kind investment will fund specifically.

stories.Headline: MiTAC Computing unveils full-stack infrastructure to scale agentic AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
MiTAC Computing Technology Corporation unveiled a comprehensive AI infrastructure ecosystem at the SC26 event in Chicago on November 17, 2026. The company showcased these innovations at Booth 4615 to demonstrate how full-stack solutions overcome common enterprise AI deployment bottlenecks. This new ecosystem aims to scale agentic AI by addressing critical compute, thermal, and data challenges for modern businesses. MiTAC collaborated with several strategic partners including AMD, Canonical, DDN, Intel, NVIDIA, and Rafay to deliver these scalable architectures. The event took place at McCormick Place from November 17 through November 19 to present these high-performance server solutions.

The G8825Z5 server uses AMD EPYC 9575F or 9755 processors and AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs for the compute-intensive prefill stage. For the decode stage, the air-cooled G4520G6 uses Intel Xeon 6 processors and eight Skymizer HTX301-4S accelerator cards. Each HTX301-4S card has 256 GB of memory, providing 2 TB of aggregate memory to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model. The upcoming ORv3 44OU Helion solution will scale up to 32,768 AMD Zen 6 CPU cores for hyperscale environments. A 52U liquid-cooled rack integrates 12 G4826Z5 servers with 96 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs to increase GPU density by 50 percent.

Rick Hwang, the President of MiTAC Computing Technology, stated that scaling agentic AI requires cohesive infrastructure rather than fragmented systems. He explained that MiTAC provides the foundational full-stack solution necessary to make sustainable AI factories a reality for enterprises. The company also utilized the vision of AMD Chair and CEO Dr. Lisa Su announced at the OCP Global Summit. MiTAC aims to empower organizations to intelligently route complex workloads and maximize agents-per-watt efficiency through their new rack-scale architectures. These leadership goals focus on providing end-to-end capabilities from research and development to global manufacturing and support.

Enterprises are affected by the need for more than raw GPU power to handle the exponential surge in inference workloads. Canonical Ubuntu provides the certified operating system layer to ensure seamless deployment and enterprise-grade reliability for these AI factories. The DDN Infinia solution prevents accelerator data starvation by processing monumental data streams with ultra-low I/O latency for users. Rafay helps organizations maximize return on investment by providing dynamic GPU-as-a-Service orchestration to eliminate idling across distributed workloads. MiCoreView software grants data center managers deep telemetry and unified visibility through a comprehensive POD management solution.

MiTAC Computing is a subsidiary of MiTAC Holdings Corporation and has provided energy-efficient server solutions since the 1990s. The company specializes in high-performance computing, cloud, and edge computing using rigorous methodologies to ensure quality across all levels. They have unified their brand with TYAN server products and Intel DSG to stand out in the server technology industry. Their expertise covers barebones, systems, racks, and cluster levels to achieve high performance and integration for their global customers. The company provides customized platforms for hyperscale data centers and specialized AI applications to meet unique business needs.

The company is developing the Helion Agentic AI Rack to support next-generation rack-scale architectures for hyperscale and enterprise environments. A proof of concept with ZutaCore uses waterless two-phase direct liquid cooling to support thermal design powers exceeding 4,000W. This cooling technology achieves a heat flux over 250W/cm2 and enables an annualized pPUE of 1.03 for the G4826Z5 server. MiTAC also offers various server platforms like the G4827Z6, G2610Z6, TN85-B8261, R1917GC, R1610Z6, M2810Z6, and the liquid-cooled C2611Z6. The articles leave open the specific release dates for the upcoming Helion solution and other future hardware iterations.

stories.Headline: Sharjah Digital Department launches Agentic AI Challenge to automate government operations
stories.Summary:
The Sharjah Digital Department launched the Sharjah Agentic AI Challenge to speed up the use of agentic artificial intelligence in government operations. This initiative follows the directives of HH Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed bin Sultan Al Qasimi, the Crown Prince and Deputy Ruler of Sharjah. The event is scheduled to take place from December 8 to 10 to help automate various government services and operations. It is organized in partnership with Inception42, while Microsoft is participating as a collaborator for the duration of the challenge. The program aims to empower national talent to create innovative solutions that address real world challenges using new agentic AI technologies.

The challenge is open to the public and will include 30 participants who will work in teams of specialists and experts. These teams must develop prototypes of intelligent AI agents that can automate repetitive procedures and reduce the time for processing transactions. The program uses a design thinking approach and hands on learning under the guidance of trainers to create these practical solutions. It begins with an introductory session and three days of intensive work from 8 to 10 December in the city. The final prototypes will be presented to a specialized judging panel that will select the winning teams for the competition.

Sheikh Saud bin Sultan Al Qasimi, Director General of Sharjah Digital Department, said the Crown Prince set a clear strategic objective for them. He stated that the goal is to harness the potential of agentic AI in practical ways across various government institutions. He believes the true value of these technologies is their ability to streamline procedures and improve the quality of government services. He noted that the challenge is a practical step toward building sustainable government capabilities by combining operational experience with technical knowledge. He added that this will strengthen institutional integration and support the goals of the Sharjah Digital Transformation Strategy 2026 to 2028.

The project is designed to make a tangible difference to the lives of people by improving the overall customer experience. It affects national talent by providing them with the opportunity to develop solutions that enhance the efficiency of government operations. The initiative also aims to strengthen partnerships and integration between different entities to promote a sustainable digital transformation for the region. These efforts align with the human centred approach to digital integration that Sharjah has committed to for its citizens and residents. The challenge also supports the broader goals of the We the UAE 2031 Vision and the UAE National Strategy for AI.

The Sharjah Digital Transformation Strategy 2026 to 2028 aims to develop government services and improve the performance of various local institutions. This strategy provides the background for the current challenge to promote a sustainable digital transformation across the entire government sector. The UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 also serves as a foundation for these technological advancements in the emirate. Additionally, the We the UAE 2031 Vision guides the strategic direction for integrating advanced technology into the national infrastructure and services. These frameworks emphasize the importance of strengthening digital capabilities to maintain a competitive and efficient government for the future.

The next step involves the introductory session followed by three days of intensive practical work for the thirty selected challenge participants. Teams will collaborate to turn specific challenges into practical solutions before presenting their final prototypes to the specialized judging panel. The panel will then evaluate the work to select the winning teams based on the quality of their AI agents. The articles do not state what rewards the winning teams will receive after the competition ends on December 10. They also leave open how the winning prototypes will be implemented into actual government operations after the challenge is completed.

stories.Headline: Prime Minister Han Seong-sook forms emergency team to prevent AI cheating on 2027 CSAT
stories.Summary:
South Korea is forming a pan-government emergency response team to stop AI-assisted cheating on the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced this team on Monday, November 16, 2026, during a meeting of related government ministries. The decision follows a confession from the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam regarding AI use. This individual admitted on a Sunday YouTube appearance to using generative AI and electronic devices during both exam rounds. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea is filing a criminal complaint for obstruction of business against him.

The team will manage the national entrance exam taking place this Thursday to ensure that no advanced AI cheating occurs. Prime Minister Han ordered the Ministry of Education to review how testing sites are managed and proctored for the exam. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin visited Yeongdeungpo Girls’ High School in western Seoul on Monday to check on various site preparations. The Ministry of Education previously ran safety inspections at 1,312 testing sites across 85 test districts over three weeks. These checks included outdoor structures and measures against fires, cold snaps, and earthquakes starting on October 20, 2026.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook stated that suspected AI cheating is spreading across various exams and has deepened public concern about fairness. She said that hard working test-takers should not be negatively affected and confidence in the exam system must not erode. Han noted that existing ways of managing national exams are limited when dealing with new and sophisticated AI cheating techniques. She urged officials to use objective data to investigate any signs of irregularity found in the results after the exam. The Prime Minister believes the country must focus all its capabilities on preparing for the upcoming College Scholastic Ability Test.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin promised to spare no effort to prevent cheating and will respond with a zero-tolerance principle. He acknowledged that authorities cannot guarantee the detection of all AI-assisted cheating just days before the national college entrance exam. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea is affected by the tax accountant scandal and is pursuing criminal legal action. Other national exams are affected, as authorities will investigate potential AI-assisted cheating across 528 different state-run national examinations. Lawmakers on the National Assembly’s Education Committee in Yeouido also reviewed the preparations to block AI-assisted cheating on the test.

The government is reacting to the rise of ultrasmall electronic devices, outside help, and smart glasses used for cheating in exams. A smart glasses company representative demonstrated device functions to inspectors at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in Yongsan District. This training session occurred on November 11 to help inspectors screen students at testing sites located throughout the city of Seoul. The government is concerned that the basic principle of fairness, which upholds trust in society, is being threatened by technology. These measures are part of a broader effort to secure the integrity of the national university entrance exam system.

The emergency team will carry out both preventive and follow-up measures to ensure the fairness of the College Scholastic Ability Test. Relevant ministries must promptly prepare related measures based on the specific conditions of the exams under their own legal jurisdiction. Stricter oversight of electronic devices and smart wearables will continue even after the current college entrance exam period has finished. The articles leave open whether the current detectors will be ready in time to stop all AI cheating during the test. It remains unclear if the government can fully block all sophisticated AI tools before the exam begins this coming Thursday.

stories.Headline: Anthropic cuts high and critical vulnerability disclosure window to 30 days
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on November 16, 2026, that it had updated its coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, cutting the window for high- and critical-severity issues from 90 days to 30 days and setting a 45-day window for all other vulnerabilities. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027, while reports already in progress on that date keep their existing deadlines. The company said the change responds to frontier AI models becoming much better at discovering vulnerabilities over the previous several months. Anthropic also said it had reported some high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities more than 90 days earlier that now exceed the deadline in its current policy and have not yet been disclosed publicly. It is notifying the maintainers of those projects that they are getting an additional 30 days, after which the reports will be published on Anthropic's dashboard in line with the updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Beyond the shorter windows, Anthropic is making two related changes to how it handles reports. It will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to its initial vulnerability report, and it will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of the policy remains the same, including the seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation, which is unchanged. The update does not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

Anthropic said flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC cannot always be resolved in 30 or 45 days, and in those cases it will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Anthropic said many coordinated disclosure norms, including those in its own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities and assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. It said neither assumption holds today, because models can now help develop fixes and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another, and it is seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months, but the company no longer believes it can, and it said the changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Anthropic acknowledged that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers and said it will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible. To reduce the burden on maintainers, Anthropic said it will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project. It pointed to three programs meant to help maintainers and defenders work at the new pace: OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans the code of critical open-source projects with the company's strongest models and sends findings directly to maintainers; the Claude for Open Source Program, which offers eligible maintainers and contributors six months of Claude Ultra at no cost; and the Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude's safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work by security professionals, including open-source maintainers. The articles do not say what further steps follow beyond the January 1, 2027 start date and the additional 30 days given to maintainers of the older undisclosed reports.

stories.Headline: McKinsey and Cognition partner to show AI coding pays off
stories.Summary:
McKinsey & Company and the AI lab Cognition announced a partnership on Monday, November 16, 2026, to show that AI coding is worth its cost. Under the partnership, McKinsey will advise clients on which engineering projects to target and how to redesign teams and workflows around AI. Cognition will provide its AI coding agent, Devin, which the company says can understand, plan, write, and test code. The launch of Devin in early 2024 set off jitters among some software engineers about whether AI tools would upend their workflows and perhaps overtake their livelihoods. Since then, developers' work across industries has shifted from writing code to guiding AI's output.

Lari Hämäläinen, a senior partner in McKinsey's technology, media, and telecommunications practice, said that until the final months of 2025 many AI coding tools were most useful for narrow tasks such as looking up technical guidance or syntax details. Since then, he said, more capable AI models have made it possible to hand off longer, more autonomous coding work. He said the technology may be improving faster than organizations can redesign the processes around it, calling it a step-change phenomenon that requires a complete rethink of software and product development. In a recent McKinsey survey of more than 300 product and engineering leaders, the top quarter of organizations saw productivity more than double due to AI, while nearly 30 per cent said it had dropped. Hämäläinen said it is straightforward to have a small team experiment with an AI tool, but scaling it across 2,000 or 20,000 developers is a completely different thing.

Goldman Sachs, Cisco, and JPMorgan are among large companies becoming more selective about who gets access to which tools and how they are used, as they hunt for AI returns and ways to manage costs. Art Levy, VP of global partnerships at Cognition, said Devin can draw on multiple AI models, using pricier frontier tools for harder engineering work and cheaper models elsewhere. He said you don't need to drive a Ferrari to the grocery store, and that Devin's approach can help with large software modernization projects companies have put off. He pointed to one client where work to update enterprise resource planning software, expected to take five years, is being compressed into 18 months. Levy said the question is no longer whether you can get the job done, but whether you can get it done and are cheap at doing it.

stories.Headline: Chinese companies use outputs from US AI models to train domestic rivals
stories.Summary:
Chinese entities have increasingly used outputs from leading American artificial intelligence models to train domestic rivals, according to more than 300 documents. This practice, known as distillation, involves using a strong model's answers to teach a smaller one to solve hard problems or write code. A November 2024 study by Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers showed that 5,000 answers from OpenAI's o1 model became 10,750 bilingual training examples for Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B. These records indicate that the method has moved from laboratory experiments into mainstream industry as tighter US chip sales limits push developers toward cheaper routes.

The process requires Chinese companies to build software that automates the collection of responses, which specialist workers then prepare for training. In an April 2025 paper, Alibaba described using GPT-4 and GPT-4o to generate non-Chinese training material for smaller Qwen models. A February 2026 paper by Meituan and Shanghai Jiao Tong University detailed using GPT-4o to draft plans for coordinating AI agents. While this technique cannot fully copy a leading model, it allows selected skills to survive inside smaller systems. Alibaba has since progressed to larger releases, including its flagship Qwen4-Max model, while Meituan builds its own LongCat-2.5 multimodal model.

US officials claim that industrial-scale distillation is the primary reason Chinese models have narrowed the gap with American ones. They view the practice as a way to bypass chip export controls by drawing on capabilities that American rivals already paid to build. Chinese officials defend the method as a standard technique, and government documents encourage distillation to spread AI across the economy. A January policy package from eight agencies supports distillation for industrial uses to create cheaper systems for factories. An anonymous former Alibaba engineer described the method as a way to make one expensive query perform repeated work.

The current context involves a push by Shanghai and Shenzhen to promote techniques that reduce computing needs. Chinese developers have asked their industry regulator for guidance on where ordinary use of foreign models ends and organized collection begins. Researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University warned that heavy reliance on this process could stifle original innovation. These developments occur as officials anticipate a meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at APEC.
