stories.Headline: Princeton-led study finds human advisers use expertise unavailable to algorithms in 67% of advising actions
stories.Summary:
Research led by Lydia Liu, an assistant professor of computer science at Princeton Engineering, found that human advisers used information unavailable to an algorithm in two out of three actions taken during student meetings, including rearranging a schedule because of a health condition, encouraging a student struggling in math, or suggesting courses aligned with career goals. The paper, presented at the Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization conference in November 2025, drew on data from a six-year study at Georgia State University on AI-assisted advising. That randomized controlled trial showed students in AI-assisted advising had grades 0.16 points higher on average and a 7% higher graduation rate than the control group. Liu wanted to learn how much of the improvement came from the algorithm alone versus human expertise.

Combining student data with extensive notes from advisers, the researchers analyzed 8,385 advising actions across 5,269 meetings, and through statistical testing of student outcomes and qualitative analysis they determined that in 67% of cases advisers drew on information accessible only to humans to target their interventions. Liu said the AI tools in the Georgia State study are the same type used to predict sepsis in hospitals and recidivism in the criminal justice system, and that all these cases share an underlying problem formulation of predicting risk from an individual's data. She said it is critical to assess the human expertise required to use such tools effectively, because human intervention determines the downstream impact of an algorithmic prediction. The algorithm flags students, she said, but in most cases helping a student was something only a human could do.

Liu said that in complex fields like health, education and criminal justice, data gathered by AI tools often creates more opportunities for human intervention, not less, and that college advising is a compelling example because it depends on human relationships. She said advising is not just transactional, about delivering, getting and processing information, but also has a relational piece when students feel they have been seen by somebody, and she said it would be really sad if automation took away that important part of the experience. The paper, titled Discretion in the Loop: Human Expertise in Algorithm-Assisted College Advising, was presented at the EAAMO conference in November 2025. Besides Liu, the authors are Kara Schechtman of Princeton University, Benjamin Brandon and Jenise Stafford of Georgia State University, and Hannah Li of Columbia Business School.

stories.Headline: AI training startup Mercor valued at $20 billion in latest funding round
stories.Summary:
Mercor, an artificial intelligence training startup, raised $750 million (about Rs 7,057 crore) in a fresh funding round announced on November 10, 2026, according to Education Times. The round was a Series D investment that valued the company at $20 billion (about Rs 1.88 lakh crore). The company's three co-founders are 23-year-olds Adarsh Hiremath, chief technology officer, Surya Midha, board chairman, and Brendan Foody, chief executive officer. Hiremath and Midha are Indian-origin entrepreneurs whose estimated wealth nearly doubled to around Rs 40,000 crore each after the round. The round drew backing from Benchmark, General Catalyst, Nvidia, Salesforce, Felicis, Apollo-backed investors and Zoom.

The founders each hold 21% stakes in the company and now have an estimated net worth of $4.2 billion (Rs 40,000 crore) each, according to Forbes. Their estimated wealth rose from about $2.2 billion (roughly Rs 20,700 crore) per person at the October 2025 valuation of $10 billion. In October 2025 the company secured $350 million at that $10 billion valuation. Foody said in a post on X that Mercor increased its run-rate revenue from $1 million to $3 billion in just 27 months, which he called the fastest to reach that point. He also announced monthly gross sales of $250 million, and the company now services over 100 customers, more than double its previous number.

Foody, Hiremath and Midha are responsible for the company, and Foody said the revenue growth was the fastest to get to that point. The company plans to expand its evaluation and post-training services following the round. It also seeks to enable the creation and evaluation of AI agents using the business's own data and domain expertise. The founders became the world's youngest self-made billionaires last year at 22, according to Livemint. Midha is the youngest of the trio by approximately two months.

Livemint reported that the founders beat Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan, who was 27, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, who was 23 when he became a billionaire. Kalshi co-founder Luana Lopes Lara, 30, is currently recognised as the world's youngest self-made woman billionaire. Mercor trails rivals including Scale AI, valued at around $29 billion when Meta acquired a 49% stake last year, and Surge AI, valued at approximately $24 billion as per Forbes. The company's services have become increasingly relevant as tech companies compete to create sophisticated AI models and AI agents for specialised tasks.

Mercor was established in 2023 as a recruitment website matching freelance software developers, including professionals from India, with U.S.-based companies. It later expanded into data labelling, bringing professionals such as doctors and lawyers on board to help leading AI companies, including OpenAI, train their models. Hiremath and Midha are graduates of Bellarmine College Preparatory in San Jose, California, an all-boys school where they joined the debate team. The two were part of the first team in the school's history to take home all three top national policy debate tournaments that year. Midha was born in Mountain View, California, and raised in San Jose by parents who immigrated from New Delhi, and he took an academic leave from Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service in 2023 to found Mercor.

Hiremath studied computer science at Harvard University but left after two years to concentrate on building the startup. Three of Mercor's founders were chosen for the Thiel Fellowship, funded by billionaire investor Peter Thiel, which gives young entrepreneurs $100,000 to pursue a business idea instead of college. Mercor's latest funding is said to aid its evaluation and post-training business, as per the company's announcement. The articles do not say what specific terms, beyond the amount and valuation, the Series D round carried. They also leave open how the company will use the remaining proceeds beyond the stated expansion plans.

stories.Headline: Kaiser mental health clinicians ratify contract with AI advisory role and 17% wage increase
stories.Summary:
About 2,200 Kaiser Permanente mental health clinicians in Northern California and the Central Valley ratified a four-year labor contract, with 97% voting in favor after more than a year of contentious negotiations. The National Union of Healthcare Workers said Monday that its group of some 2,200 Kaiser mental health therapists, social workers and psychologists had voted to approve the agreement. About 80% of workers cast ballots during a several-day voting period that concluded Sunday. The contract was ratified with 97% support, the union said. Kaiser said it could not immediately respond to a request for comment about the agreement.

The contract bars layoffs through late 2029 and gives clinicians a role in advising Kaiser on AI and other technology changes. The contract includes wage increases of about 17% over the course of the contract. The union's last contract expired at the end of September 2025, and the new four-year agreement retroactively covers a period beginning from that expiration. The company will be required to notify workers in advance of changes in its model of care, including use of AI or other new technologies. The contract creates a process for a union-appointed group of mental healthcare clinicians to give advice to management on the changes and for the union to bargain over effects if the company moves forward.

Kaiser social worker Ilana Marcucci-Morris, who has been involved in the bargaining sessions, called the contract "a big victory" but said the company's behavioral healthcare still falls below the mark. She said workers "bought ourselves some time to give public leaders and legislators time to put parameters in place around AI." She said they "didn't get fully what we wanted in the language" but that it is a win that gave them time to strategize and make sure mental health care stays human. Marcucci-Morris said Kaiser had largely held firm in rejecting union language saying AI tools could be used to support, but not replace therapists. She said the company also pushed to negotiate severance and other layoff provisions, indicating that industry headwinds around AI had made layoffs "a real threat," even amid climbing patient demand for mental health services.

Kaiser spokesperson Candice Lee previously told The Times that "AI does not replace human assessment and care," but that it "holds significant potential to benefit healthcare by supporting better diagnostics, enhancing patient-clinician relationships, optimizing clinicians' time, and ensuring fairness in care experiences and health outcomes by addressing individual needs." NUHW President Emeritus Sal Rosselli said that now that the contract is ratified, workers will need to "be vigilant" to "make Kaiser fully respect the work of its clinicians and the needs of its patients." Kaiser's mental health workers in Southern California who are also represented by NUHW reached a bargaining agreement last year after a nearly seven-month strike. Workers have accused Kaiser in recent months of implementing harsh productivity metrics on clinicians, cutting into their time to respond to patient calls and emails, record notes and prepare for appointments and pressuring the staff to overbook patients. Kaiser did not immediately respond to questions about the productivity metrics.

Last fall, a group of Kaiser workers traveled to Las Vegas to protest remarks by Kaiser Chief Executive Greg Adams and pass out fliers to conference attendees about staffing shortage problems. The union had held a one-day strike in March over AI language. In October, workers authorized a three-day work stoppage, but held off on moving forward with it ahead of a scheduled mediation session with Kaiser that month. Over the summer, the union filed a complaint with the California Department of Managed Health Care over Kaiser's use of digital algorithms to screen patients seeking care. The union alleged that the practice continued despite state law requiring that treatment determinations be made by licensed providers.

Kaiser has maintained that those decisions are still being made by licensed professionals, saying in a statement to news outlet CalMatters that the tool conducts supportive screening and "does not use AI to diagnose patients, make clinical decisions, or determine medical necessity." A Kaiser spokesperson said to the news outlet that patients could still reach a live person by calling a phone number displayed during the e-visit process, and that the online screening tool was "not the only path" to care. The state Department of Managed Health Care has not yet issued a determination about the complaint. Kaiser did not respond to questions from The Times about the complaint. Marcucci-Morris said Kaiser's shift in negotiations came after the Democrats' sweep during the midterm elections that indicated some voter backlash to AI.

stories.Headline: Mavria raises $130M at a $1B valuation to build factory-made AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Mavria, a Houston, Texas-based company that enables factory-built data center infrastructure for the artificial intelligence industry, has raised $130 million across pre-seed and seed funding rounds at a $1 billion valuation. The latest round was led by Paradigm, with participation from AMP public benefit corporation, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier, and Dream Ventures. The company plans to use the capital to secure critical supply chains, expand manufacturing capacity and expand its workforce. Mavria was founded by a team with backgrounds spanning energy, software, manufacturing and infrastructure development, and its co-founders previously worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy.

The company's first product, Terrain, is a factory-built data center platform that integrates power, cooling, controls, and information technology pods into a standardized system. It uses repeatable manufacturing processes intended to reduce deployment timelines, improve cost predictability, and simplify procurement, designed for frontier AI laboratories, cloud providers, and data center developers. Terrain 01, Mavria's first data center system, is currently in production in Houston. Adam Blake, co-founder and CEO of Mavria, wrote on the company's blog post that the team believes in rapidly deploying infrastructure as a product rather than custom-building every project.

Blake is an American energy and software entrepreneur who joined the U.S. Department of Energy in early 2025 as a senior adviser to Energy Secretary Chris Wright, where he also led the agency's Department of Government Efficiency team. His responsibilities included implementing a federal directive to streamline regulatory pathways under the Atomic Energy Act, with a target of bringing three new non-commercial nuclear reactors to criticality by July 4, 2026. During his tenure at the department, Blake and his co-founders identified constraints in America's aging power grid and industrial supply chains as significant obstacles to meeting the growing infrastructure demands of artificial intelligence. The founders believe that America's ability to expand its industrial base will become increasingly important to its competitiveness in artificial intelligence.

Paradigm is a technology investment firm led by Matt Huang and Alana Palmedo that invests in companies developing technologies across artificial intelligence, robotics, cryptocurrency, and other emerging sectors. Founded in 2018, the firm manages more than $11 billion in assets and invests across stages and geographies, from early-stage financing to public markets. Its portfolio investments include drone delivery company Zipline, aerospace and defense company True Anomaly, payments platform Stripe, prediction market Kalshi, Hyperliquid, and financial services firm Citadel Securities. The firm has offices in San Francisco, New York, and Washington, D.C.

stories.Headline: Jo Gbujama summarizes 2026 state AI employment law updates and employer actions
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, JD Supra published an article by Jo Gbujama of Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP on 2026 national AI employment law updates. The article says the first half of 2026 brought significant developments regulating workplace AI. It says several states issued new rules or guidance on automated decision-making laws, disclosure requirements, and enforcement posture. It says courts continued to test the boundaries of AI-driven hiring decisions. It summarizes key developments since January 1, 2026, and closes with a practical action list for employers in affected jurisdictions.

The White House released its National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence on March 20, 2026, covering seven policy areas including workforce preparation and preemption. A draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 was made public on June 4, 2026, and would bar states from laws specifically regulating AI model development for three years. Colorado's ADMT Act takes effect January 1, 2027, and the Attorney General published proposed rules on August 11, 2026, with comments closing October 26, 2026. Connecticut passed SB 5 on May 1, 2026, and Governor Ned Lamont signed it on May 27, 2026, as Public Act 26-15. Illinois HB 3773 took effect January 1, 2026, and New York City's Local Law 144 requires bias audits within the past year and at least 10 business days' notice.

The article says Colorado enforcement rests exclusively with the Colorado Attorney General, and violations are treated as deceptive trade practices under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act with a 60-day cure period. It says Connecticut's law is enforced solely by the Attorney General, who must provide notice and a 60-day cure opportunity for violations occurring on or before December 31, 2027. It says the Illinois Department of Human Rights has enforcement authority, and individuals may pursue claims through the IHRA complaint process. It says New York City's DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine delivered remarks at a policy forum on September 30, 2026, indicating the city intends to stay ahead. It says the Colorado Attorney General's October 26, 2026 hearing drew testimony from industry groups, consumer advocates, and individual consumers.

The article says stakeholders raised questions about when ADMT materially influences a consequential decision and what constitutes meaningful human review. It says the Illinois IDHR's May 15, 2026 proposed regulations were withdrawn in June 2026, with the related hearing canceled and no revised timeline announced. It says employers deploying covered Colorado ADMT must issue a pre-use notice and furnish a plain-language explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome. It says Connecticut employers must give written notice to the Connecticut Department of Labor of whether AI was a contributing factor in a WARN Act mass layoff as of October 1, 2026. It says Connecticut's AEDT disclosure requirement starts October 1, 2027, and employers must give applicants and employees a pre-use written notice.

The article says the Colorado ADMT Act repealed and replaced the state's prior Artificial Intelligence Act. It says a federal district court stayed Colorado enforcement in xAI v. Weiser until the court decides xAI's preliminary injunction motion, due no later than 28 days after the final rules are adopted. It says the White House Framework is non-binding and creates no obligations for employers.

It says GAAIA would impose additional WARN Act disclosure obligations whenever AI serves as a substantial factor in a covered mass layoff. It says the Illinois law bars using zip codes as a proxy for protected class and requires employers to notify employees and applicants when AI is used in an employment decision. The article says the White House Framework recommends preempting unduly burdensome state AI laws while preserving states' police powers and zoning authority over AI infrastructure. It says the Framework recommends incorporating AI training into existing education and workforce programs, including apprenticeships, through non-regulatory means.

It says GAAIA leaves states free to regulate AI use in defined contexts such as employment, so state laws targeting AI in employment would likely survive. It says Connecticut's SB 5 amends the Connecticut Fair Employment Practices Act so use of an AEDT is not a defense to a discrimination complaint. It says New York City employers must disclose within 30 days of a written request what data was collected, where it came from, and how long it will be kept, unless already posted on the employer's website. The article says the Colorado stay will continue until the court decides xAI's preliminary injunction motion.

It says the Illinois IDHR's withdrawn regulations would have required employers to identify the AI product and developer, the decision affected, the purpose of using AI, the data categories collected, and the job positions involved. It says employers should treat the withdrawn regulations as the best available compliance roadmap while monitoring the IDHR for an updated proposal. It says Connecticut employers should lean toward disclosure of AEDT use until further guidance is issued because the phrase "a reasonable person would deem it obvious" is undefined. It says the article closes with a practical action list for employers in affected jurisdictions.

stories.Headline: Punjab bans camera-equipped smart glasses for 30 days from October 2026
stories.Summary:
Pakistan's Punjab province imposed a 30-day ban on camera-equipped smart glasses with hidden recording ability, beginning in October 2026, according to a report by Husain Parvez published on November 15, 2026. The order also covered miniature cameras disguised as pens or keychains, and retailers could not evade it by selling the affected devices online. Punjab authorities said they had received complaints of spying devices being used for illegal surveillance, harassment and blackmail. The authorities did not mention which models were included, and the ban was limited only to Punjab. No country has a permanent, outright ban on AI glasses, the report said.

New York banned smart glasses with cameras, microphones or computers in all 1,240 state and local courts since July 20, 2026, requiring them to be turned over to uniformed court officers for safekeeping. Ray-Ban Meta glasses with prescription lenses are also prohibited in New York courts, and officials urged visitors to pack a traditional pair. Meta glasses are banned in courts and tribunals in England and Wales, where security personnel can hold them until visitors leave. Western Australia banned AI glasses from public schools since October 12, 2026, applying the policy to students, staff and visitors with exemptions for approved medical, accessibility and educational reasons. Victoria announced similar restrictions, which will not take effect until January 27, 2027.

Smart glasses are prohibited from SAT test sites, even during breaks, unless an accommodation is granted, and scores may be canceled for violating the testing rules. Marine Corps policy at Camp Lejeune and other bases does not allow the use of smart glasses. In Australia, Canterbury-Bankstown Council banned smart glasses at its leisure and aquatic centers. UK cinemas are rolling out measures to curb camera-enabled glasses, citing privacy and film piracy issues. Royal Caribbean permits smart glasses on board but prohibits their use in casinos, medical facilities or youth areas.

Norway's government is considering temporary restrictions that could cover parks, beaches, shopping centers and gyms, but those proposals have not been enacted. Norwegian officials have not settled on which types of smart glasses would be covered, a distinction that matters because the Even Realities G2 has no camera while Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses can take photos and videos. In September 2026, Paris prosecutors opened investigations following complaints about women being filmed without consent using smart glasses, with the footage posted online. Prosecutors did not identify which brands were involved. Meta claims the white recording LED on its glasses lights up when photos or videos are taken and that the camera is disabled if its system detects tampering with the light.

Ray-Ban's documentation states that some camera-based AI functions on newer models can work without the LED being activated, since they are not saving shareable photos or videos. Mark Zuckerberg's team showed up in Ray-Ban Meta glasses during his testimony in Los Angeles in February 2026. Judge Carolyn Kuhl warned, according to the Los Angeles Times, that if your glasses are recording, you must take them off, though no recording of the proceedings was confirmed. The report said AI glasses can look like a normal pair of glasses but are becoming more unwelcome in courthouses, schools and other public places for safety and privacy reasons. The report said the list of places banning AI glasses is expected to continue to grow.

The report was published by Engadget and republished by AOL, both dated November 15, 2026, with the Engadget version timed at 11:00 am EST. The report stated that in many other countries and states, AI glasses are banned in specific places. The report did not say what would happen when Punjab's 30-day ban expires. The report did not say whether Norway would adopt the temporary restrictions it is considering. The report did not identify the brands involved in the Paris complaints or confirm any recording during Zuckerberg's testimony.

The company uses its AI world model for three stated purposes, which are predicting patient care needs, forecasting treatment impacts and optimizing referrals. stories.Headline: Microsoft report guides workplace AI security priorities as IT teams face identity risks from agents and user-built apps
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Cybersecurity Insiders on November 16, 2026, sets out practical steps for containing and securing artificial intelligence in the workplace, and it draws heavily on Microsoft's yearly Digital Defense Report as a guiding priority list for the next twelve months. The author argues that the protection of AI use is not vastly different from the security work IT teams already do, despite the large amount of hysteria surrounding the technology. The piece notes that end users are increasingly building their own apps through vibe coding and then expecting IT to handle hosting, security and support. It also observes that attacks are often described as sophisticated when the root cause is simply someone misconfiguring a basic control that every product has. The article says identity is the surface that matters most, and that the core failure is too much standing access that is too loosely enforced, a weakness red teams have exploited for years.

It explains that AI agents operate like virtual users, with an identity, access to files and resources, and the ability to carry out digital tasks on a computer, so identity must remain a priority. The author advises against blocking all AI tools, because users have become very dependent on them, and instead recommends discovering what is being used, most easily through tools that inspect network traffic and show which domains and categories are visited. Presenting that data to business owners can shock them about where data is going, which typically convinces them that AI governance is not optional. The author, writing from an IT management perspective, says technology is the quicker and easier part of the job, while understanding and working with people is what separates one professional from the rest. The article asks whether the rest of the business received adequate training on approved AI tools and understands what not to do with business data, and whether some parts of the organization would be more productive with specialized tools routed through strong security controls.

It recommends asking people what business problem they are trying to solve, rather than accepting an answer that begins with a request for AI to do something. The author also sets out an order to follow, starting with identity and seeing how far an organization can get, because that path aligns with the failures that lead to most business compromises. The article notes that few IT staff have worked in environments where they are involved with all aspects of the cybersecurity strategy, and that starting at an MSP can make it difficult to know where to begin. It says all steps have their own merits, but some matter more than others, and it gives the example that starting with data governance while allowing all users to access stored data on any device has less impact than first preventing that action within the identity project. The conclusion states that the priority remains ensuring businesses implement the fundamental security controls long considered essential, since getting these basics right creates a stronger foundation and better prepares organizations for the risks of emerging technologies.

stories.Headline: Lawyers say generative AI gives narcissistic family litigants speed and false authority
stories.Summary:
A law.com expert opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, by Elisa Reiter of Calabrese Budner and Daniel Pollack of Yeshiva University's Wurzweiler School of Social Work describes how generative AI has affected narcissistic behavior in family litigation. The authors say that generative AI did not create narcissistic behavior in family litigation, but it has given that behavior speed, scale and a veneer of authority. They describe the litigant who treats the courthouse as a stage and files a dozen motions in a month. They describe the opposing party who rewrites the history of the marriage with unshakable confidence and frames every parenting exchange as proof of the other parent's unfitness. They describe the litigant who reacts to any adverse ruling as a personal insult.

The full text of the article sits behind a subscription paywall on Law.com, so the specific requirements, changes, numbers and dates it sets out are not available. The visible portion gives no figures, no court dates and no named cases beyond the authors themselves. The page does list related coverage, including a November 16, 2026, article by Laura Lorek reporting that court filings containing hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters while subtler errors may be harder to catch. It also lists an October 22, 2026, report by Avalon Zoppo on the Fifth Circuit reassigning a case after a judge misused AI to draft a ruling, with Judge Jerry Smith writing for the appellate court. Those items are separate stories and are not part of the Reiter and Pollack piece.

The authors are responsible for the opinions in the article, and the visible text attributes the described litigation behavior to anonymous litigants rather than to any named person or firm. The article's own framing is that AI supplies speed, scale and a veneer of authority to behavior that already existed. Beyond that framing, the paywalled article does not disclose what the authors recommend or what they say should change. The surrounding coverage suggests that courts and practitioners are watching AI errors in filings, but the articles do not say what happens next in family law specifically. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Karen Nyamu denies viral Senate thumb-sucking video and says AI fabricated it
stories.Summary:
Nominated Senator Karen Nyamu denied on November 16, 2026, that a viral video showed her sucking her thumb while scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting, and she told TNX Africa that the footage had been fabricated using artificial intelligence. The clip, which drew considerable attention on social media, appeared to show the senator seated in the chamber, seemingly distracted by her phone before putting her thumb in her mouth. Nyamu spoke exclusively to TNX Africa and insisted she was being targeted through manipulated digital content. She challenged viewers to examine her manicure, arguing that her nail polish would not have remained intact had she been sucking her thumb as the video portrayed. Nyamu asked whether she could have kept her polish if she had been sucking her thumb, and she said the footage was made using AI.

She added that another one of her posts had recently been doctored as well. She challenged those questioning her conduct to consult the official parliamentary recordings, insisting the footage would expose the alleged fabrication. Nyamu said she had been on the floor debating very serious issues and urged people to check the Senate live feed for any such thing. The denial comes against a backdrop of previous controversies involving the senator and viral footage of her conduct. A month before the November 2026 denial, she trended online after yet another video showed her sucking her thumb on the floor of the house mid-session.

In March 2024, Nyamu was captured on camera scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting as Nakuru Senator Tabitha Keroche addressed the House, and the footage sparked online criticism from Kenyans who questioned her attentiveness during parliamentary proceedings. In April 2026, an ordinary photograph of Nyamu standing alongside Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah was transformed into a fabricated intimate video that circulated widely online. Nyamu is also the sponsor of the proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, which seeks to establish a framework for regulating the development and use of AI in Kenya. The articles do not say what happens next.

This strategic move allows AMD to better compete with Nvidia, which currently holds a strong position through its open-weights models. The acquisition requires the integration of pioneering model research into the future hardware, software, and systems of the company. These new capabilities aim to help developers and researchers push the boundaries of what artificial intelligence can achieve. She believes that the research from World Labs will be essential in shaping the future of their technical ecosystem. stories.Headline: Study finds AI-generated ad labels reveal only that AI played some role
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 16, 2026, in a TechXplore article republished from The Conversation examines what an "AI-generated" label in advertising actually communicates to consumers, concluding that such a label reveals only that artificial intelligence played some role without clarifying how large or small that role was. The article explains that AI might have served as one tool in a largely human-led creative process, perhaps editing an image or refining text, or it might have generated much of the finished advertisement with limited human input, and a single label can cover both extremes and everything in between. The authors note that advertising has long used disclosures, such as the "#ad" tag influencers place on social media or labels marking sponsored content, which help consumers recognize the commercial side of what they are watching or reading. Their research indicates that AI disclosures serve a different purpose, because traditional disclosures tell consumers why content is being shown to them while AI labels draw attention to how it was produced without revealing the respective roles of humans and machines.

The article reports that the distinction matters because evidence suggests disclosing AI involvement can reduce levels of trust, and other research points to overall consumer resistance to AI, although reactions vary considerably depending on what the technology is used to create. It notes that AI blurs the line between editing existing content and creating new content, since a person may still develop the idea and refine the result while the balance between human and machine contribution varies considerably, and disclosing AI involvement can invite judgments about who or what created the content, how much human input was involved and whether the use of AI was appropriate. The article says this may help explain criticism of AI-led campaigns by brands such as Coca-Cola and Gucci, and it describes how governments and platforms are beginning to address these questions through new approaches to AI transparency. The EU wants providers of certain generative AI systems subjected to strict disclosure requirements, and technology is emerging that allows digital content, including ads, to carry accessible information about its provenance and editing history.

The article reports that Meta acknowledged its "Made with AI" label appeared on content involving only minor AI modifications and did not provide sufficient context, and the company replaced that wording with "AI info" before later making the label less prominent when AI had been used to edit rather than generate content. It also describes the same ambiguity appearing in reverse, with labels reading "human-made" and "no AI" emerging to signal human authorship, and it asks whether these mean no AI whatsoever or a predominantly human process in which AI played a supporting role, since both kinds of label can obscure as much as they reveal. The authors advise consumers to take a little time to consider how they interpret AI labels, saying the term "AI-generated" tells us something but not everything about how content was produced and does not by itself mean the result is fake, poor quality or untrustworthy. They add that the label will not spell out the human role, including who developed the idea, selected and refined the output, checked its accuracy and decided what ultimately appeared, and they conclude that an AI label should be a starting point for evaluating content rather than the end.

Articles.Title: What does an 'AI‑generated' label in advertising actually tell us?

stories.Headline: New York City Council passes bill banning companies from using browsing data to set different prices
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council passed a bill banning surveillance pricing across the city's five boroughs, the New York Post reported on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The bill was sponsored by City Council Speaker Julie Menin and passed the Democrat-dominated council in a 44-5 vote. The Progressive Grocer reported on November 16, 2026, that the council had approved the legislation. The bill blocks companies from using browsing data to charge customers different prices for the same product. The surveillance pricing law has the support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The bill aims to prevent companies from using New Yorkers' personal data and algorithms to sell goods and services at different prices to different consumers. The council described it as among the strongest surveillance pricing bans in the country. Larger companies would be immediately hit with a $1,000 fine for violating the new pricing law. Small businesses will have the opportunity to first present an action plan to remedy any missteps. New York is the second city and fifth jurisdiction in the United States to ban the practice, after Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey and Seattle.

Menin said the City Council is putting consumers first by ending the deceptive and insidious practice of surveillance pricing. She said that when corporations use algorithms and personal data to charge different people different prices for the same products, it is unethical and worsens the affordability crisis. She said the council takes consumer protection extremely seriously and will continue fighting to lower prices and stop predatory corporate tactics. Menin said there are many factors driving up costs, some quite obvious to consumers, but a more subtle reason is the insidious and predatory corporate practice of surveillance pricing. She said companies set different prices for the exact same product for different consumers shopping at the exact same time, taking advantage of their demographics, web browsing history, shopping habits and social media activity.

UFCW International VP Ademola Oyefeso cautioned that New Yorkers who are not buying airline tickets or ordering groceries online, especially those with lower or fixed incomes, are still vulnerable to predatory pricing as long as the council allows electronic shelf labels to be rolled out in the city's grocery stores. He said that with these AI-powered systems, retailers can still change prices throughout the day based on a variety of factors, even without a shopper's personal data. He added that consumers in New York City and across the state need a blanket protection against price manipulation, which lawmakers can only achieve by removing ESL capabilities from brick-and-mortar stores. Critics of the bill were concerned the regulations would harm small businesses. The UFCW represents 1.2 million workers across North America, including grocery store associates.

This past June, the New York state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act, which would ban surveillance and personalized pricing, and Gov. Kathy Hochul has until the end of the year to act on the legislation. Earlier this year, the UFCW introduced the Affordable Groceries and Good Jobs Campaign to ban surveillance pricing and ESLs in grocery stores. In the U.S. Senate, the Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act, led by Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., was introduced this past February, in tandem with a House companion bill led by Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Rep. Val Hoyle, D-Ore. Proponents of ESLs argue that they are price tags that enable grocers to update prices and discounts quickly and accurately, not to change prices based on who is in the aisle, as the National Grocers Association noted in a statement last month. The NGA, which represents the independent grocery sector, has come out against the use of shopper data to set prices.

The bill was one of several pieces of legislation that lawmakers took up during their meeting Thursday, as they opted into a state program to exempt disabled veterans from property taxes while discussing a proposal to address terminal vacancies in rent-stabilized units. A new bill under consideration would address the city's over 50,000 vacant rent-stabilized apartments that have remained empty despite the city facing a vacancy of only 1.4%. The newly introduced bill, sponsored by Brooklyn Council Member Farah Louis (D-45), would require the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to analyze and develop a plan over the course of 60 days to bring the vacant rent-stabilized stock online. Louis said that with approximately 57,000 reported vacant rent-stabilized units citywide and nearly 279,000 rent-stabilized apartments in Brooklyn alone, there needs to be a clearer understanding of why these homes remain unavailable. Lawmakers also approved a bill sponsored by Republican Councilman Frank Morano (R-51) to opt the city into an Empire State law that exempts permanently and totally disabled veterans from having to pay property taxes, which passed one day after Veterans Day with a vote of 48-1.

stories.Headline: Law.com authors warn firms that wider AI use expands supervision duties and malpractice risk
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, Law.com published an article by Nicholas Cutaia and Ruth-Claire Pollioni titled "The Expanding Duty of Vigilance: How AI Adoption May Be Reshaping Legal Malpractice Risk." The article says firms are putting more AI tools like Harvey, Claude, and Legora into the hands of more lawyers, on more matters. It asks whether firms adopting AI to work faster are weakening the human oversight needed to catch its mistakes. It says the obligation to supervise that use grows along with the adoption. It examines how that gap can turn efficiency gains into malpractice risk and what firms can do about it.

The article is a 9 minute read and was published at 12:44 PM on November 16, 2026. It appears under the Artificial Intelligence topic and the Legal Technology section of Law.com. The rest of the article sits behind a subscription, and Law.com lists subscription benefits including strategic intelligence, integrated insights, personalized experience, and smart search and alerts. Law.com gives contact details at 1-855-808-4530 for the Americas and 44(0) 800 098 386009 for the UK and Europe. The page is copyrighted 2026 by ALM Global, LLC, with all rights reserved.

The article is credited to Nicholas Cutaia and Ruth-Claire Pollioni, who wrote that the obligation to supervise AI use grows as more tools reach more lawyers on more matters. They ask whether firms adopting AI to work faster are weakening the human oversight needed to catch its mistakes. They say the article examines how that gap can turn efficiency gains into malpractice risk. They say it also covers what firms can do about it. The articles give no further statements from the authors.

A related Law.com piece by Thomas F. Berner, dated November 12, 2026, argues that AI cannot replace human lawyers' judgment, character and creativity and that its output requires careful human review. A November 16, 2026 piece by Pouya Shafabakhsh says AI can help model litigation scenarios but New York practice still places settlement authority with the client. A November 13, 2026 piece by Pouya Shafabakhsh and Alexander Paykin says New York courts should not admit digital evidence casually, nor make every unsupported "deepfake" claim a ticket to expensive forensic testing. A November 12, 2026 Law.com report by Ryan Harroff says Latham's AI-fluent junior associates prompted the firm to revamp its training playbook, adjusting the schedule and curriculum for this year's academy. The articles say the affected people include lawyers, paralegals and clients.

A TechSpective article by Lila Warren, dated November 14, 2026, says AI has worked its way into courtrooms, law offices and legal research departments across the country. It says AI-driven platforms scan thousands of case files, statutes and legal precedents, completing in minutes tasks that once took junior associates hours or full days. It says AI tools help lawyers identify problematic clauses, inconsistencies and missing provisions faster than manual review. It says predictive analytics tools evaluate how courts have ruled on similar cases, and AI-driven e-discovery platforms streamline document review in discovery. It says a probate litigation attorney in California may use AI-assisted research and case analysis for complex matters like estate disputes involving contested wills or trust administration.

The TechSpective article says questions around data privacy, attorney-client privilege and the accuracy of AI-generated outputs are at the forefront of ongoing legal and ethical debates. It says bar associations and regulatory bodies are actively working to establish guidelines that keep AI use within appropriate ethical boundaries. It says over-reliance on automated tools could lead to critical errors if attorneys accept AI outputs without proper scrutiny. It says legal fees may decrease as efficiency improves, and turnaround times on documents and case updates can be significantly faster. It says AI-powered client portals and chatbots make it easier to access basic legal information and communicate with legal teams outside traditional office hours.

The TechSpective article says the most effective approach treats AI as a powerful assistant rather than a substitute for genuine professional legal judgment. It says the human element of law, including empathy, ethical reasoning and nuanced judgment, remains irreplaceable. It says attorneys who thrive will embrace AI as a tool while prioritizing the personal and professional skills that define excellent legal practice. It says the future of law is both human and machine working together toward better outcomes. The Law.com article leaves open what firms can do about the supervision gap, because that content requires a subscription.

stories.Headline: Roanoke County students question teachers' heavy AI use as school board adopts AI policy
stories.Summary:
Students in Roanoke County Public Schools are questioning how heavily their teachers rely on artificial intelligence for classroom materials, even as the school board adopted a formal AI policy on Thursday that restricts student use of generative technology. Student Advisory Council representative Addy Weaver told board members that teenagers are noticing an influx of AI-generated content from teachers while students face strict limits on when they can use the same tools for assignments. Weaver said students understand that AI is a very helpful tool for teachers and administrators who might need help with lesson plans or social media graphics, but she said the overwhelming influx of AI-generated content in schools has been a little jarring to students, and many wish for a more balanced approach. She raised these concerns during Thursday's meeting of the Roanoke County School Board.

The school board formally adopted Policy 6.42c on Thursday, codifying rules around artificial intelligence alongside the division's existing three-zone learning framework to prevent what the division calls cognitive offloading by students. District guidelines allow teachers to use AI for routine tasks such as lesson planning and administrative work, while students default to a no-AI zone for most assignments. Some coursework falls into intermediate zones where AI research tools are permitted with proper attribution, and the policy requires students to cite AI assistance when permitted while warning against letting technology replace original thinking. Superintendent Jamie Soltis asked student leaders to bring policy recommendations to their Dec. 9 meeting at the Roanoke County Career and Technology Center.

Weaver also addressed student frustration with Copyleaks, the AI plagiarism detection tool integrated into the Canvas learning management system, saying students reported that the software has been largely ineffective and creates unfair accusations with few ways for students to disprove AI-use claims. She said concerns about Copyleaks were addressed at the meeting, noting that students accused of using AI have few ways to disprove the claim within the tool's current system. Weaver said the discussion helped the council better understand how the use of certain AIs in the county is necessary and benefits both teachers and administrators, and she thanked Soltis for listening to the students' thoughts and discussions. More information is available at the schools website.

stories.Headline: European leaders meet in Dublin to discuss coordinating US and EU AI safety efforts
stories.Summary:
European leaders including Prime Minister Micheal Martin, Antonio Costa, and Roberta Metsola met in Dublin, Ireland, on November 13, 2026, to discuss artificial intelligence. This gathering highlighted the need for the United States and the European Union to coordinate on AI safety to prevent catastrophic risks. While the Trump administration has shown little interest in this engagement, recent cybersecurity incidents from American frontier labs may encourage narrower cooperation. Progress is more likely to occur through legislatures, specifically by creating a joint AI safety working group within the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue.

This proposed coordination would utilize the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue, which has met twice a year since 1999 to discuss security and trade. The effort would focus on interoperable incident reporting and establishing designated points of contact within regulatory and law enforcement agencies. It would build upon the October 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence and the bipartisan FRONTIER Act currently in the United States. European efforts include the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus, which entered into force in July 2026 to adjust compliance requirements.

The European Parliament's steering committee and a bipartisan US delegation are responsible for managing these legislative exchanges. These officials suggest that focusing on cybersecurity measures first would avoid contentious issues like data privacy or content moderation. They argue that an early dialogue with the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would ensure that new enforcement measures are compatible. This approach aims to avoid previous failures where dialogues were dismissed as talk shops or seen as attempts to export regulatory regimes.

The current US policy is a patchwork of state laws and voluntary commitments, while the EU uses a formal legal framework. Unresolved questions remain regarding the oversight of restricted models, such as the Mythos rollout by Anthropic through Project Glasswing. Legislators face pressure from constituents to deliver meaningful safety measures that address risks extending across international borders. Future efforts will seek common definitions for incident reporting, drawing on the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.

stories.Headline: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
stories.Summary:
The Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported a critical inflection point in adversarial AI on November 16, 2026. Threat actors are now deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks to execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. These adversaries include cyber criminals, espionage groups, and those conducting information operations. They use generative AI to compress attack timelines and scale their operations. This shift moves beyond basic prompting to fully automated offensive workflows.

The report identifies open source frameworks called ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI used for automated intrusions. CAIRN targeted the US aerospace sector, while PentAGI scanned Asian organizations from August to October 2026. CyberStrikeAI uses a Go-based backend API, and HexStrike AI integrates with the Model Context Protocol. Other tools mentioned include ZeroHollow for exploit development and Agent Zero for autonomous code execution. These systems automate the reverse engineering of patches to weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.

Google stated they are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly through a multifaceted defense strategy. They use a Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero for continuous monitoring and responding at machine speed. The company hardens models against misuse and proactively disrupts the projects and accounts of bad actors. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework to counter LLM-enabled tooling. Google Security Operations also deployed specialized rulepacks to detect the use of ARTEX.

Financially motivated actors affect enterprises by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources through a process called LLMJacking. These criminals resell access to high-performance AI models using underground proxy services known as LLM Mixers. State-sponsored groups and commercial Influence-as-a-Service vendors affect the public by producing synthetic media and localized personas. Cyber espionage groups target supply chains by manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors. These activities create a new defensive challenge by exploiting known weaknesses at extreme speed.

The articles note that zero-day exploits averaged 8 per month in 2025 and rose to 11 in 2026. This number spiked to 22 in August 2026, while overall disclosures nearly doubled between January and August. Previous quarterly research had only documented nascent adversary interest in these agentic capabilities. LLMs now automate labor-intensive phases like differential patch examination and dynamic protocol fuzzing. This automation reduces the window between the disclosure of a patch and its weaponized exploitation.

Threat actors will likely continue using these frameworks in global campaigns due to a low barrier to entry. Future operations are expected to move further along the autonomous scale toward fully agentic intrusions. While current tools trade stealth for velocity, future versions will likely increase in sophistication and stealth. The articles leave open how defenders will manage the increase in fake LLM-generated exploits. It remains unclear how quickly the industry can close the shrinking patch window for organizations.

stories.Headline: Vasudha Gadhiraju grounds Normal's AI rollout in cross-agency data work
stories.Summary:
The 57 cities recognized in this year's survey from the Center for Digital Government are prioritizing AI while modernizing core systems and upgrading data infrastructure, GovTech reported on Nov. 16, 2026. Leading cities are putting guardrails in place, launching AI-driven applications and adopting agentic workflows. At the same time, they're exploring new cybersecurity strategies, upgrading legacy systems and elevating the health of their data pipelines. In the face of lean budgets and rapid changes in technology, IT leaders are positioning themselves as strategic partners with city agencies. They're driving innovation while continuously improving both constituent engagement and employee experiences.

In Normal, Ill., Director of Innovation and Technology Vasudha Gadhiraju follows two guiding principles: make digital transformation a cross-agency effort, and ground the work in data. Grounded in the What Works Cities framework from Bloomberg Philanthropies, the approach now includes a cross-departmental Data Innovation Team that is helping build data governance and literacy. The town is leveraging training from InnovateUS, and it has begun to onboard AI applications, with an immediate focus on upgrading from a machine-learning-based chatbot to a true AI interface. The IT team has implemented the "Normal Forum," a platform used to document project updates and solicit constituent feedback around road safety. The town shares its public rights-of-way with Illinois State University, so safety for pedestrians, cyclists, motorists and transit users is of the utmost importance.

In Schaumburg, Ill., Director of Information Technology Peter Schaak said he was eager to embrace AI, but early on the village wanted to put some guardrails around it and to structure its approach. That has meant putting in place a high-level administrative protocol that instructs employees in effect to do good things, don't do bad things, with AI. From there he implemented a standard operating procedure, and the village did some training around both those documents to introduce and encourage the use of AI in the organization. The immediate impact of that effort has included adoption of Microsoft Copilot as the preferred internal AI tool, and the village also launched an external AI virtual assistant and an internal-facing virtual assistant, named for Serena and Louis, two swans that live on the municipal campus. The team also is working to leverage AI in short-term rental analysis tools to identify properties that are maybe not registered as rental properties but being used as short term rentals, the Airbnbs and Vrbos of the world.

In Corona, Calif., CIO Chris McMasters said it starts out with governance and security, and without that in place the city wouldn't have been able to do the things it is doing today. The IT team moved early to identify all the shadow AI already in use and then built policy around what people were actually doing with the tools, and the city adjusted its licenses to support the AI tools people were actually using, and IT worked with a startup to implement a security platform. An AI agent will tee up a graffiti complaint work order with human oversight and communicate the outcomes back to the resident, taking a process that was about 20 minutes per incident down to less than three minutes per incident. The IT team also replaced its 30-year-old ERP and HR systems with Workday last year, the culmination of two years' labor. The team also embedded an agent across the city websites that can watch when people are getting frustrated, hanging too long on a page or clicking wildly, and can prompt a human to intercept.

In Virginia Beach, CIO Peter Wallace said IT is not a call center, but a value center, and the tech team needs to deliver tangible results, and faced with budget cuts, you've got to be measurable. In Schaumburg, the IT team undertook an initiative to create worst-case scenario runbooks, and that entailed a ton of sequencing and dependency analysis and operational timing, and the team worked through all of those over the span of the year. The runbooks establish responsibilities and sequencing and assignment of personnel, a whole long list of roles and responsibilities and tasks to help the team get through a catastrophic breach. As Schaumburg built a new village hall, the tech team had to disassemble its main operations area and rebuild it in a temporary facility, and this fall the team was in the midst of taking it apart again and shifting to a brand-new facility. In Corona, IT is in the midst of consolidating city data on a single platform, and the city will use that to generate profiles about the people that engage with it, so that when it puts out things, it is much more targeted.

In Normal, Gadhiraju said the town wants to make sure people truly understand the advantages of AI and the efficiencies it brings, while also recognizing where AI may not be able to deliver at scale. She said there are so many vendors now who quickly use the word AI to sell products, and a lot of these vendors are approaching the town's departments directly, and people need to ask the right questions and not be tempted by the bells and whistles. She said data and technology and innovation should always work towards solving a problem that the community is facing. In Schaumburg, Schaak said the village's focus is on operational benefits, and it is moving out of the world of funny graphics and songs and trying to be strategic in how it deploys these tools. He said the focus is to be fiscally responsible while always leaning forward, always looking to expand services, improve services, improve response times, in an environment of continuous improvement.

In Corona, McMasters said the city is being very methodical about how it engages the public, to give them the things they want, and there is this memory the city is creating so that people's experiences with their government can be persistent. He said IT played a huge role in the project management, bringing all the departments together, executing and then leading everyone through, and outside consultants helped as well, and their involvement knocks down a lot of the bureaucracy and the politics and helps to streamline things. In Normal, Gadhiraju said across departments the town all works collaboratively, and it could not do what it is doing without the type of culture that it has, and while the city's approach to data has been years in the making, it has really come together in the past year. She said the IT team has worked to build strong data pipelines, making sure that it has good back-end connections to its systems so that data can be put to work, and there is now a dashboard that shows at a glance how well the town is doing on its goal of planting more trees than it removes, and another to help manage cellphone expenses. She said the town is truly building in the measurement in every aspect of the work it does, and she is optimistic about the new AI interface, and the town does need a chatbot, and it needs to make sure people can easily ask it questions.

stories.Headline: Massachusetts lawmakers file bills to ban algorithmic rent pricing statewide
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts state Rep. Lindsay Sabadosa, a Democrat from the 1st Hampshire district, and state Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat from the 4th Middlesex district, filed bills in the House and Senate to outlaw algorithmic rent pricing in the state. The Joint Committee on Housing reported the bills out favorably in March, and the proposals now sit before the Committee on Ways and Means. The bills respond to rent-pricing software, often called revenue management software, that many of Massachusetts’ largest landlords use at their properties. The software draws on nonpublic leasing data from nearby properties to recommend how high rents can go. Landlords using such programs have been accused of unfair pricing, intentionally leaving units vacant and colluding with others to reduce competition.

The bills would ban rent-pricing algorithms in Massachusetts, and the session ends Jan. 5. The biggest industry player is Texas-based RealPage, which claims on its website that its customers outperform competitors who do not use the service by up to 7%. RealPage’s algorithm analyzes nonpublic data from landlords using its software, including listed rent, the actual price tenants agree to after discounts and lease length, for new leases and renewals. The software also accesses data on a unit’s future demand and occupancy, including inquiries and applications from prospective tenants. A 2023 report by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council found that 21% of Greater Boston properties sold between 2004 and 2018 were purchased by an investor or speculator, and a 2025 study by the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy found that 8.9% of residential parcels nationwide are owned by a corporation.

Sabadosa compared traditional rent-setting to selling a used car, where the seller checks prices for the same or similar models and sets an asking price accordingly. She said the algorithm is a much more sophisticated way of looking at all the rents than trying to understand the maximum the market will bear in a given community. She said that for someone just trying to make money it is surely a great idea, but for thriving communities where people can afford to live it is a terrible idea, because it is constant upward pressure that pushes everybody out. Friedman said the problem is that it is distorting the market and called it kind of immoral, saying people are taking rental places where people can live and need to live off the market. Friedman said it becomes much more insidious much faster than a landlord going through Zillow or Redfin.

Demetrios Salpoglou, CEO of the real estate platform Boston Pads, said frequent price fluctuations he sometimes sees on the website cause unnecessary issues for renters and landlords. He said he has seen out-of-state landlords rely too heavily on algorithms without understanding neighborhood nuances, and has heard from confused consumers or their agents about a unit’s price changing twice daily. He said it is like over-engineering a Hyundai and calling it a Porsche, and that he has never really had a landlord say the rental software is incredible. Salpoglou said most small- and mid-sized or independent property owners he works with use real-time pricing data on his platform and may lower rent near the lease date but otherwise rarely change prices unexpectedly. He theorized corporate landlords may use the software to satisfy obligations to owners and investors, which he called, in the nicest way he could say it, a CYA.

In 2024 the U.S. Department of Justice and several states, including Massachusetts, sued RealPage and some of the largest landlords in the country, alleging the practice illegally decreases competition. In November of last year RealPage and the DOJ reached a settlement requiring the company to stop using non-public competitor data in price recommendations, not to use active lease data to train its models and to remove or redesign features that limit price decreases. RealPage did not admit wrongdoing and said in court documents that it continues to believe the use of non-public data led to more efficient and procompetitive pricing and reduced vacancies. Massachusetts and other states continued their case, and two landlord defendants, Greystar Management Services and LivCor, have settled, while the case against RealPage, Camden Property Trust, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company is ongoing. Attorney General Andrea Campbell said in January 2025, when the state joined the case, that her office will seek to hold accountable those who betray renters’ trust and undermine a fair and competitive housing market.

Neither Sabadosa nor Friedman was optimistic the state legislation would pass this session, and Friedman said she thinks the proposal could make it into larger housing-related legislation next session. New York was the first state to ban the technology, with the prohibition taking effect in December 2025, and California and New Jersey have since followed suit. RealPage sued New York seeking to overturn the law, arguing it violated the company’s First Amendment rights to free speech and dissemination of information, and in late September a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law while the case plays out. New York Attorney General Letitia James has appealed the decision. Sabadosa said one advantage of Beacon Hill being a little slow-moving is seeing the laws pass in other states and the immediate legal challenges, and that they are looking at what the courts identified as issues and redrafting to be responsive.

stories.Headline: Bank of England and FCA find 94% of firms have formal AI governance
stories.Summary:
On 26 October 2026, the Bank of England and the UK Financial Conduct Authority published the results of their fourth survey on AI in UK financial services, which updates the regulators' evidence base on how firms are using, governing and managing AI. The survey supports the regulators' ongoing work against the backdrop of evolving AI capabilities and adoption, and it sits alongside the FCA's recent publications on AI and the final report of the Mills Review. The results offer useful insights into the practical pressure points emerging as firms move from experimentation towards more widespread, and potentially more autonomous, deployment of AI. The survey found that 94% of respondents now report having formal AI governance arrangements, although ongoing oversight is less developed.

The survey is the fourth of its kind and was published on 26 October 2026 by the Bank of England and the FCA, and it examines how firms are using, governing and managing AI. The survey draws out key themes and what they may mean for firms as deployment becomes more widespread and potentially more autonomous.

The Bank of England and the FCA are responsible for the survey, and the results reflect what respondents reported about their formal AI governance arrangements, with 94% saying they have them. stories.Headline: Chicago Public Schools restricts student access to Gemini and ChatGPT over safety standards
stories.Summary:
Chicago Public Schools restricted students’ access to generative AI tools, including Gemini and ChatGPT, because the programs do not meet its safety standards, which were first enacted in 2024. The district said the tools respond to user prompts, meaning students could ask them to solve math problems or write essays. Teachers can still use district-approved AI tools for instruction, such as generating images or turning textbook chapters into podcasts. The district’s guidance also says parents can opt their children out of AI access. Google recently announced that Search and other AI features will be turned off by default on K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.

Google will not offer an AI-free version of Search, so schools that reject all of Google’s AI offerings will also lose access to Google Search. The changes are scheduled to take effect early next year. CPS, one of the nation’s largest districts, is still deciding how to respond, and the school system wants an AI-free search engine and may have to look elsewhere to find one. A CPS spokesperson said the district was actively exploring all options to independently suppress the AI overview that appears at the top of Google searches. If CPS cannot provide students access to the search engine without its AI feature, the district will look to other search solutions, the spokesperson said.

A Google spokesperson told Chalkbeat that the company was taking steps to improve its search functions for classrooms, such as through piloting its Guided Learning feature, which uses AI to walk students through a problem step-by-step rather than providing quick answers. Cassie Creswell, executive director of Illinois Families for Public Schools, which led the rally in Chicago, said that if AI is so embedded into Google’s search engine, then it might be time for schools to step back and reassess whether to use Google at all. Creswell said that really shouldn’t be our gateway to human knowledge, and so we need to draw a line there. Creswell also told reporters that schools really need real policy, not just a guidebook with suggestions that dump the burden on teachers and kids. Reese Mackey, a 16-year-old Kenwood Academy High School junior, said at the protest that students are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer.

About 30 people huddled together outside Google’s office in Chicago’s West Loop on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, shouting chants such as “Hey Google, nice try. We don’t want your Gemini.” Most of the protesters were parents and educators, but the demonstration included some students who voiced their own skepticism about whether AI is beneficial for themselves and their peers. Protests also popped up Wednesday in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Illinois Families for Public Schools and a mix of CPS students, parents and school board members protested outside the Google office.

Michilla Blaise, current school board member for District 5b who was just reelected, said she believes AI is creating larger gaps in learning in the communities she represents on Chicago’s West Side. The American Federation of Teachers is signing agreements with AI companies, while parents are raising concerns about student privacy and consent. Recently, South Carolina mother Nikki Anderson objected to a classroom assignment that used AI to show her 6-year-old daughter what she might look like at age 25, and she asked in an Instagram post where they got consent for AI image processing. Anderson wanted to know which AI company received her children’s photos and what happened to the images afterward, and Charleston County School District said it stopped similar assignments after parents raised concerns. A lawsuit claims a North Carolina girl accessed Gemini through Google Search despite her school blocking AI chatbots, and her parents allege she used Gemini to plan a suicide attempt that was ultimately discovered and stopped.

The national AFT and its New York City chapter recently announced an agreement with Anthropic establishing binding terms for Claude for Teachers, which prohibits Anthropic from selling student and teacher data or using it for targeted advertising. The unions already had ties to the AI industry, including a five-year, $23 million partnership with Anthropic, Microsoft and OpenAI to train teachers to incorporate AI into their classrooms. That $23 million training deal did not include privacy agreements, but the unions reached a separate privacy agreement with Microsoft in September and are still negotiating one with OpenAI. Anthropic’s agreement covers Claude for Teachers, which is used only by adults, and it does not cover the companies’ other applications used in schools.

The AFT still has no privacy agreement with Google or Meta, leaving Chicago’s dilemma unresolved. CPS approved at least three generative AI tools, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini Notebook, after accepting contracts that bar the companies from using student data to train their AI models, according to CPS’ AI Tools page. The district also backtracked on its planned rollout of implementing Google Gemini in high schools for the 2026-2027 school year after community pushback, according to CPS’ AI Access Overview. More broadly in Illinois, the state’s education board introduced guidance earlier this year on how schools can use AI responsibly, though its suggestions are non-binding.

Some cities are putting stringent AI policies in place, most notably New York City under Mayor Zohran Mamdani, which just before this school year started banned the use of student-facing AI, including chatbots, from preschool through eighth grade. At the end of October, Chalkbeat obtained a list of nearly 40 products flagged by the city’s Education Department for their AI usage, such as Grammarly and Kahoot. Illinois Families for Public Schools wants CPS to place a three-year moratorium on the technology in schools and opt for what it calls human-centered education, and it urged school board candidates to sign on in the recent election. About half of the incoming Chicago Board of Education members, including President-elect Jessica Biggs, did so.

The Illinois Families for Public Schools pledge also calls for installing a chief privacy officer at the district to protect student data, limiting screen time across all grade levels, and barring the collection of biometric data such as face scans and fingerprints. Sweeping Democratic wins in last week’s midterm elections could shake up the political environment for AI companies, with potential for reverberations throughout the education sector. Data centers, the controversial facilities that power AI, proved to be a key issue this election cycle, with nearly 40 jurisdictions across the country approving ballot measures to limit their expansion. Creswell said she hopes that we have swept people into office who are not beholden to the tech industry and they’re beholden to their constituents.
