stories.Headline: Scott Loughlin says AI agents on personal devices test whether BYOD programs can survive
stories.Summary:
Employees who use personal devices for work are increasingly running artificial intelligence agents that can read work email, open files and act across applications without a person at the keyboard, and Scott Loughlin, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader in Washington, DC, wrote in a Bloomberg Law column published on November 16, 2026, that this raises the question of whether bring-your-own-device programs can survive agents in their current form. In a Gartner survey conducted in early 2026, 88% of employees with an enterprise AI tool also used personal AI tools for work, and those tools will likely increasingly include AI agents. Loughlin wrote that the core controls of a BYOD program, a company-managed container for work apps, monitoring of corporate systems and the ability to remotely wipe work data, were designed for apps that people operate and may not work as well for devices running AI agents. Because an agent works inside the employee's logged-in session, company records may show the employee doing what the agent did, and the agent's history and memory sit in the provider's cloud under the employee's account, beyond the reach of a remote wipe. Loughlin wrote that none of this requires hacking, but the exposure is real and no new AI statute is needed to create it, with personal data given to an unapproved agent raising issues under the GDPR and US state privacy laws, protected health information entered into a personal agent possibly being a HIPAA breach, and routine flows of source code or pricing undercutting trade-secret protection.

He wrote that EU law restricts the scope of employee monitoring and may require works-council consultation, and that US laws can limit employers' access to employees' personal accounts. He described three models likely to be applied role by role: access-only BYOD, in which personal devices reach corporate data only through a managed browser, app or virtual workspace; a sanctioned agent, in which an enterprise agent lets the organization control the agent even when it does not control the device; and company-owned devices for people in the most sensitive roles. He noted that the May 2026 guidance on agentic AI from CISA, the NSA and other governments recommends giving agents their own short-lived credentials and requiring human approval for high-impact actions. Loughlin recommended that organizations assign ownership at the leadership level, naming an accountable executive, adding personal and unsanctioned agents to the enterprise risk register and reporting on them to the board committee that oversees cybersecurity risk. He also recommended revisiting the BYOD agreement to address which agents may touch company data, employee disclosure duties, a narrow commitment to preserve and produce work-related agent data, and offboarding certification that connectors are revoked and work-related memories deleted, covering phones and tablets and calibrated to local employment and privacy law.

He advised updating legal-hold and e-discovery playbooks to add agent prompts, outputs, logs and memory to custodian questionnaires and hold notices, mapping roles and controlling the connection points where the law allows, updating incident response with scenarios for a hijacked or misused personal agent, and aligning related policies so they cross-reference each other. Loughlin wrote that organizations that plan ahead will be better positioned to demonstrate reasonable governance to regulators, courts and customers, and that agent risks are developing quickly enough that organizations are changing their BYOD programs in the short term before settling on a longer-term model. He wrote that it is a good idea to make the sanctioned path easier than the personal one and to focus controls on the connection points the organization owns. He wrote that BYOD rests on the premise that a company can manage the risk of devices it does not own, that agents using employees' credentials on those devices test that premise, and that BYOD is unlikely to disappear but programs are likely to change.

stories.Headline: Judicial codes of conduct bar judges from using AI to make decisions
stories.Summary:
Judicial codes of conduct forbid judges from using artificial intelligence to make decisions, but some judges have turned to the technology for administrative tasks and academic purposes, according to a Law360 report published on November 16, 2026. The report, written by Steven Lerner, said hurdles still remain before more judges adopt AI in their work. The article did not name any judges, courts or specific tools involved in the reported use. It also did not give figures on how many judges have used AI for administrative or academic work. The report said the judicial codes of conduct bar judges from using AI to make decisions, which limits how far the technology can go in court work.

It said some judges have used AI for administrative tasks and for academic purposes despite that restriction. The article did not describe which administrative tasks or academic uses the judges have pursued. It also did not say what specific hurdles are holding back wider adoption. The report gave no dates, numbers or names beyond the publication date and the author. The article did not identify any official, court or agency as responsible for the reported hurdles, and it did not include any statements from judges or other people about the issue.

No one was quoted in the available text, so there are no remarks to paraphrase. The report did not say who sets or enforces the judicial codes of conduct it described. It also did not say whether any court has issued guidance on AI use by judges. The available article did not provide context on how many judges currently use AI or how the reported hurdles might be addressed.

It did not say what happens next, whether rules might change or whether more judges are expected to adopt the technology. The report ended without naming any next steps, hearings or proposals on the issue. Because the articles carry too little for a longer story, no further details can be added beyond what is known. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democratic control of Congress shifts AI policy toward risk-based oversight, Carrillo, Ellison and Braithwaite write
stories.Summary:
Democratic control of Congress will shift the national debate regarding artificial intelligence policy on November 16, 2026. This political change moves the focus away from the deregulatory agenda previously established by the Trump administration. The new leadership intends to implement a risk-based approach that emphasizes accountability for various impacts. This strategy specifically targets the economic, consumer, and public safety consequences of deploying these technologies. The new policy framework requires a stronger focus on consumer harms, fairness, safety, and transparency.

Congress may also increase its scrutiny of cybersecurity measures and the power costs associated with data centers. Businesses must prepare for a higher volume of investigations even if no new laws are passed. Companies are encouraged to demonstrate that they have implemented strong safeguards to protect the public. Pablo Carrillo, Bradford Ellison, and Dominic Braithwaite are the authors responsible for analyzing these upcoming regulatory shifts.

They suggest that the government will likely push for tougher oversight to ensure that AI systems remain safe. The authors indicate that the shift toward accountability will redefine how technology companies operate within the United States. They believe that the focus on risk will replace the previous trend of reducing government interference. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US, Israel, UAE and Qatar sign pact to protect AI supply chains and infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The United States, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar signed the San Francisco Declaration on Sunday to protect critical infrastructure and AI supply chains. This agreement strengthens regional cooperation with Washington as the Trump administration attempts to reduce the technological advantages currently held by China. The pact was finalized just before President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping this Thursday. These diplomatic efforts occur while a major scandal involving the chipmaker Nvidia creates further tension in the global race for artificial intelligence.

This accord is a component of Pax Silica, a broader initiative launched in December 2025 to secure advanced manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, and critical minerals. The San Francisco Declaration establishes a common understanding regarding sensitive technologies and proposes the creation of five specific working groups. These groups will focus on resilience, security hubs, supply-chain cooperation, AI adoption, and the development of policy frameworks. While the document does not explicitly name China, it aims to coordinate global partners to challenge Beijing's dominance over the industries that support AI.

The United States State Department is responsible for the agreement and issued a press release explaining the need to safeguard the foundations of AI. Officials indicated that the pact creates a shared understanding of the critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies required for the modern economy. The initiative seeks to build a new grouping of partners specifically tailored for the AI economy to ensure long-term economic security. This strategic move is intended to stabilize the technology race during a period of uncertainty caused by the crisis at Nvidia.

stories.Headline: UC Law San Francisco launches a three-day certificate lab for building legal AI tools
stories.Summary:
The legal technology hub known as LexLab at UC Law San Francisco announced a new educational program on November 13, 2026. This initiative is called the Law and AI Certificate Lab, which is designed as a three-day course for building legal tools. The intensive program will take place from December 1 to December 3 for a small group of participants. It provides a condensed version of the AI curriculum that the law school typically offers its students over a full semester. The course requires the participation of up to 24 individuals, including lawyers, government officials, academics, and technologists.

These attendees will use specialized technology provided by companies such as Legora, Harvey, and the website builder Replit. The curriculum focuses on the actual development of artificial intelligence tools while addressing important ethical considerations. This training allows professionals to build and evaluate their own software solutions within a short timeframe. Adjunct professor Damien Charlotin, who created the AI Hallucination Cases database, is directing the program alongside adjunct professor Erin Fraser.

Fraser also serves as an associate at the firm McDermott Will & Schulte while helping to lead this lab. These directors intend for the course to support professionals in navigating the complexities of modern legal technology. They aim to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and the practical application of AI in legal settings. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies lose $4.2tn in market value since June as AI trade reverses
stories.Summary:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse, according to a Financial Times analysis. The article, published on 16 November 2026 and written by Clara Murray, reports that data centre construction stocks have lost $4.2tn as the boom in the AI trade unravels. The report is an analysis piece, and the available text does not name the individual companies involved or give a precise date in June for the peak. The article as supplied is behind a subscription paywall, so the full details of the analysis are not available in the text provided.

The report places the losses at $4.2tn in market value across global manufacturing, utility and mining companies since June. It links the decline to the AI "picks and shovels" trade, the bet on the suppliers and builders behind the artificial intelligence boom, which the analysis says has swung into reverse. The text does not give a breakdown by sector or country, and it does not say what share of the $4.2tn falls on data centre construction stocks specifically. No further figures, dates or named companies appear in the article as supplied.

The article is attributed to Clara Murray of the Financial Times, and the available text does not include any direct comment from her or from the companies concerned. The report is presented as an analysis rather than a news report based on named sources, and the text provided does not say who supplied the figures behind the $4.2tn estimate. No executive, official or analyst is quoted in the material available, so no one's remarks can be paraphrased. The article's own framing is that the AI trade has unravelled, and that framing is the only characterisation the text supports.

The context given is the boom in the AI trade, which the article says has unravelled, and the "picks and shovels" label for the suppliers and builders that rose with it. The text does not say what happens next, whether the decline is expected to continue, or how the companies or investors have responded. Because the full article sits behind a paywall, the details that would normally follow, such as named stocks, regional splits and forward-looking comment, are not in the material provided. The available text supports only the scale and direction of the losses and the link to the reversing AI trade.

stories.Headline: Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on sensitive computer chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on evidence of sensitive computer chip smuggling during his tenure as secretary. These ex-employees describe his leadership as chaotic and marked by micromanaging. The accusations surfaced as scrutiny grew following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. China has denied these spying accusations, calling them a smear attempt.

The department stopped adding firms to the Entity List, which bans advanced chip sales to adversaries. No companies were added between October 9, 2025, and the present, the first such gap since 2008. In May 2025, Lutnick rolled back an interim final rule from January 2025 to avoid stifling innovation. A new rule now requires licenses for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This rule was directed by the National Security Council and the Department of Treasury.

Howard Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, are responsible for the department's export control enforcement. Former staff claim Kessler micromanaged every minor decision and blocked enforcement against suspected smugglers. They allege the career workforce felt stymied and unable to perform their duties. The Commerce Department and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed frustration that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia are affected by the scandal involving suspected agent Alice Huang. Reports suggest $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips reached Chinese firms through her links since 2023. An OpenAI researcher found evidence that banned Nvidia chips trained top Chinese AI models. Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025. These smuggled chips provided roughly a quarter of China's acquired computing power.

The Biden administration first issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023. Lutnick began running the department in February 2025, shortly after firing veterans Matthew Borman and Eileen Albanese. This sparked an exodus of up to 50 skilled staff members over 18 months. Departed experts included specialists in AI, Russia, diversion, and chips. The department also pivoted to allow sales of Nvidia H20 and H200 chips to China.

Key roles in the Bureau of Industry and Security remain vacant, including the chief of staff. The principal deputy assistant secretary roles for export administration and export enforcement are also unfilled. It remains unclear if the department will fill these positions or change its enforcement approach. The articles leave open whether the decision to sell H20 chips was made by Trump. They do not state if further investigations into Alice Huang will occur.

stories.Headline: Pierre school officials draft AI classroom procedures after survey
stories.Summary:
The Pierre School District has spent the past several months working to address the growing use of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with district officials meeting alongside a staff committee to develop procedures for AI use after a community survey was conducted earlier this year. Superintendent Donavan DeBoer said he entered the role knowing that discussions about AI would be necessary as the technology becomes increasingly common, not just in schools, and he noted that AI has been a frequent topic at education conferences and professional retreats because of how quickly the technology evolves. Drawing a comparison to the introduction of cellphones in schools, DeBoer said educators learned that simply allowing students unrestricted access often created challenges that continue today, and he said the district needs to put guardrails on AI sooner rather than later because having some sort of plan is better than having no plan at all. District conversations began earlier this year with an AI-focused survey sent to staff, students and parents, and about 1,655 responses gave the district a starting point for committee discussions as members work toward establishing AI procedures for the 2027-28 school year. Eighty percent of students surveyed said they had used AI before, and nearly half of those students said they use it monthly or more often, while of the 832 student respondents, 309 said they use AI for homework help and 412 said they use it for research, with others reporting use for writing assistance and studying.

Of the 209 staff members who responded, about half said they had used AI for tasks including lesson planning, and most respondents agreed AI can help teachers save time, though many also expressed interest in additional training, recommended tools and established expectations for student use. Across all respondent groups, students, staff and parents expressed awareness that AI tools can sometimes produce inaccurate information, and DeBoer said many students also voiced concerns about academic integrity similar to those expressed by adults in the community. The district has since formed an AI committee that has met twice, and the group includes principals representing the elementary, middle and high school levels as well as Technology Director Bryan Linn, with DeBoer saying he and Linn are currently working to draft procedures and protocols for AI use. The committee plans to meet again in January to further develop those ideas before sharing them with building leadership teams for additional feedback, and DeBoer said he hopes to bring a proposal to the school board this spring and receive approval before the next school year. Currently, websites such as ChatGPT and Gemini are blocked on student devices because of privacy concerns, though DeBoer said the district may have opportunities to incorporate more secure AI tools into classrooms for activities such as project brainstorming or creating renderings in technical education courses.

DeBoer said he does not intend this to be a hard and fast policy because the world is moving at warp speed and the district's AI expectations and protocols will change as things change, and he said the district is looking at a set of processes and procedures to guide staff on consistent expectations for students rather than a policy that would constantly need revision. DeBoer said he expects AI use to be more common at the high school level than in elementary or middle school classrooms, particularly as students prepare for college, technical school and future careers where the technology is becoming increasingly prevalent, and he noted that AI-detection tools used during grading are not always accurate, prompting some teachers to return to pen-and-paper assignments to avoid concerns about misuse. While the district continues to develop expectations for classroom use, officials also hope to help teachers identify effective AI tools, provide additional training and continue evaluating the technology as it evolves, and results of the district's AI survey are available on the district website. AI policy is expected to remain a topic of discussion at Pierre School Board meetings, and the board meets at 5:30 p.m. on the second Monday of each month at the district administration building, with meetings open to the public.

stories.Headline: St. Paul student says Turnitin flag gave her a zero as district lacks AI policy
stories.Summary:
A St. Paul Public Schools student wrote in a MinnPost opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, that she received a zero on an English essay that Turnitin flagged as 32 percent AI-generated, dropping her grade to a D on the night before her last day of sophomore year. She said she had earned a 98 percent in the class before that and had not used AI for any part of the essay. When she offered the next morning to rewrite sections with pen and paper, her teacher said that was not necessary because she knew the student's writing style and believed the work was original. The teacher had previously raised concerns about Turnitin, an AI detection tool used by the district.

The piece says the district has no official school board AI policy, although Phil Wacker, the district's high school curriculum supervisor, acknowledged Turnitin's limitations in September 2025, particularly for students whose first language is not English, according to St. Paul Publishing. At that time nearly 30 percent of the district's students were English learners. The SPPS Board of Education recently announced a goal of adopting an AI policy by the end of the 2027-28 school year, with details still vague and the board saying the policy will include expectations for how the district prepares students and staff to use, question, evaluate and create with AI. Wacker said conversations about a policy are happening.

The student argues that administrators, not students, should fix the problem, and that she sees a lack of urgency. She writes that the time spent debating a policy means the conversation will take her class's entire high school career, and that some students use AI and have found ways to avoid detection. Turnitin assigns a score based on the percentage of suspected AI sentences, measuring burstiness, or spontaneity of word choice, and sentence length, and the company claims human writing tends to be inconsistent and idiosyncratic. The student notes that her flagged essay was about how high school writing structure strips individuality from students' work.

stories.Headline: Trump launches five billion dollar Genesis Mission to advance science through AI
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump launched a five billion dollar government effort to advance science through artificial intelligence. This initiative, called the Genesis Mission, began in November 2025 via an executive order. It started at the Energy Department and now includes more than 15 federal agencies. The president also issued a second order in June to speed up quantum technology development. These actions occurred during the second term of President Donald Trump.

The Genesis Mission uses Energy Department data, computing power, and facilities to build shared AI tools. In 2025, federal agencies spent about 4.2 billion dollars on AI research and development. The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy released a 123 page report in July. The Energy Department aims to develop error corrected quantum computers by 2028. The Office of Science has a total budget of 8.4 billion dollars for fiscal year 2026.

Darío Gil is the undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy. He called AI, quantum science, and supercomputing the three legs of a transforming stool. Gil stated that 400 million dollars for Genesis is small compared to the total budget. John Sarrao is the director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California. Sarrao said Genesis created an inflection point for scientists who already used AI.

Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University leads a project combining huge datasets from observatories and instruments. She said the idea is conceptually powerful but noted her cosmology grant was reduced. Brad Marston is a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. Marston said he wants all fields supported because AI and quantum were once backwaters. Researchers in public health and climate research have faced funding cuts and delays.

The National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health launched Genesis efforts in biology, health, and space. SLAC is involved in 20 Genesis projects and leads two of them. The Energy Department funded nearly 300 projects this year, including nuclear fusion and electric grid simulations. Celia Merzbacher of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium said quantum computing is at the start of a marathon. Some Genesis funding came from a 2025 budget law and some from the department budget.

The government will continue using AI to speed up the development of nuclear reactors. Agencies will keep lining up research spending with the priorities of the current administration. Scientists will continue working on quantum sensors, quantum materials, and quantum error correction. The articles do not say how the government will balance funding for other science fields. It remains open whether the department will talk with scientists about these budget trade-offs.

stories.Headline: California passes first-of-its-kind law guiding attorneys on AI in discovery
stories.Summary:
The California legislature recently passed a first of its kind law to provide guidance for litigation attorneys navigating the complexities of artificial intelligence. This new legal framework was introduced to help legal professionals who are currently struggling to manage the rapid integration of AI into their daily practices. The legislation aims to offer a necessary flashlight for those foraging through the proverbial forest of emerging technology. It specifically addresses the challenges that arise when attorneys must handle discovery in an increasingly digital and automated environment.

The new law requires a shift in how attorneys approach the discovery process when artificial intelligence tools are involved in the creation of documents. It changes the landscape for litigation by offering specific assistance to those who find themselves knee-deep in an artificial intelligence world. While the provided text does not list specific section numbers or dates of enactment, it establishes a new standard for the state of California. This regulatory change is designed to clarify the obligations of lawyers when using these advanced tools during legal proceedings.

Patrick Fanning of Lathrop GPM reported on the development and noted that the guidance was much needed for the legal community. He suggested that the legislature has provided a way for attorneys to better understand their roles in this new technological era. Fanning highlighted the difficulty lawyers face when trying to balance innovation with the strict requirements of the law. His analysis indicates that the legislation serves as a critical resource for those managing complex litigation.

The broader context involves a wave of litigation regarding whether prompts and chat histories in generative AI are protected from discovery. Courts are currently distinguishing between factual materials and litigation strategy to determine if work product protections still apply. There is a growing concern that using consumer AI platforms may defeat confidentiality due to existing privacy policies. Legal experts are now watching to see if this California law goes far enough to protect email communications from open AI engines.

stories.Headline: US states enact nearly 30 AI laws in 2026 as federal deregulation lags
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CIO on November 17, 2026 and written by David Talby, says the administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. It says states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning attention to how businesses use AI. It says AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level while becoming more regulated in practice. It says an AI application meeting requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. It says consequences of inadequate governance are growing as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes.

The article says the White House issued an executive order last year seeking to limit conflicting state AI regulations and establish a more consistent national approach. It says an executive order does not automatically invalidate state laws. It says California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53), effective this January, requires covered frontier AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report critical safety incidents. It says New York's RAISE Act establishes similar obligations beginning in January 2027. It says California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed 11 more AI safety bills into law in September, capping a 2026 legislative year that saw nearly 30 AI-related measures enacted.

The article says Illinois in July 2026 enacted the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), effective January 2027, requiring covered frontier model developers to implement safety frameworks, report serious incidents and, for the largest developers, undergo independent compliance audits. It says the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA) took effect this year and establishes an intent-based liability model rather than a broad pre-deployment risk assessment requirement. It says Colorado in May 2026 enacted SB 26-189, replacing its earlier AI law with a framework governing automated decision-making technologies used in consequential decisions including employment, lending and housing. It says beginning January 2027 covered businesses will face disclosure and other obligations, while consumers gain rights concerning inaccurate personal data. It says Colorado also enacted the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements Act (HB 26-1263) in May, introducing requirements for conversational AI services including disclosures and protections for minors.

The article says the European Union's AI Act is moving into active enforcement. It says the EU in July 2026 adopted the AI Omnibus amendments, simplifying certain requirements and extending implementation deadlines for high-risk systems into 2027 and 2028. It says the underlying framework remains intact, with obligations addressing transparency, prohibited AI practices, general-purpose models and high-risk applications. It says the same application could face different requirements depending on where it operates, which individuals it affects and how its outputs influence decisions. It says the same underlying model might power a low-risk productivity assistant and a highly consequential employment application.

The article says organizations may have approved several enterprise AI platforms while individual departments independently integrate models into customer service, analytics, software development and decision-making workflows. It says third-party vendors continue embedding AI into existing products, often expanding an organization's AI footprint without corresponding governance processes. It says agentic AI systems are increasingly capable of accessing sensitive information, interacting with enterprise applications and taking actions versus generating responses. It says 280 laws were passed just this year, with weeks to go. It says David Talby is the CEO of John Snow Labs.

The article says federal lawmakers may eventually establish a national AI framework that supersedes some state requirements, and courts may also reshape the regulatory landscape. It says CIOs can't assume simpler, streamlined rules are coming. It says even with a unified federal approach, multinational organizations will face distinct international obligations. It says the best-prepared organizations will understand where their AI operates, understand its risks, continuously evaluate its behavior and demonstrate appropriate oversight. It says federal deregulation does not equal enterprise deregulation.

Articles.Title: The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer - CIO

stories.Headline: Emory Law launches AI and the Law concentration as firms adopt generative AI
stories.Summary:
Emory University School of Law launched a formal AI and the Law concentration, one of five law schools in Georgia, as a surging number of law firms go all-in on generative artificial intelligence. The concentration offers fluency in the latest technology that is rapidly transforming legal work, and the ethical dilemmas posed by that technology are a big part of the specialized study. Ifeoma Ajunwa, one of three Emory Law professors leading the concentration, was named among the Top 50 Legal Innovators in Academia for 2026. The national honor was recently announced by The National Law Review and Wickard and recognizes those shaping the future of legal education. Ajunwa said the subject combination is key.

The concentration began in the fall, and other law schools offer formal courses in AI and the law but not a specialization, including University of Georgia School of Law and Georgia State University College of Law. Ajunwa said she taught the topic 21 years ago, and students now are prepared for a world where AI is in everything. A published report by a global organization on recognition of new legal types found 65% of the largest law firms have fully implemented generative AI, and 82% of lawyers at the biggest firms are involved in it. The report found 32% of lawyers at firms across the U.S. use generative AI, 75% of lawyers at firms with 51 to 200 attorneys use it, and 11% of lawyers at firms with 2 to 10 attorneys use it. A survey shows 34% of lawyers at firms with 51 to 200 attorneys make more use of AI than last year, and 32% said they plan to increase their use.

Ajunwa said students express enthusiasm about the technology and also apprehension as it becomes more widespread, and she said she pursues a pipeline program to fund law jobs for students. She said society often gets negative AI while it cannot afford to ignore it, and she said people are overwhelmed or frightened by what AI can do. She said society has to think about what is true and how AI determines functions, especially for people who have been marginalized. She said the good consequences come with the bad and the unknown.

She said AI saves lawyers many hours of work, which benefits clients, and she said some lawyers have relied on unchecked artificial intelligence and learned it cannot be accurate. She said AI cannot be trusted to write legal work, and she said the technology can secretly surveil workers and raise the risk of copyright infringement. She said students shared their thoughts and warned that AI could do harm, and she said some feel mixed about the benefits and the feelings behind it. She said AI can be good if someone uses it for productivity, and she said it depends on how you use it.

Sang Hun Chung, a second-year student, said he worked on a summer task involving AI and found it sensitive and repetitive, and he said he designed a policy to protect trade secrets and other information. Chris Nelson, a student, said several students noted security regulations and other laws, and he said there is a lack of guardrails for artificial intelligence. Ajunwa said her current course includes mapping the patchwork of laws, and she said she teaches students who typically train to be top lawyers. Ryan Zanaslazky, a 20-year-old student, said he told the chatbot where he was and it said it was a specialist, and he said he plans to be a lawyer for great future.

Adina Dattu, a student, said there is such a need for research skills, and she said she will develop legal research skills and learn manually. Donald Yau, a student, said AI will not be reliable without those skills, and he said there is fear of being completely replaced by future generations of AI.

Articles.Title: Emory Law takes leading role in AI-centric legal education - The Atlanta Journal-Constitution

stories.Headline: New Jersey assembly committee advances bills to regulate AI in insurance and tenant screening
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced legislation to regulate artificial intelligence in insurance, housing and the workplace at a November 16, 2026 meeting of the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee. The committee took up bills limiting AI use in insurance claim denials, regulating automated tenant screening and imposing new requirements on electronic monitoring of employees. Lawmakers also considered measures requiring greater transparency from data center developers. Assemblyman Chris Tully (D-Bergenfield), the committee chairman, said the legislation reflects the need to protect consumers as AI becomes more widely used. The proposals drew concerns from businesses about higher costs and restrictions on emerging technology.

One bill, A5494, would prohibit certain uses of artificial intelligence in denying homeowners, automobile and flood insurance claims. It advanced with Assemblyman Chris DePhillips (R-Wyckoff) abstaining and every other committee member voting in favor. A second bill, A5495, would regulate automated tenant screening systems used to evaluate prospective renters. It also advanced with DePhillips abstaining and the remaining committee members voting in favor. The committee held a discussion-only hearing on A4981, which would regulate AI-based electronic monitoring systems used in employment and public services.

Assembly members Heather Simmons (D-Glassboro) and Cody Miller (D-Monroe) are sponsoring that proposal, along with 16 other Democratic co-sponsors. Tully said AI systems can improve efficiency and tackle fraud, but that people must be protected from automatic denial by algorithms. He said that when a major decision affects someone's life, there must always be a human in the loop. Tully said mandating human oversight establishes common-sense guardrails to use these powerful tools responsibly. DePhillips said he abstained on both bills because proponents and opponents did not seem that far apart and he saw an opportunity for both sides to collaborate.

Assemblyman Balvir Singh (D-Burlington) said he felt like he was learning to ride a bike while riding it. Assemblywoman Carmen Morales (D-Bloomfield) defended the insurance proposal as a consumer protection measure and said it really is about transparency. Insurance industry representatives raised concerns that the restrictions could limit their ability to use new technology and leave companies at a competitive disadvantage. Nicholas Kikis, vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, did not take a position on the tenant screening bill but warned that AI has made it increasingly difficult for landlords to detect fraudulent applications. Kikis pointed to income verification, saying documents landlords previously could verify with relative ease can now be altered using AI.

Jeff Kolekowski of the New Jersey Builders Association raised similar concerns without taking a formal position on the bill. Anthony Russo of the Commerce and Industry Association of New Jersey said the monitoring bill would add a high cost to companies that invent those technologies and that they would have to pay to have it approved. Russo said that if the bill goes through, it just adds to the cost of doing business. Jack Ramirez of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association said the bill's definition of artificial intelligence was too broad and could subject ordinary business tools to additional regulation. Eric Richards, legislative affairs coordinator for the New Jersey AFL-CIO, said AI has the power to change the very nature of work and that without oversight AI companies pose tremendous risk to working people.

Richards said the bill puts clear common-sense ground rules for how AI can be used in the workplace and makes sure an employer can't spy on you when you're off the clock. A5224 would require data center developers to disclose certain information to the public and elected officials before preliminary site plan consideration under the Municipal Land Use Law. S4304, sponsored by State Sens. Linda Greenstein (D-Plainsboro) and Brian Stack (D-Union City), would prohibit agreements intended to conceal certain information about data center developments, and its Assembly counterpart is A2774. Greenstein said that if you don't play by the rules of open government, you don't get to build in New Jersey, and that confidentiality agreements could prevent residents and local officials from learning the full extent of a project's electricity demands and environmental effects.

Chris Sotiro of the Climate Revolution Action Network said the developers are not interested in transparency but are interested in hiding. A2774 advanced with bipartisan support, with DePhillips, the only Republican present at the hearing, voting in favor, and Assemblyman Greg McGuckin (R-Toms River) was absent. Earlier this year, Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation sponsored by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Summit) that redirected $250 million in unused data center tax credits to the New Jersey Economic Development Authority. The measure passed the Legislature with nearly unanimous support.

The hearings illustrate the competing pressures facing lawmakers as they try to establish protections for consumers, tenants and workers without imposing restrictions that businesses say could discourage innovation or make new technologies more expensive to use. The articles do not say when the full Assembly or Senate might vote on the bills. The articles do not say what happens to A4981 after the discussion-only hearing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Letitia James launches an AI safety and enforcement unit led by Cristy Phillips
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on Tuesday the creation of a new unit aimed at protecting New Yorkers from potential risks associated with artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, according to a report from WRGB. The AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit, known as the ASSET Unit, will focus on enforcing AI safety laws, protecting consumer privacy and addressing potential threats involving cybersecurity, digital scams and online safety. The unit will also oversee enforcement of New York's Responsible AI Safety Education Act, which takes effect on January 1, 2027, and requires developers of certain advanced AI models to publicly disclose their safety measures and promptly report security and safety incidents. According to the Attorney General's Office, the new unit will also develop policy proposals and provide technical expertise to support investigations across the agency.

The initiative builds on existing efforts to address AI-related risks, including scams involving AI-generated celebrity impersonations and potentially harmful chatbot interactions, the report said. The office highlighted several laws the unit will help enforce, including the SHIELD Act, which requires businesses to maintain reasonable data security practices to protect personal information. The RAISE Act establishes safety and transparency requirements for developers of certain advanced AI models beginning in January 2027, and new chatbot safety legislation prohibits unsafe chatbot features for children beginning in June 2027. General Business Law Article 47 requires AI chatbots to make reasonable efforts to identify and respond to suicidal ideation and to notify users they are interacting with AI rather than a human. New York Penal Law 245.15 criminalizes the dissemination of intimate images with intent to harm, including certain AI-generated or altered images.

James said that promising new technologies like artificial intelligence should never come at the expense of New Yorkers' safety and privacy, and that her office has always stepped up to enforce the law to protect New Yorkers when big tech companies try to take advantage of them. She said the ASSET Unit will lead the way in ensuring AI and other emerging technology are developed safely and for the benefit of all New Yorkers. The ASSET Unit will operate within the Office of the Attorney General's Economic Justice Division and work closely with its Bureau of Internet and Technology. Cristy Phillips, who previously served as special counsel for the Economic Justice Division, will lead the unit, according to the Attorney General's Office.

The announcement places New York among the states moving to regulate artificial intelligence through both new disclosure requirements and dedicated enforcement staff. The RAISE Act's disclosure and incident-reporting duties for developers of certain advanced AI models begin on January 1, 2027, while the chatbot safety provisions for children take effect in June 2027. The ASSET Unit's work will draw on the SHIELD Act, Article 47 of the General Business Law and Penal Law 245.15 alongside the newer AI statutes. The unit will also provide technical expertise to support investigations across the Attorney General's Office, the report said.

Articles.Title: NY Attorney General James announces new unit to oversee AI safety and enforcement - WXLV

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI can cut emissions across iron and steelmaking
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in Carbon Neutral Systems examines how artificial intelligence can accelerate decarbonization across the iron and steel industry by optimizing process efficiency, enabling feedstock substitution, and supporting carbon capture, utilization, and storage. The study was authored by Xidi Shang, Wuliang Yin, Jianxin Pan, Min Wang, Hua Wang, Kai Yang, and Qingtai Xiao. It synthesizes findings from 133 representative investigations identified through structured database searches covering research published between 2000 and 2025. The review was published on November 16, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article appeared under the site's Technology section with a reading time of five minutes.

The authors highlight that the global steel sector accounts for approximately 7 to 9 percent of direct industrial carbon dioxide emissions. Traditional blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace configurations generate roughly 70 percent of global crude steel output. Electric arc furnace operations currently produce approximately 41.5 percent of crude steel in the European Union and 68.0 percent in the United States. The review maps five technological pathways under evaluation across global producers, ranging from conventional coal-fed blast furnace systems paired with carbon capture to scrap-fed electric arc furnaces, hydrogen-based direct reduction, and electrolytic ironmaking. The article's subject of research is artificial intelligence applications in low-carbon iron and steel metallurgy.

The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries. They state that most models lack comprehensive representations of dynamic cross-unit couplings among material, energy, and carbon flows, which restricts route-wide optimization across entire industrial complexes. They note that industrial datasets suffer from noise, missing values, regime drift, and a scarcity of validated operational logs for emerging hydrogen or electrolytic pilots. Because metallurgical operations depend strictly on thermodynamic conservation laws, the authors say unconstrained black-box learners risk outputting nonphysical predictions when extrapolating outside training domains. The review concludes that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks, supporting verifiable, plant-wide carbon reduction across the steel industry.

The authors highlight that broad deployment of newer hydrogen and electrolysis technologies faces substantial hurdles, including capital requirements, infrastructural bottlenecks, and high operational costs, requiring system-wide optimization within existing facilities while cleaner routes mature. They report that multimodal perception frameworks combining two-dimensional photographic images with three-dimensional point clouds have achieved material granularity recognition rates exceeding 90 percent. Vision-based monitoring tools detect bosh pressure channel anomalies eight to sixteen minutes prior to operational disruptions, according to the review. Digital-twin structures integrated with deep residual networks identify carbon emission deviations, categorizing operational anomaly severity with reported classification accuracies exceeding 97 percent.

In electric arc furnaces, artificial neural networks estimate endpoint carbon concentrations, achieving reported hit rates of 96.67 percent within an error margin of 0.05 percent carbon. The review delineates the baseline operating structure of integrated steelmaking, where raw-material preparation, blast furnace reduction, converter refining, and rolling units share significant energy flows and off-gas networks. Sintering, pelletizing, and coking supply the burden materials required for blast furnace operation, wherein fossil carbon acts simultaneously as a chemical reducing agent and an energy source. Conventional chemical analyses remain accurate but require offline sampling that cannot provide high-frequency process feedback.

Echo state networks, variational mode decomposition, and swarm intelligence algorithms generate multi-step forecasts of blast furnace gas production and gasholder storage levels, driving root-mean-square errors below 0.05 across benchmark industrial datasets. The article's references cite Shang, X., Yin, W., Pan, J., Wang, M., Wang, H., Yang, K., & Xiao, Q. (2026), published in Carbon Neutral Systems, volume 2, issue 1. The review states that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks. The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries.

The article does not state when or whether such plant-wide architectures will be deployed. It does not give a timeline for the five technological pathways it maps. The article does not report any response from steel producers or policymakers to the review. It does not state the review's conclusions on costs for the hydrogen and electrolysis routes beyond the hurdles it lists.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could erase many jobs forever and urges lawmakers to act
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the 71 year old cofounder of Microsoft, published a 6,000 word essay earlier this year titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical,” in which he warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out careers over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. In the essay he called for certain jobs to be “human reserved” and said AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing, adding that many jobs will disappear forever. He wrote that the transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that the world is not preparing adequately for that transition. He also said that if the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

The warning arrives alongside new figures on job losses, as Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on November 5, 2026, that AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, which is approximately 20 percent of all cuts. Gates had already raised his concerns in September, when he appeared on NBC News’ Meet the Press with Kristen Welker and was asked whether AI is powerful enough to end all of humanity. He responded that AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that there has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools. He added that self regulation is not enough and that legislation needs to be passed, with politicians and law enforcement offering safeguarding and monitoring.

The essay sets out Gates’ view that the coming shift will be turbulent and that choices made now are critical, and it calls for some roles to be set aside for humans rather than left to machines. His September remarks place the responsibility for safeguards on lawmakers and law enforcement rather than on the industry alone, since he said self regulation is not enough. The Challenger, Gray & Christmas count of 121,401 AI cited job cut announcements in 2026, about 20 percent of all cuts, gives a measure of how far the disruption has already gone. The articles do not say what steps, if any, governments or companies have taken in response to his call for legislation.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel superintendent Mark Bedell asks parents to weigh banning or embracing student AI use
stories.Summary:
Anne Arundel County’s public school system faces a decision soon on whether to ban students’ use of artificial intelligence or embrace it, The Baltimore Banner reported on 11/17/2026 at 5:30 a.m. EST. Superintendent Mark Bedell has been asking parents to tackle that question, along with what to do about cellphone use in schools, at a series of community meetings. Bedell organized the meeting series because he pledged to listen to community members’ feedback before making any AI policy recommendations of his own. The last two meetings were planned for this week, with families invited to gather on Tuesday at Annapolis High and on Thursday at Meade High from 6 to 8 p.m. The roughly three dozen parents who gathered Thursday night at Southern High in Harwood expressed a mix of excitement and fear about the new technology.

The draft AI policy under consideration by Anne Arundel’s school board is light on specifics. It requires AI tools to be vetted for educational value before adoption and emphasizes that the technology may not replace employees’ duties. It also directs the district to establish expectations, conditions and limitations for students’ use of AI. The board is set to update and finalize the policy next month. Bedell said Thursday during the meeting at Southern High in Harwood that the district will learn how to adjust to this AI era, even though it has everyone a little nervous.

Bedell conceded in an interview that he doesn’t know how to give older students access to AI and prevent them from using it to cheat. He said the district has always been able to figure out how to put guardrails in for new technology, but for this technology it just hasn’t figured it out yet. He said a few themes have emerged from the meetings he’s attended, with many parents asking the district to teach students how to use AI safely. Others have asked for AI to be banned outright for children in elementary and middle schools, just as cellphone use at school is banned for those grades. Other parents have begged Bedell to keep AI out of their children’s schools altogether.

Attendee Tamara Bauer said she loves AI and uses it often in her personal life, and the district’s priority should be teaching students to use AI safely and appropriately. Bauer is a mom of two and the principal at the Center of Applied Technology South, an Edgewater high school offering job training, and she attended with her son Levi, a fifth grader who was the youngest kid there. Bauer said that when Levi needs help with his math homework, she sometimes scans his worksheets and feeds them into an AI model, asking it to explain step by step how to find the answer rather than show her the answer. She then helps guide her son to do the work, and she said a child working alone would be less deliberative. Hillary Klemmt, a parent affiliated with the Schools Beyond Screens coalition, which advocates for evidence-based education technology policies, asked why the district is rushing to embrace AI blindly and why it is using children as guinea pigs when there is so much at stake.

A procession of speakers who testified at a board meeting last month all had the same message: Ban it. Some parents argued AI can’t and shouldn’t be avoided, even though students may use it to cheat, while others said it stifles creativity and has no place in schools. The Banner’s related coverage included a report on Oct 23, 2026, that Anne Arundel parents and teachers urged the school board to restrict AI in classrooms. Another related report on May 5, 2026, covered what to know about Anne Arundel schools’ trial run with AI-powered weapons detection. Jessica Calefati, an education investigative reporter at The Baltimore Banner who covers the Anne Arundel County schools and Maryland’s child welfare system, wrote the story.

The final two meetings were scheduled for Tuesday and Thursday from 6 to 8 p.m., at Annapolis High on Tuesday and Meade High on Thursday. The school board is set to update and finalize the draft AI policy next month. Bedell has not yet outlined his own AI policy recommendations, which he pledged to make after listening to community feedback. The articles do not state what the board will decide or when Bedell will present his recommendations. The articles do not state how many meetings Bedell has attended or how many people testified at last month’s board meeting.

stories.Headline: National Whistleblower Center hires Attention Studio to lobby for AI whistleblower protections
stories.Summary:
The National Whistleblower Center added Attention Studio as an outside lobbying firm in 2026 while it pushes the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, which remains in committee in both chambers of Congress. Attention Studio reported $100,000 for the third quarter in a filing signed on Nov. 9, and it is the only registrant on record for the center that quarter. Two lobbyists are named on the filing, Olivia Konar, a policy associate, and Ava Smithing, a founding partner, and both also appear on the firm's new client registration for the center. The bill would bar employers from retaliating against employees and independent contractors who report artificial intelligence security vulnerabilities or violations of AI-related laws.

The legislation would also bar contracts that waive those protections and give whistleblowers reinstatement and back pay. The filing lists S. 1792 and H.R. 3460 and says the lobbying urged Senate and House offices to cosponsor the bill and support committee action before the end of the 119th Congress. It names the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and the Commerce Committee. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) sponsors S. 1792, which was introduced May 15, 2025, and referred to the HELP Committee, and Congress.gov shows 13 current cosponsors, five of them original, with no later committee or floor action. Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) sponsors H.R. 3460, which was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, and its cosponsor page shows 10 current cosponsors, one of them original.

A coalition letter dated June 10, 2025, backs S. 1792, and its 22 signers include Americans for Responsible Innovation, the Center for Democracy & Technology, the Government Accountability Project, Public Knowledge, and the National Whistleblower Center. The signers say fear of retaliation, including over confidentiality agreements, can deter insiders from disclosing AI risks, and they argue protections support transparency, accountability, public safety, and national security. The letter cites a June 2024 public statement by more than a dozen current and former employees of leading AI companies. Both bills wait in committee, S. 1792 in the Senate HELP Committee and H.R. 3460 in the House Education and Workforce Committee, and the filing's stated goal is committee action before the 119th Congress ends. Attention Studio is a new outside firm for the center, which makes the firm's work on this bill the change to track.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could eliminate many jobs and urges safety nets and retraining
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates published a new essay warning that artificial intelligence could eliminate many jobs, and he expanded on the warning in an October 22 appearance on The Verge's Decoder podcast with host Nilay Patel. The essay and podcast remarks were reported by Laura Grande on November 16, 2026. Gates wrote that many jobs will disappear forever. He said entry- and mid-level positions face the greatest immediate danger. He expects disruption to spread across law, medicine, manufacturing, construction and hospitality.

Gates wrote that the change will hit these industries rapidly over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. He said the scarcity of white-collar skills will disappear and pointed to telesales, telesupport and accounting as jobs that could be heavily affected. He acknowledged new jobs will emerge but warned that without the right policies there could be far fewer than exist today. He wrote that there is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era. He said his big concern is a 20-year transition period with winners and losers and a lot of disruption.

Gates called for stronger safety nets and retraining programs, along with taxes on AI and robots. He proposed setting aside Human Reserved roles that society chooses to keep in human hands. He warned that waiting until people are already displaced or underemployed will be too late. He cited Stanford research finding workers ages 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations had a 16% relative employment decline after researchers controlled for firm-level shocks, while employment among more experienced workers remained stable. He wrote that the jobs at most risk are entry- and mid-level.

On Nov. 5, Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that U.S. employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October. AI was blamed for 1,265 of them, bringing the year-to-date total to 121,401, second among reasons for job cuts behind economic conditions at 130,531. October's AI-related total was the lowest monthly figure recorded so far in 2026. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' November 6 report said employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment held at 4.1%. The BLS found 2 million Americans had been unemployed for at least 27 weeks in October, accounting for 27.6% of everyone out of work.

Gates helped put a computer on nearly every desk as Microsoft co-founder. The warning comes as AI starts showing up more often in employers' layoff announcements, though it isn't the only reason companies are cutting jobs. Gates believes AI presents a different problem from downturns because a position automated out of existence may never come back. Once one business uses AI or robots to cut costs, competitors may feel pressure to adopt the same technology. Workers could then face retraining while trying to cover bills without their previous income.

Turning Gates's ideas into policy could take years. The article says workers can begin preparing sooner by calculating monthly household costs, including housing, groceries, utilities, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments and essential medical expenses. It gives examples: costs of $4,000 per month would require $24,000 for six months, $36,000 for nine months and $48,000 for one year. It says saving $500 per month would produce $6,000 in one year before interest. The article leaves open whether Gates's timeline will hold and how his proposed policies would be enacted.

stories.Headline: Mayo researchers find AI EKG analysis flags hearts over 16 years older as a 65-year-old seeks the test
stories.Summary:
A 65-year-old man booked his Welcome to Medicare visit after reading about a Mayo Clinic discovery, according to 24/7 Wall St. Researchers found that an AI analysis of an electrocardiogram could identify patients whose hearts appeared more than 16 years older than their actual age. That warning was associated with increased cardiac risk in people with a particular inherited heart condition. He wants to know what his own EKG might reveal. The article was published on November 16, 2026, by Gerelyn Terzo.

Medicare covers a standard screening EKG once during the first 12 months of Part B if he receives a referral during his welcome visit. The visit costs nothing if the provider accepts assignment, and the deductible does not apply to it. The EKG works differently, with the patient paying 20% after the Part B deductible, which rose to $283 in 2026 from $257. If the visit comes early in the year before any deductible is paid, he may owe the entire approved charge for the EKG. At a hospital-owned clinic, he also owes the hospital a copayment.

Mayo cardiologist John Giudicessi said the technology could eventually help doctors recognize dangerous disease before conventional tests reveal obvious abnormalities. The findings were highlighted on October 23, 2026, and drew on a registry of 1,049 patients with genetic forms of cardiomyopathy. Researchers still need to validate the findings in another group of patients. The article states the findings do not mean an otherwise healthy 65-year-old whose EKG suggests an 81-year-old heart necessarily faces the same risks. The AI-estimated heart-age gap greater than 16 years was flagged in patients with LMNA-related cardiomyopathy, an inherited disease that can cause heart failure and dangerous arrhythmias.

Medigap Plan G pays the 20% coinsurance but leaves the Part B deductible to the patient. The AMA's temporary Category III codes for emerging technology include 0764T and 0765T, which describe AI-assisted EKG risk assessment for cardiac dysfunction such as low-ejection fraction, pulmonary hypertension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Providers bill 0764T as an add-on to standard EKG codes 93000 and 93010. Since January 1, 2025, Medicare's hospital outpatient payment system has paid those codes as separate services, according to a 2026 vendor coding guide that cites CMS. The guide lists no physician-office rate.

The article says the codes do not establish how a clinic would bill for the Mayo-style heart-age estimate. It found no published Medicare price specifically for an AI heart-age estimate, nor confirmation that the cardiac-dysfunction codes apply to it. Medicare's Advance Beneficiary Notice, Form CMS-R-131, generally must be given before treatment when a provider expects Medicare to deny an otherwise covered service as medically unnecessary. An ABN is not required for services Medicare excludes altogether, so the absence of one does not mean nothing is owed. The article advises asking for an itemized estimate separating the standard EKG from any AI analysis.

The article advises getting the billing code and the price of each service before agreeing to the additional test. It says to ask directly whether the AI analysis is billed separately, and to whom. If an ABN is handed over, the article says to read which box is being checked before signing. A patient can turn down the AI portion and still get the covered screening EKG. The article advises booking the visit early, within the first 12 months of Part B, after which Medicare covers an EKG only as a diagnostic test requiring symptoms or a medical reason the doctor writes down.

stories.Headline: Nigerian lawmakers and experts urge AI regulation to curb digital misinformation at Abuja forum
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers and communication experts called for stronger safeguards against digital misinformation at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on Monday, warning that misuse of artificial intelligence and social media could undermine public trust and weaken democratic institutions. Tajudeen Abbas, speaker of the house of representatives, was represented by Julius Ihonvbere, the house majority leader, and said misleading information could spread faster than institutions could respond. He said technology improves access to information but has also increased the capacity to misinform, manipulate and distort public discourse. Abbas urged public relations and communication professionals to promote public understanding, institutional credibility and democratic participation, and said responsible communication is a condition for the effective functioning of democratic society.

Abbas said artificial intelligence offers opportunities in research, information access and efficiency but could also be used to generate falsehoods, impersonate public figures and manipulate democratic debates. He urged public institutions to communicate accurately and transparently, asked the media to uphold independence and verification, and called on technology companies to take responsibility for misuse of their platforms. He said the proposed Abuja Declaration should establish common principles around accuracy, transparency, freedom of expression, institutional accountability and ethical AI use. Osita Izunaso, senator representing Imo west and chairman of the senate committee on capital market, called for regulation of artificial intelligence to prevent its misuse. He urged social media users to verify information before sharing it and warned against treating everything published online as factual.

Kete Omenugha, the first female vice-chancellor of Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University, called for communication ethics to become a compulsory course in Nigerian universities, irrespective of students' disciplines. She cited an incident in which a false WhatsApp voice note claiming examinations had been postponed by two weeks caused some students to stop preparing and travel home. She also warned against the use of AI to create offensive caricatures of lecturers, vice-chancellors and fellow students, saying many people carry scars all through their lives. Emmanuel Dandaura, vice-president of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations, urged practitioners to move beyond publicity and persuasive content to embrace strategic leadership, ethical conduct and institutional accountability. He warned that artificial intelligence had made deception cheaper, faster and increasingly convincing.

Dandaura said in a presentation titled "Redefining Public Relations: Nigeria's Gold Proposition for a Changing World" that the value of practitioners should lie in sound judgement, accountability and moral courage rather than merely producing persuasive content. He said machines can produce persuasive content better, so the enduring value of public relations must lie in judgment, accountability, moral courage and the ability to counsel institutions toward responsible conduct. The forum highlighted the need for responsible communication, ethical use of AI and stronger regulatory frameworks to address the spread of false and manipulative narratives. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the proposed Abuja Declaration.

stories.Headline: Xero pushes AI tools for accountants as small business adoption lags
stories.Summary:
Xero, the financial software firm, is pushing AI offerings for accounting practices even though adoption among small businesses remains at an early stage. Xero estimates that across the UK, US, and Australia, some 77% of micro-businesses and 68% of small businesses are at an early stage or have not adopted AI. More than half of medium and large businesses actively use some form of AI, even something as basic as AI chat. CEO Sukhinder Cassidy said Xero has seen this sort of adoption curve before in the cloud space. The current nascent take-up is not slowing the firm's own push into AI offerings for when the customer base is more receptive.

Customer surveys show AI tools save the average accounting practice in the UK and Australia more than seven hours a week. More than 100 XeroForce workflows are already running day-to-day while the platform is still in alpha. More than 500 customers are on the waitlist for the data. One million customers have used Xero's generative AI features over the last 12 months, and monthly users are up ninefold year-on-year. Customers can adopt AI from Xero in two ways, by using packaged solutions on key Xero surfaces or by building their own workflows using the firm's infrastructure, data and tools.

Cassidy said that four to five years ago Xero was largely an accounting product, which gave fewer ways to deepen engagement and usage. He said the 3x3 strategy has helped Xero evolve into an AI-powered multi-product platform. He said Xero wants to deliver a category-defining experience for small businesses and accounting partners across accounting, payments and payroll. He said these higher-value jobs can expand average revenue per customer, absolute gross profit dollars and cash generation. He said Xero is delivering AI solutions designed around customer value and that adoption is growing.

Soon-Ee Cheah, Xero EGM of AI Products, said accountants and bookkeepers spend much of their time on tasks that live in between the software they use. He said this work, such as getting data out of Xero, combining spreadsheets, e-mailing a client and waiting for replies, is unbillable, manual and exhausting. He said XeroForce is a natural language agent builder that lets practices create agents without writing a single line of code. He said users can build an agent from scratch or use pre-made templates to get one running in just minutes. He said XeroForce looks at connected tools such as Xero, Office 365, Outlook and Calendly and works out how to put steps into a coherent workflow.

Sarah Lawrence, CEO of Australian accounting and advisory firm Hot Toast, said the firm has been Xero-only for over a decade. She said Xero was the first platform in the firm's technology stack and gave her flexibility and lifestyle as a business owner and for her team. She said team members are all up the East Coast of Australia with clients all across Australia, so they can service them instantly via the cloud platform. She said the Xero platform has been used as an all-inclusive workflow tool for everything from Accounts Payable to Receivable, to Payroll, to Reporting. She said AI will be another game changer and that accountants are naturally the trusted partner for clients and small businesses because they already sit in the data.

The article says each technology shift changes how small businesses, accountants and bookkeepers work, from desktops and the Internet to mobile, cloud and now AI. It says Xero has been at the forefront of these shifts and led customers through them. It says AI offers an even more transformative opportunity for Xero's customers. It says one of the more interesting user adoption curves to watch in the AI sector in 2026 has been the take-up in Finance. It says how Xero's pitch evolves in 2027 as XeroForce expands its footprint will be something to keep an eye on.

stories.Headline: Universal Music Group (ENXTAM:UMG) Stock Could Be 26% Above Fair Value As AI Lawsuit Pressure Builds
stories.Summary:
Bailey Pemberton wrote an article on November 15, 2026, about Universal Music Group. The company faces pressure from a lawsuit involving an AI music platform. This legal dispute may affect how the company monetizes its recordings. Investors are now questioning if the current market value matches expected cash. The stock has fallen 21.1 percent over the last three years.

The current share price is 17.63 euros for the company listed as ENXTAM:UMG. A Discounted Cash Flow model shows the stock could be 26 percent above fair value. The group generated about 1.46 billion euros in free cash flow over twelve months. The company has a price to earnings ratio of 98.9x. A copyright lawsuit was filed against the AI music platform known as Suno.

Simply Wall St produced the analysis using AI automation and historical data. They stated that their articles are not intended to be financial advice. The analysis does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. They aim to provide long term analysis driven by fundamental data. The firm has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

FundamentalContrarianInvestor believes the stock is 24 percent undervalued due to catalog quality. This investor notes that the company controls 39.76 percent of U.S. catalogue consumption. A bearish analyst argues the stock is 47 percent overvalued because of AI. This analyst says lower margin formats could absorb benefits before they reach profit. Warner Music Group is mentioned as having 19.80 percent of U.S. consumption.

The company has seen a long stretch of weak share returns recently. Investors are weighing catalog strength against new digital formats and AI deals. There is a push to clarify how AI can use label catalogues. The business is compared against 53 different AI infrastructure stocks. Some analysts look at how executive pay and priorities tilt the future.

The company recently signed a multiyear agreement with an AI music platform. Future value depends on whether Streaming 2.0 and AI deals reward shareholders. The articles leave open how the Suno lawsuit will influence long term cash. It remains unclear if future cash flows will stay steady or race higher. The analysis may not factor in the latest price sensitive company announcements.
