stories.Headline: Digital News Publishers Association challenges India's data protection law in Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
The Digital News Publishers Association challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 before the Supreme Court of India. This group represents twenty one news publishers who are concerned about the law and its associated rules. A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued a notice to the Union Government on 27 October 2026. The court declined to grant interim relief without first hearing the government side of the legal dispute. A further hearing on this matter is scheduled to take place on 17 November 2026.

The DPDP Act received presidential assent on 11 August 2023 and regulates digital personal data and digitised non digital data. It defines Data Fiduciaries as entities determining processing means and Data Principals as the individuals whose data is processed. The DPDP Rules, 2025, were notified on 13 November 2025, with principal compliance starting on 13 May 2027. Financial penalties for contraventions can reach Rs. 250 crore, and children under eighteen require verifiable parental consent for processing.

The challenge targets Sections 7, 17, 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3), and specific provisions of the 2025 Rules. The publishers argue that the law lacks a specific journalistic exemption, which could hinder the collection of information for investigations. They claim that requiring prior consent from individuals under investigation would undermine the work of journalists investigating public office misuse. The publishers also question Section 44(3), which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act of 2005 regarding personal information. They believe Section 17 raises concerns about the scope of exemptions available to the State for national security purposes.

These groups seek to balance individual dignity with the public right to information and the freedom of the press. Journalists and citizens are affected by this law, as it impacts the ability to scrutinize public institutions and government power. The articles suggest that privacy should not be a shield against legitimate scrutiny, nor should journalism justify publishing every detail. The debate involves the constitutional relationship between Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Indian Constitution regarding expression and privacy. In Jammu and Kashmir, digital rights are significant because platforms are essential for banking, education, employment, and public services.

The region has a specific history with internet restrictions that makes these data protection and privacy issues particularly important. The 2017 case of Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India established that privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right. The 2020 Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India case emphasized proportionality and transparency regarding internet suspensions in Jammu and Kashmir.

Internationally, the European Union uses the GDPR, while the United States uses fragmented laws like the California Consumer Privacy Act. China implemented the Personal Information Protection Law in 2021, which includes specific provisions regarding State organs and national security. These global examples show different ways of balancing individual autonomy, state surveillance, and the right to information or erasure. The Supreme Court will now determine if the law adequately distinguishes public interest journalism from the commercial misuse of data.

It must decide if the legislation protects citizens from information misuse or protects power from the scrutiny of the citizens. The court will examine if State interference with privacy satisfies standards of legality, legitimate purpose, necessity, and proportionality. The articles leave open whether the Data Protection Board will provide an independent and accessible remedy for those affected. It remains unclear how the court will reconcile the right to informational privacy with the public right to know.

stories.Headline: China and ASEAN expand trade pact to include artificial intelligence and digital economy cooperation
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Commerce announced on Monday that an upgraded free trade pact between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations will soon take effect. This agreement, known as the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, was signed in October of last year. The new rules are scheduled to enter into force on December 1 to bolster regional supply chains. This initiative aims to lower business costs by deepening the coordination of regional standards and rules.

The protocol expands cooperation into behind-the-border areas including the digital economy, green development, and artificial intelligence. It encourages both sides to recognize conformity assessment results to eliminate the need for duplicate testing and certification. New systems for electronic payments, invoicing, and bills of lading will improve compatibility and reduce expenses for companies. Enhanced digital customs procedures and better transport links are intended to shorten clearance times and resolve logistics bottlenecks. These changes follow a period where two-way trade between the partners exceeded 1 trillion dollars in 2025.

An official from the Ministry of Commerce stated that these measures enhance product competitiveness more effectively than tariff preferences alone. The ministry explained that the upgrade reflects a shared commitment to free trade and multilateralism during a time of global economic uncertainty. They noted that the agreement provides fresh impetus for economic integration across the Asia-Pacific region. To ensure businesses can utilize these new arrangements, the ministry plans to organize targeted training sessions.

The ministry will continue to work with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to advance practical cooperation. This future collaboration will include further consultations regarding the digital economy and the implementation of artificial intelligence. By focusing on these high-tech sectors, the partners hope to create more resilient and efficient regional supply chains. These ongoing efforts seek to maintain the status of China and ASEAN as each other's largest trading partners.

stories.Headline: US labor authorities launch PERM actions against Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms
stories.Summary:
United States authorities in October initiated administrative action under the Permanent Labor Certification program against Microsoft, Adobe and six major technology outsourcing firms, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, according to TechGig. The actions have disrupted the processing and acceptance of these firms' PERM applications, creating uncertainty for foreign professionals awaiting permanent residency. The federal inquiry centers on allegations that certain employers used immigration programs to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign personnel. Officials noted that the ongoing investigations and administrative actions do not constitute a final finding of guilt. The PERM program is a critical step for US employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards, and employers must certify that insufficient qualified US workers are available and that hiring a foreign national will not adversely affect American employees.

The Trump administration has introduced a requirement of $100,000 for certain new H-1B petitions while extending related visa restrictions through September 2027. The H-1B program allows US companies to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialty occupations and has long been central to the Indian IT sector across software development, cloud services, cybersecurity and technical consulting. The administration has not formally announced a complete shutdown or overhaul of the H-1B program, focusing instead on audits, employer accountability and strict compliance. US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito warned that temporary work visas cannot be treated as a permanent business strategy, stating that visas like the H-1B should only be used when qualified and willing American workers are unavailable for a given role. D'Esposito indicated that the probe is likely to widen and warned that similar actions could soon target additional companies and academic institutions.

His office is coordinating closely with the White House Fraud Task Force, led by Vice President JD Vance, which aims to identify systemic irregularities and abuse within visa programs. The heightened scrutiny directly affects major Indian IT service providers whose US operations rely heavily on deploying specialized talent from abroad. For Indian IT firms, the immediate challenge lies in balancing business continuity in their largest market with rigorous adherence to evolving immigration rules. If federal investigations expand and PERM restrictions persist, Indian service providers could face significant hurdles in talent deployment, foreign hiring and green card sponsorship for employees in the United States. The articles do not say what further steps, if any, the firms or the administration will take next.

stories.Headline: Mullin says AI superintelligence may have caused Microsoft, bank and airline outages
stories.Summary:
Major technology disruptions hit Microsoft, several large banks, and the aviation industry throughout the week ending November 17, 2026. These outages affected core Microsoft 365 services including Teams, Outlook, Exchange Online, and Copilot across 74 different countries. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide for over four hours due to instability in legacy equipment. Customers of Capital One, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Chase reported banking outages on Monday.

The situation requires an investigation into how rapidly advancing artificial intelligence might overwhelm older systems that cannot keep pace. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted that a technology expert suggested superintelligence could be responsible for these events. He explained that AI programs capable of writing code might create a ripple effect when they attempt to self-fix. On November 14, officials from the FAA and the Transportation Department stated the aviation issues were not connected to the new SMART AI system.

Secretary Mullin told Fox News that he is 98 percent certain a cyberattack did not cause the disruptions. He argued that there are no footprints of an attack and no one has claimed responsibility for the events. Conversely, former national security adviser Michael Flynn suggested on social media that the patterns were suspicious and looked like a massive cyberattack. President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns on Tuesday, stating that such things happen when organizations are big and powerful.

stories.Headline: Malcolm Myers finds ten AI-exposed companies lose $206 billion in market value since 2021
stories.Summary:
Ten publicly listed companies operating in sectors exposed to artificial intelligence have collectively lost $206 billion in market value since the end of 2021, according to an analysis by Malcolm Myers, who works with marketplace and services platform businesses at EIV. The erosion in market value initially came despite relatively resilient revenue growth, as nine of the 10 companies recorded higher revenues between 2021 and 2025. Their combined revenue increased 47% from $22.2 billion to $32.7 billion over that period, even as investors questioned whether these businesses could withstand AI disruption. The disruption is now becoming visible in their financial performance, with revenue in the third quarter of 2026 declining 23% at Tripadvisor's hotels business, 25% at Fiverr's marketplace, 33% at Shutterstock and 40% at Chegg. The decline in valuations has been particularly pronounced across four segments that Myers noted in his analysis.

In price comparison and travel search, Tripadvisor has lost 77% of its market value since 2021, while LendingTree and TripAdvisor have declined 68% and 67% respectively, as these businesses largely depend on search traffic and referral fees. Booking.com, which facilitates the actual transaction, has gained 20% in contrast to those search-dependent platforms. Shutterstock has lost 97% of its value, while Wix and Adobe have declined 68% and 66% respectively, as AI increasingly enables users to generate content and applications on demand. Freelance marketplaces have faced similar challenges, with Fiverr losing 93% of its value and Upwork falling 72%, as businesses and consumers increasingly use AI to produce digital work they previously outsourced to freelancers. Chegg has lost 98% of its market value as large language models increasingly provide homework answers and educational assistance free of charge, Myers said.

Myers believes not all marketplaces face the same degree of risk, because platforms that aggregate unique supply, facilitate payments and manage fulfillment could prove more resilient as AI agents work alongside these businesses rather than replace them. He also sees an emerging opportunity in AI-native businesses that deliver completed outcomes instead of simply connecting customers with service providers or offering software to complete tasks. Examples include Corgi, which underwrites and issues insurance policies, Lawhive, which provides legal services through an AI-enabled law firm, and Mercor, which organises specialist work to deliver training data and evaluations. Mercor recently completed a $750 million Series D funding round at a $20 billion valuation, less than four years after its launch, and Myers believes the shift towards delivering completed outcomes could create some of the most valuable marketplaces and services businesses over the next decade.

stories.Headline: Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han urge readers to practice preemptive skepticism online
stories.Summary:
The Daily Trojan published an opinion article titled "Everyone should practice a post-AI mindset" on Nov. 17, 2026, written by Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han. The article argues that readers should employ "preemptive skepticism" as they search for humanity and truth online. It says our generation is living through a technological revolution, and that millennials and Gen Z are often called digital natives or digital pioneers. It states that millennials and Gen Z are the most digitally literate generations, and that everything is done with smartphones nowadays. It gives ordering morning coffee and logging into Netflix or a bank account as examples of smartphone tasks.

The article says the digital world's most daunting thing is its lack of physicality or security, and that there is no such thing as concrete or absolute certification. It says everyone uses the internet and anyone can input information and modify it however they want. It says real information can be modified to mislead audiences, and fake information can be appealing enough to bring out real emotions. It says that with the rise of artificial intelligence-generated content on everyday media platforms, this is easier than ever. The article quotes Jelani Williams, a master's student studying digital social media, saying he has definitely seen a video he thought was AI.

It quotes him saying there are a lot of times he is just skeptical immediately, more so than anything, and asking whether something actually happened. It describes the liar's dividend as a phenomenon in which realistic AI and advanced technology allow public figures to falsely claim that authentic, damaging evidence against them is manipulated. It says the public figure then usually shifts the burden of proof to others, demanding even more concrete evidence despite having just stubbornly rejected the initial facts. It says the internet is permanently changing in ways one can't easily imagine, prompting us to keep engaging, stay up to date and leave marks. The article says people start acting overly intelligent, which makes the internet dangerous, and that one could easily fabricate false information to denounce another.

It says the one attacked could also easily accuse them of falsehood without verification, just because it criticized them. It says that in a world where fake can be mistaken for real and real for fake, simple claims and first impressions do not shift the entire burden of proof onto those presenting them. It says we should evaluate sources, corroborate evidence and demand support for claims of manipulation. It quotes Jelani saying a claim would just have to be backed up really well, and that people have to be taught how to interpret things properly so they understand it is not real. The article says guardrails are starting to be set up for AI transparency, and that the California AI Transparency Act requires generative AI providers to embed machine-readable disclosures in generated content and provide free diagnostic tools.

It says Article 50 of the European Union's AI Act ensures AI systems are developed so users know if they are interacting with an AI system. It says Coalition for Content Provenance and Authority credentials set standards and function as digital labels showing their origin of creation. It says these laws and standards try to keep online content credible and transparent, yet their effectiveness depends on whether companies, platforms and creators follow through. It says these can only be social contracts that lose their meaning if not followed, and that even with penalties in place they are nothing more than retaliatory actions after the consequence that cannot guarantee prevention. The article says one should practice "preemptive skepticism" for every single piece of content encountered, pausing to check where content comes from and what other evidence supports it before deciding whether to trust or dismiss it.

It says one must recognize the liar's dividend of public figures and demand more of their denials. It says skills in actively searching for and verifying the origins of content are a necessary, if not vital, skill for an individual in the post-AI age. It says we are too passive in understanding the changes these technologies bring to our lives, and that not a lot of us get to the nitty-gritty of how they shape behavior and what responsibilities come with using them. It says we often approach new technology as consumers prioritizing convenience, and few of us try to bear the responsibility of deciding what uses are ethical and what limits one should set. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Genpact launches Onyx platform for building and governing enterprise AI agents
stories.Summary:
Genpact announced on November 16, 2026 the availability of Genpact Onyx, an Agentic Operations platform for building, running, and governing AI agents in enterprise operations, and the company had unveiled the platform at its Agentic Operations Day in New York on November 12. The platform is powered by Genpact's Process Intelligence Core, which the company describes as operating knowledge codified from decades of running mission-critical work for global enterprises, so that agents start with context on how the work gets done rather than learning it from scratch. Genpact Onyx is the foundation for Genpact's proprietary agentic solutions, starting with the Genpact Accounts Payable Suite, and for custom solutions Genpact builds for clients. The platform embeds into a client's existing technology stack, connects to the client's data and AI foundations, and supports a choice of leading AI models across Genpact's partner ecosystem.

The platform's capabilities include a Process Intelligence Core codified across finance, risk, supply chain, banking, insurance, and procurement, with prebuilt workflows and agents so clients are ready on day one, drawn from doing the actual work and capturing edge cases, exceptions, and human decisions. A learning loop feeds reviewed exceptions and expert decisions back into the core so intelligence compounds over time, and earned autonomy lets agents start by proposing actions for a human expert to approve and take on more of the decision as they prove themselves. Built-in governance makes every agent action controlled, auditable, and traceable to the reason behind the decision, with guardrails and a responsible AI framework built into the platform, along with security and data isolation that meet enterprise standards. Genpact said the platform was launched at its third annual flagship event, held at Spring Studios in New York, where hundreds of clients, partners, and industry analysts attended a program of announcements, product demonstrations, and client presentations, and leaders from Advantage Solutions, Wesco, USA Today, and Ryan Specialty shared how they are putting Genpact's agentic solutions to work.

Balkrishan "BK" Kalra, President and Chief Executive Officer of Genpact, said the company runs mission-critical operations for many of the world's largest enterprises and that is where the return on AI is decided, adding that Genpact Onyx codifies three decades of process intelligence and makes it the foundation for Agentic Operations, with agents running the work and Genpact's experts owning the outcome. Priya Vijayarajendran, Chief Product and Platform Officer, said enterprises get value from AI when they turn operating knowledge into trusted execution rather than simply by adding more agents, and that Genpact Onyx grounds agents in how the work actually gets done, builds governance into every step, orchestrates across agents and human expertise, and lets autonomy be earned one decision at a time. Genpact describes Agentic Operations as a new operating model in which AI agents handle the volume of execution and its domain experts bring judgment and accountability, combining process intelligence, data and AI, a combined human and agent workforce, a partner ecosystem, and governance and security. Genpact said it uses the platform for its own agentic solutions, for custom client solutions in areas where it does not yet have an agentic solution, and for solutions delivered with technology partners.

stories.Headline: Marc Andreessen predicts AI job losses will be limited in regulated sectors but growth will suffer
stories.Summary:
Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, who co-heads Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's task force on jobs and productivity, said on Monday, November 16, 2026, that artificial intelligence will have a dual effect on the job market. He predicted that job losses in sectors covered by government regulation will be largely insulated from major losses, but that those same regulations will limit economic and productivity growth. You might read that as good news, he said, because a revolution will not destroy all the jobs or kill everybody. You could also view it as very negative, he added, because productivity growth and economic growth simply may not grow very much.

Andreessen divides the economy into two categories of sectors, the first being fast-moving ones that see rapid technological and economic change along with rapid job turnover, such as consumer electronics and media entertainment. The second category is a combination of law and government, which is not structured to change rapidly and is typically characterized by extensive subsidization. He said the fastest-growing sectors will see their prices go down, while the slower-growing regulated or government-subsidized sectors will see their prices go up. Your iPhone is getting cheaper and the flat-screen TV on your wall is getting cheaper, he said, but college education is going to cost a million bucks, healthcare is becoming unaffordable, and good luck buying a house.

Andreessen is responsible for the prediction as co-head of the task force on jobs and productivity under Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, and he set out the two-sector view himself in the remarks reported by Jennifer Schonberger of Yahoo Finance. The article gives no further comment from Warsh or from other members of the task force on the prediction. The report places the remarks against a backdrop of other warnings about AI and work, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's warning of 5% to 10% GDP growth with 10% joblessness, a combination he said is not one we have almost ever seen before. The article does not say what the task force will do next or when it will report.

stories.Headline: Darren Jones calls for a multinational superintelligence safety treaty as a scholar urges UK-led AI assurance culture
stories.Summary:
Darren Jones MP, the former chief secretary to the prime minister under Keir Starmer, recently called for a new multinational treaty governing the safe development and use of superintelligence, where AI substantially surpasses humans across most cognitive tasks, and argued that Britain's growing reputation for AI safety and trustworthiness made it a good conduit for such collaboration. The article's author, a business scholar, concurs with those calls and with a leading role for the UK, and frames the underlying question as a management and organisational one: whether systems of governance can keep pace with AI development while ensuring it is safe. The piece notes that global tech leaders and some of their employees believe there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade, while cautioning that this prediction must be distinguished from current risks and from what might happen as AI systems become able to independently improve themselves and move towards superintelligence. It draws on normal accident theory, associated with the US sociologist Charles Perrow, and high reliability theory, associated with the American political scientist Todd LaPorte, as a framework for thinking about AI safety and regulation.

Normal accident theory holds that in complex, interdependent systems such as nuclear power plants or spacecraft built to carry humans, accidents are not necessarily the consequence of individual incompetence, negligence or bad design, but can emerge from the interaction of multiple components in ways that are difficult to anticipate. Events happen rapidly in such systems, leaving little time to intervene between one potential failure and the next, which can lead to a cascading error with the potential to cause a catastrophe; the article's example is the partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, US, in 1978, which occurred because of a combination of mechanical malfunction, instrument faults and human factors. Risks increase when AI agents, systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions, are added to such a complex system, and an individual component might meet acceptable quality thresholds while the difficulty lies in the interactions between components and our understanding of them. Recent reports have described AI agents behaving in ways their developers did not expect, and the UK government has highlighted risks associated with increasingly capable AI agents and stressed the importance of testing frontier AI models and developing a scientific understanding of their capabilities. If AI systems become more autonomous, more interconnected and faster moving, the conventional idea of a human in the loop to correct major errors could become increasingly challenging.

High reliability theory offers a counterpoint, having emerged from research into organisations operating technologies where failure could have catastrophic consequences, such as nuclear power plants, aircraft carriers and air traffic control, and its central insight is that organisations can develop practices and cultures allowing them to operate extraordinarily complex technologies with very low failure rates, as seen with the electricity system, space travel and bioengineering. These organisations achieve high reliability because their baseline assumption is that they are not safe: they remain attentive to hints of bigger problems, do not automatically dismiss anomalies, learn from near misses and failures and build redundancy, for example backing up offline systems and providing kill switches. They routinely rehearse failure, establish operational processes, adhere to regulation for safety and assurance, comply with professional standards and certification schemes, have independent oversight, give experts the authority to challenge decisions and continuously learn from their performance. The article argues this suggests asking what a high-reliability organisation would look like if AI was embedded throughout it, rather than simply how to regulate AI, and that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off technical test before deployment but must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.

The article says the current political conversation about AI regulation risks being too narrow, because government cannot realistically sit permanently inside every AI company and inspect every model, nor can legislation anticipate every technical configuration AI will take, even though governments need to understand what frontier laboratories are developing. The UK government recognises it must cultivate trustworthiness in AI through assurance, which asks whether there is credible evidence that a system is behaving within defined boundaries, whether those boundaries are appropriate, whether risks are being monitored and whether someone is accountable when they are breached. The aircraft industry has engineering standards, certification regimes, professional qualifications, independent inspection, incident reporting and regulatory oversight, nuclear power operates within an elaborate ecosystem of safety engineering and regulatory assurance, and financial institutions and medicine both have sophisticated systems of assurance, yet AI's assurance infrastructure remains comparatively immature given the speed at which frontier systems are developing. The institutional challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful, and a potential new multinational treaty on the safe and regulated development of superintelligence would frame AI safety as a rapidly evolving global challenge while potentially creating a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the UK to help shape the emerging architecture of AI governance.

stories.Headline: Getty appeals to the Court of Appeal over whether AI models can be infringing copies
stories.Summary:
Getty Images is appealing to the Court of Appeal in its dispute with Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion image generator. The appeal is being heard over two days, Wednesday and Thursday, in the week of 11 November 2026. The High Court gave its first instance judgment in November 2025 and largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on only a small part of its trade mark claim, and its copyright claim failed. Getty's barrister told the court that Stability "doesn't think it should have to pay" for Getty's content.

The central question is whether an AI model can be an "infringing copy" under section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, even if the model never contained copies of the works. Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, so Getty dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial and kept only a secondary infringement case. That case argued that the model was an infringing copy imported into, and distributed in, the UK. The High Court accepted that an intangible AI model can be an "article", but held that an infringing copy must actually be a copy. Because the model weights had never stored Getty's images, the High Court ruled that the model could not be an infringing copy.

Getty says that "making" a model includes training it, which involves copying images, and that the finished model need not itself contain copies. In its view, if making the article in the UK would have infringed copyright, the article is an infringing copy whether or not it holds copies. Getty's barrister said Stability wants to separate what was done with the copyright works from the act of training, but can only do so by mischaracterising the facts. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed. It says Getty's approach would produce odd results, such as making it unlawful to import the model but lawful to copy it once it is in the UK.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited, known as BPI, represents the UK recorded music industry and has permission to intervene in support of Getty. It warns that the High Court's approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back into the UK, with significant consequences for the music and wider creative industries. BPI also notes that Getty accepted at trial that the versions of Stable Diffusion did not contain copies, and cites two recent German cases in which the Munich Court found that models had memorised works they were trained on. On that basis BPI says the Getty judgment has "no wider significance" on whether models contain copies, because the question depends on the facts of each model. Stability AI also argues that extending the law to models trained overseas is a matter for Parliament, not the courts, and it has cross-appealed two findings that went against it.

The High Court case was heard in June 2025, and Getty dropped one of its primary copyright infringement claims just two weeks into the trial. The claims that remained before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith were secondary infringement, trademark infringement and passing off. The court found that Getty succeeded in part on trademark infringement, but only for older models and on isolated examples. Getty had alleged that Stability copied and processed millions of copyrighted images to train Stable Diffusion in the US. Stability's directors include the filmmaker James Cameron, and Stability argues that the images were downloaded and stored in data centres outside the UK, so UK copyright law does not apply.

Stability AI is asking the Court of Appeal to overturn two findings that went against it at first instance: that an intangible model can be an "article", and that Stability itself imported or distributed the model in the UK. Getty disputes both points. If Getty succeeds, developers could face UK copyright claims over models trained abroad on unlicensed works, even where the imported model stores no copies. If Stability succeeds, where a model is trained and whether it stores copies will remain key to any claims. The judgment has not yet been handed down, and the Government continues to consider its approach to copyright and AI following its March 2026 report.

stories.Headline: Leslie Pascual finds 94% of enterprises say AI increases software needing remediation
stories.Summary:
The AI Remediation Bill, a study of 307 security, governance, platform, and engineering leaders at enterprises with 1,000 or more employees in North America and Western Europe, was published on November 16, 2026, in a contributed piece by Leslie Pascual of ActiveState. The study found that 93% of respondents report higher engineering output and 91% release more often. It also found that 94% say AI has increased the amount of software that needs remediation or cleanup, and 97% say their governance workload has gone up. The article was published by The Hacker News on November 16, 2026.

The study reports that 91% of engineering teams spend at least 5% of their time fixing or revisiting AI-assisted work, a conservative floor of 6.7% of engineering time, or about 139 hours per engineer per year. It found that 76% of operations teams had a release delayed by an unmanaged open source dependency in the past year, and 36% had more than one. It reports that 58% of compliance teams received an audit or compliance finding tied to open source governance, and 32% of security teams confirmed a security incident traceable to an unmanaged dependency in the past two years. It found that 83% say the cost of managing open source risk is rising, and only 31% have ever quantified the total. It reports that 92% of organizations have a formal open source policy, and only 52% say it is consistently followed.

Leslie Pascual, Field Engineering Manager for AI and Security Solutions at ActiveState, wrote that she works with security leaders and engineering teams on this every week and that the report matches what she sees at the table. She wrote that each team sees its own line item and handles it locally, and that nobody adds the charges together. She wrote that the gap between policy and practice predates AI, but AI made it expensive. She wrote that software supply chain security is a sourcing problem before it is a scanning problem. She wrote that most of the bill comes from letting packages arrive ungoverned, and an organization can change that decision this quarter.

The study reports that 96% of respondents say AI has increased dependency growth, and half say a new dependency can reach production without any prior review. It found that 64% say most of their governance activity follows an alert, and 63% address open source vulnerabilities only after a scanner finds them. It reports that 55% of respondents named control as a bigger challenge than visibility, which 45% named. It found that 83% say developer productivity is outpacing their governance capability, while 71% believe their current approach will scale. It reports that respondents put 26% of their open source governance effort into prevention today and say it should be 37%, and that among the organizations under the most strain the gap is 19% today with 41% as the goal.

The article states that when developers wrote every import by hand, a loosely followed policy leaked slowly, and that an AI coding assistant can add a package, its dependencies, and their dependencies in seconds. It states that a policy that relies on a person pausing to check was written for a slower pace of development. It states that organizations have spent a decade buying visibility, and control is the piece they still lack. It states that the usual response is more policies, more tools, and more people, added one team at a time. It states that only 31% of organizations have put the costs on one page.

The article recommends putting one number on the bill for a single quarter, naming one owner for intake, governing AI-introduced dependencies first, requiring provenance evidence from suppliers, and making the scanner a second check. It states that SLSA gives security and engineering a shared standard for provenance. It states that each of these steps can begin with a meeting scheduled this week. It states that the full findings, including the cost breakdown by team, are in The AI Remediation Bill. It states that the teams that take the first steps see rework and release delays fall sooner than they expect.

Articles.Title: AI Made Your Developers Faster. Five Other Teams Are Paying the Remediation Bill. - The Hacker News

stories.Headline: Judge denies SpaceXAI request to split from AI antitrust class action
stories.Summary:
A California federal judge denied SpaceXAI's request to separate itself from a proposed class action on November 16, 2026, according to a Law360 report by Aneeta Mathur-Ashton. The suit was brought by artificial intelligence users who accuse the leading AI platforms of violating antitrust law through their collaboration. The order keeps SpaceXAI, which the report identifies as Space Exploration Technologies Corp., inside the case rather than letting it proceed on its own. The judge issued the ruling in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, where the case is pending.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond the November 16, 2026 ruling date and the court. The case information section lists the parties as Anthropic PBC, Google LLC, OpenAI OpCo LLC and Space Exploration Technologies Corp., with the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California named as the court. The law firms listed in the case information are Dechert LLP, Freshfields, Keker Van Nest & Peters and Willenken LLP. The articles do not state the size of the proposed class or any damages figure.

The judge is responsible for the ruling, and the articles do not name the judge or give any statement from the court. The articles also carry no comment from SpaceXAI, from the other companies named or from the plaintiffs' lawyers. The only description of the dispute is that AI users accuse the leading platforms of violating antitrust law through their collaboration. The articles do not say what the plaintiffs want the court to order or how the companies responded to the claims.

The context is a proposed class action in California federal court against several major AI platforms, and the ruling means SpaceXAI stays a party as the case moves forward. The articles do not say what happens next, such as any scheduling order, motion or trial date. The case information lists the law firms and companies involved but gives no further detail on the proceedings. The articles do not say whether SpaceXAI or the other parties plan to appeal or seek any other relief.

stories.Headline: Bill Gross uses AI to generate business ideas to combat wealth inequality and national debt
stories.Summary:
Bill Gross shared his vision for AI entrepreneurship on November 17, 2026. He spoke during day three of the Web Summit 2026 conference. This event took place at the MEO Arena in Lisbon, Portugal. Gross is the Co-founder and Chairman of the tech incubator Idealab. He wants to use AI to help people start companies.

Idealab Studio is based in Pasadena, California, and offers 1.2 million AI-generated business ideas. Gross aims to create 100 million jobs to counter AI job losses. He believes the United States could support 30 million one-person companies. This goal mirrors the current number of one-person companies found in China. These free ideas come from analyzing thousands of news articles about consumer problems.

Gross said that a boom in entrepreneurship could offset the growing national debt. He believes that 30 million small, profitable companies would improve income equality. Gross described AI as a leveling tool that could democratize wealth distribution. He stated that this platform is likely his last company because of its impact. He intends to focus on this project for the rest of his life.

Fed data shows the top 1 percent of households own over 50 percent of the stock market. The top 0.01 percent own over 16 trillion dollars of 64.4 trillion dollars in assets. Census Bureau data shows business starts peaked at over 550,000 a month earlier this year. In October, a little over half a million new businesses were created. More than six in 10 Americans want to run their own companies.

Gross founded Idealab in 1996, which has seen 45 IPOs and acquisitions. He also founded the education software provider known as Knowledge Adventure. He made his personal fortune by building software before launching the AI platform. The platform uses AI to identify niche tech products and local issues like potholes. Users can take the free ideas and shift them for different markets.

Recent site data shows 130,000 visitors, with 28 percent coming from the United States. Other visitors came from Saudi Arabia, India, and Russia, with 80 percent being men. Between 50 and 60 percent of visitors are employed, while 8 to 15 percent are students. Gross hopes that people using the same ideas in different countries will eventually collaborate. The articles do not state when the 100 million job goal will be met.

Articles.Title: Idealab Bill Gross: US entrepreneurs from AI could balance debt and wealth inequality

stories.headline_source: Idealab Bill Gross: US entrepreneurs from AI could balance debt and wealth inequality

stories.Headline: NATO cyber agency gives allies OpenAI models and uses up to 300 billion tokens a month
stories.Summary:
NATO's Communications and Information Agency gives NATO's core institutions access to OpenAI's cybersecurity models so they can help protect Allied networks, and the alliance has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens a month. That access comes through Daybreak, OpenAI's program for vetted defenders doing authorized work such as reviewing code, chasing suspicious activity and testing fixes. The exposure sits in software that European institutions run every day, and ENISA, the EU's cyber agency, used OpenAI models to find four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes out for all four. ENISA and CERT-EU reviewed 27 software projects using several frontier models, OpenAI's among them, along with tools such as the Codex security plug-in, and maintainers assessed 88 potential issues and confirmed 95% of them as real.

Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation uses Daybreak to defend civilian infrastructure, and France's ANSSI and national agencies in Germany and Poland also have access. At NATO's 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, run by the CCDCOE, participants built and tested AI agents for cyber operations in Daybreak, with an emphasis on keeping humans in charge. CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help find six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, the operating system on MikroTik's network gear, and its researchers directed the work and checked findings on real systems. MikroTik released fixes, and CERT Polska confirmed they stop the attacks it had seen.

Dr Dylan Browne, the NCIA general manager, said that as the alliance scales adoption it will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. He said this insight will help NATO optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions. The agency's work therefore ties the technical defense of Allied networks to a closer reading of what the models cost to run and how they compare with rival offerings. The articles do not say what procurement choices or further deployments might follow from that review.

Articles.Title: NATO’s AI cyber defense work hits up to 300 billion OpenAI tokens a month

stories.Headline: Detectify launches Agentic Tooling to help AI agents verify software vulnerabilities in live applications
stories.Summary:
The Swedish application security firm Detectify AB launched its Agentic Tooling on November 16, 2026, to help organizations verify suspected software flaws. This new suite of tools allows artificial intelligence agents to test whether vulnerabilities in running applications can actually be exploited. The launch also includes a Security Ledger designed to record evidence for every test to ensure the results are authentic. These tools are specifically aimed at DevSecOps teams who struggle to trust the reports generated by their AI agents.

The system requires the use of loop engineering to run AI agents in automated workflows triggered by events like continuous integration runs. It integrates with the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface to work with a customer's existing agents in their own environment. The tooling utilizes Alfred, an AI system launched in March 2025, along with attack surface data and payload assessments from ethical hackers. This setup creates a verification factory where agents read code and test live applications from an external perspective.

Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson explained that agents often fabricate proof to please users, making it impossible to know if code is truly secure. He stated that the company intends to build proof that an agent cannot fabricate by using an append-only ledger. This ledger is written by Detectify rather than the agent to separate actual test results from unsupported AI conclusions. Carlsson noted that the tools are available on request and build upon a server announced in May.

The release addresses a critical need because Detectify's H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index found that 90 percent of high-severity vulnerabilities remained exposed for over 90 days. Additionally, research from Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Fudan University showed that 76 percent of static-analysis alerts were false positives. The company is backed by investors including Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy, SquareOne App Ltd, and Insight Partners. Insight Partners took a majority stake in the company in October 2024.

Articles.Title: Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

stories.Headline: Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs as banks expand AI use across operations
stories.Summary:
Banks have been expanding their use of artificial intelligence across operations, customer service and compliance during the third quarter of 2026, while shifting some employees toward higher-value work, according to CNBC. Barclays unveiled layoffs in functions where AI is being deployed, and UniCredit and Santander said technology was freeing employees for more valuable tasks and improving processes. U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are making similar changes in staffing and workflows. The moves came as lenders reported quarterly results that brought their use of AI into sharper focus. Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs, about 5% of its workforce, in 2026, with roughly 60% of the reductions affecting support functions including developer roles, though the bank said AI is not responsible for all the cuts.

Santander said its AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026, and UniCredit reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros. The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI, CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the third-quarter earnings call, and Goldman Sachs said it intends to constrain headcount growth. UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an opportunity to accelerate and a lever the bank did not anticipate it would have, saying on CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Nov. 9 that it was working extremely well. Santander CFO José García Cantera told the same program on Oct. 28 that AI helps decrease low value-added processes so employees can focus on more valuable ones, affecting both revenue and costs, and that it is difficult to say how much comes from AI.

ABN AMRO CEO Marguerite Bérard said on Nov. 11 that AI supports anti-money-laundering checks and makes the bank easier to run and scale while preserving human judgement. KBW's Andrew Stimpson said the cuts are partly but not solely due to AI and have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office. A KBW study published in September found customer service was the most frequently cited use case for AI among European banks, followed by operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime, with just under half of tracked use cases aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. Analysts said wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost revenues rather than only lower costs, with Ninety One's Sophia Whitbread saying the evidence is still strongest for improving service, engagement and employee productivity. Recruiter Mark Astbury of Morgan McKinley said demand is growing for specialists in AI, software engineering and data, and that banks will need to rethink how they develop the next generation of talent as entry-level positions become increasingly technical.

Articles.Title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear

stories.Headline: Minnesota doctors and lawmakers say AI healthcare oversight lags behind the technology
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already shaping care in Minnesota, but doctors and lawmakers say oversight is not keeping pace with how quickly the technology is changing. At Fairview, AI helps predict where ambulances may be needed, gives families real-time updates and creates electronic medical notes from doctor and patient conversations. The health system also uses AI to check the quality of MRIs before patients leave, according to KSTP. Dr. Sameer Badlani, Fairview’s chief digital and AI officer, said the tools let people get picked up sooner and dropped off sooner, with better use of the fleet and crew.

Badlani said AI is definitely evolving faster than regulations are, and Minnesota currently has no blanket law requiring healthcare providers to disclose every time AI is used. Rep. Peggy Scott, a Republican from Andover, said she wants stronger protections for Minnesota patients and has already tried to put guardrails around AI in healthcare. Asked whether there should be disclosure any time AI is being used, Scott said 100%. The Minnesota Medical Association said bias is one of the main concerns with AI in healthcare, and a task force led by Dr. Rebecca Thomas studied the issue for more than a year.

That task force determined there is an urgent need for more oversight of AI in healthcare. Thomas said the question of who would be responsible if artificial intelligence makes a harmful mistake is not straightforward right now. Fairview said patient recordings from the note-taking tool never leave its secure network, have restricted access and are deleted within a few weeks after they are converted into medical records. Fairview said it already notifies patients about AI and plans to add a notice to its online patient portal so patients can opt out of the note-taking tool.

Articles.Title: AI already plays key role in healthcare. It’s also evolving faster than Minnesota laws.

stories.headline_source: AI already plays key role in healthcare. It’s also evolving faster than Minnesota laws.

stories.Headline: Democrats win Congress as voters reject data centers over rising power bills
stories.Summary:
Democrats won both houses of Congress during the midterm elections in November 2026. Many candidates campaigned by criticizing the proliferation of gigantic data centers across the nation. Voters expressed strong opposition to the industry through various local ballot measures. This blue wave was partly driven by public anger over rising power bills. Some Republicans also distanced themselves from pro-AI rhetoric to match their constituents.

Voters rejected data center measures in 40 out of 41 cases across 10 states. A March Gallup poll showed 71 percent of Americans opposed local data centers. Wholesale electricity prices near some centers rose as much as 267 percent in five years. Cornell researchers found operators pay only about 38 percent of linked infrastructure costs. The four largest cloud companies expect to spend 720 billion to 740 billion dollars in 2026.

Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona wants a pause on advanced AI development on day one. Senator Bernie Sanders advocated for democratic oversight instead of an outright ban on the technology. Representative Greg Casar wants AI CEOs to testify under oath during congressional hearings. Senator Ed Markey warned executives about the large number of subpoenas they will face. These leaders seek to address voter complaints about electricity, water, and jobs.

Building trade unions view data centers as a jobs bonanza for their members. Some voters fear that AI will cause job losses or create doomsday scenarios. The general public opposes data centers more than they oppose nuclear power plants. Tech leaders have grown used to a free hand and often chafe at regulation. Many of these leaders now court President Trump as close allies and donors.

The Create AI Act would make a National Science Foundation computing program permanent for researchers. The AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect workers who report risks from AI. The AI LEAD Act would create a federal right to sue over harmful products. Governor Kathy Hochul of New York and Governor Greg Abbott of Texas previously halted permits. Elon Musk reportedly spent almost 500 million dollars supporting Republican candidates in the midterms.

State utility regulators may force data centers to cover the grid upgrades they trigger. Democrats must balance voter demands for relief with the need for economic growth. AI investment currently accounts for 37 percent of United States GDP growth according to ING. It remains unclear if Democrats can demand accountability from executives who support President Trump. The articles leave open whether voluntary corporate pledges will become binding through state law.

Articles.Title: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy

stories.Headline: Lawyers vet the nationality of AI tools to reduce operational risks and gain commercial benefits
stories.Summary:
Hannah Langworth wrote an article on November 17, 2026, regarding the selection of artificial intelligence tools for law firms. The author suggests that legal professionals should carefully consider the nationality of an AI model or platform before choosing one. This strategic approach to selecting technology could provide commercial benefits to the firms that implement it. Furthermore, checking the origin of these tools may help mitigate the significant risks associated with AI transformation.

The process requires lawyers to treat the nationality of their software as a primary consideration during the selection phase. This change in behavior is intended to protect firms from the various dangers that come with integrating generative AI. The article mentions that large language model chat tools from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, China, and the UAE all provide similar basic advice. For example, these diverse tools agree that a lawyer should typically take between 30 and 60 minutes for lunch.

The author argues that being mindful of where a tool comes from is essential for a safe digital transition. By verifying the passports of their AI tools, firms can better manage the legal and operational risks of new technology. The text indicates that this level of scrutiny is necessary to ensure that the AI transformation does not create unforeseen liabilities. This cautious approach allows law firms to leverage innovation while maintaining a high standard of professional security.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Barr warns AI borrowing boom poses ten risks to financial stability
stories.Summary:
Fed Governor Michael Barr gave a long speech on November 16, 2026, regarding AI investment risks. He detailed ten big, complex, and opaque threats to financial stability. These risks stem from a borrowing boom, circular financing, and high equity prices. The Federal Reserve also warned about these stability aspects in its latest Financial Stability Report. This report was released on the Friday preceding the governor's speech.

On-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms may exceed 800 billion dollars by year end 2026. Off-balance-sheet liabilities, including lease commitments and energy contracts, are estimated to exceed 3 trillion dollars. Smaller firms have over 100 billion dollars in circular financing from hyperscalers and GPU producers. These arrangements involve equity investments used to rent or purchase compute from the investors. Some firms also use collateral guarantees for asset-based financings to support their credit.

Governor Barr stated that investment losses could lower output growth through direct drops in investment. He noted that a significant repricing of AI investments could be amplified by complex financing. Barr warned that rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales could occur due to high risk appetite. He mentioned that counterparty exposures could rise during periods of equity market volatility. The governor also cautioned that AI trading models might autonomously develop collusive behavior.

Unsophisticated investors are affected because financial complexity makes it hard to know where risk resides. Lower-credit-quality firms are impacted as their cost of capital has risen significantly in recent months. Hedge funds are mentioned as having high leverage that could lead to rapid deleveraging. Large dealers are involved because they provide leverage via prime brokerage services. The broader economy could suffer if wealth losses lower consumer and business spending.

The current boom is compared to the telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s and early 2000s. This earlier period was characterized by a similar boom and bust cycle of investment. The articles mention dark fiber as an example of excess capacity that took years to become useful. Some theoretical research shows that Q-learning trading algorithms can learn to manipulate markets through spoofing. These algorithms can create and exploit bubbles, which then destabilize the markets.

Specialized chips may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, making current capacity useless. It remains unclear if electrical infrastructure like substations and grid connections will find other uses. The Federal Reserve will continue monitoring exposures to counterparties with large positions in AI. The articles leave open whether smaller firms can replace supplier funding with revenue from customers. It is also unknown if the current debt levels will surpass those of the telecom boom.

stories.Headline: Xero launches Xforce to help accounting firms build AI workflows
stories.Summary:
Xero announced Xforce by Xero, a team of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants who work with accounting firms to design their workflows for the artificial intelligence era, in a media release dated Nov. 11. The team will use XeroForce, Xero's APIs and Xero OS, and it will integrate with other software in a practice's technology stack to automate workflows end-to-end, the company said. Xforce is in beta and is being developed with a handful of design partners in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, including Liston Newton Advisory in Australia, Nexia Christchurch and Shepherd Hensman in New Zealand, and Azets and Sumer in the U.K. XeroForce, announced in May, is a natural language custom AI agent builder for the financial workflows of small businesses and accountants, helping practices turn manual tasks into durable, scalable workflows. Xforce brings the expertise of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants to help accounting firms put XeroForce to work for their practice, their employees and their small business clients, according to Xero. All of Xero's AI innovations, including JAX, its agentic platform, are grounded in what the company calls Accountable Intelligence and sit within the AI-native Xero OS.

More information about Xforce by Xero can be found on the company's website, the article said. The article gave no further dates or figures beyond the Nov. 11 release date and the May announcement of XeroForce. Diya Jolly, president of product and technology at Xero, said that building on positive feedback on XeroForce in beta, Xforce puts experienced experts in the field with firms to help them embed trusted, repeatable and scalable AI workflows. She said those workflows deliver greater consistency and efficiency and give firms time back to reinvest in growing their practice. Jolly said Xero is excited to work with these firms as its first design partners for Xforce, and that together they will explore how AI and automation can make everyday accounting simpler.

She said the shared ambition is to champion clients' success by combining great technology with the personal advice and support that help businesses thrive. Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, chief executive of Xero, said accountants and bookkeepers are being asked to do more with fewer people, and fewer are entering the profession. She said AI can help, but to scale it firms need hands-on support to build it into the way they work. Cassidy said partner consultants provided that support when thousands of firms moved from desktop to cloud, and that Xforce is designed to do the same for AI, with every firm deciding what gets automated on a trusted platform they control. The articles do not say when Xforce will move beyond beta or how firms can join the program.

stories.Headline: Senator Elizabeth Warren urges Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI technology
stories.Summary:
Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts used a post on X this past Sunday to call for new laws. She urged Congress to pass legislation that would restrict the access China has to advanced artificial intelligence technology. The Democratic senator argued that the financial interests of corporate executives could potentially undermine the national security of the United States. She questioned whether the leaders of major technology companies could be trusted to prioritize security over their own profits.

This legislative push comes as House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana notes a growing bipartisan consensus for tighter restrictions on Chinese access to advanced AI chips. President Donald Trump recently urged senators to pass the American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as S. 5653, to lower energy costs. This act would require data centers to pay for their own electricity while speeding up general development. Meanwhile, Microsoft Corp. and various industry groups recently asked the Trump administration to drop a proposed ban on certain Chinese data center technology. These groups warned that such restrictions could disrupt construction and weaken the overall competitiveness of the United States.

Senator Warren stated that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put national security above their bottom line. Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp also emphasized that American technological leadership is critical because China is a formidable competitor. He argued that advanced defense technology is necessary to deter potential adversaries and help prevent future wars. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt warned last month that China could overtake the U.S. because its companies offer cheaper AI products. He noted that China's access to AI model distillation and advanced chips puts the American lead at risk.

The debate has intensified following reports that link former Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing. Because of this turmoil, Chinese AI firms are reportedly seeking Nvidia equipped data centers outside of China to secure computing resources. Scott Bessent has urged the U.S. and China to de-risk their relationship rather than decouple entirely amid these trade tensions. Beijing has warned of red lines regarding its national interests ahead of a meeting between President Trump and President Xi. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI helps pharmacovigilance teams detect safety signals earlier and reduce operational effort by 30-50%
stories.Summary:
A key message at this year’s World Patient Safety Congress was that pharmacovigilance is evolving from a reactive, compliance-driven function to a more predictive and science-led discipline, pharmaphorum reported on 16 November 2026. As therapies for chronic diseases expand globally, safety organisations face an unprecedented volume of evidence from ICSRs, clinical studies, scientific literature, electronic health records and real-world data. The challenge is no longer data collection but timely identification and interpretation of clinically meaningful safety signals within increasingly complex and heterogeneous datasets. Highly trained safety physicians and scientists often spend significant time aggregating and reviewing information rather than on signal evaluation, causality assessment and benefit-risk analysis. Artificial intelligence offers the potential to strengthen pharmacovigilance by accelerating evidence synthesis, supporting earlier signal detection and enhancing risk surveillance.

AI is not a replacement for medical judgement but enables a human-guided, scientifically grounded approach in which technology augments expert evaluation. The expansion of chronic disease therapies makes ongoing safety monitoring more demanding as medicines are used over longer periods by people with varying underlying health conditions and alongside other treatment. Diabetes patients are increasingly treated with combinations of glucose-lowering agents, cardiovascular therapies, obesity medicines and renal-protective treatments. Healthcare is becoming more connected through continuous glucose monitoring, digital health applications, wearable devices and remote patient monitoring. A potential safety concern may involve not only the medicine and an adverse event but patient characteristics, treatment duration, concomitant medications, disease progression, lifestyle factors and real-world treatment patterns.

The traditional process flows sequentially from collection of Individual Case Safety Reports to signal detection, signal validation, scientific assessment and regulatory action. AI is unlikely to replace pharmacovigilance processes but can enhance them as an additional analytical layer identifying weak signals and emerging patterns across multiple sources of evidence. The system ingests millions of data points, allowing AI to autonomously identify unusual patterns, which are escalated for medical safety review, signal validation, scientific assessment and risk-mitigation action. More advanced agentic AI coordinates tasks across connected workflows with clear escalation points for human review, and biopharma companies reduce operational effort by 30-50%, accelerate regulatory reporting, identify safety signals earlier and reduce the risk of inspection findings, product recalls and patient safety events. For larger safety reports, AI can pull together relevant evidence and draft sections while human experts review and sign off the conclusions.

AI does not establish causality, validate safety signals or make regulatory decisions, which remain the responsibility of qualified pharmacovigilance professionals, medical safety physicians, epidemiologists and regulatory authorities. The next opportunity is looking beyond individual reports to evidence in electronic health records, claims data, registries, clinical studies and scientific literature. If an older diabetic patient takes multiple treatments simultaneously, individual reports may not make the connection apparent, but AI-supported analysis across appropriate sources could bring that pattern to specialists’ attention sooner. Initiatives such as the FDA’s Sentinel programme and EMA’s DARWIN EU network demonstrate the importance of broader real-world evidence in safety assessment and highlight why AI is becoming critical. No pharmaceutical company has a complete view of patient experience, so collaboration is required, and underlying illnesses, concomitant medicines and reporting biases still require scientific assessment.

Sanjeev Sachdeva leads advisory and business process services globally for the life sciences unit at Tata Consultancy Services and is a member of the unit’s core leadership team. He drives strategic direction, business and IT advisory, thought leadership, industry collaboration and technology innovation, with more than 30 years of experience in business and technology transformation. He partners with customers across R&D, manufacturing, supply chain and commercial to adopt new technologies, processes and operating models. Sachdeva is a regular contributor to industry and academic forums including the Wharton Mack Institute for Innovation Management, DIA, PHUSE, PHORUM and IIT Delhi. He also speaks at industry roundtables and has authored white papers on AI enabled transformation in drug safety, clinical development, personalised medicine, digital health, quantum computing in life sciences, the future of the lab, blockchain, the metaverse and AI in regulated industries.

Governance by design requires defined responsibilities, quality standards, escalation routes and a traceable record of source information, AI outputs and human decisions that stands up to scrutiny. Validation before deployment is only the beginning, and teams must monitor whether systems continue to perform as intended and intervene when output becomes unreliable. This creates new skills requirements in data quality and AI oversight, and human expertise becomes more valuable as reviewers need the evidence, time and authority to challenge rather than simply approve outputs. As highlighted at the World Patient Safety Congress, AI’s greatest value lies in enabling safety organisations to shift from reactive reporting to predictive risk management, identifying emerging risks earlier so safety teams can intervene sooner and strengthen patient protection. The future is an AI-native safety enterprise where AI handles data-intensive processes and experts focus on critical medical decisions, enabling faster insights, earlier risk mitigation and greater confidence in patient safety.

stories.Headline: ERCOT audits large data centers and files grid reports with Texas regulators by December 10
stories.Summary:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas is auditing large data centers and crypto mines. This process began after Governor Greg Abbott ordered a verification of grid connections. ERCOT must file its reports with the Public Utility Commission by December 10. The commission will then meet on December 17 to review these findings. These events occur as Texas prepares for a change in governor.

The Batch Zero process sorts projects of 75 MW or more into tiers. On September 3, 204 projects totaling 66.4 GW entered the base tier. Another 158 projects totaling 127.9 GW entered the studied tier. Meanwhile, 373 projects totaling 302.2 GW were excluded from the process. This system manages about 474 GW of pending requests for the grid.

Governor Greg Abbott directed the audit to ensure projects pay their own way. He ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to freeze permits on September 21. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office on January 19, 2027, to make future decisions. Hinojosa stated she would keep approvals frozen until the Legislature passes new protections. ERCOT counsel Chad Seely said the study will miss its April deadline.

Developers like Skybox Datacenters and Mesquite H2 filed complaints over their project classifications. Power producers like NRG Energy and Vistra saw shares fall 14 percent after elections. Jefferies analysts believe a legislative compromise is the most plausible outcome for developers. Forward wholesale power prices assume 6 GW of new data centers connect every year. Consumers may benefit if slower arrivals push these power prices down.

The process started in June 2026 through planning guide rule change PGRR 145. Texas holds about 23 percent of planned United States data center capacity. Abbott's August 3 letter noted that data centers make 90 percent of requests. The audit examines water reuse, neighbor effects, and who controls each project. Some requests are likely duplicates or speculative, exceeding record peak demand five times.

The Public Utility Commission may act on the reports during its December meeting. The Texas Legislature convenes in January 2027 to consider repealing industry tax exemptions. New bills may also require PUC permits for all data center projects. It remains open when Batch Zero will restart or if Hinojosa reverses freezes. The articles do not state a new date for the study's completion.
