stories.Headline: ControlUp launches AI Visibility & Usage Insights for IT to track AI tool adoption
stories.Summary:
ControlUp announced AI Visibility & Usage Insights on November 17, 2026, a new capability giving IT a unified view of AI tools adoption, usage, and experience across the organization. The company said IT teams can see how employees use AI applications including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Notion AI, and others. ControlUp described itself as a company reinventing IT operations with its AI platform. The announcement said the capability helps IT get more value from their AI investments. David Marshall published the VMblog article on November 17, 2026, and GlobeNewswire carried the release from San Francisco dated November 17, 2026.

Gartner projects generative AI model spending will grow from $13 billion in 2025 to $139 billion by 2030, citing Forecast: AI Spending, Worldwide, 2025-2030, 3Q26. The capability includes a unified AI application inventory showing Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Codex, and Notion AI, with application type, user counts, and top-used models. It includes adoption and usage insights tracking active employees, total usage, and average usage per user across devices and platforms. It includes AI experience scoring with an average AI score and per-application scores, platform and environment context on browsers, operating systems, and device groups, and comparison of physical PCs with remote desktops including VDI and desktop-as-a-service. It includes PII risk visibility tracking sensitive data such as API keys and banking information, and flexible filtering by app, browser, platform, operating system, or device tag.

Bob Johnson, SVP Global Partnerships & Alliances at ControlUp, said employees are adopting AI tools faster than IT can track, leaving admins unable to answer basic questions about shadow AI, adoption, or spend. He said the capability gives IT a clear picture of AI tool adoption to guide governance, plan training, and optimize AI investments based on real usage, not guesswork. The release said IT teams can drive AI adoption by seeing where licensed users are active and where adoption is lagging. It said they can improve employee experience by spotting underperforming AI applications early. It said they can plan investment with confidence by comparing adoption and performance to decide where to expand, consolidate, or add enablement, and establish usage guardrails with a shared, evidence-based view of the AI tools in use.

The release said AI adoption is accelerating across the enterprise as employees use a growing mix of AI assistants, coding tools, and embedded AI features. It said IT teams are being asked to manage spend and demonstrate value, yet many lack a clear picture of the AI application footprint, including which tools employees use, on which devices, and where more support would help. The release said the capability gives IT a data-backed baseline and a clear view of the AI footprint in their environment. It said Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise usage varies by browser and operating system, and that AI adoption and performance differ by how people work. The release said ControlUp is reinventing IT operations with an AI platform built on real-time data, intelligent decisions, and automated action to help IT teams detect, resolve, and prevent issues before they impact the business.

The release said the platform delivers Autonomous Endpoint Management, unifying Digital Employee Experience capabilities with agentic AI to move organizations beyond reactive troubleshooting toward proactive, intelligent operations at scale. It said ControlUp ONE integrates real-time signals with AI-driven decisioning and automated remediation to reduce operational complexity and consolidate fragmented toolsets. It said IT works smarter, employees stay productive, and disruption becomes the exception, not the rule. stories.Headline: Upstage and Cohere partner to build sovereign AI solutions for enterprises
stories.Summary:
The South Korean artificial intelligence startup Upstage announced a strategic collaboration with the Canadian firm Cohere on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. These two companies signed a partnership agreement on November 16, 2026, at the Seoul office of Upstage to develop sovereign AI solutions. This joint effort aims to help both organizations expand their presence within the global enterprise AI market. They intend to provide specialized services for businesses and institutions that must follow strict regulatory requirements.

The partnership requires the integration of the Solar Pro and Solar Mini large language models from Upstage with the North enterprise AI agent platform from Cohere. Upstage will also include its Document Parse processing platform to enhance the combined technical capabilities of the new solution. These services will be available through cloud-based virtual private clouds or via systems installed locally for maximum security. This approach allows organizations to maintain complete control over their own data while utilizing advanced AI tools.

Upstage CEO Kim Sung-hoon, Cohere co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez, and Cohere Asia-Pacific President Chang Hwa-jin are the leaders responsible for this agreement. While the articles do not provide direct quotes, the executives indicated that the collaboration focuses on security-focused enterprise clients. They expressed a shared goal of providing sovereign AI solutions that prioritize data privacy and institutional security. The leadership team believes this integration will better serve the needs of high-security corporate environments.

The companies plan to move beyond the South Korean market to expand their partnership across the broader Asia-Pacific region. This expansion will focus on delivering enterprise AI solutions that allow various organizations to keep their sensitive data secure. By targeting this region, the firms hope to establish a strong foothold in the growing demand for sovereign AI. They will continue to develop tools that balance high-performance artificial intelligence with strict data sovereignty.

stories.Headline: CloudKeeper reaches Select tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track
stories.Summary:
CloudKeeper announced on November 17, 2026, that it had achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track, according to a press release carried by The Manila Times. The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers, and the Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through four tiers, which are Certified, Select, Preferred and Global Premier. The recognition builds on CloudKeeper's existing relationship with Anthropic and adds to its capabilities in helping businesses implement and manage AI solutions.

Drawing on its expertise in cloud infrastructure, FinOps and AI, CloudKeeper will support organizations building with Claude, including implementing Claude through Amazon Bedrock and addressing their AI infrastructure, governance and cost optimization needs. The company says putting AI into production involves decisions beyond selecting a model, such as how applications connect with existing systems, where workloads run, how usage is governed and how costs are managed. With experience across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, and offerings such as FinOps for AI and Generative AI Launchpad, CloudKeeper helps customers navigate these considerations. The announcement builds on CloudKeeper's earlier appointment as an authorised Anthropic reseller, which lets customers access Claude models through Amazon Bedrock within AWS.

Deepak Mittal, the CEO of CloudKeeper, said the company has spent over 15 years helping businesses make better decisions about their cloud investments, and that AI raises important questions about infrastructure, consumption and long-term costs. He said CloudKeeper wants to help customers get the most out of what they are building with Claude while keeping the economics in view, and called the recognition a meaningful step in that direction. Aman Aggarwal, the COO, said the interesting work begins when a team takes Claude from a promising capability and makes it useful in its own environment, which means connecting it with existing applications, making sound architecture choices and putting the right governance in place. He said the company's engineering and cloud teams work across these challenges and that the recognition supports the work being done with customers.

CloudKeeper describes itself as an outcome-driven AI and cloud cost optimization partner that combines FinOps expertise, proprietary technology and hands-on execution. With over 15 years of cloud cost optimization experience, it says it has helped more than 500 global companies reduce cloud and AI spend by an average of 20% across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Its outcome-based model delivers ongoing savings without upfront costs or long-term commitments, according to the release. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the two relationships strengthening CloudKeeper's ability to support customers with both Claude access and implementation.

stories.Headline: Senator Maria Cantwell accuses the Commerce Department of failing to stop AI chip flows to China
stories.Summary:
Senator Maria Cantwell accused the Commerce Department of failing to stop China from getting advanced AI chips in a November 15 letter. She claimed that Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to take action, which she argued undermined the national security of the United States. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also accused the department of weakening export controls by resisting the blacklisting of a Singaporean company. This company, called Megaspeed, is at the center of a scandal involving the export of Nvidia processors to Chinese customers. The accusations follow reports that the Commerce Department delayed action despite repeated warnings about risks to America's technological AI advantage.

Cantwell urged Lutnick to use the 2018 Export Control Reform Act to strengthen enforcement and prevent restricted technology from reaching barred companies. The dispute involves Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that US authorities suspect helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips subject to export controls. The Trump administration imposed a 25 per cent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, creating a perverse financial incentive. Cantwell cited 1.2 billion dollars in Nvidia stock held by Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm controlled by the sons of Howard Lutnick. These financial conflicts raise questions about whether business interests were put ahead of national security during the export approval process.

Senator Cantwell stated that America cannot maintain AI leadership if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury, Pentagon, State Department, and US Trade Representative's Office favored blacklisting Megaspeed for months. Bessent noted that the Commerce Department, which is in charge of the trade blacklist, had not been in favor of this. A spokesperson for Lutnick, Kristen Eichamer, declined to comment on the letter but confirmed that Lutnick agreed to testify soon. Cantwell alleged that the department suspended a probe into Megaspeed and resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as security threats.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday that a growing consensus in Congress now favors new restrictions on China's AI access. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Senator Jim Banks of Indiana argue that export decisions should face much greater congressional oversight. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is affected by reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive and suspected spy. Megaspeed is affected by the investigation, though the company denies the allegations and says it conducts a legitimate and lawful business. China has also denied the allegations that restricted chips were transferred to its customers through the Singaporean technology firm.

The New York Times reported in October 2025 that US authorities were investigating if Megaspeed helped Chinese customers obtain restricted Nvidia chips. Megaspeed stated on Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has not violated export rules. A November 9 New York Times report alleged that the Commerce Department may have delayed the investigation into the Singaporean company. The controversy involves the diversion of restricted American computing technology to China to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology. These events occur as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January of the coming year.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has summoned Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Senators Warren and Chris Coons wrote to Lutnick, Marco Rubio, and Stephen Miller to preserve all documents regarding Nvidia exports. These officials were given until November 17 to confirm that the preservation directives for communications and documents had been issued. US officials are also scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering. The articles leave open whether Megaspeed actually breached US export rules and how Washington will handle future semiconductor export decisions.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electronics and SK hynix more than double combined cash holdings on AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korean chip giants Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. saw their combined cash holdings more than double over the past year. Corporate filings released on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, revealed this surge was driven by a global artificial intelligence boom. The two companies benefited from strong demand for high bandwidth memory and other advanced memory chips used in AI data centers. This massive increase in liquid assets occurred as the companies capitalized on the growing needs of the AI industry.

Combined cash, cash equivalents, and short-term financial instruments reached 329.23 trillion won, or 246.33 billion US dollars, by the end of September. This total rose from 136.3 trillion won a year earlier and increased by 51.32 trillion won from 277.91 trillion won at the end of June. Samsung Electronics held 214.77 trillion won by September, nearly doubling its previous year record of 108.44 trillion won. SK hynix reported 114.46 trillion won in liquid assets, which more than quadrupled from 27.85 trillion won a year prior.

The companies are responsible for these financial gains through their cumulative operating profits in the first three quarters of this year. Samsung Electronics posted approximately 254 trillion won in operating profits, while SK hynix reported approximately 181 trillion won. These figures were detailed in their respective quarterly reports to explain the sharp rise in their cash reserves. The reports indicate that the financial growth is a direct result of the current AI-driven chip boom.

The broader context involves a global shift toward AI data centers that require specialized memory hardware. This trend has allowed these South Korean firms to accumulate vast amounts of capital in a very short period. The articles do not specify further future plans or next steps for the companies beyond the reporting of these current financial figures. They continue to operate as dominant players in the global semiconductor market during this period of high demand.

stories.Headline: ROBOTERA deploys humanoid robots across China Post network in Guangdong to tackle labor shortages
stories.Summary:
Beijing Xingdongjiyuan Technology Co., Ltd., known as ROBOTERA, deployed humanoid robots across the China Post Group Guangdong Branch network on November 17, 2026. This initiative represents the most geographically extensive use of embodied intelligence robots within the logistics sector to date. The rollout covers 11 postal hubs located in eight different cities across Guangdong Province. These cities include Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Jiangmen, Shantou, Shanwei, Jieyang, and Heyuan.

The project requires the integration of robots into high-volume sorting and cross-regional logistics coordination tasks. These machines utilize a self-developed five-finger dexterous hand for flexible parcel handling and offer multiple power options for continuous operation. Since a pilot began at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026, the robots have processed over 1,500 parcels per hour. This system includes adaptive speed control and irregular-item rejection to prevent collisions, jams, and missed items.

The joint implementation between ROBOTERA and the China Post Group Guangdong Branch aims to solve persistent labor shortages and high workforce turnover. ROBOTERA stated that their robots fill capacity gaps by performing strenuous frontline tasks during peak shopping seasons. This shift allows human employees to move into higher-value roles such as quality control, operations coordination, and robot maintenance. The company uses an AI-native, full-stack technology approach involving foundation models and motion control to build industrial productivity.

Guangdong serves as a critical testing ground because it is the largest province in China by express parcel volume. The company has already expanded its integrated solutions to postal operations in East China to adapt to various sorting-line configurations. ROBOTERA intends to continue collaborating with industry partners and logistics operators to integrate embodied intelligence into more real-world workflows. This ongoing effort seeks to establish a new engine for productivity across the broader logistics industry.

stories.Headline: Tencent releases Hy4 flash to provide cost efficient AI for professional workflows
stories.Summary:
Tencent announced the release of Hy4 flash on November 17, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, to power high speed and cost efficient AI deployment. This new model is the latest addition to the Hy model family and is designed to support everyday professional productivity workflows. The company developed this tool to provide a stronger balance of intelligence and efficiency for real world tasks for its users. It aims to deliver exceptional cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility across various types of professional digital work. The release follows the launch of Hy4, which joined the ranks of leading open source AI models on November 4.

Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters, including 64 billion Engram parameters, with only 12 billion active parameters and 1M token context length. It costs US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens for its users. The model is available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom, QQ, ima, and Marvis, with OpenRouter integration coming very soon. From now until November 30, users can access the model for free on WorkBuddy or get 50 percent off via TokenHub. It uses hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram features, with a KV cache size 1/24 of Hy3 and 1/6 that of Hy4.

The Tencent Hy team made specific engineering choices across the pipeline to achieve this level of cost performance and strong practical utility. They used megakernel, 4-bit quantization, and DFly techniques to reach decoding speeds that exceed 150 tokens per second for low cost deployment. The team built an internal benchmark called WorkIndex based on typical WorkBuddy tasks to focus on deliverable quality and task turnaround time. They stated that reinforcement learning was used to cut the average end to end task output tokens by 50 percent for efficiency. The team recommends Hy4 flash for everyday tasks like deep research, document processing, PowerPoint generation, simple front end displays, and computer use.

Internal WorkBuddy users participated in a blind evaluation of 259 tasks in 27 categories to test the effectiveness of the new model. These 85 users reported satisfaction levels close to Claude Haiku 5.5, while noting the shortest task completion time among all models. The model slightly outperforms Hy4 Preview, which has 770 billion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, in overall effectiveness for users. Per task costs are 1/13 of Hy4 Preview, 1/20 of Hy4, and 1/8 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max tier peak hour pricing for tasks. Users are directed to the more capable Hy4 for complex tasks such as long horizon software engineering to ensure the best results.

Tencent was founded in Shenzhen, China, in 1998 and has been listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong since the year 2004. The company is a world leading internet and technology firm that develops innovative products to improve the quality of life for people. Its communication and social services connect more than one billion people globally to help them stay in touch and access transportation. The business also covers financial technology, including payment, credit, wealth management, and insurance sectors, to support partners and their digital upgrades. Additionally, the company publishes some of the most popular video games and high quality digital content to enrich interactive entertainment experiences globally.

Tencent Hy plans to open source Hy4 flash with frequent iterations to continuously improve its practical utility and efficiency for real world work. The company will continue to push the boundaries of intelligence while delivering exceptional cost performance for its various professional AI tools. Hy4 previously ranked second among Chinese models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and first among open source models on Agent Arena. The articles do not state the specific date when the open source version of Hy4 flash will be released to the public. They also leave open the specific details regarding the upcoming integration with OpenRouter and any future pricing changes after November 30.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a November 2026 public offering using a governance structure to protect its public benefit mission
stories.Summary:
The San Francisco startup Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering on Wall Street during November 2026. This transition to a public company will test the commitment the firm made at its founding to prioritize the benefit of humanity. The company intends to use a governance structure that protects its broader mission against the pressure of financial interests. This approach follows the example of its rival OpenAI, as both are designated as public benefit corporations.

The company has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a public benefit fund, while its founders committed to donating 80% of their wealth. To maintain accountability, Anthropic created a Long-Term Benefit Trust composed of independent trustees with expertise in national security, public policy, AI safety, and social enterprise. This trust holds a single share of Class T common stock with no economic rights, allowing the five trustees to vote as a unit. The trust elects three board directors, while other shareholders, including founders with a 50.1% voting majority, elect another three. A seventh director is nominated by the trust and Class T holders but requires consent from a nominating committee likely controlled by the founders.

The company stated in its regulatory filings that it strives to bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts decisive influence over human undertakings. Sarah Kreps, a professor at Cornell University, noted that the real test occurs if the public benefit becomes costly or conflicts with profits. Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley, explained that the trust cannot determine everyday management decisions and may struggle to remove a majority of directors. Gadinis added that becoming a public company will likely increase transparency because security laws and investors will demand more information.

The company faces potential competitive pressure from open-source Chinese models that may lack the strict guardrails Anthropic currently employs. Experts suggest that measuring a public benefit is much more difficult than measuring profits, especially within the Silicon Valley bubble. Other public benefit corporations include Warby Parker, Lemonade, and Veeva Systems, though none are as large as Anthropic. The firm will now be required to report its finances and be more transparent than it was as a privately held entity.

stories.Headline: Family physician Mara Gordon uses an AI scribe on her phone to draft notes but reviews and signs each one
stories.Summary:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., wrote in a piece published November 17, 2026, that a reader asked whether to worry about an artificial intelligence scribe recording private medical conversations. The reader said her doctor had started recording office visits with an AI scribe and that she said yes when asked if she was comfortable. The reader said that in hindsight she felt a little freaked out. Gordon wrote that AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Gordon wrote that doctors use them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Gordon wrote that she first asks the patient if they are comfortable using the service. Gordon wrote that if the patient says yes, she starts recording using an app on her smartphone, usually set down on the desk in the exam room. Gordon wrote that the scribe uses "automatic speech recognition," which records the conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. Gordon wrote that sometimes, when a family member accompanies the patient, the app needs to distinguish between three or more voices. Gordon wrote that when the visit ends, the recording is transcribed and a large language model geared toward medicine converts the raw transcript into a medical note.

Gordon wrote that the notes follow a standard format specific to the specialty and the type of visit. Gordon wrote that the notes reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making. Gordon wrote that she is ultimately responsible for the content of the AI-generated note and always reads them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them. Gordon wrote that when the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, she almost always ends up editing them to make her clinical decision-making more clear.

Gordon wrote that she talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego who specializes in clinical informatics. Gordon quoted Kim saying that an overburdened doctor seeing too many patients has an AI tool offered that seems like a great solution but no time to adequately review everything. Gordon quoted Kim saying the note goes into the chart and another AI tool reading the notes propagates errors throughout the chart. Gordon wrote that she comes across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time and that it is hard to know how much is related to AI and how much to human error. Gordon wrote that many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients, and that health equity advocates fear this means unequal access that could further widen health disparities.

Gordon wrote that she has been an eager adopter in her own primary care practice. Gordon wrote that she uses an app on her phone that records her conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record. Gordon wrote that it saves her time and helps her focus more fully on her patient, so she can make eye contact rather than stare at the computer screen. Gordon wrote that she shares her patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship. Gordon wrote that she worries corporate health systems will pressure doctors to use time saved with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients, and that artificial intelligence might one day put her out of a job.

Gordon wrote that there are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Gordon wrote that most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, though some use a desktop computer or a separate recording device. Gordon wrote that she uses her personal smartphone, as do many physicians she knows, and that she once got notification pings from her book club's group chat while recording a patient visit, which made her put the phone in "do not disturb" mode. Gordon wrote that conversations are not stored on her device but uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note, and that most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time. Gordon wrote that HIPAA means the program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy, and that the software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step, encrypting it, controlling access, protecting against data breaches, and being liable if data is leaked.

Gordon wrote that she recently saw a patient with metastatic cancer who did not believe he had cancer despite multiple conversations with her, his oncologist, and his surgeon, and that she had even, with his permission, called his spouse. Gordon wrote that the AI scribe did not get this tricky situation right and that the note simply said the patient had been misdiagnosed rather than reflecting the nuances of the conversation. Gordon wrote that she often catches other errors, like mistaking a patient's gender or age, and that the scribes are known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not," where the difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe companies delete recorded conversations within a set period of time as a security feature, to protect patient privacy and protect doctors from lawsuits, and that there is widespread concern the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits. Gordon wrote that some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could assess the quality of AI-generated notes or study physician-patient communication, and that for now recordings of regular appointments, unless a patient is enrolled in a research study, are not used for research.

Gordon wrote that most of her patients readily agree to the AI scribe, but occasionally patients worry the data isn't really secure or could be used to identify them in the future. Gordon wrote that if a patient doesn't want the AI scribe, she just takes notes on the computer while they talk, as she did for years before the scribes became available. Gordon quoted Kim saying AI is "just everywhere" and it would be impossible to separate it, and that software relying on machine learning is used for billing, clinical decision-making, and communication between the doctor's office and patients. Gordon wrote that AI is often used in risk calculators, like tools that estimate a patient's risk of heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure, and in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis based on vital signs and lab values. Gordon quoted Kim saying it is basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you."

Gordon wrote that she asked Kim, a primary care doctor like her, whether AI would replace them in the coming years, and whether an AI scribe that could ask the same questions she does could generate a treatment plan as good or better than the one she recommends. Gordon wrote that Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care, possibly for the better if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer. Gordon wrote that the article ends there, leaving Kim's ultimate answer about replacement unstated. Gordon wrote that readers can send health questions to thrive@npr.org. Gordon wrote that she is happy to have robots help with her administrative tasks but still takes pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence.

stories.Headline: Google Project Zero cuts vulnerability disclosure to 90 days as AI speeds attacks
stories.Summary:
Google's Project Zero team of security researchers announced on 16th November 2026 that it has replaced its long-standing "90 + 30" disclosure policy with a new approach it calls "Full X", under which a vulnerability is made public X days after it is reported to the vendor. As of 13th November, X stands at 90 days, meaning the extra 30 days of soak time that previously let patches reach users before technical details became public has now been removed entirely. The team said the change is needed because large language models now let attackers find vulnerabilities more efficiently and make it more likely that several parties will discover the same flaw independently. Project Zero said it is now finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where it once found only a few a year, which has made the old system of negotiating with vendors increasingly unmanageable.

The policy sets out two further reductions on fixed dates, with X dropping to 60 days on 2nd February 2027 and the policy moving to "Full 30" on 3rd January 2028, when vulnerabilities will be disclosed just 30 days after reporting. The team also said AI has cut the time needed to reverse-engineer a patch and work out which vulnerability it fixes, adding that patch soak time is no longer meaningful when attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins said on X that he understands what Google is trying to do but does not agree with it at all. He said the number of CVEs found in 2026 is double that of 2025, so security fixers face double the workload while getting two thirds of the time to do it, and he warned that at some point the dam is going to break.

Ivan Milenkovic, vice president of risk technology at security vendor Qualys, said vendors will object and some have already warned Google that tight deadlines push them to fix the reported bug ahead of a more severe one, which he called a fair response, though he said the alternative was letting attackers set the deadline. He described the previous 30-day soak time as a comfort blanket that is now being removed, and warned that saying "we patch monthly" now means an organisation is slower than disclosure. He advised organisations to focus on the half-life of vulnerabilities as a key metric, saying boards should stop asking how many critical vulnerabilities they have and instead ask how many days a fixed bug stays unfixed in their estate. The articles do not say what further action Google, vendors or regulators will take beyond the scheduled reductions in 2027 and 2028.

stories.Headline: Utah tests AI that diagnoses acne and prescribes treatment without a doctor visit
stories.Summary:
Utah is running a first-of-its-kind experiment to test whether artificial intelligence can safely deliver health care, including diagnosing patients and prescribing medication without a patient seeing a doctor, according to KUTV. The state's Office of AI Policy is overseeing pilot programs with seven companies testing different applications of AI in health care, and one of those companies is Nolla Health, which operates the Nolla Derm app. That app allows patients to receive an acne diagnosis and prescription without ever seeing a doctor face-to-face, the station reported on November 16, 2026. Patients older than 18 and not pregnant can download the app, pay a subscription fee and upload five pictures of their acne, after which the trained AI system makes a diagnosis and recommends treatment. Dr. Zaid Fadul, chief medical adviser for Nolla Health, said the AI can prescribe only from a list of five to eight approved generic medications commonly used to treat acne, and the app prescribes Nolla Derm creams rather than oral medications.

During the first phase of the pilot, Fadul and a second physician must review and approve every prescription before it goes to a patient, and if the AI performs well in that stage the program can advance to later stages giving the technology more autonomy. Utah's Office of AI Policy said the pilot programs will go through three stages and can operate for a maximum of three years, with independent evaluators selected by the state but paid by the participating companies determining whether the technology is safe and appropriate before it advances. Current laws governing patient safety and privacy apply to all the pilot programs, and Utah law currently allows only humans to practice medicine. Zach Boyd, director of the Utah Office of AI Policy, said Utah does not have enough doctors and other health care professionals to meet growing demand, and the goal is to find out whether AI can take on some routine clinical tasks so physicians can focus on more complex issues such as cancer.

Boyd said he does not believe AI will replace doctors anytime soon and acknowledged that AI will make mistakes, just as human providers do, but he said the technology will have to perform at least as well as a human provider before the state allows it to advance. Fadul said acne medication is relatively low-risk and a good way to test AI prescribing for patients who often struggle to get a timely dermatologist appointment, adding that he wants to increase access to physicians rather than replace them. Michelle McOmber, president of the Utah Medical Association, questioned whether AI should be placed between doctors and patients, saying it is not appropriate to take the physician out of the loop when prescribing medication, though she said AI could help doctors with paperwork and administrative tasks. If the pilot programs are successful, their results could help guide the state in making regulatory changes, according to the report.

Articles.Title: Utah tests if AI can safely diagnose patients, prescribe medication - KUTV

stories.Headline: South Korean law and accounting firms launch AI compliance certification service
stories.Summary:
Three South Korean law and accounting firms launched a new AI compliance-certification service on November 17, 2026. This professional service was developed by D&A LLC, LIN LLC, and Deloitte Anjin LLC to assist companies. These organizations want to help businesses assess and demonstrate their adherence to domestic and international rules. The firms created this tool as companies expand their use of artificial intelligence across various operations. The certification process requires an evaluation of corporate AI management frameworks against several specific regulatory requirements.

It measures these frameworks against the South Korea AI Basic Act, the EU AI Act, and various international standards. The service assigns compliance grades to companies based on how well they meet these legal obligations. These grades are intended to help businesses defend themselves against potential litigation over AI-related harm. The developers of this service believe that public certification can bolster the legal defenses of companies using this technology.

They stated that the tool helps firms demonstrate compliance with newly introduced artificial intelligence rules and existing business regulations. By obtaining these grades, companies can show they have taken necessary steps to manage risks. This approach allows businesses to prepare for future regulatory changes while maintaining their current technological growth. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI offers a free classifier to vetted groups and pauses ChatGPT for 24 hours on flagged abuse attempts
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced a new image classifier on Monday, November 16, 2026, at a press briefing in Washington, DC, according to The Verge’s coverage. The tool detects potential child sexual abuse material, including AI-generated imagery. OpenAI is offering free access to vetted organizations. The announcement has two halves: a detection tool for investigators and platforms, and new friction inside ChatGPT for users who try to find abusive material. OpenAI said it will also give developers guidance on detecting this type of content and train law-enforcement personnel on using AI in investigations.

OpenAI said the classifier can tell AI-generated abusive imagery apart from authentic imagery involving children. Access is free for vetted organizations, and OpenAI has not said how many groups are receiving access. OpenAI said new ChatGPT warnings will interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and direct users toward specialist help. When the warning triggers, OpenAI said it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. OpenAI said it reports all identified CSAM on its platforms to NCMEC.

OpenAI attributed the wording in coverage to the company as a whole, and the coverage includes no direct quote from an individually named OpenAI representative. OpenAI frames the tool around efficiency, saying a classifier that ranks and flags files can shrink investigators’ exposure and speed the path to cases where a living child needs help. OpenAI says its Stop It Now helpline regularly hears from people who report that an AI chatbot sent them there, though OpenAI has not published a count of those contacts. OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. The public coverage does not establish the classifier’s official product name, a release price beyond the free tier for vetted groups, technical accuracy, model specifications, training-data details, or how many organizations are receiving access.

The Internet Watch Foundation, a UK hotline, reported 3,440 AI-generated CSAM videos in 2025, up from 13 in 2024. IWF classified 65% of those videos, or 2,233, as Category A, the most severe tier under UK law, and 30%, or 1,027 videos, as Category B. Childlight data reported on November 16, 2026 put referrals of AI-generated material to the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children at about 4,700 in 2023 and more than 400,000 in 2025, an implied two-year change of about 8,400%. Google and Microsoft have long offered hash-matching, content classifiers, and reporting or moderation tools, Meta uses automated detection, hash databases, human review, and NCMEC reporting, and Thorn’s Safer platform gives trust-and-safety teams tools to detect, review, and report CSAM. Small nonprofits and under-resourced police units stand to gain the most from free access, but only if the vetting process is quick enough for them to use.

For most of the past two decades, the fight against online child abuse imagery rested on a shared database model in which platforms hashed known files and compared uploads against them. A hash catches a file someone already identified but fails on a freshly generated image that no one has seen. A classifier can flag new material, which is why synthetic abuse pushes the industry toward models. Classifiers produce false positives and false negatives, and hashes mostly do not. OpenAI’s distinct move is the bundle, pairing a free classifier for vetted groups with developer guidance, police training, and user-facing warnings inside its own product.

The public coverage does not explain how removal of a flagged conversation interacts with preservation for investigators. Whether the tool reliably separates synthetic from authentic imagery is the open question, because OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. Readers should expect child-safety groups to ask for a model card, an audit path, or both, and the sources reviewed for this story contain no evidence that either is public. How often each layer of OpenAI’s stack fires is not public. More to follow.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Offers Free CSAM Tool, Adds 24-Hour ChatGPT Pause - shattered.io

stories.Headline: Mullin says an expert blames AI for recent system outages while Duffy calls the situation a head-scratcher
stories.Summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he spoke with an unnamed technology expert who blamed artificial intelligence for the series of system outages over the past few days, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the situation a head-scratcher. Several cyber mishaps have occurred since last week, including issues with Microsoft systems, a nationwide ground stop due to a telecommunications error, several major online banks and banking services experiencing system failures, and an issue with United Airlines's system. The scenarios happening in tandem have caused concern that America's technological infrastructure is at risk. Mullin told Fox News that he spoke with a technology expert, whom he clarified was not SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who suspected AI could be attempting to fix problems when added to older systems.

Mullin said the expert told him these programs are not designed to work as fast as AI, so when a program able to write code goes in, it self-fixes, and as it starts self-fixing itself it is like doing a change order on a house, where changing one thing starts everything else changing. He described that ripple effect as causing systems to be overrun that were not designed to run as fast as AI technology is today. Mullin again clarified there is no evidence that the outages affecting aviation, banking, and Microsoft are the result of a cyberattack. He said he could tell with 98% certainty that this is not a cyberattack, noting that no one is out there taking claims for it and that they are not seeing the traffic or the footprints going in and out, so nothing points to it being connected other than what the cyber guy briefed him on about three hours earlier.

Duffy also recognized the apparent pattern of technology failures but mainly discussed the issues facing aviation, saying he was just learning about the issues facing United Airlines while pointing out the banking and Microsoft incidents occurring in the same time span. He said the United problem is not an FAA systemwide problem but that it is a head-scratcher, and that as of right now he does not know the root cause of United. Duffy said he asked the FBI to come in just to make sure to put people at ease that this was not a hack, and he said he thinks it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error. The Department of Transportation has said the flight stoppage Friday evening was due to a disruption caused by an L3Harris contractor upgrading a telecommunications line from copper wire to a fiber-optic cable, and that as the contractor installed the new router, the new technology is claimed to have overloaded the air traffic control system, leading to the ground stop.

Articles.Title: Mullin says expert blamed AI for tech outages as Duffy calls situation ‘head-scratcher’ - Washington Examiner

stories.Headline: LVMH media division and OpenAI sign strategic AI agreement to deploy ChatGPT Enterprise across 17 brands
stories.Summary:
LVMH Group's Media Division and OpenAI announced on 16 November 2026 in Paris that they signed a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division's publications and to make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement covers deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, which will let them build AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work. The two sides said their shared ambition is to let teams experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting. The partnership also enhances the presence of the division's content in ChatGPT, which will provide summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identify sources and include direct links to the original articles. The division, known as Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands including Les Echos, Le Parisien, Challenges, Paris Match, L'Opinion, Investir, L'Agefi, Historia, Capital Finance, Connaissance des Arts, Radio Classique, Mezzo and medici.tv.

It has 1,800 employees, nearly 700 of them journalists, and reaches more than 27 million people in France every month. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation, with the stated goal of giving them more time for investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field. The partnership is described as a company-wide initiative that will extend across all the division's publications, with training tailored to each person's use cases to support the rollout. Michèle Benbunan, CEO of LVMH Group's Media Division, said the agreement will position the publications at the forefront of the media industry and that integrating AI will become an everyday asset for all its teams, adding that the division is delighted to work with a partner whose expertise and reputation are recognised worldwide. Emmanuel Marill, Managing Director for EMEA at OpenAI, said quality journalism depends on the people who investigate, verify facts and help audiences make sense of information, and that OpenAI wants to help put AI to work for everyone across the division while respecting editorial independence.

He said the aim is to help teams spend more time on what makes their journalism valuable, and that the partnership will give ChatGPT users access to high-quality journalism that keeps pace with the news. The announcement frames the deal around two pressures on the division's business: newsrooms gaining time for investigation and analysis, and personalisation, which the announcement calls a major priority in an increasingly crowded information landscape. It says AI is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications. The announcement also says the partnership will support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation by streamlining operations, improving efficiency and encouraging innovation and creativity. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the rollout and the training.

stories.Headline: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 16, 2026 that it was sharing new results measuring model performance, safety and cost in clinical and administrative workflows, and that it was working with Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare and CVS Health. The company said computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing and moving between applications. OpenAI said healthcare teams, developers and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians. OpenAI said it built a demo using synthetic patient data in which a patient messages a clinician about lower back pain. OpenAI said the agent reviews visit notes, physical therapy records and prior imaging in the EHR, drafts an MRI order, an encounter note and a reply, then prepares a prior authorization request in the insurer's portal.

OpenAI said it evaluated GPT-6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes, shaped by physician input. OpenAI said 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe, and physicians selected "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments on a five-point scale. OpenAI said GPT-6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points on HealthAdminBench, an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers, while GPT-6 Luna earned 91.8% despite costing 98% less at 8.5 cents per task. OpenAI said both models were evaluated at maximum reasoning effort. OpenAI said organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs, and that organization data is not used to train OpenAI foundation models.

Lagan Khare, Executive Director of Engineering at CVS Health, said less time on administrative work means more time for care and that this is a win for teams and everyone served. Madhu Nutakki, CIO of Cigna Healthcare, said moving from concept to deployment in under eight weeks shows what is possible when AI, care management expertise and the right guardrails come together. Nutakki said it means getting better, more complete insights to case managers sooner so they can focus on supporting patients with personalized, compassionate care. OpenAI said CVS Health uses validation checks and human oversight, with screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. OpenAI said data remains within CVS Health enterprise-controlled infrastructure, governed by their enterprise AI Governance team and established responsible AI policies, and that production data is not used to train foundation models.

OpenAI said CVS Health is using computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals and supporting specialist consults. OpenAI said one production workflow cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend, and another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day. OpenAI said CVS Health is open sourcing its Agent Kit, built with OpenAI's Agents SDK. OpenAI said Abridge is developing computer-use agents for care plans across applications, including those without APIs, and that its planned inpatient use case builds on the clinical conversation. OpenAI said Cigna Healthcare case managers previously had to navigate more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather context, and computer use can now bring relevant information together in seconds.

OpenAI said healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. OpenAI said when a clinician recommends an MRI, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient's medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request. OpenAI said its partners build software used in hundreds of health systems, coordinate care for members globally, and deliver care to hundreds of millions of patients. OpenAI said Ambience built additional controls, and that in a demonstration the agent stops and asks the clinician when the record is ambiguous, then waits for approval before submitting. OpenAI said health systems set which actions the agent can take, can pause it at any point, and get a step-by-step log for audit.

OpenAI said healthcare organizations can contact its sales team, and existing customers can ask their workspace administrator to enable computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI said U.S. clinicians can sign up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account today and experience computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI said developers can build healthcare applications with the OpenAI API and explore its computer use guide. OpenAI said organizations must use eligible services covered by their Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI and the required security and retention settings to support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information. OpenAI said it hopes these advances enable healthcare teams to spend less time moving information through systems and more time caring for patients.

Articles.Title: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams

stories.Headline: OpenAI gives £1m to The King’s Trust to help 25,000 young people build AI skills
stories.Summary:
The King’s Trust announced a major partnership with OpenAI on 16 November 2026, and OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support the work. The partnership is designed to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training. The program aims to support those young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy. The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The partnership forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The King’s Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market. The program will combine opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience, and The Trust is working with employers, AI specialists and young people on the skills needed. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026 found that 68% of 16, 24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects. The Trust says it has supported more than 1.3 million young people over 50 years and wants the next generation to gain the skills and confidence to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Jonathan Townsend, UK Chief Executive of The King’s Trust, said AI could create enormous opportunities for young people if they have the chance to develop the skills and confidence to use it. He said the partnership would help thousands of young people build practical AI skills, gain recognized qualifications and prepare for a rapidly changing world of work, and he thanked OpenAI for its support. Tom Duff Gordon, VP and Head EMEA Policy at OpenAI, said young people who are out of education or work deserve a real foothold in the AI economy. He said OpenAI is committing £1 million and its AI expertise to help reach up to 25,000 young people with practical skills, recognized learning and support toward education and employment.

The Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, reflecting on a shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn. He said young people deserve to be equipped for a changing world of work, and that AI will bring disruption as well as opportunity. He said it is vital that young people get a fair share of the opportunity and do not bear the cost of the disruption. For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment that builds on wider efforts including OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

Articles.Title: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership

stories.Headline: Holiday Extras executives use personal AI dots to surface data and flag issues
stories.Summary:
Holiday Extras, a UK travel technology company that helps travelers book airport parking, hotels, lounges and transfers, published an OpenAI customer story on November 16, 2026 describing how two of its executives use personal AI assistants called dots. Liam Thompson, the company's VP of AI Innovation, named his dot Beast, and the day after Holiday Extras launched a new feature in its app, Beast noticed the launch without being asked, pulled data from Google BigQuery through a ChatGPT plugin and brought him the results. David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, named his dot Brian and calls him on his morning commute to talk through the meetings ahead and to request reports built from connected company data. When some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the issue, went back through David's email and surfaced a list of people who might be affected. Liam said he talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings and spends at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with him, and Beast reminds him about replies he has not sent and finds answers from past conversations.

Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but said he was not comfortable giving them much information, while with anything OpenAI in the company environment he knows he can trust it, and he gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive and laptop. Liam, who trained as a designer, also gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop to animate 3D characters for an app, work he says would have taken him several days and that Beast did in about ten minutes. Holiday Extras gives employees ChatGPT Enterprise as a foundation for using AI and Codex to turn expertise into working software, with dots simplifying the work in between. David said that by the time he gets into the office and sits at his desk, the report is there and ready to go, and that what he likes most about Brian is that he is thinking about things David has not even thought about. Liam said it relaxes him having Beast there because if he misses something, Beast has probably already covered it and is keeping an eye on all the things going on.

Liam's advice for anyone getting started is simply to create a dot and start a conversation, adding that there is no excuse not to get started and to just go. For Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work, and David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they are learning so others can see what is possible and try it for themselves. The company says the next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something or making everyday life a little easier. That builds on the ambition behind the company's work with OpenAI, giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

Articles.Title: At Holiday Extras, dots get to work before anyone asks

stories.Headline: Kingston building official Steve Knox proposes AI plan review software as council members raise privacy concerns
stories.Summary:
Kingston’s Building Department has proposed using an artificial intelligence-based application for plan reviews as soon as early next year, and several Common Council members raised privacy concerns when Director of Building Safety and Zoning Enforcement Steve Knox presented the idea to the Finance and Audit Committee. Knox proposed spending an additional $54,700 in startup costs for the software, which would be integrated with the department’s existing City Squared system used for online application reviews. The software is a yearly subscription, and Knox said the city would incur further annual costs to keep using it. He estimated the software could produce reports that now take three to four days in hours, and he told lawmakers he hopes to implement it as soon as early next year. The committee reviewed the request as part of the Building Department’s $2,046,724 request under Mayor Steve Noble’s proposed $69.4 million budget plan.

Lawmakers questioned Knox about data collection, privacy and potential errors by AI, and the promises of faster reviews did little to sway them. Michael Tierney, D-Ward 2, said he is cautious about the city outsourcing public data to companies and wants to know more about the firm’s data collection and retention policies. Common Council President Andrea Shaut said she is no fan of AI personally or professionally, questioned how data and privacy are handled and questioned the accuracy of AI, saying it gets things wrong, though she said she could see some value if there are reassurances about privacy. Teryl Mickens, D-Ward 5, said the application sounds like an amazing tool but raised concerns about how personal data is used and asked whether it would reduce the number of department personnel involved in permit review. Knox said most of the review process is done by three people in the department.

Bob Dennison, D-Ward 6, said that aside from concerns about who owns the data he thinks the software is a great idea, and that an automated turnaround for a building review would save time and complaints that reviews take too long. Knox assured lawmakers the software will still have a human component, with reports subject to review by staff, and said he does not expect it to result in staff reductions. He said the department eliminated a proposed code enforcement director position from its 2027 budget and that the software would help alleviate the need for the position, with some accusatory work on code violations shifted to the Corporation Counsel’s office. Sara Pasti, D-Ward 1, asked whether the software had been tested, and Knox said it had not been tested but that the department looked at a number of companies and systems before deciding this was the best fit. Lawmakers also asked whether the department had reached out to similar municipalities that have used the system, and Knox said, “We certainly can reach out to them and ask.”

Marissa Marvelli, a historic preservation professional, asked what effort the department is making to fully digitize the permit application process, saying even the online process still requires some handwritten forms and is stuck in early aughts. She said contractors have told her their online applications sit in an under review state for a long time with no indication whether more steps are needed, and Knox said the department hopes to move to a fully digital system by July 2027 and that the AI system could help avoid applicants getting stuck by sending emails asking for documentation and answering general questions. Knox said the department has reviewed around 600 units over the past four years and expects that number to increase. At the end of the presentation, Tierney questioned why the department waited until budget season to come before the committee at a special meeting instead of a regular committee meeting. The use of AI by area governments has drawn controversy, and on Thursday, Oct. 22, the Ulster County Sheriff’s Office announced it would not move ahead with AI-assisted report writing after a trial period and axed plans to add Motorola automatic license plate reading cameras, a decision that came as County Executive Jen Metzger signed an executive order banning AI surveillance technologies within her own administration, an order the sheriff supported.

Articles.Title: Proposed use of AI software concerns Kingston Common Council - Daily Freeman

stories.Headline: Vincee Cole compares ten AI training data vendors and names Surge AI the top pick for expert data
stories.Summary:
Vincee Cole published an overview of ten AI training data vendors on November 16, 2026. The report compares these companies based on their services, public pricing, and long-term outlook. Surge AI is named the top pick for expert human data and evaluations. Labelbox is highlighted as the best choice for enterprises wanting software and managed labeling. Mercor raised 750 million dollars at a 20 billion dollar valuation on November 10.

The list includes Surge AI, Scale AI, Mercor, micro1, Snorkel AI, and Invisible Technologies. Labelbox offers a free tier and services from about 8 dollars per hour. Prolific charges a 42.8 percent fee plus participant pay of at least 8 dollars hourly. Bright Data sells web datasets starting from 250 dollars per 100,000 records. Other vendors like iMerit and Scale AI do not publish their real price points.

Surge AI claims OpenAI and Anthropic cited its benchmarks in 2026 model releases. The company says Microsoft used its human evaluations for the MAI-Thinking-1 model. Scale AI told Forbes its revenue reached 870 million dollars in 2024. Mercor states its network now includes more than five million recruited professional experts. Scale AI reports working with 90 percent of leading generative AI model builders.

Frontier labs, government agencies, and enterprises are the primary buyers for these data services. Researchers and AI product teams use Prolific for online studies with vetted participants. Healthcare and automotive companies utilize iMerit for compliant medical and LiDAR labeling. Teams training models on web data use Bright Data for scraping tools. Only three of the ten compared vendors publish real price points for buyers.

Demand has shifted from simple image labeling to paid experts like doctors and engineers. Reuters reported that Surge AI made more than 1 billion dollars in 2024 revenue. Meta bought a 49 percent non-voting stake in Scale AI for 14.3 billion dollars. TechCrunch reported in July 2026 that Mercor had a run rate of 2 billion dollars. Scale AI named Francis deSouza as its chief executive officer in July 2026.

Expert data and agent training are expected to stay in demand through 2028. Simple labeling tasks are predicted to become automated over the coming few years. The report suggests buyers budget for a paid pilot before signing any contract. Some companies may transition into defense and enterprise AI contractors rather than neutral labs. The long-term potential for benchmarks to become a second business remains an open possibility.

stories.Headline: Apollo embeds six evaluators inside OpenAI for four months to test whether training incentivizes subversion
stories.Summary:
Apollo Research announced on November 16, 2026 that six of its evaluators will work inside OpenAI for four months to investigate whether its models attempt to subvert alignment or control mechanisms during training, evaluations and internal deployment. The team will examine four questions, namely whether training incentivizes subversion, whether evaluations can elicit it, whether subversion occurs during internal deployment and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. The scope covers attempts to undermine a model's own alignment or controls as well as those of its successors, and the arrangement is meant to move external scrutiny beyond Apollo's earlier approach of evaluating after post-training and shortly before public release. Apollo considers that timing insufficient for testing misaligned behavior such as scheming or for examining non-public uses during internal deployment, and it describes the pilot as an ambitious first step rather than a full embedded evaluation. For the training-incentives assessment, OpenAI committed to provide relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints, while detailed access arrangements for the other assessment claims remain to be agreed.

The assessment is confined to agreed claims, models and time periods, and OpenAI may withhold in-scope items when it deems that reasonably necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks or intellectual-property protection, but it may not withhold information or staff access simply because the material is unfavorable. OpenAI must tell Apollo that withheld items exist and give written reasons, and where it considers this feasible and relevant it must identify withheld records by category and approximate volume, while Apollo can request broader access through a designated contact and escalate refusals without any guarantee of expansion. The evaluators will work on OpenAI hardware using separate channels that can be monitored, they will by default lack access to general staff channels such as Slack, and formal conversations must be logged, with Apollo required to stop substantive discussion and route follow-up through its contact if another employee raises confidential information. Apollo plans two public reports, the first on training incentives for subversion and the second on evaluations, internal deployment and the detectability of subversive reasoning, each describing methods, conclusions, limitations, questions that could not be assessed and supporting evidence that can be published. OpenAI will review the reports and may request redactions of confidential information including evidence supporting findings, but it may not redact Apollo's verdicts or request redactions merely because a finding is unfavorable, and it can redact evidence it considers sensitive intellectual property whether or not that evidence directly contributes to a finding.

OpenAI will share the unredacted reports with its board's Safety and Security Committee, and claims based on employee discussions require OpenAI's formal attestation unless Apollo establishes them independently, with Apollo allowed to disclose a declined attestation and explain its effect without revealing the underlying confidential information. Separate meta-transparency rights let Apollo describe publicly the engagement's scope and conditions, the access requested and received, material withheld or delayed and the reasons given, requested report removals and their significance, and any pressure it believed shaped its work, all without prior OpenAI review. Apollo regards those meta-transparency rights as a minimum standard for every evaluation engagement, arguing that undisclosed restrictions can make absent problems look reassuring even when the absence reflects limits on investigation or disclosure. The pilot's conclusions will therefore need to be read alongside its account of access and publication limits, since the same verdict can carry different weight depending on what the evaluators were able to inspect and disclose.

stories.Headline: LangChain raises $300M Series C at a $3B valuation to fund its LangSmith agent management software
stories.Summary:
LangChain, an AI agent management startup, raised $300 million in a Series C funding round led by CapitalG, the company announced on Friday, November 13, 2026, according to TechGig. The round included participation from Singapore's GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP and Sapphire Ventures, and it values the company at $3 billion. That figure is more than double the $1.25 billion valuation LangChain held a year earlier, when it raised $125 million. LangChain began in 2022 as an open-source project that addressed tasks early large language models found difficult, such as web searching and API calls, and it later shifted its focus to managing AI agents. The funding supports LangSmith, the company's agent management software, which is designed to be model, cloud and ecosystem agnostic so that businesses keep ownership of their intelligence.

LangChain reports 7,000 LangSmith customers, including startups Harvey, Rippling and Clay as well as enterprises Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce. In a separate deal reported by Axios, Operand, which uses AI to do due diligence for private equity firms, raised $31 million across a seed round and a Series A led by Khosla Ventures at a $220 million valuation. Operand CEO Ram Gorthi told Axios Pro exclusively that the company focuses on non-traditional data sources to help firms get an edge and on AI to process a higher volume of data. Mirendil, an AI lab founded by former Anthropic researchers, announced a $1 billion Series A led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital on Thursday, November 12, 2026, but its release names no valuation, according to TechTimes.

The training bill the company cites, less than $10 million in compute, covers only its smallest model, and the company says agents wrote over 99% of the code for that model. The round arrives 141 days after Mirendil's $200 million seed at a $1 billion valuation, and no independent evaluation of any Mirendil model has been published. Bloomberg reported in September that the company was in talks to raise up to $1 billion at a $5 billion valuation, with Kleiner Perkins leading and Andreessen Horowitz in discussions to participate, but no source reviewed confirms the final terms match that report. For context, TechTimes notes that typical 2024 U.S. medians were about $3.1 million for a seed round and $12.4 million for a Series A. The articles do not say what happens next for LangChain, Operand or Mirendil beyond the funding announcements themselves.

stories.Headline: MinoHealth AI Labs warns of bioweapons threat after model designs thousands of toxins
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MinoHealth AI Labs in Accra, Ghana, removed guardrails from their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked the system to design toxins instead of medicines. The team uploaded their findings to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025. This experiment exposed the threat of AI designed bioweapons. The lab founder then issued warnings about the dual use of such technology.

The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. Software scored all of these as likely toxic, with some resembling deadly ricin. The lab used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery. Moremi Bio was developed by a 20 member team in a modest bungalow. The project received 149,533 dollars from the Gates Foundation in 2023.

Founder Darlington Akogo said he and his team were all shocked by the results. He warned that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat to the world. Akogo questioned if DNA synthesis companies would stop someone from making these designs. He believes the United Nations should create a working group to study AI risks. He also suggested that the world needs tighter controls over synthesis.

Brenda Obuya of Kenya's Ministry of Information says the need for regulation is echoing through government. Adam Abdullahi says this shows African institutions are contributing to AI governance. Ken McCallum of MI5 stated that bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk. Ayantola Alayande noted that lay users could now generate this output via chatbots. Peter Garraghan said his team broke the Kimi model in one day.

MinoHealth Labs was founded in 2016 to solve Ghana's health worker shortage. In 2022, a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment with chemical weapons. Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences in October 2025, and OpenAI launched GPT Rosalind in April. AI drug discovery investment grew from 4.1 billion dollars in 2023 to 8.4 billion in 2025. Some labs screen orders, but Akogo says AI could hack this process.

The International Gene Synthesis Consortium is working with developers to detect AI designed sequences. Heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind called for mandatory checks in the U.S. in June. Moremi Bio is now proposing drug candidates for cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is developing diagnostics for malaria and mpox through a European Union consortium. The articles leave open if governments will mandate these screening laws.
