stories.Headline: Tiny Corp opens second tinybox red preorder at $89,000 after first batch sells out
stories.Summary:
Tiny Corp began taking preorders on November 5, 2026 for a desktop machine called the tinybox red that holds four of AMD's Instinct MI300X data center accelerators, and the first batch of 25 units at $60,000 sold out within three days. The cards inside are refurbished, they come without warranties, they are capped at 500W each, and they are linked only over PCIe 5.0. A breakdown posted by the AI Quanting account on X noted that the store page already showed the machine as out of stock a few days after the listing went live. Tiny Corp has now opened preorders for a second batch of 50 units at $89,000, which is about 48% above the launch price and roughly $29,000 more per box.

On paper the machine offers 768GB of GPU memory, 21.2TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth and 10.44 PFLOPS of FP8 compute, which are exactly four times AMD's own per-card figures of 192GB of HBM3, 5.3 TB/s and 2.61 PFLOPS of dense FP8. The listing quotes the dense number rather than the 5.22 PFLOPS AMD lists with structured sparsity, so the published specification is the more conservative one. The host is a 32-core water-cooled AMD EPYC Genoa platform with 192GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB boot drive, four 1TB drives in RAID 0, two 10GbE ports and an OCP 3.0 slot. Two standard 1,700W ATX power supplies feed the 54V the GPUs need through a converter, so the box runs on one 220V circuit or two 110V circuits, and Tiny Corp claims it stays under 50dB.

Tiny Corp is the company behind the machine and it is the party taking the preorders, while the account AI Quanting on X is credited with spotting that the first batch had sold out. Tiny Corp says the second batch will be delivered in Q1 or Q2 2027, though it stops just short of committing to either date as a firm timeline. The company also claims the box stays under 50dB, which would make it far quieter than the rack servers MI300X cards normally live in. The cards themselves are refurbished and come without warranties, which is part of how four data center accelerators fit into a desktop box.

The context is that MI300X cards normally live in rack servers, and Tiny Corp has squeezed four of them into a box that runs off ordinary wall power. The first batch sold out within three days at $60,000, and the second costs nearly 50% more than the former. The second batch of 50 units is now on preorder at $89,000 with delivery penciled in for Q1 or Q2 2027. Beyond that shipping window, the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Preferred Networks taps Samsung Foundry and Semifive to build 3D-IC AI inference chip
stories.Summary:
Japanese AI company Preferred Networks has chosen Samsung Foundry to manufacture the logic chips for its next-generation AI inference semiconductor, the MN-Core L2000, with South Korea's Semifive acting as turnkey partner. The two companies disclosed the collaboration on the 17th at SC26, the supercomputing trade show held in Chicago. Tokyo-based PFN is responsible for the processor architecture and logic design, while Semifive handles design implementation, memory supply, packaging, testing and mass production. The chip uses a 3D-IC structure that stacks the compute chip and DRAM vertically, which the companies describe as the first commercial application of such a design. Tape-out, the handoff of the completed design to manufacturing, is targeted for the first quarter of 2027, and the L2000 series is the successor to the MN-Core L1000, which is scheduled for launch in 2027.

According to PFN, the new chip targets more than double the memory bandwidth of the L1000 by creating hundreds of thousands of data pathways between the compute chip and the DRAM. Because the memory is attached vertically, components such as the interposer needed to connect chips side by side are eliminated, and the company expects manufacturing costs to fall as well. Vertically stacking chips still poses challenges, since heat dissipation is difficult and securing manufacturing yields is tricky, and industry observers expect considerable process tuning before 3D-IC reaches a stable mass-production stage. Cho Myung-hyun, CEO of Semifive, said 3D-IC is a next-generation solution that can overcome the supply constraints of HBM, and that starting with the collaboration with Japan's PFN the company will lead commercialization of next-generation AI semiconductors. He has previously described the technology as offering wider bandwidth and lower power consumption than bundling eight HBM4 chips.

The collaboration is a case of the foundry-to-design-IP alliance in the AI semiconductor supply chain being reshaped around a Japanese customer. With HBM procurement emerging as a bottleneck, the attempt to secure bandwidth through vertical memory stacking has now been connected to an actual mass-production line. That development is expected to make the push to reduce memory dependence a new variable in the competition for design services and foundry orders. Semifive plans to expand the technology's application beyond data-center AI chips to robots and smart devices.

stories.Headline: Tim Cowen proposes robots.txt terms and antitrust action to curb platform power over publishers
stories.Summary:
Tim Cowen, the chair of the antitrust practice at Preiskel & Co LLP, recently addressed the struggle publishers face when negotiating artificial intelligence rights with dominant platforms. He argues that publishers are often forced to accept unfair commercial terms because they depend on these platforms to reach their audiences. Cowen believes that companies like Meta act as monopoly distributors, which gives them undue bargaining power over content they did not create. This power imbalance makes it difficult for publishers to refuse content collection without risking their visibility to readers.

To address this, Cowen proposes a framework where publishers use robots.txt files to set separate terms for search indexing and other AI uses. His plan allows web crawlers to index sites for free while requiring explicit permission and payment for any other material usage. He suggests that regulators should use the U.K. Competition Act, EU Article 102, and the Digital Markets Act to ensure fair licensing payments. Additionally, he wants authorities to stop Google from bundling its Gemini AI service with its monopoly search product to give rivals a fair chance.

Cowen stated that distributors should not be able to impose their will on content creators who lack meaningful negotiating power. He explained that the Movement for an Open Web provides a consortium for businesses to challenge these dominant platforms collectively. According to Cowen, the commercial value of digital content varies by time and importance, so individual website owners should set their own prices. He believes that public availability of a website does not mean the owner surrenders authority over how that material is subsequently used.

Articles.Title: Publishers Push to Keep Search Access While Setting AI Terms

stories.Headline: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness fund buys back AI stocks and takes a $440 million stake in SharonAI
stories.Summary:
Leopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to financial markets at the end of the third quarter, according to a new regulatory filing reported by CNBC on November 17, 2026. As the fund got back on its feet, Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while the IREN and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million respectively, and the Fermi stake has a value of more than $11 million. The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF and data center power play Bloom Energy, with Sandisk and Nebius being key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.

All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since September 30, with SharonAI at the top of that list after a 58% loss in October and an 11% fall so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October while Nebius declined 35%, and last week Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast. It is not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff, because the 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter. The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel, and the fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak before that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.

Aschenbrenner, who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness, re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time, and the Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off. Stocks tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology, fears spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September. In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company. Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

Samsung Electronics accelerated its investments in artificial intelligence semiconductors through the third quarter of 2026, as revealed in a quarterly report on November 16. The company spent 56.9 trillion won on facilities and 41.8 trillion won on research and development to secure future growth engines. These financial efforts coincided with a rise in global market shares for the company's flagship smartphones, televisions, and semiconductors. The semiconductor business unit led overall earnings growth, recording sales of 356.3358 trillion won.

The facility investment plan requires 52.7509 trillion won, or 93 percent of the total, to be concentrated within the semiconductor division. This funding aims to strengthen next-generation memory technologies and expand production capacity for advanced system semiconductor processes. The company also signed a foundry supply agreement with Tesla worth 16.54 billion dollars that lasts until 2033. Market shares grew to 22.1 percent for smartphones, 29.5 percent for televisions, and 38.3 percent for DRAM.

Company officials stated that these investments are necessary to prepare for a mid-to-long-term increase in demand for AI infrastructure. They noted that the expansion of the AI ecosystem and premium products helped increase the market share of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8. The company also highlighted the importance of mass producing HBM4 and 1c-nanometer DRAM to maintain its top position in the memory market. They are currently expanding cooperation with major clients including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Hong Kong Techtronics, and Supreme Electronics.

The company continues to secure a stable customer base by signing multi-year supply contracts with global big tech and AI cloud firms. It also maintains a strong intellectual property portfolio, having registered 8,411 patents in South Korea and 8,470 in the United States this quarter. Total worldwide patents have now reached 302,751 since the first United States registration in 1984. Samsung will continue targeting the global number one position for televisions for a twenty-first consecutive year.

stories.Headline: Nvidia accepts CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and appoints CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Nvidia experienced a major leadership change when the board accepted the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on November 11, 2026. The company officially announced this decision the following day, leading to the appointment of Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim CEO. This shift is expected to weaken the dominance of Nvidia in the artificial intelligence semiconductor market. Consequently, Samsung Electronics is positioned to become the primary beneficiary as the industry moves toward a more diversified ecosystem.

The changing market requires a shift toward custom chips, known as application-specific integrated circuits, such as AWS Trainium and Google Tensor Processing Units. KB Securities projected in a November 16 report that non-Nvidia customers will account for 65% of Samsung Electronics high-bandwidth memory shipments by 2027. By that same year, Nvidia is expected to represent 38% of global demand for this memory, while Google will take 37% and AMD will take 13%. Other customers are projected to make up the remaining 12% of the global demand landscape.

Kim Dong-won, the head of research at KB Securities, stated that uncertainty regarding leadership at Nvidia will likely encourage customers to diversify their supply chains. He noted that the rush by Amazon, Google, and AMD to commercialize their own AI accelerators is accelerating this structural change. Kim further explained that while the leading figure may be gone, the overall empire of artificial intelligence will continue to grow larger. He expressed confidence that Samsung Electronics can grow because it maintains the broadest customer base outside of the Nvidia ecosystem.

This transition is occurring as Big Tech companies increase efforts to develop in-house chips and expand the AI inference market. Samsung Electronics is also pursuing growth through processing-in-memory technology, which was showcased via the LPDDR5X-PIM product at the FMS 2026 conference last August. LS Securities suggested that moving computing operations directly into memory could improve efficiency and increase the strategic value of these components. Industry observers are now watching to see if Samsung can successfully increase its market share during this period of diversification.

stories.Headline: Quantum X and Everest Cloud sign MOU to bring quantum and AI services to six South Asian markets
stories.Summary:
Quantum X and Everest Cloud signed a memorandum of understanding on November 6, 2026, to bring Quantum X's quantum computing and AI infrastructure products to customers across six South Asian markets, according to a press release from Quantum X. Everest Cloud is the Kathmandu-based cloud services brand of Digital Network Solutions Pvt. Ltd. The non-binding agreement gives Everest Cloud's customers access to Quantum X's EntangleX platform and broader AI and data infrastructure solutions in Nepal, India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. It also establishes a reciprocal arrangement under which Quantum X will promote Everest Cloud's services to U.S. customers, with both companies planning joint sales and technical integration. The MOU has a two-year initial term and is non-binding, and the parties intend to sign a definitive Channel Partner Agreement within 90 days.

Under the reciprocal, non-exclusive arrangement, each party earns commissions on revenue from customers it refers, with registered leads protected for twelve months and the option for either party to resell the other's products. The go-to-market plan includes joint sales calls, co-branded proposals, bundled offerings, joint marketing and technical integration between the two platforms, overseen by dedicated partnership managers and quarterly senior leadership reviews. Quantum X has not attributed a revenue estimate to the partnership and will report on referred customers as they are secured. Emil Assentato, Chief Executive Officer of Quantum X, said the next phase of quantum and AI will be decided by access rather than hardware alone, and that Everest Cloud already serves the banks, telecom operators, universities and data centers EntangleX was built for.

Ujjwal Roy, Head of Strategy and Chief Scientist of Quantum X, said working with Everest Cloud gives EntangleX a trusted local channel into these markets while giving U.S. organizations access to reliable cloud infrastructure from the region. Arun Khatri, Chief Executive Officer of Digital Network Solutions Pvt. Ltd., said the partnership opens the U.S. market to Everest Cloud and gives its clients access to quantum computing and advanced AI infrastructure through a trusted local partner. Khatri said the MOU lays a strong foundation for the company's vision of becoming a "Local to Global" company from the Himalayas.

The partnership gives EntangleX its first international route to market, through a cloud provider serving enterprises, banks, telecommunications operators, government bodies, universities and data centers across the six markets. IBM, Tata Consultancy Services and the Government of Andhra Pradesh have announced plans to deploy an IBM Quantum System Two in Amaravati, and India's National Quantum Mission is funding research and startups nationwide, while Amazon Web Services and IBM already offer quantum computing as a cloud service. EntangleX is a hosted circuit simulation and labs platform, live at entanglex.co as a minimum viable product, where users can build circuits gate by gate in a visual editor, send larger simulations to a hosted job queue and use Agentic Labs to turn a plain-language description of an experiment into a draft circuit. SliceX, Quantum X's platform for GPU slicing and security within the slices, has proven its ability to slice, but completion of the security issues between the slices is still subject to funding.

stories.Headline: Media Nov Records files a copyright strike that removes Samantha Shokin's folk song recording from YouTube
stories.Summary:
Media Nov Records issued a copyright strike against musician Samantha Shokin last month. This action caused YouTube to remove her recording of a Bulgarian folk song. Shokin had originally uploaded the track to YouTube two years after a pandemic recording. The company claimed ownership of the five year old recording of the song. Shokin discovered the company was an AI content mill abusing automated detectors.

The company claims it existed since 1996 but was founded last year. It lists addresses at a Los Angeles apartment and the Black Church in Dublin. Corporate paperwork shows shareholders based in Turkey and a registration in Ireland. Media Nov Records operates 500 YouTube channels featuring AI art and looping beats. These channels use AI powered content recognition and automated DMCA takedown systems.

Media Nov Records told 404 Media it works with various music partners. The company claimed Shokin and Loopmaster emails had gone to a spam folder. They initially asked Shokin for original audio files and evidence of her ownership. Later, they retracted the request because the video had not generated any revenue. They stated this retraction was not a waiver of any held rights.

YouTube denied two counterclaims from Shokin before eventually reinstating her original video. Shokin felt vindicated but unhappy that a journalist had to intervene for results. Copyright lawyer Alfred Steiner said the company was likely using AI tools slipshodly. He noted that filing takedowns for rights not held can create legal liability. Small parties often lack the resources to fight such fly by night entities.

Shokin first found her voice in a popular track with four million views. DJs had purchased her voice in a Folk Legends pack from Loopmasters. Loopmasters apologized and granted her royalties after she discovered the unauthorized sample sales. The song, Bre Petrunko, is a public domain folk song with no writer. Philip Koutev popularized a version in 1963, which the Smithsonian now owns.

Media Nov Records intends to initiate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute. The company did not explain why it brought Philip Koutev into the conversation. It also failed to identify which catalog work triggered the notice against Shokin. The articles leave open whether the company will actually pursue further legal action. It remains unclear how many other creators are affected by these automated strikes.

stories.Headline: Tax partners say AI token models complicate corporate value and tax treatment
stories.Summary:
Corporate capital structures have long centered on debt and equity, but artificial intelligence and token-based business models are beginning to complicate that framework, according to a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 17, 2026 by Megan Lisa Jones, a tax partner at Holland & Knight, and Fotis Konstantinidis, a managing director at Stout. Technology companies can now combine stock with tokens, token warrants, digital incentives, access rights, and governance mechanisms, while AI businesses develop new ways to monetize services. The result is a structure in which economic value may no longer reside entirely in corporate equity, and where tax treatment can be far less settled than for traditional stock and debt. A token does not necessarily represent ownership in a legal entity, and its value may instead depend on network growth, utility, scarcity, trading demand, or contractual rights.

The article says the IRS treats digital assets as property rather than currency under Notice 2014-21, so a sale or exchange of a token generally produces gain or loss, and receiving tokens as compensation, as payment for goods or services, or through staking or an airdrop can result in ordinary income. The guidance explains how a holder is taxed when it receives or disposes of a digital asset but does not say what a particular token is, and there is no comprehensive authority on whether a token is stock, debt, a partnership interest, an option or forward contract, or simply property. A token that is a security under the Howey test is not necessarily stock or debt for tax purposes, and a corporation generally does not recognize gain when it issues its own stock, but there is no comparable rule for tokens. Tokens issued to employees and service providers raise questions of timing, valuation, and withholding, including whether a Section 83(b) election is available, and in an acquisition tokens delivered to selling holders are unlikely to count as stock of the acquirer.

The authors say the law in this area has not caught up with the technology, with no comprehensive statute, regulation, or ruling addressing whether a token is debt or equity, and existing guidance deals only with specific fact patterns such as hard forks, airdrops, and staking. They advise companies to expect to take positions without clear authority, document the basis for them, and revisit them as guidance develops, and say tax advisers should be involved when the token is designed rather than after it has been issued. For management teams and boards, they write that the most important question may be the simplest, namely what business problem the token is solving, followed by understanding the economic rights being created and how those rights interact with existing shareholders. The article says the opportunity is real because AI and digital assets may allow companies to create forms of ownership, participation, and economic incentive that were difficult to implement through traditional capital structures alone, but that greater flexibility comes with greater complexity.

stories.Headline: Google and Mandiant report that cyber criminals now deploy autonomous AI tools to run multiple stages of attacks
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group released its GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold report on Monday, November 16, 2026, and the report was developed with the cybersecurity firm Mandiant. The research draws on incident response investigations, global threat actor tracking and security monitoring, and it found that cyber criminals have moved beyond using AI to assist with individual tasks. According to the report, threat actors are increasingly deploying autonomous tools that can carry out multiple stages of cyber attacks, using large language models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits and execute attacks at machine speed. Researchers found that attackers are increasingly using open source, multi-agent frameworks to automate activities that were previously done by humans, sometimes with no human help at all.

One public sector example cited in the research is the late-summer exploitation of PaperCut print management software, which is used by more than 70,000 organizations, including universities, libraries and government agencies. In August, attackers exploited two vulnerabilities that, when combined, allow unauthenticated remote code execution, and four days after the initial vulnerability disclosure there was a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations, likely using large language models. By the numbers, the Cloud Security Alliance reported that the attack reached 48 countries and 395 organizations, including 204 compromised instances in the education sector. Attackers have not changed long-standing access methods such as using compromised credentials and exploiting unpatched systems, but what has changed is speed and scale, with high-velocity attacks that leave visible forensic trails.

Researchers say hackers are now more sophisticated when using AI, and they expect attacks to involve even less human intervention and to become harder to detect. The report attributes the shift to threat actors building full attack frameworks rather than relying on simple prompts, and it points to machine-speed execution as a defining feature of the activity. The articles do not name individual attackers or identify who is responsible beyond describing them as threat actors tracked by Google and Mandiant. The articles do not say what specific steps organizations should take next or what further action Google or Mandiant plans.

stories.Headline: Club Champion fitter Drew Koch uses AI Co-Pilot to guide a driver fitting but picks the winning shaft himself
stories.Summary:
Earlier this year, Club Champion leaned heavily into artificial intelligence with its proprietary AI Co-Pilot system, and a Plugged In Golf writer recently watched the system in action to see whether it could replace fitters completely. The fitting was one of his friends fitting another, and the fitter was Drew Koch, a Plugged In Golf staff writer and master club fitter with Club Champion. The golfer was Alex, who is 51 and a very solid player looking for a driver to replace his eight year old PING G400. Alex came in viewing his driving as consistent and reliable but not a big strength. The fitting started with Alex making ten swings with his current gamer while Drew talked him through what he was seeing in the numbers.

All of the Trackman data was then fed into AI Co-Pilot, and the system generated five shaft recommendations ranging from a 60 gram stiff flex to a 40 gram senior flex. Shaft testing started with the Fujikura Ventus Blue 5-S, and after a couple of swings Drew saw it was a poor fit for Alex's smooth transition. The data from those swings went into AI Co-Pilot, the recommendations changed slightly, but Drew went off script and pulled the Fujikura Ventus White in 4-R, which was not on the list but was in line with the smooth, 40 gram option the system suggested. Results with the Ventus White were excellent, with club and ball speed up and smash factor crossing the 1.5 threshold several times. Drew fed that data into AI Co-Pilot, which generated more new ideas but began to hone in on Alex's preference for something lighter and softer, and a couple more shafts were tested but nothing outperformed the Ventus White.

With the shaft choice locked in, Drew asked AI Co-Pilot which head would be a good fit, and the system returned two options: the PING G440 LST that Alex was already using to test shafts and the Titleist GTS2. Both options performed well, but there was little question that the PING was the better option for Alex. Alex picked up roughly 8 MPH of ball speed, over 7 yards of carry, and over 18 yards total while painting the center line. The author wrote that AI Co-Pilot, with well over 50,000,000 data points in its system, shows the range of possible solutions, simultaneously narrowing the field and keeping options open.

He added that unlike human fitters, AI is not going to get stuck in a rut of solving the same problem the same way every time, and with access to every fit from every fitter it is constantly finding the newest, best solution. The author said that while AI Co-Pilot started with a wide net during the shaft fitting, once it had enough data it was able to speed them toward the final answer with the club head. Toward the end of the fitting, Alex noted that he was getting tired, and having to only test two driver heads was extremely helpful in making the fitting efficient. The author argued that in an AI fitting there is no conversation, just ten shots and a bunch of numbers, and the AI does not understand who the golfer is as a player, what they are trying to achieve, what brands they love, or what sound they hate.

He said the AI cannot pull the plug on a bad combination the way a human fitter can, seeing one bad swing as just one data point where an experienced human fitter sees a golfer fighting a shaft that is never going to work. He noted that in the fitting he watched, the best combination did not come directly from AI Co-Pilot's list of suggestions, and Drew was able to get to it faster because of his experience and knowledge of Alex's swing. The author wrote that he is sure some people once worried that launch monitors would replace club fitters, and the same with interchangeable heads and shafts, but neither did and AI will not either. He said all of these things are tools that a skilled club fitter can use to deliver a better fit for the golfer.

He concluded that if you want the best fitting, you want the best human fitter using the best technology, meaning the best launch monitors, the most hittable combinations, and the smartest AI, all of which he said can be found at Club Champion. The article was published on November 17, 2026, by Matt Saternus, editor in chief at Plugged In Golf, who founded the site in 2013 and has over 16 years of golf industry experience. Saternus lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago with his wife and two daughters. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Springer Nature reports 6.3% revenue growth as AI and open access lift research publishing
stories.Summary:
Springer Nature reported financial results for the first nine months of 2026, with growth in its academic publishing business driven by increased journal output, expanding open access agreements and continued investment in AI-enabled publishing technology. The publisher reported group revenue of €1.47 billion for the nine months to September, up from €1.43 billion in the same period last year, representing underlying growth of 6.3%. Adjusted operating profit increased to €427.8 million, with underlying growth of 7.7%. Its Research division remained the principal driver of performance, generating revenue of €1.15 billion, with underlying growth of 7.4%, while adjusted operating profit in the division rose to €369 million, reflecting underlying growth of 8.4%.

The company reported a 12% increase in published research articles during the period, compared with estimated market growth of approximately 8%, with growth recorded across its fully open access, Nature and Springer journal portfolios. During the first nine months of 2026 it signed 23 new transformative agreements with national consortia, government bodies and research institutions, bringing its total number of transformative agreements to 105, covering more than 4,500 institutions worldwide. The company also launched 54 journals during the period, including Nature Progress Oncology, npj Nephrology, BMC Sustainability and Scientific Reviews, a multidisciplinary sister publication to Scientific Reports, and the launches included 17 titles in its Discover portfolio. More than 62% of manuscript submissions were processed through SNAPP, the publisher's integrated AI-enabled publishing platform, during the first nine months of 2026, and the company reported progress with Nature Research Assistant, its AI-powered research tool, which is currently in beta testing with more than 25,000 users.

Frank Vrancken Peeters, CEO of Springer Nature, said the performance in the first nine months of 2026 was again led by the Research segment, and that this continued momentum is driven by leadership in open access, the use of AI-enabled tools and continuous investment. He said the company has updated its guidance and now expects underlying revenue growth for the Group of at least 6% in 2026 with at least 30bps of margin expansion. Springer Nature said it had completed its 2026 contract renewals, while negotiations for the next renewal cycle, which began in September, were progressing as expected. The company said AI-enabled technology remains a central element of its publishing strategy, with investment focused on improving editorial workflows, strengthening research integrity and supporting researchers.

Nature Research Assistant is scheduled for launch in early 2027 and continues to achieve customer satisfaction scores above 80%, including for newer features such as Manuscript Adviser, introduced earlier this year. Beyond publishing workflows, Springer Nature reported growth in its text and data mining services and new ARC3 licensing partnerships with corporate customers, which enable organisations to access scientific content within AI-powered environments. Its books business also recorded revenue growth across print and digital formats, and the publisher introduced the first titles from its new Nature Books imprint at the Frankfurt Book Fair in October. The company completed the disposal of its consumer media businesses, selling Scientific American to LabX Media Group in June and Spektrum to GeraNova Bruckmann in July, which it said represents a further concentration of its portfolio on its core research publishing and related activities.

stories.Headline: National Insurance Crime Bureau reports AI mentions in questionable claims rise over 1,400%
stories.Summary:
The National Insurance Crime Bureau, a nonprofit based in Oak Brook, Illinois, published its 2026 threat assessment on November 16, 2026, reporting that mentions of AI in questionable claims rose by more than 1,400% from 2025 to mid-2026 across auto, liability, cargo and workers' compensation lines. The report identifies three converging threats: AI-enabled identity schemes, organized crime networks that mix digital and physical tactics, and professional networks of attorneys, medical providers and auto repair firms working together to inflate claims. Fraudsters are using widely available tools to generate fabricated medical records, synthetic identities and doctored accident photographs at a volume that existing claims workflows were not built to handle. A separate Verisk study published in March 2026, based on surveys of 1,000 US consumers and 300 claims professionals, found that 36% of consumers would consider digitally altering a claim image or document even if it broke insurer rules, rising to 55% among Generation Z. On the insurer side, 76% of claims professionals said manipulated media submissions had grown more sophisticated over the past year, while only 32% were confident their organization could identify a deepfake. The report also found more than 1,600 transnational, interstate and state-level organized crime rings operating in 2025, running schemes that span staged accidents, vehicle theft and complex multi-party fraud.

The NICB describes predatory legal and medical networks as systematically exploiting the litigation system, turning low-severity incidents into mass litigation and driving settlement values well beyond the underlying loss, and it has focused legislative efforts on fraud in litigation funding. The FBI estimates non-health insurance fraud costs the US at least $40 billion annually, and fraud losses inflate loss ratios, which in turn drive premiums. In commercial cargo, total supply chain crime incidents across the US and Canada held roughly steady in 2025 at 3,594 events against 3,607 in 2024, but estimated losses reached nearly $725 million, a 60% year-on-year increase, according to Verisk CargoNet's January 2026 annual analysis. The average value per theft rose 36% to $273,990, confirmed cargo theft cases rose 18% year-over-year, and California, Texas and Illinois accounted for just over half of all incidents, while New Jersey, Indiana and Pennsylvania each recorded significant increases. Pranay Mittal, vice president of Travelers Investigative Services, said in a statement issued alongside the NICB report that shared insight is the industry's strongest defense because every insurer holds a piece of the picture, and that working with NICB and other fraud-fighting partners helps investigators spot patterns sooner and focus investigations with greater precision as new threats emerge.

Aimee Stidham, president of the International Association of Special Investigation Units, a global nonprofit headquartered in Albany, New York, and claims SIU manager at Hiscox USA, said in a statement issued alongside the report that the fight against insurance fraud is no longer undertaken by any single organization, and that today's most effective anti-fraud initiatives are driven by collaboration, intelligence sharing and a shared commitment to protecting policyholders. The NICB is integrating business intelligence across its member companies, authenticating digital evidence and building infrastructure to flag emerging fraud patterns earlier, while its field agents work alongside law enforcement to disrupt cargo theft operations directly. For brokers placing cargo or logistics cover, the articles say policies underwritten against 2023 or 2024 loss assumptions may no longer reflect current exposure, and carriers are tightening terms, adding exclusions and demanding stronger chain-of-custody controls from clients, conversations that now fall to brokers to initiate. Policyholders and industry professionals can report suspected fraud to NICB at reportinsurancefraud.org.

stories.Headline: Arthur Hayes names four tokens he expects to pump before the AI bubble ends
stories.Summary:
Arthur Hayes named four tokens he expects to pump before the AI bubble ends, calling the group the "Four Horsemen" in a post on X, according to a BeInCrypto report published on November 16, 2026. The call came after Bitcoin fell to nearly $62,000 on November 15, its lowest level since July. Hayes said the four would pump and then usher in the end of the AI bubble. The post follows his June exit from Hyperliquid, NEAR and ZEC, which he had grouped as a "holy trinity" two weeks earlier, and he sold ZEC after a vulnerability surfaced in its Orchard shielded pool.

His targets are $2,800 for Ethereum, $1,800 for Zcash, $6 for NEAR Protocol and $40 for Venice Token, the token of the privacy-focused AI platform Venice. He sized the trade small to medium because his conviction is low, writing that if the music is playing you have to dance, and he attached no timeframe to the targets. The $2,800 ETH target sits $2,200 below the $5,000 year-end level he forecast in August. Hayes said he kept only Bitcoin and ETH as core crypto holdings.

Hayes argues that a burst would trigger a financial crisis and a wave of central bank money printing he calls the "Big Print," which he expects to send Bitcoin sharply higher after an initial drop. In August he called the AI boom a credit bubble and said Bitcoin could reach $1 million. On-chain investigator ZachXBT has accused Hayes of pumping tokens such as ZEC and Worldcoin before selling to his audience. The trade rests on a $1.5 trillion AI debt wave that Hayes says has absorbed dollar liquidity, and if that debt avoids a crisis the trigger he describes never arrives and the pump loses its stated end point.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora says AI leaders push an unnaturally negative narrative about their own technology
stories.Summary:
Nikesh Arora, the chief executive officer of Palo Alto Networks, criticized leaders of advanced artificial intelligence companies during a Semafor event on November 16, 2026. Speaking with Mat Honan from MIT Technology Review, Arora claimed that these industry figures are promoting an unnaturally negative narrative regarding their own technology. He argued that the current obsession with potential risks is overshadowing the immense benefits that this fast-moving technology could provide to the world. According to Arora, the people who should be championing the advantages of these tools are instead focusing on their dark side.

Arora described artificial intelligence as a transformational technology that could democratize intelligence and uplift a huge amount of humanity across the globe. He suggested that a villager in India could use these tools to summarize multiple websites and access the best available intelligence. Regarding the difficulty of building new data centers, he believed that scarcity of computing capacity would actually accelerate innovation in compression technology. However, he acknowledged that these growing capabilities intensify cybersecurity risks by making it easier to find vulnerabilities in software written over the last 50 years.

The executive warned that as more software weaknesses are discovered and exploited, companies may be forced to take systems offline to apply necessary patches. He stated that there is no quick solve or panacea for these security challenges, but believed the industry would eventually grind through them. Arora maintained that every technology possesses a dark side, yet the potential for positive global impact remains the more important story. He concluded that the industry must power through these inevitable security hurdles to realize the full potential of the technology.

stories.Headline: TrustYou adds SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder to its Customer Experience Platform
stories.Summary:
TrustYou, a hospitality technology company headquartered in Munich, Germany, announced on 17 November 2026 that its Customer Experience Platform now opens on three conversational entry points built around jobs hotel teams do every day. The first, SummaryAI, has already read every new review across all sources so each property starts the day with its priorities set. The second, Ask TrustYou, answers any question about guest feedback and lets users follow up and dig deeper within the same conversation. The third, Report Builder, is new today and handles reporting for hotel teams.

A team describes a report once, including the KPIs, the properties and the comparison periods, and CXP then builds it, keeps it on schedule and delivers it as a PDF or Excel file in each recipient's language. That delivery reaches owners and boards who never log in to the system. All three tools work on one principle, which is that a user describes the outcome and CXP delivers it, so hotel teams act on guest issues sooner and guest insight reaches every role without training or analyst support. Multi-property groups get back the days each month they now spend consolidating reports across dozens or hundreds of properties, where quality and operations teams produce reports for general managers, owners, boards and regional leadership, and each audience expects its own KPIs, format and language.

Benjamin Jost, Founder and CEO of TrustYou, said hospitality is becoming conversational on both sides of the front desk, with guests already talking to AI to plan and book their stays. He said that on the guest side the company already closes the loop, because its Customer Data Platform sends every message and its agents answer every reply. He said staff should be able to work the same way with every system a hotel runs, so that you say what you need and it gets done. He described SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder as CXP's biggest step yet toward that vision, where opening it means the reviews are read, asking gives the answer and describing the report means the board has it every month.

SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder are live for all CXP customers, according to the announcement. TrustYou describes itself as hospitality's memory, a platform that unifies what guests feel, what they do and what they ask in a single system, and it says more than 100,000 hospitality businesses have used it since 2008. The company says its AI Review Summaries turn guest reviews from all relevant sources into structured, benchmarked insight for over 2 million properties worldwide, and that the same verified insight reaches travel platforms, booking engines and AI assistants via API and MCP. TrustYou is headquartered in Munich, Germany, and serves hospitality brands in over 165 countries.

stories.Headline: Tom Lee says AI trade remains structurally intact despite Nvidia leadership scandal
stories.Summary:
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 12 percent from its October 6 record close by November 5, 2026. This decline followed the November 12 resignation of Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares lost about 35 percent of their value since October 6, which represents a loss of roughly 2 trillion dollars. The company experienced its worst week in 19 months, with shares dropping another 4.1 percent on Monday.

The Nasdaq closed at 24,315.00 on November 5, which was 11.9 percent below the October 6 record close of 27,599.79. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is currently serving as the interim leader for Nvidia. While Nvidia shares fell, rivals Broadcom and AMD saw their stock prices rise on the day Huang resigned. The market now awaits quarterly results from Nvidia on Tuesday and a potential Nasdaq debut for the AI developer Anthropic this week.

Tom Lee, the head of research at Fundstrat Global Advisors, believes the artificial intelligence trade remains structurally intact. He argues that the current slide is driven by emotion, headlines, and margin selling rather than a fundamental wall for the industry. Lee suggests that capital is dynamic and could flow toward SpaceX or Anthropic if Nvidia becomes less central. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co added that while Huang's exit cost Nvidia 1 trillion dollars in valuation, it will not stop 3 trillion to 4 trillion dollars in expected spending.

The leadership scandal has weighed on AI shares for several weeks as investors react to the loss of the founder. Future funding for the sector may broaden beyond a single chipmaker if the upcoming events go well. However, a stalled debut for Anthropic or a cut to the outlook for Nvidia could test the resilience of the trade. Analysts continue to monitor whether the industry can move past the loss of its most prominent leader.

Articles.Title: Tom Lee Sees No Cracks in the AI Trade Despite Nasdaq's 12% Drop

stories.Headline: Edge Group CTO Chaouki Kasmi leads work on laser and autonomous drone capabilities
stories.Summary:
The Edge Group has been developing a high-energy laser capability to counter various aerial threats, according to a report published on November 17, 2026. This organization is also working toward the creation of a fully autonomous drone capability for future operations. These technological advancements are being led by the group's chief technology officer, Chaouki Kasmi. The company is focusing on these specific areas to enhance its overall defense and aerospace portfolio. The new laser systems are intended to defend against drones and other air or missile threats.

These capabilities require the integration of advanced artificial intelligence to manage autonomous drone flight and targeting. The project involves the Abu Dhabi Government and utilizes sophisticated unmanned aerial systems to achieve its goals. No specific dates for the full deployment of these systems were provided in the report. Chaouki Kasmi, the chief technology officer for the Edge Group, is the primary official responsible for these developments.

He confirmed that the group is pursuing both the laser and autonomous drone capabilities. However, Kasmi remained guarded regarding the specific extent of the work being done on the laser systems. He did not provide detailed technical specifications or a timeline for the completion of these projects. More to follow.

stories.Headline: ILO study finds AI and streaming reshape pay and working conditions in media and culture
stories.Summary:
The International Labour Organization published a study on 17 November 2026 examining how streaming and artificial intelligence are reshaping pay and working conditions in the media and culture sector. The report, titled Trends in remuneration and working time: Recorded media and live performance, looks at how creative workers are paid, how their working time is counted, and how digitalization and AI are changing both. Streaming has moved recorded media from physical sales and downloads toward subscription and advertising-funded services, and in recorded music streaming accounted for about 70 per cent of global industry revenue in 2024. AI adds a further layer because voices, images and performances can now be replicated, translated and reworked in new ways, which raises questions of consent, control and remuneration.

The study identifies three main ways AI can affect pay and work. First, AI systems can use existing works and performances as input, as when a recorded voice-over artist's voice is used to generate new dialogue, which raises issues of licensing, attribution and payment. Second, AI can generate or modify content, helping small production firms cut costs through tools such as subtitling and translation, but it may also reduce demand for some types of work or increase competition from AI-generated content. Third, AI can change job tasks, as when an editor spends less time on an initial cut and more on reviewing and correcting AI-generated material, and the question is whether those new tasks are reflected in pay, working time and skills. The report also cites a United Kingdom survey in which 61 per cent of screen directors said they had not fully understood the rights they were granting when signing their contracts.

Workers' organizations emphasize transparency and the need for creative workers to share in the value of later uses of their work, while employers and producers stress upfront investment, uncertain commercial returns and clear rights to finance and distribute the work. Collective agreements can clarify how such uses are permitted and paid, and the report points to the 2023 United States TV/Theatrical Agreement and a 2025 German film industry agreement, which include negotiated provisions on consent and remuneration for some uses of performers' digital replicas. The ILO's human-centred approach emphasizes transparency, human oversight and social dialogue, and the report says social dialogue can support a negotiated transition that promotes adequate remuneration, human creativity and viable enterprises. The report also notes that the ability to benefit from AI is highly uneven, since smaller enterprises and workers in less connected markets are likely to have less access to finance, skills, technology and the systems to manage rights and payments.

stories.Headline: S&P Global rates AI-linked debt as analysts warn concentrated exposure may magnify credit risk
stories.Summary:
S&P Global has taken a central role in rating a growing wave of AI linked debt instruments that are attracting institutional demand, according to a report published on November 16, 2026. S&P Global Ratings has assigned relatively high grades to structures backed by AI related projects that are drawing capital from insurance companies. Analysts have raised concerns that complex repayment terms and concentrated exposures within these AI themed securities could magnify credit risk. The report says the growing use of S&P Global ratings on AI related debt should not be the only factor investors consider today. The report says S&P Global operates in the capital markets industry as a provider of benchmarks, data and analytics, and its credit ratings on AI related debt directly influence how insurers and other large investors assess and compare risk across this emerging segment.

It says the S&P Global narrative rests on the group using AI, data and capital markets activity to turn complex financing trends into high margin, repeatable services. The report says the main condition for this thesis is that S&P Global converts its investments in AI driven productivity, private markets transparency and energy data into high margin growth across divisions. It says the news leans into the catalyst that S&P Global can monetise an 8 trillion dollar maturity wall through more structured and themed issuance. The report says the catch is that concentrated exposure to a handful of tech borrowers means those ratings are now more exposed to a single theme than traditional diversified securitisations. It says that pressure point sits squarely in the risk section that already flags dependence on healthy issuance volumes and investor confidence in Ratings.

The report says that if analysts start questioning whether AI related tranches are understood as well as they are scored, it gives critics of traditional ratings models fresh material, including at rivals like Moody's and Fitch. It says the more scrutiny builds, the more investors may look at S&P Global's own debt disclosures and risk frameworks for clues. The report says raw headlines about AI debt only become useful once you link them back to the S&P Global Narrative, because that is what turns a single theme into a full investment decision. It says readers might want to see where analysts expect the business to be a few years from now and how far that is from today. The article is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that it is not intended to be financial advice.

stories.Headline: Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts AI agents will recommend most major corporate decisions including layoffs
stories.Summary:
Michael Ioffe, the cofounder and CEO of the startup Arist, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on November 16, 2026, that AI agents will increasingly recommend major corporate decisions, including layoffs, while executives keep the final say. He predicted that within the next few years the majority of significant enterprise shifts, such as products being launched or layoffs being made, will be recommended by agents. Arist uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data and recommend solutions to business problems, and it already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500. Ioffe said the technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours, a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Ioffe said an executive will always make the final call, and he sees AI's biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster rather than replacing executives or consultants.

Before an agent can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it must understand what is happening inside a company, so Arist's agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions and weigh responses against information such as an employee's tenure, performance and past engagement scores. Ioffe said that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization, and that the agents will push back if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want. He argued that employees may be more candid with AI agents than with another person, and he said that if a company can get to the truth much faster, a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup. Ioffe said he did not set out to compete with consulting firms, and he described how at 19 he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform before shifting Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies and becoming one of OpenAI's early partners. He noticed that companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem and then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it, and in his experience the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time, which prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing problems.

He pointed to a major software company whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why. The prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of "AI washing," or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons, and the article says that even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work, according to previous reporting cited in the article. The article also notes that gathering information through AI agents could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.

stories.Headline: Stephen Ferrara launches AI + Nurse Academy to give nurse practitioners a foundation in AI
stories.Summary:
Stephen Ferrara, a doctor of nursing practice and family nurse practitioner, was named Medscape's Nurse Practitioner of the Month in a feature published on November 17, 2026, recognizing his work helping nurses navigate artificial intelligence. He is the chief executive officer and founder of AI + Nurse Academy, an educational platform that gives nurse practitioners a foundation in AI, which he launched in October 2025. Ferrara said his motivation comes down to trying to fix a system he feels is not working as intended for the people it is designed for. Early in his clinical career, he realized state law did not allow him to do things he had been educated and prepared to do, such as performing licensing physicals for people pursuing a barber career, and he turned his attention to overcoming barriers such as full practice authority laws.

The academy currently offers nurse practitioners and registered nurses a 60-minute continuing medical education module, and upon completion users receive a certificate of completion and one accredited hour of continuing education. Participants can also join a community of peers to ask questions, share concerns and exchange experiences, with responsible use as the company's guiding principle. Ferrara said the main goal is to expose every nurse to what generative AI is, what it means for their practice, and to prompt them to consider how they will integrate it thoughtfully into clinical practice. He explained that he wants nurses to understand where AI makes mistakes and how it can affect patient outcomes, stressing that keeping a human or clinician in the loop means AI does not make any decisions without a human or clinician reviewing it.

Ferrara said that in nursing school he was taught that at the end of the day it is your license to lose, and that if you adopt a tool it is your clinical judgment on the line regardless of whether you choose it or are told by administrators to use it. He pointed to flaws in the research large language models rely on, such as the lack of robust cultural, socioeconomic and ethnic studies in certain patient populations, and said he wants the human between AI and the patient to be able to discern whether a recommendation is pertinent. He said it is his core belief that AI can potentially make him a better clinician through rapid access to information and the ability to personalize it to patients, but that it is not magic. He said clinicians are ingrained to do no harm and asked how AI can be made to better anticipate things and patients rather than spewing things that are not necessarily helpful.

Before retiring from his Columbia appointments earlier this year, Ferrara served as inaugural associate dean of AI, spearheading strategy and programs to ensure nurses gained foundational AI literacy, and he moved from assistant to full professor of nursing at Columbia University in New York City. As associate dean of clinical affairs and chief clinical officer for the ColumbiaDoctors Nurse Practitioner Group, he expanded services to include house calls and integrated mental health services, achieving Patient-Centered Medical Home recognition. As president and immediate past president of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, he advocated for the Improving Care and Access to Nurses Act so nurse practitioners can practice to the top of their license and education. Ferrara reported receiving profits from AI + Nurse Academy, and the article says the path starts with a basic framework and AI literacy and ideally ends with improved patient outcomes, with nurse practitioners determining what happens in between.

stories.Headline: Pearl engineering leader urges CIOs to measure cycle time and rework to gauge AI productivity
stories.Summary:
Nazar Yaremchuk, senior director of engineering at Pearl, wrote in CIO on Nov 17, 2026 that AI can write code in seconds but that is only the first stage of software development. He said AI-generated output can introduce errors, miss internal requirements or require extensive rework, so the time saved upfront can quickly disappear. Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. Yaremchuk said that if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren't so clear-cut. A report from Bain & Co found AI coding tools help developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%.

Yaremchuk said CIOs need to look at the entire process, from the initial idea to software in production, to understand whether AI is improving productivity. He said AI adoption metrics such as token usage and developer participation show how much a company is using AI, but not necessarily whether it is becoming more productive. He said a more useful approach is to track engineering cycle time, end-to-end lead time, review and rework time, and software quality. He said these measures are most useful when considered holistically, and leaders should assess whether quality is consistent or improving and whether review and rework are consuming too much time. He said establishing a baseline before expanding AI use, then tracking these measures over time, can help CIOs distinguish genuine improvements from shifts in where work happens.

At Pearl, Yaremchuk said, the team asked AI to help create pipeline automation, but it generated GitHub Actions workflows for an engineering environment that uses Azure DevOps and Jenkins. He said astute engineers caught the mismatch during review and had to rewrite the integration, and the code was plausible but didn't account for Pearl's actual infrastructure. He said Pearl has a quality-control process that combines AI-assisted review with human oversight based on risk, with lower-risk changes such as unit tests often reviewed primarily by AI while critical production-facing code still receives human review. He said Pearl's AI reviews identify an average of 16 errors per 10 pull requests, including security and architectural issues. He said the goal is not to remove humans from the review process but to use automation to catch issues efficiently and reserve human judgment for decisions where risk and complexity warrant it.

Yaremchuk said Pearl tracks engineering cycle time and has seen it decline month over month in 2026 as its use of AI-generated code has increased. He said that in September 2026, the average pull request Pearl released to production was 75% AI-generated, and 45% of all pull requests were written entirely by AI, with no line edited by a person before commit. He said savvy organizations have taken advantage of AI to automate repetitive tasks so that engineers can focus more on architecture, complex problem-solving and validating results. He said enterprises introducing AI agents that can execute multistep tasks and work together will need to rethink how they assign, supervise and evaluate that work, with clear permissions, defined responsibilities and appropriate oversight. He said of critical importance is determining where human judgment remains essential and how teams should adapt as more work becomes automated.

Yaremchuk said the priority for CIOs should be to redesign engineering workflows around the capabilities of AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes. He said this starts with establishing a baseline for development speed and software quality, then measuring how both change as AI adoption increases. He said it also means using the results to adjust workflows, review requirements and the allocation of engineering time. He said AI investments should be held accountable to the same business outcomes as any other technology investment, and more code, more tokens and broader adoption can indicate progress but can be misleading. He said the real measure of AI productivity is whether an organization can deliver better software faster, with quality and security intact.

Yaremchuk has nearly 20 years in software delivery and over a decade leading engineering organizations, and he oversees architecture, DevOps, security and AI adoption across a 280-person engineering organization at Pearl. He led a transformation that increased production releases from one to approximately 400 per week and now champions AI-native software delivery. He is completing an Executive MBA at Oxford Saïd Business School. The article was published Nov 17, 2026 and runs 5 minutes.

stories.Headline: Academic librarians expect AI to drive change and want to lead AI literacy, Elsevier study finds
stories.Summary:
A global study from Elsevier found that 83 percent of academic librarians surveyed expect artificial intelligence to be the biggest driver of change in academic research, while 81 percent also named the misuse of AI as the greatest threat to the integrity of the scholarly record. The findings come from the Librarian of the Future report, which draws on responses from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders. The research highlights the increasingly strategic role librarians could play within universities as institutions respond to technological change, evolving research needs and growing concerns around research integrity. Almost all respondents, 95 percent, expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years.

The report says 82 percent of respondents believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers, and 76 percent believe librarians should contribute to AI governance. Despite these expectations, only 30 percent report that their institution has implemented an AI policy, which suggests a significant gap between the adoption of AI technologies and the development of institutional frameworks to manage their use. More than three-quarters of respondents, 76 percent, anticipate greater collaboration between libraries and other university departments over the next five years. The findings also point to the growing importance of leadership, influencing skills and the ability to navigate complex institutional decisions as librarians take on broader responsibilities.

Ann Gabriel, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Networks at Elsevier, said librarians have always been essential to research, but the study shows an opportunity for their expertise to play an even more strategic role. She said that as AI transforms how research is discovered, conducted and evaluated, librarians bring a unique combination of technical expertise, ethical judgement and trusted relationships across their institutions. She added that ensuring they have the skills, support and visibility to contribute fully will be important as universities navigate this next phase of change. Jim O'Donnell, University Librarian and Professor at Arizona State University, said librarians long thought they were in the book business, or perhaps the information business, and that the survey shows the community now broadly recognises it is in the research business.

The report suggests that librarians are increasingly positioning themselves as partners in the wider research process, rather than solely as providers of information resources. Alongside AI literacy and governance, demand is expected to grow for library expertise in open access, research data management and research integrity. The report identifies responsible AI adoption, trusted information and research integrity as areas in which librarians could play a more prominent role in supporting researchers and institutional leadership. Elsevier says it will continue working with the global library community to explore how the profession can respond to these changing demands, and the full report is available at Librarian of the Future.

stories.Headline: Hariharan marks 50 years in music and raises concerns about AI
stories.Summary:
Legendary playback singer Hariharan sat down with The Hindu to mark a remarkable milestone of 50 years in the music industry, a career that has spanned more than 15,000 songs across 10 languages and 30 ghazal albums. In the conversation he discussed his musical journey and the roots that bridge Mumbai and Chennai, the two cities that shaped him. He also spoke about his training under legendary masters and about recording with Kishore Kumar during his long career. The interview was published on November 16, 2026, and was updated the same day at 5:36 pm IST. The conversation also covered the record-breaking success of his Hanuman Chalisa rendition, which he cited among the highlights of his career.

Beyond the numbers, Hariharan raised profound concerns about what he called the AI dilemma in modern music. The interview framed his career through the scale of his output, from thousands of film songs to three decades of ghazal albums. It presented his journey as one that connects the North and South of Indian music through his own life and work. Hariharan is the figure at the centre of the interview, and the account of his career and his concerns is presented in his own words as given to The Hindu. The article does not attribute any statement to anyone else and does not set out any decision, policy or change arising from the interview.

It reports his reflections on 50 years of singing, on the masters who trained him, and on the artists he recorded with. It also records his worries about artificial intelligence in music without describing any step he or anyone else plans to take. The context the article gives is the milestone itself, half a century in the industry measured in more than 15,000 songs, 10 languages and 30 ghazal albums. It places his story between Mumbai and Chennai and traces his training under legendary masters and his recordings with Kishore Kumar. stories.Headline: Philippines residents protest planned US led AI and manufacturing hub
stories.Summary:
Local residents in the Philippines held protests on Monday against the upcoming visit of President Trump to Manila. These demonstrations center on a planned artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub located just north of the capital city. The project serves as the first major action for Pax Silica, which is an international initiative led by the U.S. State Department. This effort aims to secure high-tech manufacturing supply chains that do not rely on China.

The proposed industrial hub will cover more than 4,000 acres of land in the Philippines. This project follows the December 2025 announcement of Pax Silica, which has since attracted over 25 participating countries including India, Japan, Israel, and the United Kingdom. The Philippines officially joined this initiative in April, leading to the current plans for the manufacturing center. The Marcos administration claims this development could create between 100,000 and 130,000 new jobs for the local population.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. expressed great excitement in October, calling the hub a grand opportunity to move the country up the value chain. Conversely, advocate Maninging Vilog argued that the project only benefits the United States while grabbing local lands. Protester Kaiser Cortina questioned why farmers and bus drivers should care about artificial intelligence. Representative Antonio Tinio noted that opposition to AI data centers is a global issue seen across Southeast Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia.

The U.S. government is pursuing this strategy because of long-standing concerns regarding Chinese access to advanced chips and hardware. Recent attention increased following reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Participants in Pax Silica signed a declaration on Sunday regarding the protection of critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies. stories.Headline: Damac chairman Hussain Sajwani says his Anthropic stake earned more in under two years than 30 years of investing
stories.Summary:
Hussain Sajwani, the 72-year-old chairman of Dubai-based luxury real estate developer Damac Properties, said at the Bloomberg Invest Dubai forum that what he made in 30 years he made in Anthropic in less than two years, according to Livemint. His comment came as Anthropic, the AI startup behind Claude, prepares for a Nasdaq IPO on Wednesday at a valuation of $1.4 trillion. The listing is expected to make all seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Christopher Olah, Jared Kaplan, Jack Clark and Sam McCandlish, multi-billionaires, while around 50 early employees are projected to cross the $100 million threshold in stock wealth. Sajwani said he expects his investments in AI firms, including Anthropic, to draw billions in returns.

In July 2024, Damac Group announced notable investments in AI companies, including $50 million in Anthropic, as one of the top investors who bought into the company from the cryptocurrency exchange FTX. The group also invested in Elon Musk's xAI and in Mistral, a France-based AI company behind one of the best European open-source large-language models. Sajwani said at the time that the group was excited to be part of the AI revolution and to contribute to the growth of the industry, adding that its investments in Mistral, Anthropic and xAI underscored its dedication to fostering innovation. He said that between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, the group is making a few billion dollars of profit.

Sajwani founded Damac Properties in 2002, and according to Forbes he started out in the food services business, catering to the US military and construction giant Bechtel, before shifting to real estate in 2001 after Dubai allowed foreigners to own property. Forbes puts his net worth at $15.3 billion, making him the 185th richest man in the world. Damac Group, his multi-billion-dollar conglomerate, divides its investments into seven core areas: real estate, capital markets, hotels and resorts, manufacturing, catering, high-end fashion and data centres, with a footprint across North America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Its notable activities include Damac Properties, the acquisition of Italian fashion house Roberto Cavalli and Swiss jewellery brand de GRISOGONO, the 50-storey DAMAC Towers Nine Elms in London and a luxury resort in the Maldives.

stories.Headline: Taisei launches a 150 million dollar fund for AI and robotics startups
stories.Summary:
The Japanese construction company Taisei announced on Monday, November 16, 2026, that it is establishing a new investment fund. This 153-year-old firm is dedicating 150 million dollars to support various startups specializing in robotics and artificial intelligence. The company intends to use these technological advancements to find viable workarounds for a shrinking domestic workforce. This strategic move aims to modernize the business by integrating automation into its traditional construction processes.

The fund will be managed by Pegasus Tech Ventures, a firm based in Silicon Valley that serves as the general partner. This partnership will focus on searching for new investments in automation and related fields through the year 2036. Taisei also plans to target startups that provide liquid-cooling infrastructure and high-density power solutions. These specific investments are intended to support the company as it expands its efforts into the construction of AI data centers.

Anis Uzzaman, who serves as the founder and chief executive officer of Pegasus, explained the purpose of the venture. He stated that the primary objective is to transform a traditional construction firm into a leader enabled by robotics and AI. Uzzaman further noted that the fund will help the company secure the necessary infrastructure for modern data centers. Pegasus currently manages over 2 billion dollars in assets and has previously worked with other Japanese companies like Aisin and Japanet Holdings.

This initiative comes as Japanese businesses struggle with chronic labor shortages, rising wages, and a general backlash against foreign workers. These economic pressures, combined with sliding domestic spending, are pushing more companies to adopt robotic solutions. Taisei has already shown interest in this sector by investing last year in a fund run by Met Fund Advisors. That previous investment focused on emerging startups coming out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

This initiative was unveiled during a visit to Yokosuka in Kanagawa Prefecture.

The new guidelines will require an update to the basic AI policy that was originally compiled in July 2024. These rules will focus on three pillars, including the requirement that humans make all final decisions and accept responsibility for the results. The framework also aims to transform data into a defensive power for the nation. Finally, the ministry seeks to balance the fast spread of AI with the need for enhanced safety.

Minister Koizumi is responsible for this shift and told reporters that the government will not hesitate to revise policies. He explained that revisions are necessary because the field of artificial intelligence changes very rapidly. The minister stated that the government wants to show a new direction for national security. He believes that utilizing AI and data will strengthen the overall defense capabilities of the country.
