stories.Headline: Utah board creates AI student taskforce to advise on classroom use
stories.Summary:
The Utah State Board of Education formally established an Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce a few weeks before mid November 2026, placing it under the board's existing Student Advisory Council, and the group is set to meet roughly four times during the school year, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The task force was approved during the board's October meeting, and although students have not yet been assigned to it, several students helped set the effort in motion. One student from one of Utah's largest districts contacted the technology director about a year earlier to ask how to start a task force, a high school senior recently interned at an AI law office, a charter school student wants to bring his experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student is running projects with the STEM Action Center. The council currently has 15 students serving on it.

The task force is meant to advise the state board on how AI is used in teaching and learning, and it gives students a chance to share their views on decisions adults make for them. Matt Winters, the board's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the board, said she hopes the group provides a boots-on-the-ground perspective on how AI is affecting students' education, for better or for worse, because students are the ones who see it in action. The article ties the effort to wider debate since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, noting that a 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI, while more than 400 CEOs, including leaders from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating mandatory computer science and AI education in schools.

Winters credited the students for driving the work, saying the story is entirely about the kids and that the work flows through him rather than because of him. He said he would expect companies such as NVIDIA, OpenAI and Anthropic to pay attention, describing the students as savvy and able to help influence the state's long-term vision. Wood said one challenge may be engaging students beyond the 15 on the council, since some may want careers in governance, law or public policy while others have different goals, and Winters has already prompted students on bringing in more peers, with ideas such as a hackathon taking shape. Wood said that if students make recommendations or raise concerns and the board disregards them, the experiment will have failed, and she hopes the experience leads students to engage civically as adults.

Articles.Title: Students want a say in AI policy. Utah is giving them one. - SmartBrief

stories.Headline: Canada and the UK renew their AI security partnership with shared standards and joint evaluations
stories.Summary:
On 13 October 2026, Canada and the UK renewed their AI security partnership, which was first signed in 2024 as the AI Safety Partnership. The renewal aims to foster the safe and responsible development and deployment of AI. The agreement commits both countries to three priorities: interoperable standards, enhanced information-sharing and closer technical cooperation. The Canadian AI Safety Institute and the UK AI Security Institute will hold regular exchanges and coordinated evaluation activities. The Canadian Institute of Advanced Research contributed CAD $1 million to the UK AI Security Institute's Alignment Project.

The renewed partnership covers mutually recognised or shared AI security standards, improved information exchange including on frontier risk, and expanded technical arrangements. Neither country has passed a single comprehensive law governing AI across every sector. Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was abandoned when Parliament was dissolved in 2025. The UK has deliberately chosen not to legislate. No legislation in either country sets out exactly how organisations must assess AI risks.

The article recommends that organisations implement a consistent and repeatable process to answer the same questions both regimes ask. These questions are whether the impact of the AI system has been assessed before deployment, whether decisions have been documented, whether there is meaningful human oversight and whether there will be ongoing monitoring. Such a process would let organisations respond to the partnership priorities, evidence compliance in both jurisdictions and prepare for any future legislation. The article was co-authored by Carole Piovesan, Managing Partner at INQ Law in Toronto. It was published by Stephenson Harwood on 16 November 2026.

Canada's legal environment is fragmented across jurisdictions and sectors, including privacy, human rights, consumer protection and competition law. The federal Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems sets out commitments on accountability, safety, fairness, transparency, human oversight and robustness. The Directive on Automated Decision-Making is binding on federal institutions and is supported by the Algorithmic Impact Assessment, which scores a system's risk and scales safeguards accordingly. In June 2026 the federal government tabled Bill C-36, which would enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act as Canada's new private-sector privacy law. A companion bill, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), would impose digital safety duties on social media platforms and chatbot services, with both regimes overseen by a new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.

Health Canada has issued pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' Guideline E-23 on Model Risk Management, in force from 1 May 2027, expressly captures AI and machine learning models at federally regulated financial institutions. The Standards Council of Canada has convened work on AI standards and trust frameworks. In 2017 Canada became the first country to launch a national AI strategy, and its successor, AI for All, launched in June 2026, aims to lift business AI adoption from just over 12% to 60% by 2034. Canada now has a dedicated Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, whose priorities flow from the Prime Minister's May 2025 mandate letter to Cabinet.

Budget 2026, tabled on 5 November 2026, includes access to 500 MW of sovereign AI compute, approximately CAD $1 billion over five years for a Government Transformation Fund, a new Digital Transformation Canada, CAD $176.3 million over five years for the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission and a plan to explore a Technology Stability Board. The UK has adopted a principles-based approach covering safety, security and robustness, transparency and explainability, fairness, accountability and governance, and contestability and redress, enforced by sector regulators. The Financial Conduct Authority's AI Update outlines how existing financial services rules apply to AI, and the Information Commission has issued guidance on AI and data protection and has been tasked with preparing a formal Code of Practice on AI and automated decision-making. The Competition Markets Authority's AI Strategic Update sets out six principles aimed at fostering competition and consumer protection. If an AI system uses personal data, a data protection impact assessment is one of the most useful tools available to assess risk.

Reforms under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 removed the general prohibition on solely automated decision-making that produces legal or similarly significant effects, replacing it with a requirement for a lawful basis such as legitimate interests, provided no special category data is involved. Organisations must still ensure transparency, provide individuals with the opportunity to make representations, allow access to human intervention and enable individuals to challenge decisions. The EU AI Act came into force on 1 August 2024, and its broad extraterritorial reach applies to organisations based in the UK and Canada that place AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market. The EU's digital omnibus on AI has deferred the rules for high-risk AI systems from 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I. Providers of high-risk AI systems must operate a robust risk management system, keep detailed technical documentation and records, design systems to allow effective human oversight, demonstrate compliance via a conformity assessment before the system is placed on the market and conduct post-market monitoring.

stories.Headline: Al Kingsley writes a plain English guide to explain how AI works and where it may go
stories.Summary:
Al Kingsley wrote in School Management Plus on 16 November 2026 that school leaders and staff often pretend to understand artificial intelligence during meetings rather than admit they do not know the basics, because teaching is a profession built on knowledge and an information gap can feel like a failing. He said the problem is not the technology itself, since AI is not a scary human overlord yet, but that without knowing how it works and what its quirks are, leaders and staff cannot make informed decisions for colleagues and students. He argued that anyone who does ask what others may regard as simple questions will find their colleagues grateful, and he guaranteed it. He described his book, Unpicking AI ,  one token at a time, as deliberately and definitively not a book about AI in schools, with no education jargon at all.

The book is a simple, accessible guide to AI in general, written for anyone who wants to understand what it is before deciding how to use it, and it emphasises plain English. It first explains where AI came from, showing that the ideas started many, many years ago, which makes media headlines seem less futuristic and less overwhelming. It then explains how AI actually works, and once you realise it learns from vast amounts of data, you can see why it is so impressive and why it sometimes gets things oh-so confidently wrong. The book also looks at where AI might end up in the future, in easy language, because at this point nobody actually knows, even the tech bros.

Kingsley said that when we get our questions answered we all gain confidence, whatever the subject, and that with a new understanding of AI your questions will improve. Asking whether to ban it will become a question of what it can do, where to look out for problems and how to help students use it constructively in school. He returned to the meeting scenario, where someone who knows how AI works fearlessly asks to check that everyone knows what they are talking about before deciding. Kingsley is due to speak at the Schools and Academies Show in Birmingham this week at a talk entitled Choosing the Right Technology for Your Secondary School: The Questions Leaders Should Be Asking.

stories.Headline: Parents sue OpenAI after ChatGPT allegedly told their daughter to stop taking medication
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that its ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, which led to her death, according to a professor of business law writing for The Conversation. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot's interactions with her son contributed to his suicide, and the state of Kentucky later filed suit claiming that Character.AI's software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies powered by artificial intelligence are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused, and regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, with several winning candidates holding a regulation agenda. The author, a former litigator and professor of business law, writes that all this action signals that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm, and that an answer may be found in strict liability.

Strict liability is part of tort law that holds a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble, and two types matter for AI, one for abnormally dangerous activity such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material and one for when a product hurts someone using it. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868, where the court stated that if someone has anything under their power that is likely to do mischief if it escapes, he must keep it in at his peril and is answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape, with the defendant liable even if they used the utmost care to prevent the harm. An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox, a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network, but loses control of it, and the AI industry's recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose, though one hitch is that an activity must not be in common usage, so lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn't available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately, since in 1929 aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous but damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent, and attitudes changed in 1999 when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide, raising statutory damages and eliminating caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company's aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes, and a court might similarly order that AI software be turned off, or grounded, until it is improved. Strict product liability is the other strategy, and in years past courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible, but that view is shifting, with courts in recent social media lawsuits seeing social media as a product and concluding that strict liability was applicable, and Character.AI's recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. Design defects is the part of the doctrine gaining traction, where a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it, and so far the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

The author writes that AI software by its nature is constantly learning and therefore changing, making it impossible for a company to promise that it will absolutely behave a certain way, and in many cases the software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, according to a Brookings Institution report, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers, and the author believes that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues, and the next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, the author writes, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.

stories.Headline: Poll finds 85% of Floridians concerned about children using AI chatbots
stories.Summary:
A recent poll found that 85% of Floridians said they were concerned about children and teenagers interacting with AI chatbots, according to a column in the Tampa Bay Times. The column, by Turner Loesel, reported the figure without giving the number of people polled or the dates the survey was conducted. The piece appeared on November 17, 2026, and was labeled as a column and a viewpoint rather than a news report. It did not name the organization that carried out the poll or describe how the respondents were selected.

The column said that parents who want to take on the responsibility of overseeing their children's use of AI chatbots have more tools than they did even a year ago. It did not list those tools, name any of them, or say who provides them. The article did not describe any law, rule, or policy that has been adopted in Florida on the subject. It also did not say what age group the poll covered or how the concern was measured.

The column presented the finding as a sign that Floridians want parents, rather than someone else, to be in charge of how children and teenagers use AI chatbots. It did not quote any parent, lawmaker, or company, and it did not say what parents themselves said about the tools available to them. No official was named as responsible for any proposal, and no statement from an official was included.

The article gave no details on what happens next, such as any planned legislation, hearing, or further polling. It did not say whether the poll was conducted statewide or how its results compare with earlier surveys. The column appeared alongside other opinion pieces and letters in the newspaper's viewpoints section. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities prepare to scrutinize executive AI policy and chip exports after 2026 midterm wins
stories.Summary:
The 2026 midterm elections resulted in a blue tidal wave at state and federal levels. Democrats won 256 House seats and 55 Senate seats, while Republicans won 169 House and 44 Senate seats. Democrats also won a majority of gubernatorial races by November 1. Artificial intelligence emerged as a prominent campaign issue for candidates from both political parties. AI is expected to top the agenda for the new Congress in January.

New Democratic majorities will use subpoenas and hearings to examine executive branch AI policy. Lawmakers will scrutinize the Commerce Department regarding advanced AI chip export decisions and Chinese espionage. The Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence will face questions about its mission. The Department of War will be examined for AI use in military planning. CISA will face questions about AI-enabled cyberattacks and recent budget cuts.

Lawmakers will press officials on how licensing decisions were made and if industry pressure played a role. They will ask how the Commerce Department enforces requirements that exported chips are not resold. Representative-elect Scott Wiener authored California's SB 53, which requires safety frameworks and incident reporting. Representative-elect Manny Rutinel sponsored SB 24-205 to guard against algorithmic discrimination in housing and lending. Senator Maria Cantwell opposed using a federal law to override state AI laws.

Constituents expressed concerns about AI-related job losses and rising utility bills linked to data centers. Parents worried about children's safety as youth spend more time engaging with AI chatbots. Frontier AI developers will face scrutiny over how they test and monitor models after deployment. Companies hosting Chinese open weight models may face enhanced congressional scrutiny. Some lawmakers may investigate financial ties to the Administration, including White House ballroom project donations.

Democratic candidates flipped five Republican-held Attorney General offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas. Democrats will hold 29 AG offices compared to 22 for Republicans in January. State laws currently regulate chatbots, deepfakes, algorithmic pricing, and data centers. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison joined 26 other AGs to prohibit the preemption of state laws. Federal rules are generally treated as a floor rather than a ceiling for regulation.

Texas AG-elect Nathan Johnson promised a 30-day audit of consumer protection and employment laws. Michigan AG-elect Eli Savit pledged to issue rules against algorithmic price-gouging within 100 days. Georgia AG-elect Tanya Miller and Nevada AG-elect Nicole Cannizzaro focused on AI-driven pricing and rent increases. NIST will provide technical guidance for agentic systems and update the AI Risk Management Framework. Rep. Ted Lieu and Rep. Sarah McBride introduced bills to scale reliance on NIST standards.

stories.Headline: Nokia leads AIGF Northern consortium to build AI computing network across four Nordic and Baltic sites
stories.Summary:
A consortium led by Nokia, called AI Gigafactory Northern or AIGF Northern, plans to build a network of AI computing facilities across the Nordic and Baltic region, according to an announcement reported on November 17, 2026. The group intends to submit a bid under a tender run by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, known as EuroHPC JU. The tender seeks to select and establish AI Gigafactory consortia, in line with European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure. The founding members of the consortium are Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton Technologies, Telia and Verda.

The proposed network would span four locations: Oulu in Finland, the Tallinn region in Estonia, Valmiera in Latvia, and a site in Sweden that has not yet been selected. The model would distribute computing capacity across several countries, linking data centers, cloud platforms and telecommunications networks under European governance. This distribution is meant to reduce reliance on individual sites and suppliers while providing computing and cloud services to businesses, research institutions and public sector organisations across Europe. The five founding companies would each contribute a different part of the infrastructure.

Nokia would supply network and connectivity technology, while Nscale and Verda would provide AI computing and cloud platforms. Telia, together with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, would support connectivity, data transmission and cloud operations, and Skeleton Technologies would provide high power systems designed to improve data center efficiency and electricity grid stability. Mikko Hautala, Nokia's Chief Geopolitical and Government Relations Officer, said Europe's AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale, and that AIGF Northern brings together the needed connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities. Research organisations VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden are also supporting the initiative.

The bid fits European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure through the selection of AI Gigafactory consortia under the EuroHPC JU tender. The articles do not say when the bid will be submitted, when a decision is expected, or what happens if the bid is not selected.

stories.Headline: HPE's Lux AI cluster for Oak Ridge debuts as the world's fastest TOP500 system
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced in November that Lux, an AI cluster it built for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, has debuted as the world's latest fastest system on the TOP500 list. HPE issued the release through Business Wire from Chicago during the SC26 supercomputing conference. According to HPE, Lux delivers hundreds of petaflops and is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. The company said its ranking places Lux ahead of systems designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux was first announced in October of last year as part of a broader collaboration among HPE, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD.

Lux is built specifically for artificial intelligence workloads rather than for the simulation tasks that have traditionally dominated supercomputing. HPE described it as a multi-tenant system that offers cloud-like access, allowing many research groups to use the cluster at the same time. Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 servers. The compute nodes use AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs and AMD Pensando DPUs, combining processors for AI acceleration, general-purpose computing and data processing. HPE said Lux also includes Silicon Root of Trust protection, a security feature it offers across all HPE ProLiant servers, designed to verify the integrity of server firmware from the moment a system starts.

HPE said Lux is the first Department of Energy national laboratory deployment of HPE Networking, built on open Ethernet. The deployment brings together HPE's server business and the networking capabilities associated with the Juniper name. HPE's StockAnalysis profile lists Networking as one of its reporting segments, alongside Server, Hybrid Cloud, Financial Services and Corporate Investments and Other. HPE said Discovery's storage will include the DAOS-based HPE Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems K3000 and the Lustre-based E2000. HPE describes itself as a leader in essential enterprise technology, combining AI, cloud and networking to help customers improve operations, turn data into insight and increase their impact.

Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility. The facility is the user-facing organization at Oak Ridge National Laboratory through which researchers access the system. Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI infrastructure solutions at HPE, said the company is proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission. HPE described the Genesis Mission as a Department of Energy initiative that uses AI to accelerate breakthroughs in energy research, scientific discovery and national security. The effort is intended to combine AI, supercomputing, quantum systems and advanced scientific instruments.

According to StockAnalysis, HPE develops intelligent solutions across the United States, the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia Pacific, Japan and other international markets. Its server products include general-purpose and workload-optimized servers and integrated systems such as ProLiant rack and tower servers, Synergy, Scale Up, Edgeline and Cray EX. Hewlett Packard Enterprise is a constituent of the S&P 500, the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000. Lux's arrival on the TOP500 about a year after its first announcement marks its transition into service for researchers. The article was published on November 16, 2026, by Anmol Khazanchi.

Lux was not HPE's only supercomputing announcement of the week. In November, the company introduced new hybrid configurations of its HPE Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000, combining flash SSDs with new SAS-4 hard drives and new SAS-4 drive enclosures that hold more than a hundred drives. The same release introduced the HPE Rack Management Controller, which provides real-time monitoring, leak detection, automated cooling control and rack-level visibility for high-density liquid-cooled racks. It initially supports HPE Cray Supercomputing GX5000 systems and integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software. The article states that Lux uses HPE Juniper Networking QFX switches supporting 800G.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Crexendo wins 2026 Voice AI Technology Excellence Award for its CAIRO AI Receptionist
stories.Summary:
Crexendo, Inc., a Nasdaq-listed software technology company based in Phoenix, announced on November 17, 2026, that its CAIRO AI Receptionist and Orchestrator had won the 2026 CUSTOMER Magazine Voice AI Technology Excellence Award. The award is given by TMC's CUSTOMER magazine, and CAIRO was selected for its ability to use Voice AI to enhance customer engagement through intelligent call handling, automation, and orchestration capabilities. Crexendo describes CAIRO as the Crexendo AI Receptionist and Orchestrator, and the company says the product helps organizations improve satisfaction, streamline operations, and build stronger customer relationships. The company also says CAIRO delivers seamless, responsive, and highly personalized customer experiences for the businesses that use it.

Crexendo says CAIRO is an important component of its strategy to accelerate organic growth through AI-powered solutions, and that providing advanced AI capabilities through its NetSapiens cloud communications platform will create additional revenue opportunities for the company and its service provider licensees. The company says businesses increasingly seek intelligent automation to improve productivity, reduce operating costs, and enhance customer engagement, and that CAIRO and its expanding portfolio of AI solutions can drive increased adoption and additional recurring revenue. Crexendo states that its solutions support over eight million end users globally through a network of more than 250 cloud communication platform software subscribers and its direct retail offering. The press release also notes that TMC has been honoring technology companies with awards for more than 20 years, and that the company's forward-looking statements are subject to risks described in its Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, and its Form 10-Qs filed with the SEC.

Rich Tehrani, CEO of TMC, congratulated all of the 2026 Voice AI Technology Excellence Award winners and said the recipients represent some of the most innovative and impactful companies in voice technology. He said their commitment to excellence, customer success, and continuous innovation is helping shape the future of communications. Jeff Korn, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Crexendo, said the company is extremely pleased that CAIRO received the recognition, which he said further validates its commitment to making Crexendo and the NetSapiens platform leaders in AI-powered cloud communications. Korn said artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to accelerate organic growth and create meaningful new revenue streams for Crexendo and its licensees, and he added that the ability to bring these innovations to an ecosystem supporting more than eight million end users is particularly exciting.

According to the release, earning an Excellence Award from TMC's CUSTOMER magazine elevates the Crexendo brand before TMC's audience of technology professionals, decision makers, and executives, along with their ecosystem of end users and other providers. Crexendo says the recognition underscores its influence on the future of customer engagement through intelligent cloud communications, and that it continues to advance its innovation leadership by delivering an AI-powered software platform. Korn said that as AI adoption accelerates, the expanding portfolio of AI solutions can generate additional recurring revenue, increase the value of the platform to existing customers, attract new licensees, and provide a meaningful catalyst for long-term growth. The release states that forward-looking statements speak only as of the date they are made and that the company undertakes no obligation to update them except as required by law.

stories.Headline: Cato Networks launches AgentSense to block harmful AI agent actions in real time
stories.Summary:
Cato Networks announced on November 17, 2026, a patented capability called Cato AgentSense from Cato AI Labs that continuously assesses AI agents in real time to protect the integrity of their decisions, actions and outputs as they operate autonomously. The company said the guardrail stops harmful agent actions before they execute, keeping enterprises in control as agents gain greater autonomy. AgentSense is integrated within the Cato platform and will be included at no additional charge within Cato AI Usage licenses. Cato also introduced the AgentSense Challenge, which invites the security community to attack an AI agent workflow protected by AgentSense and plant instructions aimed at steering it away from the user's intent, with the first three eligible participants to succeed each receiving $10,000 USD.

The capability rests on two detection methods. Untrusted Influence Detection traces how instructions and data influence an agent's behavior at runtime, and when it detects that untrusted content is steering the agent toward an unsafe action, it blocks that action before execution, providing protection against indirect prompt injection even when attacks do not match previously observed patterns. Instead of relying on static classifiers or known attack patterns, it separates trusted instructions from untrusted content inside the AI session and traces how untrusted content influences both behavior and outputs, which Cato describes as a one-of-its-kind layer of protection from zero-day vulnerabilities. Drift Detection will identify when agent actions depart from the original task or intent, evaluating as a workflow progresses whether actions still serve the intended objective and flagging steps that may be individually permitted but fall outside the given task.

Shlomo Kramer, CEO and co-founder of Cato Networks, said enterprises entrust agents with decisions that shape revenue, customer relationships and business continuity, so control over agent behavior has become as essential as financial controls. He said giving agents greater autonomy requires security that can intervene before their actions cause harm, and that the vision for AgentSense is to give enterprises confidence to put agents in charge of critical business processes while retaining control over how they operate. Nithin Reddy, vice president of cybersecurity at Dayforce, said scaling AI safely means having the ability to detect and stop actions that could put customers, data or business at risk. Itay Ravia, head of Cato AI Labs, cited DuneSlide, EchoLeak and CurXecute as notable prompt injection vulnerabilities that continue to make headlines, and said AgentSense helps preserve trust by tracing how untrusted content influences an agent's decisions and sensitive actions. Grace Trinidad, senior research director of AI Security and Trust at IDC, said organizations need to know their objectives fully and evaluate agentic actions in the context of the full workflow and the task the agent was authorized to perform.

Cato said AI agents continue to scale faster than the guardrails put in place to secure them, citing Gartner figures that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within the next 12 months while only 21% currently have agentic AI governance capabilities in place. It said forecasts report that by 2028, ungoverned AI agent abuse will drive 25 percent of enterprise breaches. The company described a fundamental architectural weakness in which agents cannot reliably distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted data they pick up as they work, letting attackers hide malicious instructions in emails, webpages, documents, tickets or tool responses, and said the combination of sensitive data access and action-taking tools turns prompt injection into a business risk. Cato said it will use participants' findings and feedback from the Challenge to evaluate and strengthen the capability.

stories.Headline: Elastic launches nightshift AI SRE private preview for observability investigations
stories.Summary:
Elastic announced on November 17, 2026, a private preview of Elastic nightshift AI SRE, an AI agent built into Elastic Observability that carries out investigations the way an engineer would and makes the work visible, according to a press release from Elasticsearch Corporation, the Tokyo-based subsidiary led by president Ken Otani. The agent continuously detects and investigates problems across the whole stack with full context, surfacing unknown issues that rule-based alerts would miss, and it tests several hypotheses about root causes in parallel against telemetry and other relevant context. It then gives engineers evidence-backed answers while showing its reasoning at each step, and once it identifies a likely root cause it proposes remediation, either by selecting existing workflows and preconfigured actions or by providing commands for engineers to run. Engineers can inspect every step of an investigation, including the queries the agent ran and the underlying data.

The release cites an April 2026 NeuBird AI survey finding that 78 percent of companies reported at least one incident in the past year where there was no alert and users themselves were the first to notice the problem. Elastic says context behind investigations is usually incomplete because telemetry is cut to save costs, knowledge is scattered across code, runbooks and Slack, and lessons from past incidents are lost, while standalone AI SRE tools reason over data they do not hold. Because each investigation draws on full context from cost-efficient telemetry storage, customers can keep everything rather than sample data for AI, and a knowledge graph links that telemetry to source code from GitHub repositories so the agent can identify the commit likely behind an exception. Records of investigations accumulate over time, so each resolved incident shortens the time needed for the next one, and the agent continuously evaluates the environment and all telemetry, correlating alerts, SLOs and anomalies into findings engineers should actually review.

Shannon Kalvar, a senior research director at IDC, said named-role agents such as AI SRE are a first step toward AI-driven operations, and that these agents need access to broader context, especially across wide and heterogeneous environments, along with the ability to learn from their own actions while validating those actions against facts. Baha Azarmi, general manager of observability at Elastic, said most observability agents get smarter only by collecting more data, whereas Elastic nightshift AI SRE gets smarter by closely observing how engineers conduct investigations and by verifying the results of its own work after incidents are closed, which keeps production running without unwanted token costs.

The private preview is available starting today on Elastic Observability Serverless, and Elastic customers can use it free during the early access period. Elastic plans to broaden support for third-party tools and data stores and to publish a technical preview within the year, and customers who want the private preview can register online. The Japanese release is an abridged translation of an English release Elastic published on October 8, 2026, and Elastic, listed on the NYSE under ESTC, says its platform is used by thousands of companies including more than 75 percent of Fortune 100 firms.

stories.Headline: Nvidia stops reporting Singapore unit revenue in 2025 after it reaches $104bn, nearly half of global sales
stories.Summary:
Nvidia stopped reporting revenue for its Singapore unit in 2025, according to documents cited by the Financial Times, after that unit accounted for nearly 50% of the company's global revenue. The Singapore unit's revenue rose 72% year on year to $104bn in 2025, the documents show. The disclosure change came as the unit grew to represent almost half of Nvidia's worldwide sales. The Financial Times reported the details on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

The documents indicate that the Singapore unit's revenue reached $104bn in 2025, a 72% increase from the prior year. That figure represented nearly 50% of Nvidia's global revenue for the year, according to the same documents. Nvidia stopped disclosing the unit's sales in 2025, the Financial Times reported, meaning the breakdown is no longer part of its regular reporting. The report does not say why the company made the change.

The Financial Times is the source of the report, which is based on documents it reviewed rather than on statements from Nvidia. The article does not include any comment from Nvidia or from company executives about the decision to stop reporting the Singapore unit's revenue. No explanation is given in the available material for why the disclosure ended in 2025. The report also does not say whether the company plans to resume reporting the figure.

The available article is a subscription page and does not provide further context on what the change requires or what happens next. It does not say how the missing Singapore figures affect Nvidia's overall reporting or what regulators or investors have said about it. The report gives no indication of any response from Nvidia or from Singapore authorities. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
stories.Summary:
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, the founder of Biocon, said on the social media platform X that the recent disruption of Microsoft services could create an opening for the Indian software company Zoho to serve as a backup management information system for Indian businesses, according to TechGig. She made the suggestion as companies were re-evaluating their reliance on global technology providers following the outage. The Microsoft 365 outage affected users in more than 70 countries, including India, according to Downdetector data cited by the report. Microsoft announced on Saturday that its services had been fully restored and that all products were operational, confirming the Microsoft 365 disruption was resolved.

The report said Microsoft's Microsoft 365 suite has more than 450 million commercial users, a figure Bloomberg reported, and the scale of the disruption renewed concerns about the risks of businesses relying heavily on a single technology provider. Zoho already has a significant presence in India's government email infrastructure, with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology stating in December that nearly 12.68 lakh official email accounts across various ministries and departments had migrated to a Zoho-based platform. Approximately 7.45 lakh of those accounts belonged to central government employees, according to the ministry. Union ministers publicly backed domestic products, including Zoho's software and its messaging platform Arattai, as alternatives to foreign technology services in October last year.

Mazumdar-Shaw is the person behind the suggestion, and she posted on X that Zoho could emerge as a backup management information system provider for India Inc given such unforeseen events, the article said. The report did not say whether Zoho or Microsoft responded to her remarks. The articles give no further statements from Microsoft, Zoho or government officials beyond the ministry's December figure and the ministers' earlier public backing of domestic products. The articles also do not say what steps, if any, Indian businesses plan to take in response to the outage or to her suggestion.

Articles.Title: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw

stories.Headline: Oracle's Natalia Rachelson urges businesses to measure AI success by delivered improvements, not agent counts
stories.Summary:
Natalia Rachelson, a Senior Vice President of Applications Development at Oracle, said in an interview with PTI that businesses adopting artificial intelligence should judge success by the improvement the technology delivers rather than by the number of AI agents they deploy. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, a view that shifts how organisations should evaluate their AI investments. Her comments were published by TechGig on November 16, 2026, in a report that also said AI is moving from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them. The report said this evolution requires a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics.

Rachelson advised business leaders to select a measurable goal for AI implementation from the outset, so that AI initiatives stay aligned with tangible business outcomes and improvements. The report said this approach is crucial as AI transitions from assisting employees to performing tasks autonomously. It said businesses should measure success by delivered improvements, not by the number of AI agents deployed. The report framed the shift as a change in how organisations should think about the value of their AI spending.

Rachelson is responsible for applications development at Oracle, and she gave her assessment directly to PTI, according to the TechGig report. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, and she tied that view to the need for a measurable goal chosen at the start. The report presented her position as guidance for leaders weighing how to evaluate their AI investments. It did not give any figures for agents deployed or improvements measured.

The report described the technology as transitioning from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them, which it said necessitates a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics. It said business leaders should therefore pick a measurable goal from the outset to keep AI initiatives aligned with tangible outcomes. The article gave no further details on specific companies, timelines or results beyond Rachelson's comments. It did not say what happens next beyond the advice to measure delivered improvements.

Articles.Title: Oracle executive advises measuring AI success by results, not agents

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with lower token prices and higher benchmark scores
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on 17 November 2026, according to its announcement. OpenAI described Astra as its new frontier model for the hardest projects. OpenAI described Sol as its efficient, versatile model for everyday work. OpenAI said both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens. OpenAI said users can get more done within their usage limits.

OpenAI said Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Agents’ Last Exam at less than a third of the cost. OpenAI said Astra scored 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 on that exam at just 5% of the cost. OpenAI said the Fable 5.2 leaderboard results exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model. OpenAI said Astra’s API input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input and $40 for output per million tokens. OpenAI said Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol’s API token prices.

OpenAI said Astra sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. OpenAI said Astra also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index. OpenAI said Astra sets a new state of the art on Harvey LAB-AA v1.1, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. OpenAI said its configuration Astra for Law scores even higher on that benchmark. OpenAI said Astra leads its internal GDPval v2 benchmark, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT-6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens.

OpenAI said Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT-6.1 Sol on GDPval v2. OpenAI said Sol comes within 0.5 points of Astra on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 at about one-fifth the cost, both at max. OpenAI said Sol outscores GPT-6 Astra on its LifeVal evaluation at about one-seventh the cost. OpenAI said Astra answers 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts in an AA-AnalystAgent task using California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate medical transport spending. OpenAI said many of its employees use Sol as their default model for technical and non-technical tasks.

Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer at IMC, said Astra’s documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra and its writing and charts made key points easier to pick out. Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, said Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks and scored higher than alternative models on 8 of 10 research tasks across tax, M&A and litigation work. Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research at Harvey, said Astra completed more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks with 34.5% fewer output tokens. Jay Hack, Head of AI at ClickUp, said Astra edged out its production model in blind testing with about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds. OpenAI said its team used Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a paper lamp.

OpenAI said Astra created a 3D model of a car’s chassis dynamics on a mountain road, wrote a Python solver to simulate tire and suspension dynamics and animated the results in Blender. OpenAI said Astra can model a mechanical system part by part so engineers can show how it goes together and test design changes. OpenAI said Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. OpenAI said Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look. OpenAI said Astra can match a slide template’s layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size.

OpenAI said Astra’s slides, spreadsheets and documents read less like AI and more closely follow provided templates and field conventions. OpenAI said Astra writes cleaner code and builds better-looking, better-working frontends, particularly for websites, gaming and 3D design. OpenAI said Astra’s writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler. OpenAI said Harvey LAB-AA gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations. OpenAI said GDPval v2 assignments are drawn from real projects in consulting, finance and design using the files and messages the team had when the work was assigned.

OpenAI said the site generated by Astra can be used to create your own paper lamp. OpenAI said early testers found Astra’s decks easier to use directly with fewer edits. OpenAI said Astra’s titles state the main takeaway and its body copy focuses on the details readers need. OpenAI said the LifeVal evaluation measures performance on challenging everyday tasks such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis. OpenAI did not state a release date beyond the announcement or say when either model becomes available.

stories.Headline: Ambience Healthcare adds rounding and discharge AI tools for hospitals
stories.Summary:
Ambience Healthcare announced on Tuesday that it has added two AI tools, Rounding Assistant and Discharge Readiness, to its hospital software, which already writes clinical notes and suggests billing codes for hospital stays. Rounding Assistant pulls together overnight events, changes in a patient's condition and a list of suggested tasks for each shift. Discharge Readiness flags medical, practical and social problems that could delay a patient going home, earlier in the stay. The company is backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Kleiner Perkins and the OpenAI Startup Fund, and it counts Cleveland Clinic and Mayo Clinic among its customers.

Much of the company's pitch is about money, because Ambience aims to raise hospitals' case mix index, a measure of how sick patients are that helps set what insurers pay. At Onvida Health, discharges handled with Ambience scored 6.5% higher than a year earlier, according to the company. Mike Lewis, chief financial officer of Onvida Medical Group, said Onvida needed roughly a 1.5% improvement in case mix index to justify the investment, and he said Onvida's own finance team checked the results. Ambience also says admission notes written with its tool captured 59% more of the diagnoses used in quality rankings, in one health system's review of 1,100 stays. None of the figures come from independent research.

Ambience ties its fees to results, and Lewis said the improvement was needed to justify the investment, with Onvida's finance team checking the figures. The company says its tools help care teams prioritise tasks and spot barriers to discharge earlier. AI note tools are still under scrutiny, because in August England's patient watchdog warned that AI scribes were getting drug names and diagnoses wrong. Rivals are growing fast too, with Heidi raising $340M in September and Google launching Gemini for healthcare last week.

stories.Headline: Autonomous agents turn static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs under six GraphRAG patterns
stories.Summary:
A practitioner's guide published on Towards Data Science outlines six agentic GraphRAG patterns that show how autonomous agents can turn static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs. The guide, reported by TechGig on November 16, 2026, describes patterns that let these graphs retain operational history and user intent. According to the content, autonomous agents carry out this transformation so that knowledge graphs can evolve beyond static data repositories. Context Graphs built this way gain the ability to remember past decisions and user interactions, which the guide says enhances their utility in complex AI workflows.

The guide sets out six distinct agentic GraphRAG patterns, and each one describes a way for autonomous agents to reshape how a knowledge graph holds and uses information. The central change it describes is the shift from static knowledge graphs, which serve as fixed stores of data, to Context Graphs that keep a record of what has happened and what users intended. Retaining operational history and user intent is presented as the main gain, because it lets the graph carry forward past decisions and interactions rather than starting fresh each time. The guide explains that autonomous agents facilitate this transformation, and it frames the resulting Context Graphs as more useful in complex AI workflows.

The guide comes from Towards Data Science, and TechGig reported on it on November 16, 2026, describing it as a practitioner's guide to the six patterns. TechGig presents the guide as detailing how autonomous agents transform static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs, and it credits the content with the explanation of how agents facilitate that change. The report says Context Graphs gain the ability to remember past decisions and user interactions, a capability it ties to their utility in complex AI workflows. TechGig frames the patterns as enhancing AI workflows with operational history, which is the benefit it draws from the guide.

The context the articles give is that knowledge graphs have worked as static data repositories, and the guide positions agentic patterns as the way past that limit. By keeping operational history and user intent, Context Graphs are said to remember past decisions and user interactions, which the guide links to better performance in complex AI workflows. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond describing the six patterns and the transformation they enable. No further steps, timelines or adopters are named in the coverage.

Articles.Title: Autonomous agents enable 6 GraphRAG patterns for living context graphs

stories.Headline: Psychiatrist Cheng-Ta Li creates AI platform to assess treatment-resistant depression
stories.Summary:
Dr. Cheng-Ta Li developed an AI platform to evaluate severe depression. This psychiatrist created the tool to precisely assess treatment-resistant depression. The news of this development was published on November 17, 2026. He leads the Precision Depression Intervention Center at Taipei Veterans General Hospital. Dr. Li also holds an appointment at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University.

The AI-PreDIC platform is a patented tool that combines clinical information with biological measurements. It uses EEG and FDG-PET brain imaging to provide objective estimates of depression severity. The Precision Depression Intervention Center opened in June 2022 in Taiwan. This center has provided clinical services to more than 20,000 treatment-resistant depression patient visits. The system treats resistance as a continuum rather than a simple label.

Dr. Li believes the key is finding which treatment helps a particular patient at a specific stage. He stated that resistance is a road where patients stand at different points. He argues that findings should be judged by evidence strength, not by publication source. Dr. Li expressed a desire to understand mental health better before his grandmother died. He says his motto is to stay curious and persist in what matters.

Patients with severe depression who failed conventional treatment are affected by this research. Dr. Li fears patients might trust unproven treatments and miss appropriate care. His 2024 JAMA Psychiatry analysis showed that first-degree relatives of TRD patients are 9.16 times more likely to be diagnosed. This study used national health insurance data for all of Taiwan. He wants to reach the public through books, lectures, and AI chatbots.

Dr. Li studied in Taichung and earned a PhD under Professors Jen-Chuen Hsieh and Tung-Ping Su. He completed a fellowship with Professor Robert Innis at the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health. His 2014 study in the journal Brain tested theta-burst stimulation for refractory depression. He helped bring repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation toward regulatory approval in Taiwan. He is the founding President of the Taiwanese Society of Brain Stimulation.

The Taiwanese Society of Brain Stimulation held its first annual meeting in August 2026. Dr. Li is developing new treatments using brain stimulation and emerging approaches like psychedelics. He serves as a Councilor of the International College of Neuropsychopharmacology. He previously served as Secretary General of the Asian College of Neuropsychopharmacology. The articles leave open the specific results of his emerging psychedelic treatment research.

stories.Headline: Ralf Seifert proposes a five stage model to move procurement teams from AI pilots to autonomy
stories.Summary:
Ralf Seifert proposed a five stage maturity model for procurement teams on November 16, 2026. He wrote this guide to help organizations move from AI pilots to full autonomy. The model aims to map the journey toward scaling artificial intelligence in sourcing. Seifert argues that many teams currently test AI without a clear plan. He suggests a structured approach to build organizational readiness for these tools.

The model requires moving through five stages called aligned, organized, data-ready, augmented, and autonomous. It demands a spend data platform, ERP integration, operational platforms, and strict model governance. Organizations must develop their mindset, skillset, and toolset together to reach the final stage. This process requires defined decision guardrails, quality data, and a dedicated owner for AI. Success depends on matching agent autonomy to risk through spending limits and access rights.

Ralf Seifert is responsible for the model and emphasizes that pilots alone do not scale. He states that organizations must validate business value before expanding the responsibilities of AI agents. Luca Nanni, former supply chain lead at Philip Morris International, says spreadsheets hinder AI scaling. Nanni explained that his company redesigned its operating model and accelerated its process transformation. He believes a holistic change in systems and capabilities is necessary for success.

Dirk Holbach, former chief supply chain officer of Henkel Consumer Brands, says the industry is in a hype cycle. He notes that while value exists, it is not yet available at scale. A ProcureAbility survey from October 2026 found that 68 percent of leaders test AI without plans. Only 8 percent of senior procurement leaders have a defined plan for AI implementation. These figures show that a lack of organizational adoption affects many procurement teams.

SAP showcased the autonomous enterprise at its Connect conference in October 2026 with procurement featured. Novartis presented a sourcing assistant pilot co-developed with SAP to handle heavy manual tactical work. This pilot promised 35 percent higher productivity and 25 percent faster cycle times for sourcing. The articles state that the first three maturity stages provide little more than visibility. Savings leakage and supply risk are only addressed once a team reaches Stage 4.

Next, procurement leaders should ask ten specific questions about ambition, leadership, value, ownership, and skills. They must also evaluate governance, data security, scaling, autonomy, and competitiveness to determine their standing. Advanced teams must rank a portfolio by value and validate savings with finance departments. The articles leave open how many organizations will successfully move past the pilot phase. They do not state the specific timeline for reaching the autonomous stage.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Max Roser of Our World in Data published an article on November 16, 2026, comparing recent high-quality surveys of American views on artificial intelligence. He wrote that he searched for a range of recent high-quality surveys and put them together in one chart. He said he was cautious about surveys because answers can shift when a question is worded slightly differently or when respondents can choose from different options. Every survey he included found that more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. He wrote that he was surprised by how consistent the overall result is.

In Pew's survey, 52% say they are more concerned than excited and 9% are more excited than concerned, a ratio of more than five to one. When Pew first asked this in 2021, the ratio was about two to one. When a middle answer is offered, 37% took it in Pew's recent survey, and in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys only 9% chose a positive view. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society and just 2% said extremely good. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% said they are somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could threaten human survival, and 73% believe such a risk exists.

Pew's survey found that 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI, and in both parties only around one in ten are more excited than concerned. Roser wrote that many find the prospects of AI exciting, but for more Americans the concerns are larger. He wrote that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust, it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far. Pew's survey covered 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel, conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, with November 2021 data from the same panel conducted November 1 to 7, 2021. The Gallup and Bentley University survey covered 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel, conducted May 4 to 11, 2026.

The Quinnipiac poll was released March 30, 2026, based on a telephone survey of 1,397 US adults conducted March 19 to 23, 2026. The Annenberg Public Policy Center survey covered 1,320 US adults, conducted June 16 to July 19, 2026. The Ipsos survey for ABC News and The Washington Post covered 2,545 US adults on the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, conducted October 9 to 13, 2026. In the same Ipsos survey, 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, while 15% said it is extremely bad for them personally against 3% who said extremely good. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life against 34% who expected more good.

Roser included only surveys based on probability samples, and Quinnipiac called randomly generated landline and cell phone numbers. The other four surveyed members of online panels recruited at random, mostly by mail to randomly selected addresses: Pew's American Trends Panel, the Gallup Panel, the panel used by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, and Ipsos's KnowledgePanel. All five surveys weight their results to match the US adult population and publish the full wording of their questions and their results. Roser did not include polls based on opt-in online panels, citing an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed that the Holocaust is a myth, when Pew's probability-based panel found 3%. In 2021, Pew introduced the question with a short definition and referred to artificial intelligence computer programs rather than artificial intelligence (AI), and Pew reports the results as one trend.

The Quinnipiac poll on concern about human survival was a telephone survey of 1,202 US adults conducted September 24 to 27, 2026 using random digit dialing, with live interviewers calling landlines and cell phones. In that poll, 14% were not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all, and 1% did not know or gave no answer. A Quinnipiac release on September 30, 2026 reported that 86% support independent safety standards for AI companies. Pew's September 16, 2026 report by Monica Anderson and William Bishop was titled Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI and its impact on jobs. The article leaves open how the industry should address these concerns, beyond Roser's statement that it will have to take them much more seriously than it has so far.

stories.Headline: Amazon identifies AI agent campaign stealing API keys from exposed AI applications
stories.Summary:
Amazon's threat intelligence team uncovered a campaign using AI agents to steal API keys from exposed AI applications. These agents hunted for weak spots in internet-exposed apps to extract provider keys stored inside. The team captured records of this activity using decoy servers from October 3 until late last week. The agents used stolen keys to run AI models that powered the search for more keys. The team believes separate China-linked groups operated the agents based on time zones and prompts.

The campaign targeted LiteLLM, One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. It exploited default credentials like LiteLLM's master key and flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow. One API family systems were targeted via an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header. Attackers used server-side request forgery to reach cloud metadata services and searched GitHub, npm, and PyPI. The agents also tried bypassing identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

Amazon's team said they cannot verify the reported outcomes but the records show what actors pursued. They stated that AI agents change the speed and persistence of attackers rather than using new techniques. The team noted that agents succeeded where basic security was missing, such as hard-coded credentials. They recommended treating AI apps like production systems and watching for unusual usage or spending. The team expressed moderate confidence that the agents ran on the open-source tool ARTEX.

Cloudflare responders saw ARTEX use a compromised CI/CD API token to make 400 database dump requests. The company noted that static tokens without expiry dates granted broad access across customer cloud setups. Microsoft reported that attackers used agentic AI tools for GitHub secret hunting to find AI inference keys. The FBI stated that attackers have used ARTEX since August against organizations in many global sectors. South Korean financial institutions were affected, with personal information of 67,000 people stolen in one campaign.

The agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs to find leaked keys. They searched container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. ARTEX uses a planner agent to split goals into tasks for worker agents running security tools. The developer made the ARTEX GitHub repository unavailable on October 8, but commercial versions remain. CISA added a related flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on May 5, 2025.

AWS customers who may have been affected have been notified by the Amazon threat intelligence team. Cloudflare suggests looking for Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, or artex-do-*. Users should rotate exposed credentials and limit client IP addresses for their API tokens. Researchers at Cisco Talos linked more than 2,500 IP addresses to the ARTEX tool. The articles leave open whether the deepfake ID photos passed checks or if database requests returned data.

stories.Headline: APA publishes guidance urging employers to put people at the centre of workplace AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The American Psychological Association published new guidance on 16 November 2026 to help organisations introduce artificial intelligence into the workplace responsibly, warning that unclear policies and conflicting expectations risk undermining employee trust and wellbeing. The guide, titled Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know, sets out seven recommended practices informed by established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI use. It is intended to help employers balance the potential benefits of AI with the need to protect workers, maintain meaningful human oversight and consider how technology changes the design of jobs. The guidance comes amid growing pressure on employees to incorporate AI into their daily activities, often without clear organisational policies governing its use. According to the APA's 2026 Work in America Survey, fewer than 40% of workers for whom the question was applicable knew whether their employer had an official policy on acceptable AI use, pointing to a potential disconnect between the pace of AI adoption and the development of workplace policies to support it.

Among the guide's recommendations are ensuring that safeguards reflect the potential consequences of AI errors, involving employees and others affected by AI systems in decisions about their introduction, and protecting opportunities for workers to develop expertise and learn through experience. The APA also encourages organisations to consider how AI might affect professional judgement, knowledge sharing and the development of skills over time, rather than focusing exclusively on efficiency or productivity gains. Developed with input from specialists in human-technology interaction and several branches of psychology, the guide includes practical examples of effective implementation and warning signs that organisations should recognise. APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr. said the rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviours and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology, and he asked whether using AI to write emails should change how someone is judged. He said psychological science can help organisations understand not just what AI tools can do, but how their use affects trust, decision-making and employee well-being, and that the guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the centre of the process.

Dennis P. Stolle, executive lead psychologist for applied psychology at APA, said purchasing an AI tool and telling people to use it without further direction is not a sound strategy. He said organisations need to invest in the people who will work with the technology, not just the technology itself, which means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed. Although aimed at employers across sectors, the guidance raises questions relevant to universities, research organisations and scholarly publishers, where AI is increasingly being incorporated into research, editorial, administrative and knowledge-management workflows. For these organisations, the APA's recommendations underline the importance of establishing clear expectations around acceptable AI use while preserving professional expertise, accountability and trust in human decision-making.

Articles.Title: APA urges employers to put people at centre of workplace AI adoption

stories.Headline: Executives trust AI over their own judgment twice as often as other workers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
New research from Charter's AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job found that executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, Fortune reported on November 16, 2026. About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers, and executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague. The same article notes that Gen Z approaches AI with some skepticism, since 69% of employed Gen Zers in the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation and GSV Ventures say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. That study surveyed 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, and only 3% of them put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI, even though 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. The survey also found that 81% of executives say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers, and that executives are 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt.

In Charter's survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI's impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. The article recalls that in 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends. It adds that misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top, because when an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences without getting a vote. Brian Elliott, Charter's executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research, says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born, and that the survey of over 5,000 AI users at work found sharper divides by career stage than by age. He says AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI's gaps show.

He says executives fact-check AI more but are also far more likely to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that a mistake might cost them their job. In his view the biggest driver may be pressure, since many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and he says that combination explains how a CFO might drop the CMO's campaign into ChatGPT and quiz her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work. The article says younger workers' wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them, from schools to employers, and that Gen Z treats AI as an assistant rather than giving it main character energy. It notes that executives are finalizing next year's budgets and AI strategies now, and that the open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader's judgment and how many on a chatbot's general answer. It concludes that leaders who treat AI the same way Gen Z does could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions.

Articles.Title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often

stories.Headline: Attackers use AI to bypass security patches and find vulnerability variants
stories.Summary:
This summer, maintainers of the vm2 JavaScript library shipped fixes for 34 sandbox-escape vulnerabilities. Anthropic's Claude co-wrote 19 of these patches, but a security researcher later used AI to bypass one. Shayaun Nejad of Rubrik performed this variant analysis for a talk in San Francisco. He presented his findings at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference.

The vm2 library sees 1 million downloads per week and uses open-source code. In June, FIRST projected 66,000 CVEs for the year, but the number is approaching 100,000. Microsoft's October Patch Tuesday addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities, compared to 180 in October 2025. Bank of America added 1,000 contractors in the second quarter to help 3,000 staff. Meta used AI for 40% of critical fixes by July, though code grew 100% year over year.

Shayaun Nejad warned that AI-assisted patches can serve as blueprints for attackers to find variants. He noted that the same bugs were often rediscovered in new testing runs. Anthropic stated that software security is now limited by how quickly humans verify and patch AI findings. David Molnar of Meta said humans are drowning in reviews and need more automation. Taesoo Kim of Microsoft warned that AI drastically reduces time for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation.

The Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are using AI for patch-gap abuse. This affects downstream browsers like Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge that use the Chromium base. Epoch AI researchers used GLM 5.3 to compromise every Firefox release from September 17 to October 26. These researchers spent 1,000 dollars in credits and 12 hours per target. The process did not trigger any provider safeguards or refusals.

Rubrik and 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs observed that AI offense currently outperforms AI defense. Off-by-1 Labs found that half of 6,080 AI patches for six vulnerabilities left attack paths open. P2Patch tests showed an AI agent successfully bypassed 41 of 101 patches. Trail of Bits found one in eight human-written patches for 2,265 vulnerabilities also failed. Anthropic's Glasswing program found 37,966 vulnerabilities, but only 217 of 7,349 public flaws were fixed.

Mozilla will stop releasing regression tests associated with security fixes to prevent patch gap abuse. Fudan University researchers used an LLM framework to find 56 incomplete patches across 62 closed-source applications. This work resulted in 19 CVE assignments and 28,100 dollars in bug bounties. Some users now employ open-weight models like Qwen, Kimi, and GLM to avoid API guardrails. The articles leave open how the industry will fully automate the review pipeline.

Articles.Title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
