stories.Headline: German students use AI for homework as PISA finds lowest scores in 25 years
stories.Summary:
Young Germans have used artificial intelligence tools for two and a half years to complete school assignments. Students use these applications for subjects like math, German, English, chemistry, and physics. Many students use these tools to solve problems or explain complex academic topics. Some students admit to using AI for homework when they feel stuck. This practice is described by scientists as cognitive outsourcing of the thinking process.

The 2024 JIM study found ninety-one percent of Germans aged 12 to 19 use AI. Seventy-four percent of these students use AI for learning and homework. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani banned AI in public schools up to eighth grade for 2026 and 2027. The KMK has issued vague statements on AI use since 2024 in German federal states. These guidelines suggest students should engage with AI in a critical and responsible manner.

Teacher Franziska Müller says some students can no longer think for themselves or comprehend texts. She notes that students often read AI prepared answers aloud during her gymnasium classes. Julian Hinn believes AI can respond better to student needs than some teachers can. He suggests introducing AI in the 10th grade for students aged 15 or 16. Hinn encourages his senior students to critically question the quality of AI solutions.

Andreas Schleicher of the OECD reported that AI chatbot users get lower average science scores. The Brookings Institution argues that AI risks outweigh benefits by eroding critical thinking and memory. Students with knowledge gaps may adopt AI errors and fall further behind their peers. Affluent children may benefit more, which the PISA study says widens the existing gap. This phenomenon is called the Matthew effect, where early success leads to more progress.

The PISA study from September evaluated 15-year-olds from more than 90 countries worldwide. German 15-year-olds posted their lowest scores in the 25-year history of this specific study. The Brookings Institution conducted research with young participants from around the world on cognitive skills. The Matthew effect is based on a biblical verse from Matthew 25:29 regarding wealth. These reports highlight a decline in independent judgment and perseverance among students.

Teachers are now more motivated to challenge students to think independently and maintain personal autonomy. Students must solve problems without AI during exams or they risk failing their courses. One student told Müller he felt unable to think for himself after a poor result. The articles leave open how to balance AI support with the development of basic skills. It remains unclear if bans or strategic integration will better prevent the dumbing down.

Articles.Title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

stories.headline_source: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

stories.Headline: AT&T COO Jeff McElfresh says agentic AI agents are reversing internet traffic toward uploads
stories.Summary:
AT&T chief operating officer Jeff McElfresh said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, November 16, 2026, that the direction of internet bandwidth is undergoing a fundamental shift, because agentic AI agents tap the network around the clock rather than in the episodic patterns created by people watching video. U.S. household upload traffic grew 19.2% year over year in the second quarter, more than three times as fast as downloads, which grew 6.1%, according to OpenVault, which tracks broadband usage for internet providers. The average subscriber now uploads 58.2 GB a month, and while households still download about 11 times as much as they upload, that ratio was 16.6 times in 2019. McElfresh, who has been at AT&T for 31 years, said watching traffic from the network's control center used to be easy to read, with clear patterns like Netflix and YouTube traffic and traffic leaving cities for the suburbs at the start of the pandemic, when many work-from-home networks struggled and video calls glitched. He pointed to an autonomous vehicle connected to AT&T's wireless network that transmits more data up into the cloud to train a model than it consumes.

Mobile operators are seeing a similar shift, since in 2025, 43 of 55 service providers tracked by Ericsson saw uplink traffic grow faster than downlink, according to its June Mobility Report. Ericsson's scenarios have uplink traffic tripling or quintupling by 2031 if AI apps, smart glasses and agents take off, though it says mobile traffic is still expected to remain downlink-dominated in the near term and warns operators that current networks are not dimensioned for sustained uplink demand. Nokia's 2026 network traffic report forecasts that AI will drive 44% of global network traffic by 2035, and that for physical AI such as robots, cars and drones, more than 90% of traffic will start in the uplink, with Nokia writing that AI is challenging the asymmetric design of traditional access networks. AT&T has a business reason to tell this story, because fiber carries traffic equally fast in both directions while cable broadband, its main home-internet rival, has historically offered much slower uploads than downloads. McElfresh called fiber the gold standard, saying it is future proof and has all of the symmetrical capabilities to be very responsive to the AI future.

AT&T plans to reach 60 million fiber locations by 2030, about 1.5 times its footprint, and signed a supply deal with Corning worth more than $3 billion in September. OpenVault's numbers give AT&T something to point to, since fiber subscribers uploaded an average of 94.1 GB a month in the second quarter against 58.2 GB on cable's DOCSIS networks, though OpenVault CEO Mark Trudeau told Light Reading in October that he attributes the upstream growth to gaming, Zoom and Teams calls and a lot of AI content creation, and cable companies are also rolling out DOCSIS 4.0, which supports symmetric speeds. Corning CEO Wendell Weeks, who shared the stage, said customers will feel the shift at home through the combination of the bandwidth delivered and the type of products AI will enable, from robots to how people use their devices. Weeks said the next frontier is inside the data center itself, where copper wiring will give way to fiber, converting signals to light within a centimeter of the processor.

McElfresh said AT&T technicians are installing fiber in 10,000 neighborhoods on any given day, adding roughly 4 million locations this year, toward the company's target of 60 million by 2030, while Ericsson's forecast window runs to 2031.

Articles.Title: The internet was built for Netflix streaming down to your couch. AT&T’s COO says AI agents are flipping it the other way

stories.Headline: Gen Z buyers use AI to shortlist homes and estimate mortgage costs
stories.Summary:
Gen Z consumers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to research homebuying, according to a 2026 Homebuyer Insights Report from Bank of America. These young buyers use the technology to shortlist properties, estimate mortgage payments, and calculate closing costs before contacting agents or lenders. The report found that 32 percent of Gen Z, 28 percent of millennials, and 20 percent of all prospective buyers or homeowners used AI tools in the past year. Most users focused on financial affordability, with 57 percent estimating costs and 55 percent learning about the general homebuying process.

The shift requires real estate firms to scale their technology, though JLL research shows 90 percent of companies are testing AI while only 5 percent have met their goals. More than 60 percent of these firms are unprepared to scale beyond pilots, and only 33 percent of workers feel adequately trained. In early 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac introduced governance frameworks for accountability and human oversight, while MISMO released a voluntary toolkit in June. Additionally, a revised law in Colorado regarding automated decisions is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

Matt Vernon, the head of consumer lending at Bank of America, stated that AI is now a meaningful first step in the journey for buyers. Despite this trend, the report indicates that 55 percent of buyers still prefer humans for touring homes and 54 percent want human legal advice. The Urban Institute noted that AI already assists with underwriting, valuation, and fraud detection to lower costs and speed up servicing. They suggested that lenders should measure success by how many more people become and remain homeowners.

The real estate industry is currently undergoing its largest transformation in a generation, which the World Economic Forum compares to the early days of the internet. Companies with C-suite sponsors for their technology programs are three times more likely to succeed than those without such leadership. The Urban Institute has launched a new initiative on AI in mortgage finance to track these developments. Future success for firms will depend on training their staff and proving measurable results to keep pace with AI-savvy buyers.

Articles.Title: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.headline_source: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI uses Kimi models to pursue scientific discoveries in biology and chemistry
stories.Summary:
The Beijing-based artificial intelligence start-up known as Moonshot AI recently announced its intention to utilize Kimi models for scientific discovery. This strategic move was highlighted by the company during a keynote address delivered at the Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon late last week. The organization is now competing with rivals from the United States to transform artificial intelligence into a powerful engine for research. By focusing on these goals, the company aims to push the boundaries of what current machine learning models can achieve. This new direction requires the development of more advanced reasoning capabilities to handle complex data in specialized fields.

The company is specifically pushing into the realms of biology, chemistry, and pharmaceutical research to find new breakthroughs. These scientific applications demand a much higher level of intelligence than those used for standard coding tasks. The transition involves moving beyond general purpose AI to create tools that can solve intricate problems in the natural sciences. Giacomo Ficari, who serves as the director of international for Moonshot AI, spoke about the potential of this shift.

He stated that the real excitement for the company lies in the field of science. Ficari explained that while finance and legal applications are at the same intelligence level as coding, science pushes that level even higher. He believes that the ability to reason through scientific problems represents the next major frontier for their technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: China’s Moonshot AI puts Kimi models into race for science discoveries

stories.Headline: Druckenmiller exits AMD and Alphabet and adds SpaceX, Palantir and AppLovin
stories.Summary:
Duquesne Family Office's third-quarter 13F showed complete exits from AMD and Alphabet, alongside new positions in SpaceX, Palantir and AppLovin, according to MarketWatch's review of the filing. Stanley Druckenmiller is still buying artificial intelligence but changing which AI businesses he owns. The filing does not show his sale prices or exact trade dates, so investors can't tell how well the exits were timed. Since then, AMD has fallen 22.35% from its October 6 close of $649.42. Since the quarter ended, Alphabet has dropped 17.54%.

AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 44.7% to $13.38 billion, and Data Center sales grew 97% to $8.55 billion. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to approximately $17 billion, and the stock trades near 191 times trailing earnings. GAAP EPS was $1.46 after a $1,097M customer warrant charge. Alphabet's Google Cloud revenue grew 103% to $30.71 billion, but capital spending reached $51.36 billion and free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion. Alphabet is now paying for its expansion partly through debt, at-the-market equity issuance and mandatory convertible preferred stock, and GAAP EPS of $2.12 missed the $2.97 estimate, ending a 12-quarter beat streak.

Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue of $984M exceeded U.S. government revenue of $953M for the first time, and the adjusted operating margin was 62%. Full-year revenue guidance rose to $8.53B, and CEO Alex Karp said the Sovereign AI moment is purpose-built for Palantir. Palantir trades near 228 times earnings, total contract value grew just 6% year over year, and shares are down 11.81% year to date. SpaceX reported revenue of $14.60B, and its Super Intelligence segment, which includes Grok and Cursor, brought in $7.60B, up 830%. That segment leases data center capacity to outside customers and expanded with the Cursor acquisition at an implied $60B equity value.

Starlink had 13.6M consumer subscribers, and SpaceX shares trade at $141.48, down 12.1% from their first available close on June 12. On Tuesday, MarketWatch reported that SpaceX got a vote of confidence from Nvidia. AppLovin's revenue rose 55.5% to $2.18B, and adjusted EBITDA reached $1.84B at an 84% margin. The company bought back $1.4B of stock during the quarter, and CEO Adam Foroughi said he believes this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term. At about 38 times earnings, AppLovin trades at a far lower multiple than Palantir, and shares are up 46.53% over the past month but down 42.13% year to date.

Earlier this year, Druckenmiller said AI-linked stocks looked disturbingly heated. In a Morgan Stanley interview, he summed up the market's view that the consensus for AI is that it will be very deflationary and lead to massive job losses. The pattern points to a preference for companies that sell AI-driven results through software, ads and connectivity, with less exposure to the chip spending cycle. AMD now trades near 191 times earnings and Alphabet's spending turned free cash flow negative. Palantir's stock trades near 228 times earnings.

Four signals to track include whether AMD delivers its roughly $17B fourth-quarter revenue target as its Helios server racks scale up. Another is Palantir's fourth-quarter revenue against its $2.649, $2.653 billion guidance, and whether contract value starts growing faster. The next 13F will show whether Druckenmiller kept, added to, or cut these positions. The filing does not show his sale prices or exact trade dates.

stories.Headline: Klarna reports 12% revenue growth and unveils an upgraded AI shopping assistant
stories.Summary:
Klarna stock initially jumped over 5% in early trading on Tuesday morning, November 17, 2026, after the buy now, pay later company reported third quarter earnings, with revenue up 12% year over year. The Swedish company announced the results in its third quarter earnings report and discussed them on its Q3 earnings call that Tuesday. On that call Klarna also announced an upgraded AI-powered shopping assistant, building artificial intelligence into its shopping browser and app, as well as iMessage and WhatsApp. Co-founder and CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski announced the shopping assistant on Tuesday's call, saying it is live with a small group of early users and pre-registration is starting. Klarna is upgrading AI features and attracting new customers in time for the holiday shopping season.

Revenue came in at $1 billion, compared to analyst estimates of $964 million. Gross merchandise volume rose 10% year over year to $36.1 billion. Adjusted loss per share was $0.19, a wider loss than the estimated loss per share of $0.13. The company saw a 19% increase in adjusted operating expenses to $350 million and reported a net loss of $65 million in Q3. Klarna reiterated its full-year outlook for gross merchandise volume, the total monetary value of all completed purchases across its network, at $149 billion to $151 billion, and for Q4 it predicts revenue of between $1.01 billion and $1.09 billion. Q3 volume in its card business more than doubled to $4.5 billion, card subscribers tripled to 2.6 million, and subscription revenue grew over 500%.

Siemiatkowski said on the call that Klarna is bringing AI and agentic commerce to the core of Klarna. In its Q3 earnings release the company wrote that heading into 2027 it sees three key opportunities: scaling Fair Financing in the U.S. and expanding it across Europe, growing the Klarna Card beyond its merchant network, and AI to accelerate growth and productivity. The company named Chris Koegel, formerly of Robinhood, as CFO, effective Jan. 1. Klarna described the US as its fastest-growing market. The report was called relatively rosy good news for Klarna.

Adobe forecasts US buyers will spend a record $21.3 billion through buy now, pay later firms like Klarna during the 2026 holiday season, up 6.6% year over year. Klarna has struggled over the past year, and the stock is down 50% since the beginning of the year. Fintech valuations may be pressured in the coming months if the Federal Reserve raises interest rates in December, as is widely expected. In the previous quarter the company missed Wall Street expectations, lowered its guidance, and announced executive transitions. The articles list related coverage including a Barron's piece saying Klarna keeps winning shoppers but has not been winning over investors.

The articles give no further background beyond the past year's struggle, the prior quarter's miss, lowered guidance and executive transitions, and the widely expected December Fed rate move. Klarna's stock jump of over 5% came in early trading on Tuesday morning. The Q3 report showed revenue up 12% year over year. The upgraded assistant was announced on the same call. The company reiterated its full-year gross merchandise volume outlook.

The articles leave open how the upgraded shopping assistant will perform beyond the small group of early users and when pre-registration will convert to wider availability. They do not say whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December. They do not give the date of the Q4 report or the size of the holiday season's effect on Klarna's results. They do not say how the CFO transition will affect the company. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Klarna stock rises on strong revenue growth and upgraded agentic AI shopping assistant

stories.headline_source: Klarna stock rises on strong revenue growth and upgraded agentic AI shopping assistant

stories.Headline: Telefonica says digital security now requires protecting trust as AI fuels fraud
stories.Summary:
Digital security is becoming a priority for citizens, businesses, and institutions in the face of rising fraud, identity theft, and content manipulated using artificial intelligence, according to Telefonica on 16 November 2026. Cybercriminals no longer seek only to breach technological systems, and increasingly they attempt to deceive people through fraud, identity theft, manipulated content, or messages designed to appear legitimate. In Spain, computer fraud ranks high among cybercrimes, reflecting the growing importance of techniques designed to manipulate people's trust. AI-based tools enable the generation of text, voice, images, and video with ever-increasing quality, and these same capabilities can be used to personalize deceptions, automate fraud campaigns, or create synthetic content intended to cause confusion. European institutions are promoting measures aimed at strengthening the protection of minors online, advocating for design models that take into account users' ages, privacy, and risk reduction from the very inception of digital platforms.

The article says digital security requires strengthening digital identity, verifying communications and transactions, embedding security by design, and promoting the responsible use of AI. It also poses social and regulatory challenges, such as protecting minors online, and age verification, privacy controls, and the creation of safer digital environments play a prominent role in the debate. The European Union has developed a framework covering operational resilience, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and user protection, including the NIS2 Directive, the DORA Regulation, the Cyber Resilience Regulation, the Artificial Intelligence Regulation, and the Digital Services Regulation. Organizations should strengthen mechanisms for protecting digital identity, improve the verification of transactions and communications, properly manage risks associated with third parties and suppliers, integrate security and privacy into the design of products and services, establish governance frameworks for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, promote training and awareness among employees and users, and periodically review prevention, detection, and response mechanisms. Initiatives focused on the digital provenance of content aim to provide verifiable information about the origin and modifications made to images, videos, or digital documents.

The article states that security is no longer an issue exclusive to technical departments but has become a shared responsibility. It says this evolution involves, to varying degrees and with differing responsibilities, manufacturers, developers, service providers, platforms, and organizations. It says the challenge is not to curb innovation, but to develop mechanisms that allow us to harness the potential of artificial intelligence while maintaining user security and trust. It says technology alone will not solve the problem, and digital trust also requires education, critical thinking, transparency, and the ability to verify information before sharing it or acting on it. It says the common goal is to build digital experiences that protect the most vulnerable users without compromising fundamental rights such as privacy.

The article says digital safety is the set of practices, technologies, and measures designed to protect people, organizations, and digital services from risks such as fraud, loss of privacy, identity theft, content manipulation, or cyberattacks. It says digital safety centers on people and their ability to navigate safely in an increasingly connected environment, unlike traditional cybersecurity, which focuses primarily on systems, networks, and data. It says digital security is a key element of the customer experience, corporate reputation, and trust in digital services, and customer trust becomes a fundamental factor in evaluating service quality and building secure digital experiences. It says the ability to offer secure, transparent, and reliable experiences will be a key factor for organizations, alongside technological innovation and the ability to respond to the needs of an increasingly connected population. It says trust is becoming an essential element for the development and functioning of an increasingly connected world.

The article says every digital interaction begins with an act of trust, and every day we perform dozens of digital actions without even thinking about it. It says for years the main digital threats were associated with malware, vulnerabilities, or unauthorized access, and although these risks still exist, digital fraud has taken center stage. It says in certain cases cybercriminals may try to convince a person to provide information, make a transfer, or hand over their credentials, rather than attempting to bypass technical security mechanisms. It says concepts such as digital identity, verification, reputation, and trust are taking on strategic importance for citizens, businesses, and institutions. It says artificial intelligence is driving some of the most significant technological advances in recent years and is also reshaping the landscape of digital risks.

The article says the history of digital transformation has been marked by technological innovation, but its evolution will also depend on organizations' ability to build and maintain trust. It says digital security is no longer just about protecting systems, and it also involves protecting the trust that enables citizens, businesses, and institutions to interact, share information, and use digital services. It says this approach addresses the challenge of facilitating citizens' access to digital technologies through innovative, secure, and reliable networks and services. It says the digital transformation is accompanied by a profound regulatory evolution, and security extends beyond technical departments. It says ensuring safe, transparent, and reliable digital experiences is essential to harnessing innovation without undermining the trust that underpins the digital economy.

Articles.Title: Digital Security: How to Protect Trust in the Face of Fraud and Artificial Intelligence

stories.headline_source: Digital Security: How to Protect Trust in the Face of Fraud and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Travel firms expect AI agent bookings to keep protection as sellers seek machine-readable offers
stories.Summary:
As artificial intelligence agents begin to take on more of the travel booking process, the industry faces a new question about how travelers will be offered protection when an AI assistant is handling the transaction, according to a PhocusWire report published on November 16, 2026. Travel insurance has traditionally been presented during checkout, where sellers can explain coverage, provide required disclosures and obtain consent from the buyer. But as booking shifts toward conversational interfaces, those familiar steps will need to be rethought by the companies involved. New Phocuswright research finds that travel companies generally expect protection to remain part of AI-driven bookings, although their requirements differ from one another.

Only 5% of surveyed companies say they would leave protection out of AI agent booking flows, which means the large majority expect it to stay in place. Travel sellers prioritize machine-readable offers and a clear business case for including protection in those flows. Technology providers, by contrast, are more interested in solutions they can deploy across multiple clients rather than single-purpose tools. The sponsored report examines what it will take to integrate travel protection into AI-driven booking experiences, including the technical, commercial and regulatory considerations involved.

The report also identifies six priorities for companies evaluating protection partners as agentic commerce evolves, though the article does not list them. The research was sponsored by Travel Insured International/C&F, and the full report is available by filling out a form on the PhocusWire site. The article does not name any individual responsible for the findings or attribute any direct statements to a person. It also does not say what happens next beyond the report's release and the six priorities it identifies for companies assessing partners.

Articles.Title: How travel protection needs to adapt as AI agents book at scale

stories.headline_source: How travel protection needs to adapt as AI agents book at scale

stories.Headline: Fed finds over 3 trillion dollars in off-balance-sheet AI commitments
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve examined the financing of the AI buildout in its November 2026 Financial Stability Report. This first close look found over 3 trillion dollars in commitments not listed as debt. The Fed released these findings on November 17, 2026. The report includes a new section titled Leverage in the Data Center Buildout. This specific section was absent from five previous editions dating back to 2024.

The report counts 1 trillion dollars in unsigned leases and 2 trillion dollars in other contracts. These obligations involve Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Oracle. On-balance-sheet debt for these seven firms should exceed 800 billion dollars by year end. The Fed notes these off-balance-sheet figures are undiscounted and not directly comparable with debt. Data used for the report ends on October 28, 2026.

Fed Governor Michael Barr said the potential maximum nominal value of obligations is above 3 trillion dollars. He warned that opacity can exacerbate selloffs when investor sentiment shifts. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stated that staff started modeling scenarios from booms to disappointments. Barr noted that guarantees show how much producers might absorb if borrowers default. He said he is less concerned about direct losses given limited debt.

Market players are worried, and 87 percent of 23 surveyed contacts named AI a salient risk. Large U.S. bank holding companies have close to 1 trillion dollars of exposure to AI entities. High-yield bond funds, life insurers, and private debt vehicles hold riskier slices of construction debt. The New York Fed found bank liquidity stress is at levels not seen since 2014. Banks would face a 151.1 billion dollar capital gap in a 2022 rate shock scenario.

Debt tied to advanced computing rose to 680 billion dollars by October, up from 130 billion in 2023. This debt now makes up 31 percent of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate issuance, up from 6 percent. Total outstanding public debt for advanced computing is estimated at more than 1.1 trillion dollars. Lucent previously committed 5.7 billion dollars in credit during the dot-com boom in 2000. The Bank for International Settlements found direct lending to AI quadrupled over five years.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Nvidia has a 105 billion dollar capped obligation for an OpenAI campus in Pike County, Ohio. The company also listed 3.5 billion dollars in guarantees on cloud partners leases as of July 26. The Federal Reserve will release its next report in the spring of 2027. The report leaves open how much larger economic exposure is than on-balance-sheet liabilities.

stories.Headline: Clay raises $115m Series D led by Wellington at a $7.1bn valuation
stories.Summary:
Clay, a New York company that sells data and AI agents to sales and marketing teams, was valued at US$7.1bn after a US$115m Series D round led by Wellington in September 2026, more than double its valuation of US$3.1bn in August 2025. The company was co-founded by Kareem Amin, who is chief executive and who sold his previous start-up Frame to Sailthru in 2012, and by Varun Anand. Clay began as a way to fill spreadsheets with better data, and its waterfall enrichment queries more than 200 data providers one after another, from ZoomInfo to People Data Labs and Hunter, until it finds a match. It now counts OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral AI and ElevenLabs among more than 17,000 customers, up from 10,000 a year earlier, and 80% of the Forbes AI 50 are Clay customers. Revenue grew fourfold in 2025, and annual recurring revenue was about US$150m in May 2026 according to a Sacra estimate.

A March 2026 pricing overhaul split data credits from Actions and cut data costs by 50% to 90%, a move designed to widen use beyond power users. Clay unifies CRM records from Salesforce and HubSpot with product usage, campaign engagement, calls and emails, then predicts the next best action and helps a team take it, while agents handle account research, lead scoring and pre-call preparation. A September 2026 update added an action that drops enriched records straight into HubSpot lists, and 24 new or updated connectors in September 2026 extended EMEA and APAC data coverage, added Canva for personalised decks and wrote records back to Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and ClickHouse. Amin now describes the goal as a self-learning revenue engine, and he has said that AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history. Scotty Huhn, engineering lead at OpenAI, has said of Clay that it allows OpenAI to move fast and drive outsized impact on GTM execution.

Customers report good numbers, with Anthropic tripling its enrichment rate, Mistral AI cutting market mapping and account scoring from two months to ten days, Intercom growing outbound-sourced pipeline by 140% and Pendo reaching 200% quota attainment. ElevenLabs lifted sales-qualified leads by 50% by cutting speed to lead to under five minutes. A new job title, the GTM engineer, has grown up around the product, and Clay is investing in the people who run it through a US$1m scholarship fund that trains GTM engineers, with its ecosystem team saying more than 50,000 people have been trained. At Sculpt 2026, its second annual conference, about 2,000 attendees from 30 countries saw agent-first building, Clay Workflows and an Inbound SDR Agent. The customer list reads like a roll call of the AI industry, with OpenAI, Cursor, Lovable, Notion and Figma using Clay alongside established software firms such as Okta and Rippling.

stories.Headline: Developers use AI tools to build clones of Adobe and Microsoft software
stories.Summary:
A group of developers has used AI-powered software development tools to build feature-exact clones of the Adobe Creative Suite, the Microsoft Office suite and the AutoDesk CAD applications, a collection known as ArtCraft, according to an InfoWorld opinion piece published on November 16, 2026. The piece says the most striking ArtCraft release so far is not a clone of an existing app but a relatively original project called Craft Anything, which it describes as a fancy agent harness for studying existing applications or websites. That tool then prompts a large language model to create your own copy of the studied software, either by reproducing its outward behavior, which the piece calls clean-room cloning, or by disassembling binaries. The writer says you never have to touch a line of code if you don't want to, calling it the no-code dream pushed to the limit.

The piece says the trend is driving development of ever-more-abstracted software tools and transforming existing tools into more abstracted ones, and it is also fostering new generations of developers for whom those tools will be their first contact with programming, and possibly their last. It notes that higher-level languages once replaced machine code, that compilers now write better machine language than people produce by hand, and that higher-level languages are now next in line to be automated away, or so the argument goes. The writer, Serdar Yegulalp, a senior writer at InfoWorld, says he does not think it is a bad idea to have a choice of abstraction levels, but he does think it is a bad idea to believe more abstraction is inevitable or always better. He says the more abstraction we put between ourselves and the work, the harder it is to know what might be wrong or how it might be better.

Yegulalp says we have not begun to understand the psychological impacts of LLM use on veteran programmers and newcomers, and that the non-deterministic output of agents makes it harder for developers to reason about the results of any given prompt. He asks whether an agent that never generates the same code twice is producing a bug or a feature, and he says some people argue there is no point in knowing what is under the hood because the work now happens at a pace and scale only other machines can handle. He calls that argument seductive to developers facing impossible deadlines but says it feels like the same kind of fatalism, and he asks how many of those expectations about velocity are genuine and how much LLM-driven work actually results in features shipped, bugs fixed and value delivered. He says those were already hard questions before LLMs came along, and that as more developers gravitate toward an agent-first way of doing things it will be harder for them to ask such vital questions in the first place.

Articles.Title: How AI is warping both developers and developer tools

stories.Headline: JetBrains CEO Kirill Skrygan says policies alone cannot govern AI agents
stories.Summary:
The article, published by InfoWorld on 2026-11-16, describes how AI agents are changing software governance as organizations accelerate AI adoption across software development. It reports that AI systems can act faster than the organizations responsible for them can understand or govern what is happening. It says organizations are thinking about compliance, data privacy, security, and model reliability while boards demand policies and regulators develop frameworks. It states that AI has significantly lowered the barriers to generating code, with assistants suggesting individual functions and coding agents working across repositories, running tests, making changes, and executing multi-step tasks. It says agents can access tools, retrieve data, write code, trigger actions, and coordinate tasks on behalf of users.

The article says the goal is to scale AI across development workflows while ensuring the people responsible for the software can still understand, verify, and stand behind what those systems produce. It says governance becomes murkier when AI agents not only generate code but test it, deploy it, open a pull request, modify multiple files, or interact with other systems. It says the distance between decision and action becomes much shorter, making it harder for humans to retain enough access to understand and monitor each step. It says developers must decide what work to delegate, what context an agent needs, and how to verify the result. It says a developer can delegate a task without delegating responsibility for the outcome.

The article says Kirill Skrygan is CEO of JetBrains, the company behind intelligent software development tools trusted by more than 15 million users and 88 Fortune Global Top 100 companies. It says he leads JetBrains as the company combines its deep expertise in code intelligence with AI to help developers and organizations build. It says most organizations already have policies governing software security, access, and compliance, but policies alone cannot govern AI agents operating across repositories, tools, and development environments. It says organizations must define what agents can access, what actions they can perform, how their work is recorded, and where human approval is required. It says these controls need to be built into the environment where development happens rather than applied after an agent has completed its work.

The article says the first control to consider is traceability, so developers understand what AI has contributed to a codebase. It says AI-generated changes must be tracked and made auditable so teams can read, review, and understand the output. It says if an agent makes changes across multiple files and runs tests, the team should identify exactly what actions were taken, what was changed, which instructions were received, and which tests were run. It says developers are ultimately responsible for software that reaches production, and customers do not care who or what wrote the code. It says accountability ultimately sits with the organization and its engineering team.

The article says the goal should not be to put a human in the loop for every individual action carried out by AI. It says organizations need to clearly define where human judgment is required, for example allowing AI to generate code and run tests automatically while requiring explicit human review for changes to production infrastructure or other critical systems. It says an AI tool that can modify application code does not necessarily need access to production infrastructure, and a coding agent that can run tests does not necessarily need permission to change deployment configuration. It says tokenmaxxing has been one of the defining AI trends of 2026, yet organizations increasingly realize AI activity and AI value are not the same thing. It says measuring usage rates, prompts, and token consumption tells organizations how much AI they are using but not whether AI is delivering better outcomes or creating meaningful business value.

The article says agentic systems can perform long, multi-step workflows and consume significant resources without a developer manually initiating every individual step. It says this is driving interest in what the industry now calls a software harness, a layer of software around AI models that can provide context and give organizations greater control over tasks and token costs. It says what works when one developer is directing one agent becomes harder when multiple agents operate across repositories, teams, and shared systems. It says the most successful organizations will not be those that deploy the largest number of AI agents but the ones able to create the clearest lines of accountability around them. It says the question is not whether organizations will adopt AI agents but how they can remain in control of them.

stories.Headline: South Korea bans all electronic devices at 1,312 test sites to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korean education authorities are scrambling to prevent AI-assisted cheating before the national college entrance exam this Thursday. Public outrage grew on Sunday after the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam confessed to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative AI. This individual missed only one of 160 questions in the first round and scored high marks in the second round. Police have opened an investigation into the matter, which follows other cases where four students used AI glasses during school and university tests.

The government will ban all electronic devices from the 1,312 test sites, allowing only scratch pads and writing utensils. Specialized personnel will be dispatched to detect AI-powered glasses that can scan tests and produce answers in seconds. Students caught with smart devices will have their results invalidated and face a ban from the exam next year. Officials are currently moving to extend this penalty to a three year ban for offenders.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for the use of all national capabilities to prevent misconduct during this week's exam. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin vowed a zero-tolerance approach and stated that the ministry will actively seek criminal punishment. While some suggest using metal detectors or physical searches, officials say these are realistically difficult to implement. Floor leader Chun Ha-ram of the New Reform Party suggested postponing the exam to ensure systematic preventive measures.

The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as Suneung, is a major life event that determines university placement and future careers. It is considered so critical that military drills and flight schedules are adjusted to avoid disturbing the test takers. A spokesperson for the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union argued that the government should change educational evaluation practices. They believe that relying on proctor vigilance is insufficient in an era where AI can easily find answers.

stories.Headline: Doosan Enerbility shares AI maintenance technologies with domestic power companies
stories.Summary:
Doosan Enerbility shared artificial intelligence-based technologies for operating and maintaining power generation equipment with domestic power companies, the company said on Nov. 15. The company held the 2026 Power Generation Operation Technology Exchange at its headquarters in Changwon, South Gyeongsang Province, according to the report. The two-day event began Nov. 12 and drew about 100 participants, including officials from major domestic power companies and university professors. Doosan Enerbility presented its in-house-developed predictive diagnostics solution Prevision, along with AI-based remote monitoring and non-destructive testing technologies.

The technologies analyze power equipment operating data to detect abnormal signs early and improve maintenance efficiency, the article says. The company also shared cases of operational support using power equipment technical data and AI data development. Participants toured Doosan Enerbility's gas turbine plant and the test center for GUARDIAN, its in-house-developed power equipment control system. Doosan Enerbility plans to strengthen its long-term maintenance and digital solution businesses in line with expanding gas turbine supply.

The articles do not name a specific person as responsible for the event or give direct comments from company officials. The context given is the company's plan to expand its gas turbine supply and its related maintenance and digital solution businesses.

stories.Headline: Guernsey Institute surveys employers on AI skills needs
stories.Summary:
The Guernsey Institute launched a survey for local employers on November 16, 2026, to identify future workforce skills. This initiative seeks to determine how students and workers must adapt to changing demands caused by artificial intelligence and new technology. Executive principal Dr Louise Misselke noted that this is the first survey of its kind conducted in 12 years. The project aims to prepare the island for different workplaces and address existing skills gaps.

The process requires gathering direct feedback from employers regarding the specific qualifications and training needed for their staff. Dr Louise Misselke believes that people must upskill and retrain, though she views these necessary changes as a significant opportunity. Simon Le Tocq, the chief executive of the business school, expects artificial intelligence to be a primary focus of the responses. He noted that the lifespan of professional skills has dropped from five years to only a year and a half.

Simon Le Tocq argued that Guernsey must compete on capability because it cannot compete on size or cost. Esther Reid, the dean at TGI University Centre, stated that the results should help keep workers on the island. She wants students to know they can return home to advance their professional learning after completing initial higher education elsewhere. The leaders emphasized that the voices of both young people and adult learners are essential to this transition.

This effort follows a previous survey from the Guernsey International Business Association in October, where artificial intelligence appeared in 80 percent of responses. The institute hopes to eventually conduct this type of data collection every year to stay current. By aligning education with employer needs, the island intends to maintain its competitive advantage through its people. The university centre will use these findings to support those looking to change careers or improve their skills.

stories.Headline: Marius Meiners predicts AI assistants will choose purchases and automate routine shopping
stories.Summary:
Marius Meiners predicts that artificial intelligence will soon choose what people buy and determine which businesses receive their money. The co-founder and chief executive of Peec AI believes digital assistants will automate routine shopping and everyday services. This retail revolution involves AI agents learning consumer needs to make purchases without being asked by the users. These agents can already search the internet, compare prices, and recommend products based on budgets and tastes. Meiners expects these tools to eventually handle everything from buying groceries and clothes to booking hotels and restaurants.

The transition requires personal AI assistants to anticipate purchases and complete routine transactions autonomously for the users. Some brands already generate between 20 and 30 per cent of sales conversions through AI searches on various platforms. These platforms include ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, which shoppers use for advice before they spend their money. Meanwhile, on-device AI marketing suggests that an iPhone 18 Pro or Pixel 11 with 12GB of RAM is necessary. These specifications are presented as the baseline for users who want to unlock a world of on-device AI.

Marius Meiners told Juliette Foster that everyone will likely have a personal AI assistant because they will be useful. He stated that these assistants will know exactly what a person wants, where they eat, and where they stay. Meiners believes this technology is another step toward making lives easier and freeing up time for the consumers. He noted that AI can make annoying decisions better than people would make those same decisions for themselves. He urged brands to ask customers how they make decisions because AI models already have a massive impact.

Retailers are affected because they risk losing customers if AI overlooks products or uses outdated prices and inaccurate information. Businesses must understand which sources AI platforms use to make recommendations to avoid losing sales to their competitors. People who enjoy shopping can still buy luxury or expensive goods themselves, while others may prefer AI automation. Gabriel Zamora and Jason Cohen discuss how cloud-reliant AI agents may reduce smartphones to glorified dumb terminals for users. They argue that compact models in phone memory are lightweight utility tools unequipped for complex thinking tasks.

The articles explain that AI agents are already capable of searching the internet and recommending products based on tastes. Some companies report that chatbots are already driving a significant portion of their total sales conversions for products. The background includes a trend where shoppers turn to platforms like ChatGPT for advice before making a final purchase. Tech giants are currently charging top dollar for smartphones while relying on remote data centers for sophisticated reasoning tasks. This architectural reality means that most on-device AI is not actually cloud-free despite the marketing from Silicon Valley.

Next, AI assistants will likely handle more personal decisions, such as arranging services suited to individual needs and habits. Brands must adapt to how AI influences consumer behavior since conventional website analytics may fail to reveal this impact. The articles leave open whether smartphones will continue to rely on remote data centers for complex AI reasoning. It remains unclear how many consumers will fully hand over their routine shopping decisions to autonomous digital agents. The text does not specify when the predicted total automation of everyday retail services will be fully realized.

Articles.Title: AI Shopping Agents Set to Transform Retail as Tech Boss Predicts Revolution

stories.Headline: ICCSD Advisory Committee urges people-centered AI and stronger governance for cultural development
stories.Summary:
The ICCSD Advisory Committee gathered in Beijing on October 26, 2026, to examine the intersection of artificial intelligence and cultural development. This meeting included 11 members and various experts representing four different countries to share their professional insights. Executive Director Xiao Lan opened the session, while Hans d'Orville served as the chair for the proceedings. The group focused their discussions on the post-2030 agenda, the International Decade of Culture, and the 2005 UNESCO Convention.

The committee determined that technological progress must remain people-centered and serve the goals of human creativity. They called for the creation of diverse cultural datasets and the implementation of stronger governance for artificial intelligence. The experts emphasized the need to protect the rights of creators and the security of intellectual property. They also recommended expanding access to digital resources and increasing cooperation between international universities. Finally, they suggested providing specialized training in artificial intelligence for cultural practitioners in rural communities and developing nations.

The participants agreed that the evolution of artificial intelligence should prioritize technological ethics, inclusiveness, and the preservation of cultural diversity. They stated that these efforts are necessary to help narrow the existing global digital divide. The meeting functioned as a platform for international exchange and dialogue among the gathered experts. These insights and recommendations are intended to support sustainable cultural development and inform the future work of the ICCSD.

stories.Headline: Greg Holmes says AI workloads will split between hyperscale and edge on latency, privacy and energy
stories.Summary:
Hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft spent over US$250bn in 2024, according to Bloomberg, and analysts project more than US$600bn in 2026. The five major tech companies exceeded US$400bn in capital expenditure in 2025. Global data centre electricity consumption reached 485TWh in 2025 and is set to rise to 950TWh by 2030. Mordor Intelligence projects the global edge data centre market to grow more than 22% annually, from roughly US$15bn to more than US$60bn over the coming decade. Between 30% and 50% of the 16GW of US data centre capacity scheduled to come online in the US face severe delays or cancellation, according to industry research.

Greg Holmes, Field CTO EMEA at Apptio, an IBM company, said workloads will be split according to latency, privacy and energy efficiency in a hybrid of hyperscale and edge. He said optimisation is part of the core economics, so cost management and taking stock of the data supply chain will be a first-order concern. He said organisations would lean towards quicker answers, so latency will matter, but the real question is at what cost per use. He said compliance and governance are growing challenges that will mean organisations need to change from an infrastructure approach to a data-centric approach. He said creating data resilience starts with a change in mindset to assigning ownership and controls to all workloads.

Holmes said growing AI workloads mean LLM inference workloads may not always benefit from being on the cloud, and arriving at that conclusion requires a real-time understanding of the cost of running the IT estate. He said key technologies include cloud-native standards regardless of where things run, and that organisations need flexibility, certainty, security and governance working together in a single environment across countries and systems. He said the industry can rally around common standards like Kubernetes, open-weight AI models and open APIs to prioritise operational needs over technology constraints. He said a consistent approach using a Technology Business Management framework turns interoperability, like AI orchestration, into a business value decision rather than a technical implementation. He said rearchitecting solutions to run from the edge takes time and highly specialised resources and needs to be an organisational priority to become a standard.

Holmes said operating more deployments on the edge means security and governance become a significant cost factor, an additional investment early on that may result in a more cost-effective, robust and scalable solution in the long run. He said technology deployment can be rapid, but skills, culture, data-driven decisions, real-time monitoring and governance are the new default. He said operational resilience to prevent downtime, data volume and taking the benefits of both environments are key. He said understanding how the business generates value through its IT estate and working with that know-how to design systems that support growth and compound value matters.

Microsoft withdrew from anchoring Nscale's planned 50MW AI data centre in Essex, UK, where grid power may not be available until the 2030s. Training frontier models demands extraordinary compute density, raw power and specialised liquid cooling, territory where hyperscale campuses retain a decisive advantage. At that scale, economies of scale help offset enormous utility consumption. Autonomous systems, smart manufacturing and real-time enterprise decision-making cannot always afford to send data hundreds of miles to a central facility and wait for an answer.

Edge environments have historically carried a broader physical and cyber attack surface, and moving data closer to the action can make it more exposed than data held within a heavily fortified hyperscale data centre. Electrical grids around the world are under strain, and securing multi-megawatt allocations for conventional centralised campuses has become materially harder. Where latency affects revenue, safety or customer experience, edge becomes non-negotiable, while highly sensitive, audit-heavy workloads requiring a hardened perimeter still favour centralised facilities. Over-investing in edge can multiply operational complexity, and relying exclusively on hyperscale can create spiralling egress costs as data moves continuously between environments.

Edge can no longer be treated as a remote branch office of the data centre and demands its own compliance, governance and operational discipline. Edge deployment offers a partial release valve by spreading demand across distributed infrastructure, but at the cost of greater management overhead and decentralised maintenance. The real discipline lies in balancing latency against total cost of ownership. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hyperscale vs Edge: The New Rules of AI Infrastructure

stories.Headline: IAB releases AI-Era Attribution Blueprint to classify AI influence on purchase conversions
stories.Summary:
The Interactive Advertising Bureau released a new framework called the AI-Era Attribution Blueprint on November 16, 2026. This system provides the advertising industry with a standardized method to classify how artificial intelligence influences a purchase conversion. The organization developed this tool to help companies decide which parties can legitimately claim credit for a sale. It aims to solve the problem of tracking complex customer journeys that involve both human and machine interactions. The blueprint requires users to identify who created the intent, who made the decision, and who completed the purchase.

Based on these answers, conversions are labeled as either Human-Owned, AI-Assisted, or AI-Executed to determine eligibility for claims. A September study by the IAB found that 45 percent of ad buyers consider comparing AI-driven and traditional journeys their biggest measurement challenge. Additionally, 44 percent of these buyers currently use direct traffic and branded search as proxies for AI influence. The IAB is responsible for this framework and stated that the blueprint should work alongside existing attribution systems rather than replacing them.

The organization is calling on publishers, agencies, AI platforms, and brands to collaborate in closing existing evidence gaps. They intend to bring various stakeholders together to share their findings as more data becomes available over time. This collaborative effort is meant to refine how the industry understands the role of AI in the buying process. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Skanska CEO Anders Danielsson sees no slowdown in AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Skanska CEO Anders Danielsson said in a CNBC interview on Monday, November 16, 2026, that the Swedish construction group is not seeing any slowdown in the building of data centers for artificial intelligence, according to a Squawk Box Europe segment posted that morning. The interview clip, which runs about four minutes and twenty-one seconds, was published on cnbc.com under a headline stating that the CEO does not see a slowdown in the AI data center buildout. In the segment Danielsson discussed the company's data center business and the obstacles facing the AI buildout, though the article gives no further figures on orders, revenue or project counts. The article names no specific projects, clients or locations, and it gives no dates for any construction work beyond the date of the interview itself.

The piece carries no statement from any other company or official, and it offers no numbers on how large Skanska's data center business is or how fast it has grown. The only change the article reports is Danielsson's public characterization of demand, namely that Skanska sees no slowdown in AI data center construction, which he presented as the state of the company's business rather than as a forecast with figures attached. The article does not say what the buildout requires in investment, energy or materials, and it gives no dates, counts or names beyond Skanska, its CEO and the CNBC program. It also does not say how the obstacles he mentioned might affect timelines or costs, because the text does not describe them.

No other numbers, dates or names appear in the article beyond the publication time of 06:00 GMT on November 16, 2026, and the length of the video. Responsibility for the remarks rests with Danielsson as CEO of Skanska, and the article paraphrases his position as seeing no slowdown in the AI data center buildout while pointing to obstacles for that buildout. The article does not quote him at length and does not say what he proposed doing about those obstacles. CNBC produced and published the segment, and the byline and reporter are not given in the text provided.

No regulator, customer or rival is named as responding to his comments. The context the article supplies is limited to the setting, a CNBC business program covering European markets, and the fact that the discussion covered both Skanska's data center business and the hurdles to the AI buildout. The article does not say what happens next, gives no schedule for future results or projects, and does not indicate whether Skanska expects the trend to continue beyond his statement. stories.Headline: Kandou AI and Neurosoft Bioelectronics win international awards
stories.Summary:
Lausanne-based Kandou AI and Geneva-based Neurosoft Bioelectronics earned prestigious international awards in 2026 for their advancements in connectivity and brain-computer interfaces. Kandou AI received the 2026 EU Innovate with TSMC Demo of the Year award in Taiwan for its chip-to-chip technology. Meanwhile, Neurosoft Bioelectronics won a gold medal in the biotechnology category of the 2026 Fujian Global Innovation and Entrepreneurship Competition in China. This achievement for Neurosoft Bioelectronics came after competing against more than 1,000 different projects.

The Tigerwing technology from Kandou AI enables high-speed and energy-efficient connectivity between chips across a circuit board. This company successfully demonstrated Tigerwing on the 4nm technology node of TSMC in June at the 2026 TSMC Europe Technology Symposium. To address data transfer challenges in AI infrastructure, Kandou AI raised a strategic round of 225 million USD earlier this year. Neurosoft Bioelectronics is currently industrializing its SOFT ECoG technology to treat epilepsy and restore motor control for people with paralysis. This firm closed a seed round of 7.5 million USD in May 2026.

Neurosoft Bioelectronics is responsible for developing high-bandwidth brain-computer interfaces to improve human health and technology. The company intends to build a large dataset of human cortical activity for use in humanoid robotics. While the provided text does not include direct quotes, it highlights the strategic goals of both award-winning firms. These companies are focusing on scaling their respective technologies to meet the demands of modern AI and medical infrastructure.

stories.Headline: FIOR's AI agent gateway passes NCC Group cyber resilience test with zero unmet claims
stories.Summary:
FIOR, a British AI security company, announced on 16 November 2026 that its AI Agent Enforcement Gateway had cleared Cyber Resilience Testing by the NCC Group, an assurance firm the NCSC assures, with zero unmet claims across 18 security principles and 69 distinct security claims, which FIOR exclusively disclosed to AI Magazine. The NCSC, part of the UK signals intelligence agency GCHQ, had published its State of the Cyber Nation report at the start of November 2026. That report warned that UK critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028. The report said AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” within the next two years to increase the scale and efficiency of ransomware attacks, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation. AI Magazine reported that an OpenAI model discovered a way to gain non-public access to Services Australia earlier this year, ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, and wrote files.

FIOR’s gateway enables organisations to identify AI agents, determine what each agent is authorised to do and enforce those permissions before actions are executed. FIOR says the gateway is built on a novel patent-pending authentication method that creates quantum-safe digital identities for AI agents without reliance on traditional certificates. FIOR describes the system as working like a passport system built on post-quantum cryptography, giving every AI agent a verifiable identity and checking what it is allowed to do before it does anything in the system. FIOR is part of the NVIDIA Inception Program, an accelerator designed for startups, and in August 2026 FIOR and Multiverse Computing announced a strategic partnership to integrate FIOR’s governance with Multiverse’s models for secure edge AI. FIOR also announced it has joined Oracle’s enhanced partner program, and its CTO James Patrick joined the business directly from Oracle, where he was Chief Field Architect for Defence and National Security.

FIOR CEO David Williams said he believes there is a degree of uncertainty in some parts on whether enterprise leaders are underestimating autonomous agents, and that most CISOs face alert overload because of the scale and pace of AI change but many have not been given the budget and instructions to manage the threat properly. Williams said one executive told him his security team are “blocking all agents”, which he called a particularly dangerous assumption that creates a false sense of security. He said an agent operating within the permissions of a compromised or legitimately acquired identity could conduct reconnaissance, collect information and execute a sequence of individually permitted actions without triggering conventional security alerts. Williams said there is no mandatory protocol, HTTP header, TLS extension or network signature that identifies a connection as originating from an AI agent, and that identifying a connection to a known AI provider does not establish its role. He said an autonomous agent could make thousands of network connections without any of them contacting an identifiable AI service, and that default-deny networking would materially reduce exposure but would not prove every permitted transaction was human-directed.

James Patrick, FIOR’s CTO, said the hardest challenge has been to create a self-sovereign system that creates a unique and quantum-safe identity for every single agent that is cryptographically protected against replay, spoofing and cloning. Patrick said FIOR strongly believes customers do not want to send information about the existence and activities of their agents outside the enterprise to identity providers to gain a security wrapper that holds their credentials in a central database, and that this has been seen many times over as not a strong security guarantee. Gemma Ungoed-Thomas, the Cabinet Office’s former Director for State Threats, Cyber and Technology and an advisor to FIOR, said she believes the UK has emerged as a global leader in the assurance of AI and AI security, and that creating a basis for strong identity is essential to reap the full benefits of agentic transformation. Lieutenant General (Retd) Sir Tom Copinger-Symes, former Deputy Commander of UK Strategic Command and an advisor to FIOR, said the UK is taking a lead in agentic identity and governance, and that a common method for securing agentic identity is fundamental and urgent for agents to communicate with those of international partners and even cross-domain communications. McKinsey estimates in its article Securing the agentic enterprise: Opportunities for cybersecurity providers that the cybersecurity market is worth US$220bn, but buyers are left trying to cut through the noise of a crowded, claim-heavy vendor landscape.

The NCSC relies on Cyber Resilience Testing to independently verify capabilities, and the global cybersecurity assurance firm NCC Group is assured by the NCSC to carry out that testing. The NCSC report was published as cybersecurity firms develop identity-based access controls for AI agents, and the UK is positioning itself as the global hub for AI security standards. The NCSC’s key facts state that NCSC chief Dr Richard Horne warns the era of cheap tech is over. The UK government is investing £60m into a new national Cyber Shield, and a Manchester AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence will build government expertise. Most cybersecurity solutions spot problems as they happen or after the fact, while FIOR’s offering is intended to work like a passport system instead.

FIOR’s gateway cleared the NCC Group assessment with zero unmet claims across 18 security principles and 69 distinct security claims, and FIOR exclusively disclosed that result to AI Magazine. David Williams said that if a security manager tells a boss “don’t worry boss we are blocking all AI” without tooling specifically designed to do this, the boss needs to have another conversation. The articles do not state when the NCC Group assessment took place, what the 18 security principles or 69 claims were, or what the gateway costs. The articles do not state whether any organisation has deployed the gateway, or what the NCSC said about FIOR’s testing beyond the Cyber Resilience Testing framework. The articles do not state what the £60m Cyber Shield or the Manchester centre will involve beyond the figures given.

Articles.Title: FIOR’s NCSC-Tested Gateway Gives AI Agents Quantum Passports

stories.Headline: Chandler Fang says t54.ai processed over 10 million AI-agent payments on XRP Ledger
stories.Summary:
XRP traded at about $0.95 on November 16, 2026, down 0.71% over 24 hours, as spot XRP ETF withdrawals and growing AI-payment activity shaped the outlook for readers searching for a Grok AI XRP price prediction. No attributable Grok forecast accompanies those developments, and the article instead assesses XRP's market conditions and payment adoption. Franklin Templeton's fund disclosed 293.1 million XRP in quarter-end holdings at September 30, up from roughly 225 million XRP at the start of the quarter. The immediate question the article raises is whether returning investment demand can support a recovery above $1 while the network expands its use in small, frequent transactions. The article distinguishes Ripple, the private technology company, from XRP, the digital asset, noting that the two names are often used interchangeably even though buying XRP gives exposure to the token's market price.

It describes the XRP Ledger as an independent distributed ledger governed through network validators, where Ripple develops payment products while the ledger supports payments, issued assets and on-chain trading. Chandler Fang, founder of t54.ai, said its x402 Facilitator had processed more than 10 million AI-agent transactions, a total the interviewer put at 11.7 million payments. Fang said activity had grown from almost nothing three or four months earlier, and he described more than 200 merchants on the network. Fang said the most common use was buying AI compute by the task, with payments of roughly $0.50 or $1 instead of monthly subscriptions costing $20 to $200.

He expects agents to move into real-world purchases over the next few quarters, and he said the startup participates in Mastercard's agentic payment program. The article also warns that other assets use the XRP or Ripple name on Solana and other networks, so its outlook concerns native XRPL XRP, including the asset held by the Franklin XRP ETF. It notes that XRP broke below $1 after a run of daily losses and that spot XRP ETFs experienced withdrawals, while an interview published by the XRPL Foundation on November 15 described millions of AI-agent payments. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Zhengzhou University researchers find AI-integrated teaching improves ophthalmology trainee scores
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University conducted a randomized trial to evaluate a new AI-supported instruction model for ophthalmology clinical teaching. Between June 2023 and June 2025, the study tracked 106 medical trainees to see if restructuring education around job competency produced measurable gains. The investigators used a random number table to divide the participants into an observation group of 53 trainees and a control group of 53 trainees. This two-year evaluation compared traditional lecture-based methods against a curriculum that integrated artificial intelligence tools into problem-based and case-based learning.

The new framework required integrating AI directly into case-based and problem-based learning formats while focusing specifically on job competency development. To measure success, the team used the Chinese Clinical Physician Post Competency Questionnaire, the Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory-Chinese Version, and the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise. The results showed that the observation group achieved significantly higher scores in theoretical knowledge, practical skills, and clinical performance, with statistical significance established at P < 0.05. These trainees also reported greater overall satisfaction with their teaching experience and showed improved critical thinking compared to the control group.

The authors, Zhipeng W. and Long L., concluded that this AI-integrated model was associated with higher short-term scores across all evaluated parameters. They noted that the study was limited by its single-center design, a relatively small sample size of 106 people, and a short intervention duration. Because the model combined several different elements, the researchers stated it was difficult to isolate the specific contribution of each individual component. They emphasized that further multicenter studies with longer follow-up periods are necessary to determine if these educational benefits can be sustained and generalized.

Articles.Title: AI-Integrated Competency Teaching Improves Short-Term Ophthalmology Scores in Randomized Trial

stories.Headline: Trump and allies fund super intelligence accelerator to expand Indo-Pacific AI access
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced a new super intelligence accelerator during a dinner in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. This initiative was unveiled as the president began his first trip to Asia following the midterm elections. The announcement occurred while leaders from the United States, Australia, India, and Japan met for the first time in two years. This event took place at the Solaire Resort immediately after the conclusion of the ASEAN Summit.

The new agreement among the United States, Australia, India, and Japan provides more than 85 million dollars in funding. These resources are intended to expand access to trusted artificial intelligence partners throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Simultaneously, the administration is taking steps to restrict the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access advanced chips from the United States. This push for superintelligence comes during a period of global upheaval involving chipmakers like Nvidia.

President Trump stated that the nations gathered for the meeting are very advanced regarding superintelligence and almost every other field. He used the term superintelligence, or SI, to describe the artificial intelligence technologies being discussed. The president made these remarks as he prepared to travel to China on Wednesday. He is scheduled to participate in a trilateral meeting later this week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The initiative arrives as national security risks surrounding artificial intelligence supply chains face intensified scrutiny. This heightened concern follows allegations of Chinese espionage and general instability within the global semiconductor industry. The administration is focusing on these security risks while expanding partnerships with key allies in the region. Further diplomatic discussions are expected to continue during the president's ongoing visits to China and Russia.

stories.Headline: Baidu AI cloud growth offsets a 22 percent drop in search advertising revenue
stories.Summary:
Baidu reported its third-quarter financial results on Monday, November 16, showing a slight decline in overall revenue. The company saw total revenue drop by 1% from the previous year to RMB30.8 billion, which equals approximately 4.60 billion dollars. This decline was largely driven by a 10% fall in revenue from the streaming arm, iQIYI, which brought in RMB6.0 billion. Meanwhile, the core online marketing business suffered a significant 22% slump, falling to RMB11.9 billion.

The company is shifting its focus toward AI, with AI-powered segments now making up 53% of General Business revenue. General Business revenue grew 1% to RMB25.0 billion, supported by AI segments that earned RMB13.2 billion. Specifically, AI Cloud Infra revenue reached RMB8.2 billion, while GPU cloud revenue surged by 191% from a year earlier. However, this growth requires massive investment, leaving the company with a negative free cash flow of RMB4.6 billion.

CEO Robin Li stated that the company's full-stack AI investments are creating meaningful growth for the business. He noted that AI Cloud Infra has evolved into a major driver of revenue for the organization. Despite these gains, AI-native marketing services fell 15% to RMB2.4 billion, and AI Applications remained flat at RMB2.6 billion. This suggests that the company is currently succeeding more as a provider of compute power than as a creator of consumer AI products.

The company continues to face a difficult balance between shrinking ad revenue and expensive infrastructure costs. Net income attributable to Baidu was RMB1.4 billion, while non-GAAP net income stood at RMB2.4 billion. The business must stabilize its search advertising losses to improve its cash flow position in the future. Baidu will continue pushing its Ernie model to maintain a position among the top tier of AI models.

Articles.Title: Baidu's AI cloud surge nearly cancels out a 22% slump in search ads
