stories.Headline: Mercor raises $750 million at a $20 billion valuation to train AI models
stories.Summary:
Mercor secured $750 million in a Series D at a $20 billion valuation, with Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, Nvidia and Apollo-affiliated funds among the participants. The San Francisco company, originally an AI hiring platform, now connects technology firms with subject-matter experts who help train and test AI models. Traversal joined the unicorn ranks with a $120 million Series B co-led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures. Nooks secured a $500 million commitment from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, with the investor taking a share of the returns generated by its capital rather than equity. Fractile, based in London and Bristol, reached a $7 billion valuation after a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint.

Fractile’s round included backing from the UK’s Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank, and its first commercial chip is due next year. In Germany, Sparxity, formerly SpiNNcloud, closed a Series A led by ICM HPQC Fund, with participation from Lockheed Martin Ventures, GlobalFoundries and the EIC Fund, bringing total funding secured by its team to $90 million. Pure Data Centres Group agreed a US$780 million growth facility with a US$1.1 billion accordion that could lift total financing to around US$1.9 billion. Physicl raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to generate targeted training data for the edge cases where models fail, working with labs including Meta and World Labs. Tel Aviv-based Bay emerged from stealth with $50 million in total funding, including a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures.

Bay’s platform evaluates each agent action in the context of the full session and decides in milliseconds whether it can proceed, and the company counts Micron, Peloton, ClickUp and Wix as customers. Finite State secured $27 million in Series C funding led by The O.H.I.O. Fund to help device makers find vulnerabilities in connected products. Ocient closed a $100 million Series C co-led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures to let agents and analysts query petabyte-scale data with built-in governance over agent access and lineage. Ballistic Ventures is seeking $490 million across two new funds, according to SEC filings. Berlin’s Pliant raised an $80 million Series C led by Seaya Nova and Speedinvest to open its B2B payment infrastructure to AI agents, letting tools such as Claude and ChatGPT connect via Model Context Protocol.

Toronto-based Blue J secured US$176 million at a US$700 million valuation, led by JMI Equity, to commercialise its AI tax research agent and expand into the UK, with nearly US$100 million to fund a secondary sale for employees and early investors. Kalepa raised a $75 million Series B at a $470 million valuation to coordinate agents across underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. Seattle’s Finpilot raised a $10 million Series A led by Lobby Capital for its agent-driven operating system for institutional investors. London’s Crediflow AI secured £1.5 million to automate commercial loan analysis. Athena took $2.5 million in pre-seed funding from a16z Speedrun to deliver commercial real estate legal work at a fixed fee per transaction, with agents drafting redlines before attorneys sign off.

Mercor’s valuation roughly doubles the $10 billion it reached last October, as AI startups took $102 billion in Q3 2026, or 64% of global venture capital. Traversal’s technology maps production systems into a form AI agents can read, letting them test thousands of hypotheses in parallel to find the root cause of software incidents, and monthly investigations have grown more than 100-fold this year to nearly 73,000. Nooks said it is on track to nearly triple annual recurring revenue by year end. Fractile is building chips designed to make inference faster, cheaper and less energy-intensive. Sparxity’s sparse-native chips target up to 44 times faster inference in ultra-sparse models.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the government wants to stop world-leading UK ideas from becoming industries elsewhere. Pure Data Centres Executive Chairman and interim CEO Gary Wojtaszek said power is the biggest limit on AI growth, and the company secures it before building capacity. Finite State CEO Matt Wyckhouse said AI-equipped attackers can now find flaws faster than manufacturers can identify affected products. Ocient expects to more than triple revenue this year.

A JPMorgan Chase report found AI-enabled companies made up about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May, up from 36% in 2019. Pliant has passed $100 million in ARR and is positioning its licensed status as a principal Visa and Mastercard member as an advantage once agents begin moving money. Kalepa has tripled revenue while remaining cash flow positive. Bay is less than a year old.

The week’s largest venture deal went to a company that sits behind the agent economy rather than selling agents directly. Investors backed the companies building, securing and powering AI agents, from a $20 billion valuation for an agent-training platform to fresh bets on inference chips, agent security and specialist tools for finance, insurance, tax and law. The common thread is a market paying for AI that does real work inside real businesses. Valuations remain high, and many of these companies have yet to prove durable margins at scale.

The growing emphasis on revenue growth, customer retention and cash flow suggests investors are rewarding AI that can show measurable commercial results. Agent security is becoming its own investment category, financing structures are diversifying beyond conventional equity, as Nooks and Blue J show, and sovereign infrastructure ambitions are increasingly shaping where chip capital lands. Capital flowed to every layer the idea requires, with Mercor and Physicl supplying the data and evaluation that make agents reliable. Fractile, Sparxity and Pure DC provide the compute and power to run them, Bay and Finite State address the security risks they create, and vertical players from Pliant to Kalepa put them to work in regulated industries.

stories.Headline: i14 raises $9m from IP Group to build brain-inspired, energy-efficient AI models
stories.Summary:
i14, an artificial intelligence company led by chief executive Tom McLeod, has raised a $9 million funding round backed by IP Group PLC, the two sides announced in an interview with Proactive published on 16 November 2026. McLeod and Eeshan Kulkarni, a principal at IP Group, spoke with Proactive's Stephen Gunnion about the company's work on energy-efficient AI models and its plans to scale the technology. The company says it is developing new AI architectures inspired by the human brain, which are designed to deliver frontier-level intelligence while using less memory, computing power and energy than conventional large language models. McLeod said the technology can keep energy and memory costs consistent as models process more information, which could remove the traditional trade-off between capability and efficiency.

The $9 million round is intended to fund product development, expansion of the team and deeper partnerships with hyperscalers, neocloud providers and AI inference platforms, including work involving AWS. Over the next 12 to 18 months, i14 aims to broaden its model offering, grow early customer adoption and make the technology more widely available. The company says wider availability could give businesses and governments greater control over their AI capabilities while requiring less computing infrastructure. IP Group, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker IPO, backed the round through its focus on deep technology and the future of computing.

Kulkarni explained that IP Group backed the funding round because of i14's scientific innovation, its research expertise and its commercial potential. He also described how the company fits into IP Group's wider deep-tech portfolio and its focus on the future of computing. McLeod set out the company's view that its brain-inspired designs could cut the memory, computing power and energy that large language models demand. Proactive noted that it has a commercial relationship with IP Group PLC and that the article was produced independently under its editorial standards policy.

The interview was published by Proactive, which covers artificial intelligence, deep technology, investment and emerging companies across its news and video channels. The articles do not say when the funding round closed, who else took part or what valuation the round placed on i14. They also do not give a date for the AWS work or say how far it has progressed. Beyond the 12 to 18 month goals described by McLeod, the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: FleetGuru develops AI agents that assess repair quotes in seconds using historical maintenance data
stories.Summary:
Australian fleet maintenance technology provider FleetGuru.ai says its platform automatically approves an average of 35% of maintenance jobs, rising to 70% for some customers. The company is developing AI agents that can assess repair quotes in seconds, using historical maintenance data to check whether proposed work and charges meet fleet approval rules. The technology aims to reduce the time spent reviewing maintenance requests and identify excessive repair charges before work is authorised. FleetGuru founder and managing director Eden Shirley disclosed the figures at the Fleet APAC Summit in Bangkok in June, where he also outlined plans to expand into Japan. FleetGuru has not specified how many of those approvals are handled by AI agents.

FleetGuru is developing maintenance data infrastructure for the Japanese market, building on its operations in Australia and New Zealand. US-based Fleetio made its AI Service Advisor generally available in September following a six-month trial. Fleetio says the system assessed more than US$1.4 billion in maintenance expenditure during the trial, helping vehicles return to service an average of 2.5 hours sooner per repair. The technology can also approve low-risk repairs automatically within limits set by fleet managers. An April 2026 Fleetio survey of more than 600 fleet professionals found that only 4.1% supported AI making high-impact decisions, including automated approvals, without human authorisation.

Barry Pryce, FleetGuru's CTO and tech co-founder, says reviewing maintenance quotes is one of the first fleet management tasks where AI agents can outperform humans. Pryce says AI agents can complete these checks in seconds, identifying pricing discrepancies that fleet managers might otherwise miss. He says an agent compares every line item against billions of data points, and that a human cannot analyse at the same speed and scale. Pryce says the AI agent works from structured historical maintenance data and does not answer from a general model's memory or the internet. He says FleetGuru has billions of data points captured from vehicle records, service history, workshop and parts pricing and policy rules.

Pryce says fleet managers can set the rules governing which repairs AI agents are allowed to approve, including limits on expenditure and supplier restrictions. He says anything outside those limits triggers human review, and every decision is logged with the data behind it so a manager can override it. Pryce says FleetGuru starts with low-risk, high-volume decisions and widens the agent's authority as the results prove out. He says FleetGuru processes close to 1 million work orders per annum, totalling hundreds of millions in maintenance costs. Pryce says cost savings vary by fleet, and even small percentage gains compound quickly.

The April 2026 Fleetio survey also found that just 1.5% of fleet professionals said they fully trusted AI-generated recommendations without human review. Pryce says the biggest barrier to wider adoption of AI maintenance approvals is proving they deliver financial savings. He says fleet managers have heard plenty of promises and are right to want evidence before handing over decisions that cost money. Pryce says the top concerns of fleet managers today are rising costs and increasing regulation. He says maintenance management is expensive and resource-intensive, and it is easy to demonstrate real savings on invoices and the time required to review and approve them.

FleetGuru has yet to provide specific figures showing how much its AI agents can reduce maintenance costs. Pryce says FleetGuru's quote scrutiny engine uses machine learning to analyse historical maintenance data and assess repair costs, rather than relying on generative AI. He says FleetGuru works primarily through fleet management companies, integrating its services with the systems their customers already use. Pryce says a telematics provider would need years to build the supplier network behind maintenance transaction data. He says the AI projects that fail will be the ones that don't deliver ROI and don't own their own data or service networks, and that FleetGuru owns both.

Articles.Title: FleetGuru reports 35% automated maintenance approvals, uses AI to scrutinise repair quotes

stories.Headline: Daisytuner raises 6 million euros to automate AI performance engineering across different chips
stories.Summary:
The German deep tech startup Daisytuner announced that it raised 6 million euros in seed funding on November 16, 2026. This funding round was co-led by Elaia and LEA Ventures, with additional participation from Seedcamp and the Amadeus APEX Technology Fund. The company intends to use these funds to expand its compiler technology, grow its internal team, and bring its Daisyflow platform to more enterprises. This technology automates performance engineering to ensure AI models run at maximum speed on any available chip.

The company will utilize its patented optimization platform and a self-learning compiler to eliminate the need for manual integration. This process converts code from frameworks like PyTorch into native code for various architectures, including AMD and Nvidia GPUs. The Daisyflow platform is already live in production and has shown that Qwen 2.5 can run 18 percent faster on AMD Instinct GPUs than the industry standard vLLM. Founded in 2024 by Adrian Schmitz and Lukas Trümper, the firm relies on research from institutions like ETH Zurich and TU Munich.

CEO Lukas Trümper stated that software currently keeps many available accelerators on the sidelines despite growing demand for compute. He noted that the company is collaborating with European hyperscalers, enterprises, and chip vendors to ensure new hardware enters production immediately. Sébastien Lefebvre of Elaia remarked that the industry needs to remove the bottleneck created by relying on a single vendor's software stack. Alexi Malikotsinas from LEA Ventures added that the technology restores control over compute efficiency and technology sovereignty to the customers.

stories.Headline: Telefónica blocks 500,000 fraudulent calls daily in Spain and launches Llamadas Molestas alerts
stories.Summary:
The articles report that AI-powered fraud could cost firms USD $11.5 billion by 2027, according to CFOtech, and that Telefónica publishes a running series of position papers and blog posts on digital security framing the problem as a question of trust. The analysis, dated November 16, 2026, pulls together what Telefónica, CFOtech, TELUS Digital, E*TRADE and a handful of named practitioners say about AI-enabled fraud, what defenses they recommend, and where the market is heading. The articles state that AI now writes the scam, clones the voice and builds the fake colleague, and that the bill is climbing. The articles state that when any voice, face or message can be faked, the old shortcuts for deciding who to believe stop working. The articles state that the Maileva hack exposed 22 million people's data recently, and that every leak of personal data hands scammers fresh raw material for convincing impersonation.

The articles state that CFOtech's report puts the potential cost of AI-powered fraud to firms at USD $11.5 billion by 2027, a figure the articles say cannot be verified from the headline alone and should be treated as a directional estimate rather than a measured loss. The articles state that Telefónica's Spanish operations block approximately 500,000 fraudulent calls every day, and that on 16 March 2026 Telefónica launched Llamadas Molestas, a service that alerts users to potentially unwanted calls using predictive models that analyze patterns associated with spam and nuisance calling. The articles state that Telefónica says its security capabilities include 12 Security Operations Centres built to detect and respond to potential incidents. The articles state that TELUS Digital lists the preferred multi-factor method as an authenticator app or hardware device, not SMS, and that high-value transactions should require two or more independent approvers. The articles state that E*TRADE's consumer-security guidance lists fraud warning signs as urgency, secrecy and demands to act now.

The articles state that Ben Colman, chief executive officer of Reality Defender, defined the problem in a KCBD report on voice-cloning scams, saying a deepfake is a piece of media, audio, video, images where a real person is either AI-generated or AI-manipulated using tools available to anybody with just a Google search. The articles state that Telefónica's guidance for organizations focuses on knowing which AI systems are in use, who uses them and what data they touch. The articles state that Telefónica recommends four moves for organizations deploying AI: discover which AI systems are in use, identify the users and the data they access, protect models against known attacks, and monitor model behavior continuously for malicious patterns. The articles state that Telefónica's AI-risk framework adds security-by-design measures such as access controls, security assessments, continuous monitoring and protection of physical and digital infrastructure, plus employee cybersecurity training. The articles state that Telefónica says industry-wide anti-fraud work increasingly combines AI-driven detection, advanced authentication, intelligence sharing and consumer education.

The articles state that Telefónica Tech applies AI and automation inside its Security Operations Centres to analyze large data volumes and prioritize threats for human analysts, and that the company says AI can improve cybersecurity by spotting anomalous patterns and emerging risks in real time. The articles state that automation takes over repetitive security tasks, freeing specialists to focus on complex decisions and incident response. The articles state that ET Edge Insights ran a piece under the headline that AI scams overtake phishing as cybercrime turns into an industrialised business. The articles state that a human fraudster might run a handful of convincing scams a day, while an automated pipeline can run thousands and tailor each one. The articles state that the confirmed picture has three parts: AI is being used to create convincing impersonations, deepfake audio and video, fake personas and other deceptive content at scale; that capability feeds AI-enabled fraud and phishing, which threaten both users' digital trust and their financial security; and the recommended response is a mix of personal habits, organizational process and technical monitoring, not a single product.

The articles state that Telefónica's published material treats deepfakes, advanced phishing campaigns and increasingly sophisticated digital fraud as the growing risks tied to malicious AI use. The articles state that Telefónica's security writing stresses that identity replication makes the authenticity of digital interactions more important for customer relations, identity verification and fraud protection. The articles state that Telefónica describes a prevention model that spans the whole incident lifecycle, from anticipation through prevention to detection. The articles state that readers once learned to spot phishing by its flaws, such as odd grammar, a mismatched logo or a clumsy greeting, and that AI removes most of those tells. The articles state that an earlier report on fake GTA VI downloads carrying the Vidar infostealer showed how quickly a hyped launch becomes bait.

The articles state that the cost has more than one layer: direct losses such as a fraudulent wire approved after a convincing fake call, then investigation and remediation costs, then the slower damage to customer confidence. The articles state that a customer who doubts a brand's messages stops acting on any of them, including the legitimate ones. The articles state that the articles stick to confirmed figures and clearly label their own judgment calls because the fraud space attracts more guesswork than almost any other corner of tech. The articles state that the articles' own read is that the training line deserves more attention than it gets, since most successful fraud still ends with a person pressing a button. The articles state that tooling shrinks the number of bad messages that reach that person but never reduces the stakes of the ones that do.

stories.Headline: Omani SMEs use AI to improve productivity and cut costs
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by CNN on November 16, 2026, discusses what it calls the originality gap and the search for competitive advantage in the AI era, though the text provided contains mostly page code rather than the article's reporting. The second article, published by Zawya on November 14, 2026 and written by a staff writer for the Oman Daily Observer, examines how small and medium-sized enterprises in Oman can turn artificial intelligence into a competitive advantage. It says AI is no longer reserved for large corporations or businesses with substantial financial resources, and that even relatively small businesses can now use AI tools for tasks that once required considerable time, specialised expertise and additional staff. Those tasks include responding to customer enquiries, analysing sales trends, managing inventory and preparing financial reports. The article says AI can help Omani SMEs improve productivity, reduce costs and become more competitive, and that the real question is not whether businesses should adopt AI but how they can use it effectively to generate tangible economic benefits.

It gives examples: a small retail business can use AI-powered tools to analyse purchasing patterns, identify popular products and forecast future demand, which helps owners make better inventory decisions, reduce unnecessary stock and minimise waste, while restaurants and hospitality businesses can use AI to understand customer preferences, manage bookings, improve marketing and respond to enquiries more efficiently. Marketing is another area of benefit, since AI tools can now assist with producing marketing content, translating communications, identifying potential customer groups and tailoring promotional campaigns, work that previously required dedicated employees or external agencies. Financial management also offers opportunities, as many small businesses struggle with cash-flow management, expense monitoring and financial planning. The article argues that SMEs play an important role in Oman's economic diversification, employment generation and development of local supply chains, so businesses that become more productive through technology can potentially expand operations, improve service quality, reach new customers and compete in regional markets. It cautions that adopting AI should not become an objective in itself, because buying software or subscribing to an AI platform does not automatically translate into higher productivity or profitability, and businesses first need to identify where they face operational difficulties and whether AI can offer a practical solution.

It says a small enterprise might begin by automating customer enquiries or improving inventory management rather than investing in expensive and complex systems, and that starting with manageable applications, evaluating results and gradually expanding their use is a more realistic approach. It also lists challenges that cannot be ignored, including data privacy, cybersecurity, the accuracy of AI-generated information and the risk of excessive dependence on automated systems. The article says government institutions, universities and the private sector can contribute through practical training programmes, SME-focused digital advisory services, collaboration with technology providers and affordable access to AI solutions, and that universities can connect research and technical expertise with real business challenges. It notes that Oman's National Digital Economy Programme and its second phase for 2026 to 2030 provide a policy framework for accelerating digital transformation and encouraging businesses to embrace emerging technologies, and that the next step should be ensuring these ambitions translate into practical improvements at the level of individual enterprises. It concludes that the competitive advantage of AI will not belong only to businesses that adopt the most advanced technology but to those that understand how to use it intelligently, responsibly and productively, and that for Oman's SMEs the opportunity now is to turn that potential into measurable economic value.

stories.Headline: Egypt health minister discusses deploying AI for 100 Million Healthy Lives initiative
stories.Summary:
Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, Dr. Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, met on Monday, November 16, 2026, to discuss strengthening collaboration and bringing the latest digital technologies into the country's healthcare system, according to a ministry spokesperson. The meeting looked at ways to develop an artificial intelligence framework for healthcare and to expand cooperation in digital health, the spokesperson, Dr. Hossam Abdel Ghaffar, said. Talks also covered proposed infrastructure and technological solutions for building integrated health systems and for making telemedicine services easier for patients to use. The discussions further explored using big data and the digital infrastructure Egypt has built in recent years, combined with advanced operational models, to streamline medical data flows and support informed healthcare decisions.

The meeting examined how to deploy AI applications in support of the "100 Million Healthy Lives" presidential public health initiative, the spokesperson said. By drawing on the large national health databases generated through these programs, the ministry aims to improve diagnostic accuracy, enable early prediction of disease and identify groups at high risk. The minister stressed the need to speed up coordination and executive action between ministry officials and private-sector representatives so that cooperation frameworks can be put into operation. He said harnessing available capabilities and expertise would support development of the national healthcare system and drive a major improvement in the quality and efficiency of medical services provided to citizens.

The meeting was attended by Deputy Minister of Health and Population Dr. Mohamed El-Tayeb and Assistant Minister for Public Health Initiatives Dr. Mohamed Hassani. Others present were Assistant Minister for National Projects Dr. Sherif Mostafa and Head of the Central Administration for Healthcare Quality Dr. Galal El-Shishini. The Head of the Central Administration for the Health and Population Information Center, Eng. Ahmed Sobhy, attended, along with Dr. Mona Khalifa, General Director of the General Administration for Presidential Initiatives. The articles do not say what steps follow the meeting or when any of the discussed systems would be introduced.

stories.Headline: Ciaran Malone speaks at ESTRO course on AI integration in radiotherapy
stories.Summary:
Ciaran Malone, a Senior Medical Physicist at St Luke’s Radiation Oncology Network and a member of the AI in Radiation Oncology working group at the National group under the NCCP, shared a LinkedIn post about a guest speaker role at an ESTRO course. The course is titled Current Use, Future Developments, and the Integration of AI, and it is hosted by St. Luke’s Radiation Oncology AI Network at the St. James’s Hospital Campus. Malone said he was delighted to be contributing as a guest speaker along with Maeve Kearney at the course. He described a great opening session to a full room led by Course Director Rob Tijssen alongside Prof. Gerry Hanna, Marie Curie Chair of Clinical Oncology and Consultant Clinical Oncologist. Malone said the session set the tone with a few standout reminders, including that imaging does not simply support radiotherapy but defines what it can do.

Malone also cited the reminder that we do not treat images, but treat patients based on the information images provide. He said he was really looking forward to sharing his perspective on SGRT and AI at the course. He added that he looked forward to learning from colleagues across the field and exploring how to best harness the technology to improve outcomes for patients. The article describes ESTRO, the European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology, as a leading European scientific society dedicated to promoting excellence in radiation oncology through education, research, and professional collaboration. ESTRO organizes courses, workshops, and educational programs for radiation oncology professionals, and it supports research and innovation in radiotherapy and cancer treatment. The society also provides opportunities for specialists to expand their knowledge and clinical expertise and connects healthcare professionals, researchers, and institutions worldwide.

ESTRO additionally promotes developments in radiotherapy, medical imaging, artificial intelligence, and precision cancer treatment, according to the article. The article gives no further details on the course schedule, the content of Malone’s talk, or any outcomes from the session. It also does not say what SGRT stands for or how AI would be used in the radiotherapy workflow. No figures, dates beyond the article’s publication, or patient data are provided in the text. The article closes with a note inviting readers to stay up to date with daily picks from OncoDaily and a copyright notice covering the site’s content.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: UKRI funds 20 Turing AI Fellows with over £39 million to tackle medicine, energy and nuclear safety
stories.Summary:
UK Research and Innovation announced 20 new Turing AI Fellows on 16 November 2026, backed by more than £39 million in government funding. The fellows will use artificial intelligence to tackle challenges including personalised medicine, clean energy and nuclear safety. The cohort includes 17 researchers supported through the Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships and three supported through the Turing AI Global Fellowships. Both schemes are delivered by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and form part of UKRI's Industrial Strategy 8 AI Priority Programme. The fellowships contribute to UKRI's wider investment of more than £11 billion in the UK's highest-potential sectors.

The Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowships started in October 2026 and will run for three years, while the Turing AI Global Fellowships start in 2027 and will run for five years. Dr Thiago Sogo Bezerra of King's College London will combine AI with novel detector technology to improve neutrino measurements, with potential applications for nuclear reactor monitoring and safety. Dr Roisin Buckley of the University of Glasgow will develop AI tools to improve understanding of underground and seabed conditions, supporting cleaner energy and major infrastructure projects. Professor Neil Cummins of the London School of Economics and Political Science will use AI to unlock more than a million handwritten wills. Professor Jocelyn Monroe of the University of Oxford will use the search for dark matter to develop more trustworthy AI systems capable of identifying extremely rare events.

Professor Charlotte Deane, Senior Responsible Owner for the UKRI IS8 AI Programme and Executive Chair of EPSRC, said AI has enormous potential to transform how society understands and tackles its biggest challenges. She said the fellowships will give outstanding researchers the freedom and support to push the boundaries of AI itself while applying it in new ways across disciplines. She said they are part of UKRI's long-term commitment to AI, building on sustained investment that helps strengthen the UK's position as a global leader. She said that by investing in exceptional people and ideas, UKRI is helping build the expertise and capability the UK needs to remain at the forefront of AI research and innovation. She said this will turn advances in AI to advance knowledge, improve lives and drive growth across the UK.

Dr Jonathan Phillips of the University of Exeter will combine AI and experimental biology to help scientists better understand and design proteins for applications in medicine, biotechnology and environmental sensing. Professor Michael Tadao Inouye of the University of Cambridge will use AI and large-scale health data to better understand disease and support more personalised healthcare. The new fellows join a growing Turing AI Fellowships community that has already helped launch start-up companies, attract significant investment, influence policy, and train the next generation of AI researchers. The application of AI across disciplines will support growth and high-skilled jobs across the UK while building on areas of established UK strength and global leadership. The cohort will help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of both AI research.

The funded projects include AI-driven precision measurements and applications in neutrino physics, led by Dr Thiago Sogo Bezerra at King's College London. Professor Cristian Bonato of Heriot-Watt University leads work on developing a real-time AI-enhanced experimenter for quantum sensing. Professor Jasmin Fisher of University College London leads work on understanding cancer through trustworthy AI and digital twins. Dr Katherine Inzani of the University of Nottingham leads atoms to devices, machine learning approaches for the dynamics of functional materials. Professor Sally Keith of Lancaster University leads BEACON, behavioural ecology AI for conservation action.

Professor Nan Li of Imperial College London leads work on manufacturable-by-design to production-ready, sustainable and trustworthy AI for materials forming. Professor Qiuhua Liang of Loughborough University leads HiPA-flood, high performance computing and AI for personalised flood forecasting and resilient futures. Professor Andrea Manica of the University of Cambridge leads work on predicting future biodiversity changes by integrating multiple lines of evidence at scale. Dr Jacob Page of The University of Edinburgh leads work on a new era for turbulence computation. Professor Ganna Pogrebna of Queen's University Belfast leads BIQUAD, behaviourally informed quantum-augmented AI agents for bias-aware human-machine collaboration in critical domains.

Professor Matthew Rigby of the University of Bristol leads a near-real time global greenhouse gas observation and emissions evaluation system. Professor Corwin Wright of the University of Bath leads a gravity wave latent inference framework for climate. Professor Jonathan May is relocating from the US, from the University of Southern California, to The University of Edinburgh to lead work on from language to intent. Professor Denny Wu is relocating from the US, from New York University and the Flatiron Institute, to the University of Oxford to lead work on a predictive mathematical foundation for scalable deep learning. Professor Roi Reichart is relocating from Israel, from Technion, Israel Institute of Technology, to the University of Cambridge to lead work on building socially intelligent AI, core AI advances for modelling behavior, interaction, and emotion.

stories.Headline: Gulliver visited our AI world 300 years ago. He left in disgust.
stories.Summary:
Jonathan Swift published his famous satire titled Gulliver’s Travels Into Remote Regions of the World on October 28, 1726. The author used the third part of this masterpiece to mock the scientists and technologists of his own era. He specifically targeted the Royal Society, which had been founded in 1660, to criticize those obsessed with impractical projects. Swift depicted a flying island called Laputa where philosophers focused on abstract mathematics and astronomy while ignoring the real world.

The story describes a society where intellectuals are so detached that they require flappers to slap them with bladders of pebbles to regain focus. This narrative serves as a critique of modern tech elites who pursue costly vanity projects and immortality fads. The author suggests that today's world is becoming dominated by error-prone algorithms and a similar lack of practical wisdom. These modern developments transform an eighteenth-century satire into a relevant dissection of our current artificial intelligence age.

Adrian Wooldridge wrote that it takes a rare genius to create a work that remains relevant three centuries later. He argued that the technologists of today repeat the same follies that Swift mocked during the time of powdered wigs. The writer believes that the isolated technicians of the past have evolved into a group that now rules the world. He suggests that the obsession with intellectual purity over mundane practicalities continues to define the current technological landscape.

Articles.Title: Gulliver visited our AI world 300 years ago. He left in disgust.

stories.Headline: Revenue cycle leaders should treat AI as part of the operating model, not a standalone tool
stories.Summary:
The article is a how-to piece on future-proofing revenue cycle management in the age of AI, published by hitconsultant.net on November 17, 2026, and it offers guidance rather than reporting a single event with named actors and dates. It does not name the people who wrote it, the organizations that contributed to it, or any specific company, hospital or vendor that has adopted the practices it describes. Because the text supplies no who, no when beyond the publication date and no concrete numbers, there is no reported happening to set out in the order a news story would require. The piece instead frames AI as a force changing how revenue cycle work is organized and argues that organizations should prepare for it deliberately.

What the article requires of readers is a shift in how revenue cycle management is planned, staffed and measured, with AI treated as part of the operating model rather than a standalone tool. It presents future-proofing as a set of changes to process, people and data rather than a single purchase or policy, and it frames the work as ongoing preparation for conditions that are still developing. The text gives no figures for cost, adoption rates, error rates, staffing levels or timeframes, and it names no deadlines, budgets or performance targets that a reader could check. It also gives no dates for when any of the described changes should begin or be completed, beyond the publication date of the article itself.

Responsibility for acting sits with the leaders who run revenue cycle operations, according to the article, though it does not name any individual, title or institution as accountable. The guidance is addressed to those who plan and oversee the revenue cycle rather than to patients, payers or regulators, and it treats their decisions about technology and workflow as the lever that determines the outcome. The article's own statements are presented as advice and framing rather than as findings from a study, a pilot or a disclosed set of results. No spokesperson, executive or expert is quoted by name, and no organization is described as having tested or endorsed the approach.

The context the article supplies is the growing presence of AI in revenue cycle work and the risk that organizations adapt slowly or unevenly to it. What happens next, in the article's telling, depends on whether revenue cycle leaders treat future-proofing as a continuing discipline rather than a one-time project, and it offers no schedule, milestone or forecast for how that will unfold. It reports no event that has occurred, no decision that has been announced and no result that has been measured, so there is nothing further to say about consequences that the text actually supports. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Axel Licha shares study showing AI contours 21 cardiac substructures in under a minute
stories.Summary:
Axel Licha, a radiotherapy clinical consultant at TheraPanacea, shared a LinkedIn post about a new study published in Practical Radiation Oncology, the official clinical journal of the American Society for Radiation Oncology, on November 17, 2026. The study is titled Multicenter Evaluation of a Deep Learning Model for Automatic Contouring of Cardiac Substructures in Adults. Alexandra Moignier and Axel Licha share first authorship, and the co-authors are Felix Felici, Loig Duverge, Martin Lange, Loic Ah-Thiane, Gregory Delpon, Anna Karlhede, Fredrik Löfman, Frida Skarf, Jonas Söderberg, Elvire Martin-Mervoyer, François Thillays, Arnaud Beddok and Loig Vaugier. Licha said the project involved months of research, collaboration and a shared ambition of making cardiac protection in radiotherapy more precise and accessible.

The deep learning model automatically contours 21 cardiac substructures in under one minute, according to the post. Of those contours, 93.8% were clinically acceptable without major corrections, and the figure was 88.5% for coronary arteries, which the post describes as among the most challenging structures to delineate. Licha framed the results as less time contouring and more time for clinical expertise, and as a step closer to more personalized radiotherapy. He thanked the co-authors and collaborators, especially Moignier, and named Elvire Martin-Mervoyer, Arnaud Beddok and Loig Vaugier for their trust, mentorship and constant support.

Licha is responsible for the LinkedIn post, and the study itself is the work of the listed authors, with Moignier and Licha as first authors. In the post he said artificial intelligence is changing radiation oncology and that he and his colleagues are part of it. He also said some publications mean a little more than others and that this is definitely one of them, adding that he is incredibly proud to share the publication. The articles do not record any further comment from the other authors or from the journal.

The articles give no further details on the study design, the centers involved or a publication date beyond the post, and they do not say what happens next with the model or its clinical use. The only stated next step is Licha's description of the work as a step closer to more personalized radiotherapy. The remaining content of the source page consists of site navigation, other headlines and a copyright notice, which add nothing to the story.

stories.Headline: Zus Health raises $33M Series B led by Drive Capital to expand its AI-native patient record platform
stories.Summary:
Zus Health, a health technology company founded and led by Jonathan Bush, raised 33 million dollars in a Series B funding round led by Drive Capital, according to an announcement reported by Fierce Healthcare on November 12, 2026. The round also drew backing from Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures and Alumni Ventures, along with existing investors Andreessen Horowitz, F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners. The new financing brings the company's total capital raised to more than 100 million dollars. Zus Health, which launched in 2021 and was named a Fierce 15 honoree in 2025, is building what it describes as an AI-native healthcare data platform.

The company said the fresh funding will support continued investment in its intelligent patient record platform, its national healthcare data network and its AI-powered clinical workflows. Zus Health has built its platform in three layers, starting with a nationwide patient record, then a data network that pulls information into that record, and increasingly AI-enabled workflows that automate care tasks. Its Zus Aggregated Profile brings fragmented clinical information into a unified, longitudinal patient record, supported by nationwide connectivity across EHR networks, pharmacy data, care event notifications and labs. The company claims that in August alone its network supported more than 110 million networked transactions, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date.

Bush told Fierce Healthcare that electronic health record systems succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations, leaving clinicians to search for records and reconcile incomplete information. He said the company is now on the last and critical piece of what he thinks the future of medical records looks like, which is standing up workflows that automate patient care tasks in a bespoke way. He added that with AI the company has an extraordinary opportunity to build workflows that make delivering care easier, faster and more effective. Molly Bonakdarpour, a general partner at Drive Capital, said in a statement that healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on reliable, connected patient information, and she said Zus has built the foundation to address that challenge at scale.

Zus Health works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, and diagnostics and precision medicine companies, and its solutions span pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management. The company plans to use the funding to build out its AI-powered clinical intelligence and capabilities and to broaden its healthcare data network connectivity. It also plans to expand its solutions to automate population health and care management workflows while enabling customers and developers to create AI-powered workflows across value-based care, specialty care and other high-value use cases. Bush noted that the company is seeing rapid growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where complex patient records are spread across multiple providers.

stories.Headline: Sumary raises a $25M seed led by Singular to expand AI accounting software across the UK and Europe
stories.Summary:
Copenhagen-based Sumary, which makes AI accounting software, raised a $25 million seed round led by Singular, the company announced in a Tech Funding News report by Sofia Chesnokova dated November 10, 2026. Existing investors byFounders, Partech and Tenity joined the round, along with angel investors including Steve Anavi of Qonto, Tuomas Artman of Linear, Stanislas Polu of Dust, Steffen Tjerrild of Synthesia, Jannick Malling of Public.com and Ben Freeman of Omnea. The round is nearly six times the $4.2 million pre-seed Sumary raised in November 2025, led by byFounders. Total funding to date comes to $29.2 million. Sumary claims it is the largest seed round ever for accounting software in Europe.

Sumary offers an AI operating system for accounting that automates workflows, checks transactions and provides insights, handling the monthly close, VAT returns and year-end for all clients and ledgers. Every step is set up for the accountant to review and approve, and a VAT return is delivered as a draft for review and sign-off. The company says firms spend 50% less time on their monthly close and 75% less time on VAT returns after three months on the platform. Sumary says it has arrangements with most of the 20 largest accounting firms across the Nordics and contracts with several leading UK firms, and customers include Deloitte, Grant Thornton and Baker Tilly. Grand View Research valued the European accounting software market at $5.4 billion in 2024 and forecasts it will reach $8.4 billion by 2030.

CEO and co-founder Pascar Sivam said accounting firms are being asked to do more with fewer people, and software has to take on the preparation properly so accountants can give their time to clients and their own teams. Sivam said the round lets Sumary bring that to firms across the UK and Europe much faster. Sivam said dozens, and probably soon hundreds, of AI accounting firms are being built, and Sumary wants to offer existing firms the chance to deliver customer value as good as, if not better than, these new entrants by adopting AI quickly. He said that with the right technology, existing firms can lead this transformation rather than be disrupted by it. Jeremy Uzan, a general partner at Singular, said Sumary has one of the strongest founding teams seen in Europe at this stage and exceptional commercial momentum, combining deep AI research with an understanding of how accounting firms operate.

Sivam started Sumary with Bastian Schneider, Lucas Rantzau, Frederik Hvilshøj and COO Frederik Skov Wacher. Sivam and Schneider are former McKinsey consultants, and Hvilshøj was a lead ML engineer at Encord and holds a PhD in explainable deep learning and generative models from Aarhus. Sivam and Skov Wacher are both moving from Copenhagen to London, which will be the company's main commercial centre, while Denmark remains the centre of its technology and AI research. The company is expanding into Europe, with the Benelux as the first market. Sumary's Copenhagen research team has created a benchmark based on actual accounting work and runs all the top AI models against it before using them with clients.

Since July, the AI accounting space has split, with some startups selling AI to established firms and others operating as accounting firms in their own right. Basis landed $100 million at a $1.15 billion valuation in February, Kabilio in Barcelona raised €10 million on November 5 and serves over 500 accounting firms, and Ravical in Belgium secured a $17 million seed round on October 29. Skalar raised €12 million in July, Integral raised an €18 million Series A in September, Dougs raised €50 million in October, and Gradient came out of stealth with $4 million that same month. Sumary says it will work with any ledger the accountant is currently using and aims to be the firm's operational partner.

The big question the article raises is whether the profession will trust tools that assist existing firms or tools used to build entirely new firms around AI. Sumary has opted to support existing firms and now has $25 million to demonstrate what it can do. The end game, according to the article, is for accountants to spend less time on drudgery and more time on advisory. The article does not say how the new funding will be allocated beyond UK and European expansion. The article does not give a company valuation for Sumary.

stories.Headline: Marsh reports AI-driven cyber incidents more than double as premiums head for 10 percent rise in 2027
stories.Summary:
Insurance broker Marsh reported on Tuesday, November 17, that artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace and scope of cyberattacks. The company recorded 105 cyber incidents for its clients during the second half of October, which is more than double the 48 incidents seen in late May. These AI enabled tools allow attackers to identify vulnerabilities like unpatched software and weak identity controls much faster than before. The FBI also warned that a hacking framework called ARTEX has been used since August to gain privileged enterprise access in under three hours. This specific tool has targeted the telecommunications, manufacturing, healthcare, and financial services sectors, including a breach of personal information for 67,000 people in South Korea.

These rising threats are driving a significant increase in the cost of global cyber insurance premiums over the next two years. GlobalData projects that premiums will grow by 6.9 percent to reach 16.6 billion dollars this year. This growth is expected to accelerate further to a 10 percent increase in 2027, bringing the total to 18.3 billion dollars. Businesses are facing these higher costs as they struggle to respond to the increasing frequency of attacks. The shift requires companies to address the asymmetry between software driven attackers and defenders who are limited by budgets and staffing.

Meredith Schnur, the cyber practice leader for Marsh Risk in the United States and Canada, explained that AI acts as an amplification of risk. She stated that a significant number of recent incidents can be attributed to attackers using agentic tools to find system weaknesses. Schnur noted that the volume of incidents has increased because organizations are taking longer to contain attacks while AI adoption scales quickly. This environment puts immense pressure on chief financial officers and chief information security officers at large enterprises. These leaders must manage larger digital footprints that are more susceptible to the new methods employed by modern fraudsters.

Articles.Title: Cyber Insurance Costs to Jump 10% Amid Rising AI Attacks

stories.Headline: US stocks decline as AI companies experience price swings ahead of Nvidia earnings report
stories.Summary:
The United States stock market fell on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, as artificial intelligence companies experienced significant price swings. The S&P 500 sank 0.9 percent, while the Nasdaq composite dropped 1.2 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 541 points, or 1.1 percent. Nvidia led the decline with a 2.9 percent drop, and other AI firms like Advanced Micro Devices and CoreWeave also shifted from early gains to losses. These fluctuations occurred as investors awaited a critical earnings report from Nvidia after the trading day ended.

The situation requires Nvidia to prove that its growth can persist following the resignation of former leader Jensen Huang. The company is now establishing a new board committee to manage global trade compliance and national security. This change follows reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with a person alleged to be a spy for China. Interim CEO Colette Kress is scheduled to speak to Wall Street for the first time since taking over the leadership role.

Market analysts suggest that AI stocks have been volatile for months due to a series of evolving concerns. These worries include the possibility that stock prices rose too high, the impact of high interest rates, and potential new regulations following Democratic victories in the midterm elections. Other market factors contributed to the decline, such as a 1.8 percent drop for Home Depot and a 2.3 percent loss for United Airlines. The broader economy remains influenced by high inflation, rising oil prices, and technical issues at major banks like JPMorgan Chase.

stories.Headline: Claude and Gemini repeat partisan language as their own in Texas election answers
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, James Talarico and Bobby Pulido won their races as Texas’s U.S. Senate and House races heated up, and voters turned to Google Search with questions about Democratic candidates Talarico and Pulido and Republican candidates Ken Paxton and Monica De La Cruz. In October, the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas asked OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini each the most common questions drawn from Google Trends. On October 9, 2026, DDIA tested OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna, Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5 and Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash, with web search on, through a service called OpenRouter. Researchers asked 39 questions, in English and Spanish, about eight candidates in four 2026 races in Michigan, Texas and Florida. DDIA researchers asked all three chatbots whether Talarico said “God is nonbinary,” a line Republicans have been using against him throughout the current campaign.

Talarico said it in an October 2021 speech on the Texas House floor against a bill that required students to play on school sports teams matching the sex they were assigned at birth, pointing to the two Hebrew words used for God in the first lines of the Book of Genesis, one masculine and one feminine. In an April 2021 committee hearing, Talarico said modern science recognizes many more than two biological sexes, in fact six, referring to intersex chromosome variations, not genders. In September 2026, he said he missed the mark on some of his past statements and explained there are two sexes plus a small percentage of people with genetic variations. Paxton has been Texas attorney general since 2015, and in May 2026 he beat Sen. John Cornyn in a runoff and became the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate. On June 29, 2026, his office as Texas attorney general, which Paxton still led while running for the Senate, published a press release touting his record.

Claude, in English, said Talarico was speaking against “a bill to ban men from women’s sports,” an exact phrase used by Fox News in an article, and three of its four sources were right-leaning outlets: Fox News, PJ Media and Public Square magazine, with the fourth a local San Antonio TV station. In Spanish, Claude sent researchers to FactCheck.org and local TV and did not borrow phrasing that can be considered controversial. In English, Claude began with “Not quite” and explained that Talarico had talked about six biological sexes, not six genders, but in Spanish it began with “Sí” and said Talarico did make a claim about “seis géneros/sexos,” using words fully extracted from the Washington Examiner and summarizing the measure as keeping “hombres biológicos que se identifican como transgénero” out of girls’ sports. Claude described Paxton’s record by copying, word for word, two lines from a press release his office published to promote him, that he “vigorously and successfully defended SB 4,” a state law that lets police arrest people suspected of crossing the border illegally, and that he “secured a major U.S. Supreme Court victory” on the state’s congressional map, using no quotation marks and not saying the words were the office’s own praise. Claude, in English, added that Pulido “has criticized Biden’s open borders policies,” copying content from a post by the Welcome Party, a group that backs centrist Democrats, including Pulido.

Gemini and ChatGPT responded accurately and in a fact-based manner, and both described the bill being discussed when Talarico said “God is nonbinary” in neutral terms in both languages, though Gemini used as sources Facebook posts made by conservative news outlets: Fox News in English, and PJ Media and Fox News in Spanish. ChatGPT also opened its Spanish answer with “Sí,” but right away added that the phrase is usually distorted and that he never said “six genders,” and in English it said “No, not literally.” Gemini got the facts right in both languages, mentioning that Talarico spoke of six biological sexes, not six genders, and later walked it back, but linked to Facebook posts made by politicians, using a social media publication made by Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s campaign as source in the English and Spanish versions, and in Spanish also linking to a post by Republican Lt. Governor Dan Patrick and to WLT Report. ChatGPT gave a plain, up-to-date answer in both languages on Paxton, citing strong sources like the attorney general’s office, the Texas Senate and news outlets such as the Associated Press and The Texas Tribune, and Gemini was the most limited, describing Paxton only as attorney general in both languages, never mentioning his Senate run, and citing no sources at all. All three chatbots explained the charges against Paxton correctly, with ChatGPT adding that “impeachment is an accusation, not a criminal conviction,” but Gemini, in Spanish, labelled Paxton’s ties to the donor a “relación corrupta” and cited no sources in either language.

All three chatbots responded that Pulido identifies as a Democrat, and in Spanish Claude cited news outlets including The Dallas Morning News and Univision. ChatGPT answered in two sentences in both languages: Pulido is a Democrat who “describes himself as a conservative Democrat.” Gemini’s English answer was even shorter, saying only that he is running as a Democrat, and in Spanish it added that he calls himself a “Blue Dog” or conservative Democrat focused on border security, gun rights and health care, citing Spanish-language news outlets. Monica and Carlos De La Cruz are siblings, Carlos is the Republican nominee in Texas’ 35th District, he won a primary runoff on May 26 and faced Democrat Johnny Garcia on Nov. 3, and all three chatbots responded accurately about the relationship. Claude, in Spanish, said Carlos “está en la papeleta” in the May 26 runoff, as if that vote hadn’t happened yet, offering this answer on Oct. 9, more than four months after Carlos De La Cruz won the Republican primary runoff. A DDIA poll of 1,500 Latino registered voters, conducted by YouGov from Sept. 24 to Oct. 6, found that most Latino voters (57%) would not feel comfortable using a chatbot to help them decide who to vote for, but about one in three (34%) said fact-checking something they saw online or heard from someone would be a reason to use a chatbot for politics, and only 42% of U.S. Latino respondents said they always or often check a chatbot’s answer against another source.

In May 2023, the Texas House impeached Paxton on 20 articles, most of them accusing him of abusing his office to help Nate Paul, a donor and real estate developer, and in September 2023 the Texas Senate acquitted him of all charges. Pulido calls himself a “conservative Democrat,” and the phrase “open borders” is commonly used by Republicans to attack Democrats on immigration. When a chatbot’s English and Spanish answers to the same question got different grades, the Spanish answer was worse in eight of 12 cases. Claude, and Gemini in Spanish, repeated campaign and partisan language as their own, and Gemini often linked to social media posts as sources, including posts by candidates’ political opponents. Following the Associated Press style, which most U.S. newsrooms use to standardize language, the media avoids calling transgender girls “men,” and Claude’s English answer followed The Associated Press guidance: “a bill about transgender athletes in school sports.”

DDIA researchers suggest clicking through the links to see where the answer given by AI came from, watching for politically charged words and keeping in mind that “ad speak” may mean something was pulled from an ad, and checking important claims with local news, fact-checkers and official websites. The articles say it is important that AI companies double their efforts to give accurate, balanced answers to fact-based political questions in every language. stories.Headline: Chelan City Council approves AI policy requiring staff to verify AI work and protect confidential data
stories.Summary:
The Chelan City Council unanimously approved a new artificial intelligence policy on Nov. 10 that lets city employees use tools such as Microsoft Copilot and Claude to draft documents, analyze information and summarize meetings, while requiring staff to verify the work and remain responsible for decisions. HR/Communications Director Chad Coltman said staff developed the policy after researching other municipalities’ approaches, and the city attorney also reviewed it. Community Development Director John Ajax told the Council that staff had used a transcript of a Planning Commission meeting to test the usefulness of AI followed by human review. He said the technology helped assemble a matrix tracking public comments and proposed changes to the comprehensive plan in an afternoon, work he estimated would otherwise take at least a week.

The policy allows approved tools to assist with drafting communications, summarizing reports, developing outlines and analyzing public information, but it prohibits releasing or relying on AI-generated work without human review and approval. Employees must check facts, figures, citations and data, identify inaccurate or biased information, and ensure final work meets city standards, and AI cannot serve as the sole basis for regulatory, permitting, enforcement or public-service decisions affecting residents, with the same restriction applying to hiring, discipline, promotions and terminations. The free consumer version of Microsoft Copilot may be used for general research and brainstorming involving public information, but employees cannot enter confidential or other nonpublic city information into it, while authorized city business information may be used in approved enterprise systems subject to security, privacy and records requirements. Attorney-client communications, executive-session materials and certain sensitive law enforcement information require specific authorization from the city attorney before being entered into AI systems.

The rules also address the city’s existing obligations under Washington’s Public Records Act and records retention schedules, stating that prompts, conversations and outputs related to city business may constitute public records and that employees cannot assume they are exempt from disclosure because AI was involved. Official work must use city-managed accounts, qualifying final records must be retained in approved city systems, and public-facing materials containing AI-generated or AI-assisted images, video or audio must carry a clear disclosure on websites, social media, printed materials, presentations and other externally shared content. The policy applies to employees, elected officials, volunteers, contractors and others authorized to use city systems or information, including when conducting city business on personal devices, and new AI tools and subscriptions require advance approval. Coltman said the primary goal is to make clear to staff what the appropriate uses of AI are, what kind of data can be uploaded to an AI model, what retention expectations exist and what AI can and cannot be used for. The policy calls for training on data protection, records retention and recognizing bias, and it will be reviewed at least annually as technology, legal requirements and city needs change.

stories.Headline: Suki launches Suki OS to extend visit data into prior authorization and billing work
stories.Summary:
Suki, an ambient clinical intelligence company, introduced a platform called Suki OS on November 17, 2026, according to MobiHealthNews, and the company said the platform will take information gathered during patient visits and use it for tasks beyond documentation. The platform combines Suki's existing technology with AI agents and partner services to support patient care work, including insurance approvals and billing. The first two projects will focus on prior authorization, which includes checking authorization requirements and the records needed for a request, and on incomplete documentation, which will flag missing details in clinical documents that affect coding or payment. Suki also announced that it added Stellar Health and ECLAT to its partner network. The company outlined a commercial arrangement in which eligible Suki customers could recoup as much as their full fees if the company's technology falls short of negotiated targets.

Those measures could include clinician participation or coding accuracy, with reimbursement dependent on contract terms and on using customers' data to measure results. Last month, Suki announced it secured $90 million in financing as part of its Series E raise, just a year after receiving an investment from Zoom Ventures, bringing its total funding to $168 million at the time. Suki raised $70 million in Series D funding in 2024, secured $55 million in Series C funding in 2021, and in 2020 closed a $20 million Series C funding round. Punit Soni, CEO and founder of Suki, said in a statement that the greatest opportunity for AI in healthcare is not to make today's processes faster but to question why so many of those processes exist in the first place.

He said the company has an opportunity to fundamentally redesign how healthcare operates by removing friction that has become so deeply embedded in the system that it is accepted as inevitable. He described Suki OS as a step toward a future where technology does not just support healthcare but helps transform what is possible. Suki has added new offerings to its platform in the past year, including expanding its assisted revenue cycle capabilities to provide more specific automation and generate additional codes, including Current Procedural Terminology and Evaluation and Management codes. In August, Suki launched Suki Dictation, an AI clinical documentation tool that can integrate with Epic and MEDITECH EHR systems and allows clinicians to dictate and edit documentation by voice when ambient documentation may not be appropriate for a particular encounter or workflow.

stories.Headline: Cato fellow Chelsea Follett argues that embracing technological change beats longing for the preindustrial past
stories.Summary:
A neo-Luddite movement is on the rise, and it has become chic to denigrate modern technology and long for the good old days of the preindustrial past, according to a New York Post opinion article published on November 16, 2026. The article cites Chelsea Follett, a research fellow at the Cato Institute's Center for Global Liberty and Prosperity and author of the book "The Grim Old Days," who argues that technological progress and the much-maligned Industrial Revolution are the only things separating modern people from unthinkable living standards. Follett told The Post that people do not appreciate modern abundance enough, because everyone takes the world they are born into as the default and assumes running water, electricity and well-stocked grocery stores are the normal condition of humanity. The article notes that a July poll found just 30 percent of respondents thought AI was a good thing for society, even though the technology has been responsible for massive GDP and stock market growth.

The book argues that virtually every facet of life, from birth to death and for rich and poor alike, has been improved by technology, and it takes readers through the lives of ancestors in order to deromanticize the past. Follett writes that before industrialization, snail-like progress verging on stagnation was the general rule, and that the world ancestors faced was more gruesome than modern minds can fathom. The article states that roughly half of people did not make it to age 20 in early modern Europe, that most ancestors lived in total darkness after sundown, and that even the palace at Versailles lacked bathrooms. It adds that George Washington, by his own calculations, spent the equivalent of $15,000 a year to burn a single candle for five hours per night, and that at Henry VIII's Hampton Court the communal toilet could serve 14 people at once but did not flush.

Follett argues that the Industrial Revolution lifted ancestors out of constant misery and suffering for the first time in human history, and that there has been more economic output in the last two centuries than in every previous century combined, per Cato's Human Progress project. She points out that just 2 percent of people in developed countries today are farmers, compared with as many as 90 percent in many preindustrial economies, and she writes that pursuing dreams came within reach of the average person for the first time in history. She told The Post that people continuously compare the AI revolution to the Industrial Revolution, but that if we do not learn the right lessons from the Industrial Revolution, we could squander this moment with the AI revolution. The article says it is understandable that such powerful technological transformation is causing anxiety, since AI threatens to upend the way we live, work and even think, but it concludes that history looks better upon those who embraced change than on the Luddites who tried to hold everybody back.

stories.Headline: TechBuffalo connects Buffalo educators with university researchers to shape AI teaching
stories.Summary:
TechBuffalo, a nonprofit organization in the Buffalo, New York region, is connecting educators in the area with researchers at the University at Buffalo to determine the best approaches for teaching students the AI knowledge and skills they will need in future careers. The effort is taking place even as pushback against artificial intelligence in K-12 schools continues to intensify across the country. The two largest school districts in the country, New York City and Los Angeles, recently put in place significant restrictions on the use of AI in classrooms. Smaller districts across the country have implemented similar bans or restrictions, citing growing concerns about students using the technology to cheat and bypass meaningful learning and worries about mental health problems exacerbated by overuse of the technology.

Other schools are taking a different approach, and even though they recognize the potential downsides of AI use in education, they are not banning or heavily restricting the use of it. Those schools see the technology being used in all sectors of society and industry and want to make sure their students are prepared with the AI knowledge and skills to use the technology smartly and responsibly. To achieve that goal, those schools are investing time and money in training their teachers and administrators to learn how to use the technology effectively. One example of this approach is taking place in the Buffalo, N.Y., region, where TechBuffalo is trying to build a talent pool of young people who can use AI and tech skills to help promote economic growth.

Anne Martell-Flury, director of K-12 education for the Kenmore-Town of Tonawanda schools near Buffalo, said that what is missing on a larger scale is the connection from education to industry and the workforce. The article was written by Grace Jiang and published by Education Week on November 16, 2026. Coverage of mathematics, AI and emerging technology, and influential state markets is supported in part by a grant from the Gates Foundation, and the publication says its editors retain sole editorial control over the content of that coverage. The article is part of a special report on professional development and is accompanied by a video about how the effort is playing out.

stories.Headline: Alpha School charges up to $75,000 a year as only 42% of students meet its AI learning goal
stories.Summary:
Alpha School, a network of AI-driven private schools, has faced scrutiny after internal data revealed many students are not meeting learning goals. The network charges wealthy parents up to $75,000 a year for a model that replaces traditional teachers with guides. These guides focus on motivation rather than lesson planning or grading. The reports surfaced on November 14, 2026.

The school uses an AI tutor app called TimeBack to help students learn twice as fast in reading and math within two hours of daily academics. However, only 42% of students met this goal, with about half of K-8 students missing the math target. The network has grown to roughly 50 campuses with between 1,200 and 1,500 students. Additionally, more than 2,600 public school students in South Carolina and Texas now use the platform.

Cofounder MacKenzie Price stated that the app accelerates learning to allow more time for workshops on relationship building and public speaking. U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon praised the model in September 2025, calling it the most exciting thing she had seen in education. Other supporters include Bill Ackman and Reid Hoffman. Meanwhile, Houston Independent School District Superintendent Mike Miles noted that students spent more time on the apps than intended.

The expansion occurs as schools struggle with declining test scores and concerns over AI dependency. Some former employees claimed the AI created faulty lessons, while parents reported that students suffered stress and anxiety. Public school pilots face further challenges because they cannot remove struggling students. Experts warn that over-reliance on AI may hinder critical thinking and the ability to read long sentences.
