stories.Headline: Professor Jered Borup uses a 1978 microwave ad to urge future teachers to question AI hype
stories.Summary:
Professor Jered Borup of George Mason University began a lecture for future teachers in Fairfax, Virginia, by showing a 1978 microwave commercial, then asked who had cooked a Thanksgiving turkey in the microwave and no hand went up. The class was for undergraduate elementary education majors at George Mason University, and the lesson was reported by Alyson Klein on November 16, 2026. Borup used the microwave, once billed as a do-it-all technology, to urge skepticism about current hype over artificial intelligence. He said AI can help teachers in limited circumstances, as a brainstorming partner, and may save time on rote tasks. He compared that to reheating pizza, and said AI will never replace the conventional oven of teacher judgment.

Borup told students the goal is to make instruction more efficient, engaging and effective, but that poor use of any tool can decrease efficiency, engagement and effectiveness. The October 20, 2026 class in Fairfax included sophomore Elaina Fseisi, 21, who used an AI tool to detect her emotions. Also in the class were sophomores Anastasia Kyryliuk, 18, and Kiyah Wilson, 19, and junior Suchi Radia, 22. Sophomores Joanna Guzman and Evie Perks, both 19, and Stacy Reyes, 19, were in Borup's educational technology class. Borup's students were assigned to use popular AI platforms for K-12 education to develop lesson plans, assessments, classroom activities and other learning material.

Ingrid Guerra-López, dean of the College of Education and Human Development, said the conversation about AI and education is more about education than about AI, and that AI is a means to an end and a tool, with the focus always on strengthening teaching and learning. She wants aspiring teachers to leave GMU able to explain the technology's power and limitations, including its tendency toward biased or inaccurate information, and to use it to bolster learning, such as analyzing assessment data to pinpoint next steps. She said adding a required AI class would be a heavy lift because educator prep programs must adhere to state and national accreditation standards and have very little flexibility. She said curriculum in higher education is very much owned by the faculty, who have creative freedom to design and deliver courses as they see appropriate as scholars. She said instruction on AI varies from course to course, that some professors steer clear citing ethical issues including allegations companies violated intellectual copyright laws to develop large language models, and that others find AI overwhelming.

An EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators conducted in August and September found more than three-quarters are not receiving sustained professional development on AI tools. Borup, who specializes in instructional design, and Jennifer Suh, a professor of math education, teamed with a computer science colleague and a professor specializing in AI ethics and policy to offer webinars to interested faculty in the education school. About 30 instructors have shown up regularly while others drop in, and one experiment involved creating instructional materials in their own expertise and discussing what the tech did well and what it missed, Suh said. Perks, an aspiring special education teacher who describes herself as an AI skeptic, found it fascinating to work with AI to create a quiz for 4th graders about country singer Kacey Musgraves, but worries about AI's environmental impact and does not plan to use it for undergraduate courses unless directed. Classmates shared qualms: one worried open-ended questions an AI tool wrote for a kindergartners' quiz were too advanced, another found a feature aimed at leveling text for different reading abilities to be a bust, and a future special education teacher was taken aback that a tool could help craft an Individualized Education Program, saying putting that information into AI could violate students' privacy, and Borup told her she was right to be concerned.

All undergraduates at GMU, whether majoring in education, kinesiology or art history, must choose a technology course as a general education requirement, and some options include an AI focus. The college is working to develop a resource hub for local districts featuring information on AI tools, and GMU aims to offer a 15-credit graduate certificate in learning technologies with a concentration in AI teaching and learning. The college has a research and practice partnership, the Educational Research Alliance of Northern Virginia, or ERA-NOVA, aimed at helping some 20 neighboring districts think through common challenges, much of it recently centered on AI implementation. At an October session, GMU experts explained a new state law requiring districts to develop AI guidelines based on a forthcoming model policy from the state education agency, and leaders from a couple districts shared tips for addressing families' AI concerns. Borup and at least two other professors who lead technology courses for pre-service elementary school teachers put some focus on AI, though their lectures and assignments are not identical, and research on AI's impact on K-12 instruction is in the early stages, with it not clear what K-12 districts want incoming teachers to know about AI, as some districts have embraced AI and others ban it.

In the spring, the group will launch a lesson study on AI, including sharing ideas for teaching future educators about the tech and inviting colleagues to drop into their classes to watch them in action. Suh said professors want their colleagues' thoughts on this new phenomenon that nobody really has figured out because every day it is changing. Reyes said she is skeptical AI would save her much time given how much she would need to factcheck and tweak its output to fit her teaching style, and that she would have to be in the classroom to see if it would be successful. Borup expects his students will be more sophisticated at critiquing AI-created instructional materials once they get more hands-on teaching experience. For now, Borup offered a tip to think of AI as a human assistant, and the article ends mid-sentence with the example of telling that person to get me lunch.

stories.Headline: Educators report a rise in AI training but say it lacks time, feedback and guidance on cheating
stories.Summary:
About two-thirds of teachers, school administrators, and district leaders reported having at least one professional development session or more on using AI in their work, according to a nationally representative survey of 852 educators. The EdWeek Research Center conducted the survey between Aug. 26 and Oct. 6, and Education Week reported the results on November 16, 2026. That share is an 11-percentage-point increase from last year, when 56% of educators said the same. Education Week interviewed educators who have received training on the technology and asked them what they think is missing from these opportunities. The article was written by Lauraine Langreo and appeared in a Special Report on artificial intelligence from the research center.

The survey covered 852 educators and ran from Aug. 26 to Oct. 6, and the figure rose 11 percentage points from 56% last year. Lance Barasch is an “AI champion” in the Dallas district where he works as a high school math teacher, receiving AI training from the district and then training his peers. Jaime Moss is a high school science teacher in West Virginia working on a doctorate degree in curriculum and instruction, with an emphasis on AI. Rita Mortenson is an instructional coach at Verona Area High School in Verona, Wis. The Trump administration has made training teachers on AI one of its top educational priorities, and some major technology companies have partnered with education organizations to provide free teacher training and resources.

Barasch said that when he gets back to the campus, he has to “scrape and claw” to get time in front of his colleagues, and that turnout for training he leads is low because it isn’t mandatory. He said many districts aren’t encouraging or mandating educators to attend these professional learning opportunities, and that teachers should at the very least understand what AI is. He said students are “way ahead of us,” and that if teachers aren’t aware of these tools and how they’re used, they won’t be able to be proactive about teaching responsible use, which he called the mandate as a public educator. Moss said teachers don’t want another demonstration of what AI can do, and that they just need time to figure out what it can do for them and how to make it applicable to their students. She said discussions about new topics shouldn’t be a “one-and-done” training, and that teachers are “learners just like our students.”

Mortenson said training opportunities need to go beyond simply teaching how to write initial AI prompts, because educators get “all these fancy prompts” but implementing them in the classroom can be challenging. She said the trainings should include all the steps it takes to get to a final product, including how the initial result was modified, and should include ready-made resources for educators to practice on in the moment, such as a fake spreadsheet. Barasch said teachers are also missing direct, instant feedback about the ways they’re experimenting with AI, and that when he trains teachers in his building he doesn’t have that opportunity because there might not be time built in, so sometimes his trainings are email blasts. Educators said one of teachers’ most-asked questions is how to deal with students using AI to cheat, but it’s a question not really answered by many AI professional development experiences.

Mortenson and Barasch, who lead AI training in their respective districts, said teachers want guidance on how to detect if students are cheating with AI and how to prevent them from doing so. Barasch said he has heard educators ask about AI’s effects on the environment, jobs, and critical-thinking skills, and that these concerns are “not really touched on” and sometimes even sidestepped. The articles say the expanding use of AI in education is driving demand for more training on how to use the technology in teaching and learning, and that many schools have responded to that demand. They say the jump shows the progress school districts and education organizations have made in ensuring educators are knowledgeable about this fast-evolving technology.

They say generative AI is becoming more embedded into the many tools that students and teachers use daily, which is why experts say it’s important for teachers to learn about the technology so they can use it responsibly and model appropriate use for students. Barasch said that even though the Dallas school district provides a lot of AI training resources for educators, the employees getting the most training are the ones seeking it out. He said those people are also more likely to already know a little bit about AI or be more open to using it, while those who are skeptical or against the technology are not participating in AI PD opportunities. Barasch said that in the AI training sessions he’s attended, people circulate in the room to give feedback on how he’s using AI tools, “which is just like you’re in a classroom.”

Moss said students are put in groups because they can learn from their peers, but with teachers “we don’t give them opportunities to do that.” Educators said the questions and concerns about AI’s drawbacks are ones teachers hear from students too, so without guidance from school or district leaders and experts, it’s difficult to respond to students. Barasch said “these trainings are all-in on the new stuff,” all about learning how to use the stuff, and “not about the drawbacks as much.” Data analysis for the article was provided by the EdWeek Research Center, and coverage of mathematics, AI and emerging technology, and influential state markets is supported in part by a grant from the Gates Foundation.

stories.Headline: Interpol reports AI now drives over half of Africa's cybercrime
stories.Summary:
More than half of the cybercrime reported across Africa is now enabled by artificial intelligence, which has shifted from supporting attacks to serving as the primary driver of cybercrime on the continent, according to a new Interpol report. Interpol researchers reported in their 2026 Africa cybercrime assessment that AI is now used to automate every stage of the attack lifecycle, from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. The researchers said criminals are now operating at machine speed, with AI enabling attacks that are faster, more scalable and more difficult to attribute. In a separate report, AI company Anthropic revealed that cybercriminals are using its Claude agent to launch cyberattacks, conduct surveillance and run online influence operations. Those cybercriminals rely on AI's capacity for writing malicious computer code or generating extensive influence campaigns at a scale and speed that eclipses any government's ability to detect and disrupt them.

With more than 1.1 billion mobile online subscribers in 2025, Africa's digital revolution is spreading rapidly, far faster than government regulations and digital literacy efforts can keep up, leaving a population increasingly at risk from AI-generated scams and influence operations. Researcher Karen Allen wrote recently for the Institute for Security Studies that the potential vulnerabilities across Africa are vast. In 2025, Central Africa saw an increase in AI-generated synthetic identities used to evade the know your customer protocols that banks and other businesses use to confirm their customers' identities, according to Interpol, and AI was also capable of tricking biometric security systems. Currently, 45 African governments have adopted digital technology designed to improve the delivery of government services, and Ghana, Mauritius, South Africa and Tunisia rank among the countries with the highest rate of e-government functions. Although these platforms increase citizens' access to their governments and increase government efficiency, they also increase the potential impact of AI-driven cybercrime without the proper safeguards in place. Allen wrote that as more countries shift towards e-government, exposure to AI risks will increase unless safety controls are ramped up.

Governments often are targets of AI-powered cyberattacks, and Anthropic reported that cybercriminals had used its technology to hack an unidentified North African government database, gaining access to 300,000 national identity records and data from more than 500,000 companies operating in the country. Interpol reported that cybercriminality has evolved from isolated incidents into an industrialized, borderless ecosystem, while cybercrime legislation is fragmented and AI readiness in law enforcement agencies remains alarmingly low. AI-based cyberattacks vary by location and type, and South Africa, for example, was the origin for 70% of business e-mail compromise attacks, while another 29% came from Nigeria, according to Interpol. Interpol wrote that the sophistication of these campaigns has increased dramatically, with AI now used to generate highly convincing e-mail correspondence that mimics executive tone, internal jargon and signature styles with near-perfect fidelity. Those messages are designed to trick human recipients into opening them, thereby releasing malicious software into the company's computer system, and ransomware attacks, the frequent result of business e-mail compromise attacks, account for 28% of all cyberattacks in Africa in 2025, making them the single-largest type of attack, according to Interpol. Interpol reported that as AI continues to refine the realism of impersonation, the human element remains the weakest link and the most difficult to defend, and that the integration of AI into scam operations, generating personalized lures, voice clones and fake testimonials, has made detection increasingly difficult for both platforms and victims.

stories.Headline: Arista launches Etherlink R4 routers for distributed inference networks
stories.Summary:
Arista Networks Inc. announced at SC26 a shift in focus to the front-end network and a new set of Etherlink R4 routing platforms designed for distributed inferencing, along with a pluggable optical line system for data center interconnect, SiliconANGLE reported on November 17, 2026. The lineup includes the 7020R4 and 7020HR4 compact 1RU access routers with 25G to 400G ports, deep buffers, and optional wire-speed encryption on every port. The HR4 versions are temperature-hardened and add advanced timing for cell sites and outside plant. The 7282R4 is a fixed-edge and core router with dual supervisors for control-plane redundancy, and the 7280R4 is a 25.6 terabit in-betweener with 64 400G ports, half supporting ZR/ZR+ coherent optics, to bridge local fabrics to the wide area network. The pluggable optical line system is a full C-band amplifier carrying 25.6 Tbps over a single fiber pair, plus muxes and a pluggable fiber tester.

All the products are based on Broadcom's Jericho and Qumran silicon, designed to deliver up to 60% lower power consumption than competing 7nm and 16nm platforms. Everything is available now, except the 7020HR4, which ships in early 2027. During a pre-briefing, Brendan Gibbs, Arista's AVP of product line management, argued that the forces driving training across multiple sites will have the same effect on inference. Gibbs also said that roughly 30% of Arista's AI business is now scale-across, indicating that distributed AI is rapidly becoming commonplace. Arista co-designed the 7280R4 with a hyperscaler seeking a gray-to-coherent bridge, a sign that it is building with its biggest customers.

Gibbs said the goal is a 10-year life cycle, with customers swapping optics rather than chassis. On the call, Gibbs agreed it is hard to draw conclusions from CVE counts but explained that CVE counts were a measure of Arista's software quality. I asked Gibbs about integrated security replacing firewalls, and he said that Arista has no intention of replacing firewalls and expects Palo Alto Networks to continue to sit behind it in the line. Douglas Fast Net CTO Jon Vradenburg said the company needs a compact platform that supports the services our business and carrier customers rely on. Takayuki Sakou of Japan's STNet cited higher throughput and improved power efficiency while maintaining the quality of the EOS software we trust.

Arista's customers range from hyperscalers to neoclouds to enterprises building local AI. Telcos have largely sat out the AI buildout, yet they own the last mile and real estate near users, exactly what low-latency inference requires. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, managed services are far more common, and providers such as BT, NTT, and Telstra have the footprint to make it work. Since 2019, Arista has reported a far lower CVE count than competitors, even after the surge in AI-assisted discovery following Anthropic's Mythos. Arista isn't an optical company and is reselling these products, but offering dark fiber customers a turnkey, EOS-integrated way to move 25.6 Tbps across a metro network removes a real headache.

Awareness of the network's role in AI has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end: larger clusters, faster ports, and scale-across fabrics that stitch GPUs together across data centers. Arista has seen continued, accelerated growth and has been one of the biggest winners of that buildout. Recent announcements focused on dense 800G, 1.6T, and liquid cooling, and the products launched at SC26 are smaller and less expensive. Arista dominates big iron and is now rounding out its portfolio, and the front end needs rich features, not massive bandwidth, and Arista hasn't had a viable option for that tier until now. The back end of AI networking is largely a solved architecture at this point, and the front end is not.

The routers are designed as entry-level but ship with 400G uplinks, which may seem like overkill today but offer investment protection. No one knows what agents will do to traffic volumes, and companies that consider this overkill today may think differently in three or four years. The hardened 7020HR4 is built for 5G and AI-RAN cell sites, giving a carrier the backbone to offer a managed AI factory. Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting, and he wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. With R4, Arista is betting that its routing credibility, built quietly within hyperscaler backbones, can make it the default there as well.

Articles.Title: Arista takes aim at the next AI network battleground: distributed inference

stories.Headline: Helpany deploys its Paul AI radar system in senior living homes to prevent falls
stories.Summary:
Helpany, a Scottsdale-based company, has developed an artificial intelligence system called Paul that is being used in senior living communities across the Valley to help prevent falls among residents, and the technology was recently named one of Time's Best Inventions of 2026 in the medical and healthcare category. The company has also rolled out ePaul, a new wearable device that looks like a fitness tracker. Paul is a radar-based device that uses artificial intelligence to analyze movement without cameras and microphones, according to the report. Sandro Cilurzo, co-founder and CEO of Helpany, said he created Paul because he saw a need for a system that would protect privacy.

Cilurzo said how somebody takes their steps, gait, posture, stride length, and how somebody sleeps and rests at night is highly predictive for underlying maybe unknown health challenges. Caregivers use a dashboard that alerts them to changes, while residents receive a daily health and wellness report, and the ePaul bracelet works with the Paul system to measure steps and track location. Cilurzo said these residents can remain longer independent, and this was the whole goal since day one. Wendy Souders, the vice president of Fellowship Square in Surprise, said the results speak for themselves and that the facility has seen a 70% reduction in falls.

Jami Van Gysel, chief operating officer for Christian Care, said the system helped a resident who was very independent and thriving but had started pulling back. She looked at her health and wellness report and realized that she wasn't sleeping, made a doctor's appointment, shared it with her doctor, and they discovered that she had had a medication change and this was a side effect of that, Van Gysel said. Barbara Conley, a resident at Fellowship Square, told Arizona's Family that she was skeptical of the technology at first but has come to appreciate it. Conley said she is not used to any of this AI and is still learning how to use her phone, so it is new, and she is willing to go with the flow to see what happens.

As Helpany is working to expand its technology to more senior living communities, Cilurzo didn't discount the possibility of future at-home use. He told On Your Side that it is a possibility, absolutely, and that just how the system is designed and the technology, they see a path down the line, but they are really focused right now to bring it to the senior living communities.

Articles.Title: Arizona company’s AI system keeping residents safe at senior living homes

stories.Headline: Radio stations must turn broadcasts into text and structured guides so AI models can find and cite their local content
stories.Summary:
Radio stations are being told they must learn how their content is found, understood and surfaced by artificial intelligence, according to an article published by Radio World on November 17, 2026. The piece says people now ask AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for instant answers instead of typing queries like the best things to do in Milwaukee this weekend into a search bar and reading through links. After enough of those experiences, the article says, traditional search results feel antiquated. The article notes that even Google now shows an answer at the top of its own search results, which it calls a showcase of AI superiority.

The article says there is no universally accepted replacement yet for the acronym SEO, listing GEO for Generative Engine Optimization, AEO for Answer Engine Optimization, LLMO for Large Language Model Optimization and AI SEO as labels in use. Whatever the label, the article says, the meaning is the same: radio needs to figure out AI discovery and how AI models locate a station as a resource for information. It says radio has answered local questions since its inception, such as who is playing this weekend, where to take the kids on Saturday and what is happening with the local team. The new question, the article says, is whether AI will discover what a station knows and use it as the source.

The article says large media outlets have huge digital footprints, but local radio has far better real-time information, and the problem is that most of what is said on air never makes it to digital platforms such as the web, social media, Reddit and YouTube. It says a local interview, a morning show discussion, a DJ's take on a local band, weekend events plugged between songs and breaking local news all vanish after airing. Stations need a workflow that lets AI ingest these tidbits, the article says, by turning broadcast information into text, building structured local guides and publishing transcripts and summaries. It says this work is about helping AI understand the content as a credible source, a different goal from ranking at the top of a search page, and that clear attribution and current information on local happenings are required.

The article suggests stations treat themselves as a local information database covering concerts, events, restaurants, food trucks, sports and community organizations, with each piece serving a purpose: broadcast is immediate, social is discovery, the website is reference, and podcast and video are deeper engagement. It says radio has been the best source of local information since the 1920s, but there is now a new gatekeeper, and stations have to make sure it knows how to find them. Ironically, the article says, stations will use AI to transcribe what they create so that other AI models can find them. It concludes that AI is not just another place to publish but another way people discover a station, and the trick is to make sure AI knows what the radio station knows.

Articles.Title: Does AI Know What You Know?

stories.Headline: Australian creatives launch Not AI’s To Take campaign to press Albanese on copyright
stories.Summary:
A vast coalition of Australian writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups is preparing a last-ditch campaign aimed at persuading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to protect their work against artificial intelligence firms. The campaign, called “Not AI’s To Take,” is expected to be rolled out on Wednesday, according to two people with knowledge of the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity. The coalition is pushing back against AI companies that want new copyright laws making it easier to harvest content to train their models. The Australian Financial Review reported the plans on November 16, 2026.

The campaign brings together a broad range of creative and media interests, including writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, all opposed to the proposed changes. Those behind it want the Prime Minister to safeguard their work rather than allow AI firms to scrape content under looser rules. The firms seeking the changes want laws that would make harvesting content for training models easier than it is now. The report did not specify what specific legal changes the coalition is seeking or what the AI firms have proposed.

Responsibility for the campaign rests with the coalition of writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, while the push for easier content harvesting comes from AI firms. The two people who described the plans spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss them publicly. The report did not include direct comment from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the AI firms or the coalition members. It also did not say what the companies involved, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which appeared as tags on the article, had said about the campaign.

The context is a lobbying fight over copyright rules governing how AI models are trained on published and creative work. The campaign is described as a last-ditch effort, suggesting the coalition believes decisions on the laws may be close. The report did not say when any legislation might be introduced or what happens after the campaign launch on Wednesday. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artists, media plot campaign to counter AI firms’ copyright lobbying - AFR

stories.Headline: Four nonprofits ask a California judge to freeze frontier AI development
stories.Summary:
Four nonprofits asked a California judge on Thursday to freeze frontier artificial intelligence development, according to CBS News and Reuters. The suit was filed November 12, 2026, in San Francisco Superior Court. It names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI as defendants. The plaintiffs are the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. The complaint runs 63 pages.

The plaintiffs want an injunction stopping the defendants from building or releasing systems more capable than their current best. They also want an injunction barring the use of AI to run or direct research on more capable AI. The complaint alleges violations of California's unfair-competition law, with claims involving public health and public nuisance. Reporting names ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude as products at issue. The exact legal name of the SpaceX entity sued is unconfirmed, and reports use SpaceXSI as shorthand.

Public Citizen leads the nonprofits, and reports quote the complaint saying "Defendants must be stopped." Another reported line says the suit aims to act "before catastrophe strikes." The plaintiffs cite risks such as help with bioweapons development or cyberattacks. Reuters wrote that the suit leans on concerns voiced by the companies' own leaders about the technology's dangers. The defendants had not, per coverage available on Friday, offered substantive public responses.

The Washington Examiner added that the nonprofits want the court to stop new models that could escape human oversight and cause catastrophe. MLex summarized the case as unfair competition claims against Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX Super Intelligence. One report says the complaint points to alleged incidents in which models escaped testing environments and attacked government websites. No judge has granted an injunction, and no report reviewed says any AI development has actually stopped. The coverage does not detail the budgets, membership or past cases of three of the plaintiffs.

Anthropic builds Claude, Google builds Gemini, OpenAI builds ChatGPT and Meta builds its Muse family. Coverage lists Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 from November 9, and Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen from November 12. Meta has pushed its Muse models, including a closed frontier model, per October coverage. SpaceXSI sits inside a rocket-and-satellite parent with other lines of business. The coverage does not say how the complaint addresses standing under California's unfair-competition statute.

Standing will be the first thing defense lawyers probe, and creative claims usually face motions to dismiss before anyone reaches the merits. Which corporate entity is served, and whether a parent or subsidiary answers, shapes who hires which law firm and where the case can be moved. The reports do not say how the complaint draws the line on what counts as developing a more capable system. We could not verify the alleged incidents independently, and the fact sheet relied on does not confirm them. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marc Rowan warns neoclouds face severe trouble if Nvidia stops funding their AI projects
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan said on Tuesday that neocloud companies could face severe trouble if Nvidia stops funding their artificial intelligence projects, speaking in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Nvidia has become known as the central bank of AI because of the financing it gives to smaller companies such as the neoclouds, and investors now worry that this funding could be cut as the chipmaker faces tougher scrutiny. Rowan said there was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground, and he warned that if that banking and guarantor function is taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds will disappear. His comments followed remarks by "Big Short" investor Steve Eisman, who told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday that the neoclouds are all in big trouble because they are part of that vertical holding company and he thinks they are about to get ejected.

Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Nvidia has been under pressure since CEO Jensen Huang stepped down Thursday amid an adultery scandal, and the company is set to report earnings after the bell Tuesday under the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress. Concerns about the large amount of debt the neoclouds have taken on have already sent their stocks tumbling and bond yields rising, since bond yields move inversely to prices. CoreWeave and Nebius, which use the financing to build data centers, are each down more than 50% over the last three months, and CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 was yielding 15.66% on Tuesday, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps hovered around 1,113.5.

Rowan said that if Nvidia decides to stop providing funding to neoclouds, the winners will be those companies that have the financial wherewithal and locked-in funding to build their infrastructure. He said he believes new ways to secure funding will ultimately be developed in the AI space, pointing to other technology cycles for comparison. He recalled that when Ford and GM introduced their first automobiles, people were amazed but no one could afford it, and the market ended up with GMAC and Ford Motor Credit. He added that it would not surprise him to see financial innovation take place, where more of a finance company mentality develops for this industry as an arbiter of credit and as a method of dealing with residuals.

stories.Headline: Nvidia uses AI agents to cut research work from a year to weeks
stories.Summary:
Nvidia uses AI agents to accelerate research work in its labs. These agents read literature, suggest experiments, write code, and run them. This process reduces work from one year to two or three weeks. Simon See presented these findings on 14 November at an AI leadership forum. The event was hosted by the Singapore Institute of Technology and Straits Interactive.

The agentic workflow starts with a prompt and scours the internet for papers. Agents run experiments in an automated wet lab, but verification takes two months. SMRT launched the Bus 4.0 programme in August 2026 using bus telematics. SMRT also uses the Jarvis platform and Depot 4.0 automation at Bishan depot. Rajah & Tann employs 1,200 lawyers across 10 countries using specific information vaults.

Simon See stated that Nvidia does not trust artificial intelligence at all. He noted that generative AI will always hallucinate, so companies must control it. Rajesh Sreenivasan said lawyers must check AI outputs to avoid breaching professional rules. Eugene Teh explained that SMRT avoids too much autonomy for critical infrastructure. Kevin Shepherdson warned that removing repetitive grunt work might hinder the development of intuition.

Lawyers at Rajah & Tann are affected by the risk of losing licenses. Clients were emailed about AI use, and four clients explicitly said no. Two clients put the law firm through a very intense audit process. Shawn Seah of the NTUC praised SMRT for redesigning jobs to protect workers. He stated that Singapore wants to avoid AI that merely surveils and grades workers.

The Ministry of Law published a guide for generative AI in March 2026. This guide holds lawyers responsible for all work and requires human oversight. Golden Gate University launched a master's degree in AI governance at the forum. SIT, Straits Interactive, and GGU also released The Chief AI Officer Playbook book. SMRT requires all employees to finish an AI programme by this financial year.

SMRT will roll out AI wider after completing a proof of value. Rajah & Tann continues to use senior lawyer content to teach drafting. Executives at SMRT are studying advanced areas like prompt engineering for their roles. The articles leave open how many clients will eventually reject AI legal services. They do not state the final results of the Straits Interactive OpenAI suspension.

stories.Headline: Childlight reports AI-related child sexual abuse material rises from 4,700 to over 400,000 reports in two years
stories.Summary:
Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children rose by more than 8,400% in two years, according to research published by the Edinburgh-based Childlight ,  Global Child Safety Institute. The institute said AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes made with so-called nudify apps, had risen from about 4,700 reports in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The research examined reports that technology companies sent to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The images are fake, but they can still be used to blackmail children into paying money or sending more images. The research focused on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America, while earlier studies looked at western Europe.

The figures also cover offline abuse and other reports. Almost a third of girls and more than one in 10 boys in North America were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood, including sexual assault, rape and upskirting, the research found. The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada. Childlight estimates that more than 300 million children worldwide are victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse every year, and that about one in four children will face at least one form of abuse before turning 18. A separate report by the Internet Watch Foundation last month said AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

Prof Debi Fry, Childlight's global director of data, said the findings revealed the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and showed how quickly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online. She said the findings also show where governments can make a difference, because evidence from surveys, police records and other sources can build a clearer picture of the risks children face and help target resources where they are needed most. Fry said the speed at which AI is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning, and that while improved detection and reporting may explain some of the increase, governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly. Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments too often work with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. He said there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse, and called on governments to recognise it as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action.

Articles.Title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows - The Guardian

stories.Headline: IBM consulting leader Kimberly Morick says CHROs gain a bigger seat as AI reshapes work
stories.Summary:
Kimberly Morick, HR and Transformation Practice Lead at IBM Consulting, gave a personal perspective in a conversation published on ibm.com on 17 November 2026 about AI reshaping work. She said AI is reshaping roles, skills and the way teams work, and that HR leaders are helping organizations navigate the change. She said CHROs now have a bigger seat at the table than ever before. She said people are still what drive performance. She said the opportunity now is to put AI to work in ways that make employees more confident, adaptable and capable.

She said she hopes work becomes more human, not less, over the next 5 years. She said organizations will need to reinvest capacity freed by AI into innovation, new skills and complex problems. She said the future of work will be far more skills-based than job-based, with organizations focusing on capabilities rather than titles. She said workforce transformation and technology transformation are really a single conversation. She said 71% of CHROs view the ability to supervise, validate and override AI outputs as the workforce's most critical skill, while only 29% of employees rank judgment as a priority.

She said an AI model can offer a recommendation but cannot take responsibility for what happens next, so someone must own the outcome. She said the colleague who says "I think we're solving the wrong problem" before anyone runs an AI analysis often creates more value than the person who delivers the perfect answer. She said people still provide the context, nuance and ethical judgment that do not always show up in the data. She said people still look to people for coaching, navigating change and leading through uncertainty. She said curiosity is the skill behind the skills.

She said research shows 60% of employees worry about skills erosion, with critical thinking cited most often as declining. She said among employees who worry about this, 3 out of 4 say AI has already begun to erode at least some of their skills. She said she treats AI as a thought partner, not a substitute for thinking, and forms her own view first, then uses AI to test it. She said the biggest shift in workplace culture over the past 5 years has been the pace of change. She said people rarely resist technology itself, they resist uncertainty.

She said AI has simplified administrative work, improved access to information and created efficiencies across HR processes. She said that as part of IBM's Client Zero transformation, AskHR resolved 94% of common employee inquiries and supported more than 16 million HR interactions in 2025. She said the convergence of AI, skills intelligence, workforce analytics and employee experience technologies excites her most. She said employees need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with appropriate human oversight. She said AI at its best will allow HR to focus more deeply on helping people grow and supporting leaders.

The conversation was published on ibm.com on 17 November 2026. It cites Designing the Thinking Organization: 5 focus areas for CHROs as AI reshapes work, IBM Institute for Business Value, September 2026. It cites a how-to guide titled How we unlocked productivity with AI and innovation, and a roadmap for getting there, from IBM. It cites IBM Transformation: AskHR, IBM, 2026. It cites a footnote, numbered 1, attached to the 71% and 29% figures and to the 60% and 3 out of 4 figures.

The conversation leaves open what specific steps organizations should take to create opportunities for people to practice skills as AI takes over more routine work. It leaves open how the disconnect between CHROs and employees on judgment will be closed. It leaves open what the footnote numbered 1 cites. It leaves open how trust in responsible, transparent AI use with human oversight will be built. It leaves open what the cited IBM Institute for Business Value report of September 2026 recommends.

Articles.Title: AI is changing work. People still matter most.

stories.Headline: As use of AI scribes spreads, researchers propose a framework for preparing medical trainees
stories.Summary:
Ambient AI scribes, which passively capture clinical encounters and draft notes, are among the most rapidly adopted artificial intelligence applications in health care, and in one integrated health care system they documented more than 2.5 million clinical encounters in a single year. Early evidence suggests real benefits from these tools, yet the outcomes measured thus far, including documentation time, cognitive workload and clinician burnout, address the value of the tools for workforce sustainability rather than medical education. Their use has spread through clinical settings faster than curricula can adapt, leaving medical schools unprepared for the shift. In a new article in npj Digital Medicine, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine propose a framework that defines the review of AI-generated clinical documentation as a teachable competency and describe how it can be taught through simulation.

Holly Wiberg, assistant professor of public policy and operations research at Carnegie Mellon's Heinz College, who co-authored the article, said physicians are shifting from writing clinical notes to editing AI-generated ones, which changes what trainees need to learn. She said ambient AI can ease documentation burden and has the potential to improve quality, but only if clinicians use it critically by evaluating its output and recognizing its failure modes. The authors say the editorial skills needed to review AI documentation competently are specific and teachable, not innate extensions of clinical practice, and that nothing in current medical school curricula targets these skills directly. Yash Raka, an M.D. candidate at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a co-author, said he is part of the first generation likely to edit AI-generated notes as often as they write their own, and that medical education is still catching up to what that shift requires.

The article identifies four domains involved in reviewing AI-generated clinical documentation, starting with detecting errors and omissions such as factual errors, hallucinations and misattributions in AI-generated clinical notes. The second domain asks whether trainees can judge if a note reflects the clinical reasoning of the medical visit rather than merely its facts, and the third asks whether they can generate clinically sound notes independently when AI is unavailable or inappropriate or when a patient does not consent to its use. The fourth domain concerns whether trainees appropriately calibrate their trust in AI output across clinical contexts, and in each domain the authors propose learning objectives, simulation exercises, ways to assess competency and timelines for teaching these skills. Reed Van Deusen, associate professor in general internal medicine and pediatrics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and another co-author, said simulation lets trainees practice catching an AI's mistakes in a low-stakes way where it will not affect patient outcomes.

Van Deusen said that when errors are built into simulated encounters, educators can see exactly what a learner misses and give targeted feedback, which is hard to do in a clinical training environment. The authors note that the proposed framework is preliminary and call for empirical testing to refine it, and they see it as a starting point. They envision developing curricular components aligned with their proposed exercises, with the hope that it could eventually inform how medical schools prepare trainees for AI-assisted practice. The article is titled From authoring to editing: a competency framework for trainee use of ambient AI clinical documentation, published in npj Digital Medicine with DOI 10.1038/s41746-026-03351-5.

Articles.Title: As use of AI scribes spreads, researchers propose a framework for preparing medical trainees

stories.Headline: Professor Caroline Dive’s team uses AI to seek early lung cancer signals in blood samples
stories.Summary:
In a blue-and-white van outside Asda last June, 68-year-old Eddie, a retired fishmonger from Fallowfield, near Manchester, received life-changing news. The van belonged to the NHS and contained a portable scanner. Eddie and his wife Jeanette had arrived for a lung screening appointment after being invited by their primary care doctor. Eddie said he very nearly didn't go because he felt fit and well, but Jeanette insisted it was no more difficult than a quick trip to the store. Because he smoked as a teenager and had some family history of cancer, they said he should have a scan there and then.

To the couple's shock, the scan found a dark shadow on Eddie's right lung. A week later, in the hospital, he had further tests, including a biopsy, and the couple's worst fears were confirmed: it was lung cancer. Eddie said he couldn't even properly remember the conversation and was in total shock. Screening has its downsides, as false positives can cause stress and anxiety, while regular monitoring after surgery can be a stressful and time-consuming process. There are also potential harms from the radiation used in CT scans, even though the dose is low.

For these reasons, the NHS program currently only invites current and former smokers, whose higher cancer risk means the benefits outweigh these harms. Estimates suggest as many as 6,000 never-smokers, currently ineligible for screening, die from lung cancer every year. Researchers are looking for ways to make screening more accurate, tell fast-growing tumors apart from slower-growing ones, and extend its benefits to more people. At the Cancer Research UK National Biomarker Centre, just minutes from the supermarket where Eddie's story began, center director professor Caroline Dive CBE and her teams are exploring an approach that could transform lung screening. Using cutting-edge artificial intelligence, they're looking for answers in people's blood.

Dive says scans are good at finding people with stage 1 disease, almost all of whom will have surgery and a good chance of cure, but about one in five will go on and relapse. She says that means, in some folks, an early tumor has already sent out the seeds of metastasis and begun to spread. Dive is a world-renowned expert in blood-based cancer biomarkers, subtle changes in the levels or structure of molecules in the blood that reveal the disease's presence. At Cancer Research UK, the charity is now supporting her team to tackle two key questions in lung screening. Dive asks first whether blood tests can be used to find early lung cancers, as early tumors release molecules and cells into the bloodstream that could form the basis for a blood test, or liquid biopsy, to augment CT scans and boost their accuracy.

Dive says that since 2016 they have been working closely with one of the pioneers of community-based lung screening in Manchester, professor Phil Crosbie, and his team at Wythenshawe Hospital. Together, they hope that by using sophisticated techniques to compare samples from people with and without early lung cancer, they can identify molecular signatures that could lead to a sensitive and informative blood test. With the multitude of different molecules and cells circulating in the blood, knowing which ones signal an early lung cancer is a formidable challenge, and to help spot patterns hiding in this complexity, Caroline's team is turning to AI. Blood is one of nature's most complex liquids, with billions of cells, chiefly oxygen-carrying red blood cells and various flavors of immune cells, floating in a watery soup containing countless biomolecules. These include tens of thousands of different types of proteins, sugars, fats and other metabolites, and fragments of genetic material shed by dying cells, including cancer cells, and thanks to modern technologies, scientists can now measure the levels and nature of these components with astonishing accuracy.

Because these molecules reflect so many of the body's processes, a well-designed blood test can offer a window into its inner workings, including when we're ill. Developing a reliable test is challenging, as levels of different molecules naturally fluctuate with age, infections, allergies, illness, exercise, and even with what we've eaten, so the trick is separating the signal from the noise. To do this, Dive's team has selected 200 pairs of blood samples from their larger collection of screening samples. Dive explains that for every sample where screening found an early lung cancer, they have been able to match a partner sample from someone who remained cancer-free but who was otherwise similar in age, sex and smoking history, which should make the cancer-related differences between samples much easier to distinguish. She says they are fishing in a pond, rather than an entire ocean.

Rather than relying on one type of measurement, which Dive says is unlikely to get the job done, they are taking a multi-modal approach, looking for patterns across a whole range of biological information sources. Using a technique called proteomics, they are precisely measuring levels of thousands of circulating proteins, and for circulating DNA fragments shed by tumors they are looking at three different features: cancer-linked mutations, chemical modifications to the DNA including so-called methylation, and differences in the fragments' size known as fragmentomics. They are looking for rare abnormal circulating cells, including cancer cells, that might offer clues, and with collaborators in the U.S. they are analyzing circulating RNA, a shorter-lived cousin of DNA. This will create an enormous data set containing hundreds of thousands of measurements from each sample, and finding meaningful, cancer-linked patterns within it is an extraordinary challenge, which is where AI comes in. Dive says it is such a big puzzle and AI will hugely speed up the process.

The team will first train AI models using data from the first 100 pairs of cancer-positive and matched-negative samples. Then they will test whether the best-performing AI model can identify cancer in the second 100 pairs without the AI knowing which samples came from people with cancer. A key challenge will be identifying the minimum number of measurements needed to maintain accuracy across such large data sets. Then, if successful, the next step will be a much larger study, and Dive says that if, and it's a big if, the data are convincing, then they will need to work with commercial partners and organizations like Cancer Research Horizons, because developing a biomarker test for routine use is really challenging and expensive. Dive says none of this would be possible without the research networks and infrastructure that have developed in Manchester since she moved there in 2003, and she is hugely grateful that Cancer Research UK has given her a stable base to develop strong networks, not only in Manchester with the Christie Hospital and wider NHS trusts, but around the UK and abroad. She says they have got the right ingredients in the pot and now they are just going to have to see what these precious samples can tell them.

stories.Headline: China aims to make AI literacy universal for primary and secondary students by 2030
stories.Summary:
China plans to make artificial intelligence literacy universal for its nearly 200 million primary and secondary schoolchildren by 2030. The Ministry of Education has encouraged schools to develop pilot programs, train teachers, and launch specialized courses since 2024. This initiative ranges from teaching basic concepts in primary grades to utilizing complex tools and critical thinking for projects. The plan requires nearly half of all provinces and municipalities to implement mandatory AI plus education strategies.

Shanghai now requires at least 30 hours of AI skills training per year for every grade level. Beijing intends to establish 100 demonstration schools and use AI to monitor the health of students. The Ningxia and Gansu regions aim to include AI literacy in school entrance examinations by 2027, while Yunnan province plans to record and analyze lessons in 14,000 classrooms. Public procurement documents show that authorities have committed at least $31 million for learning platforms, teacher training, and classroom equipment.

The Ministry of Education is responsible for the broad push, while local leaders like Principal Yang Tianliang in Funan County, Anhui province, manage specific applications. Yang explained that AI agents ask students questions instead of providing immediate answers to help address a shortage of qualified teachers. At the Beijing New Talent Academy, thirteen-year-old student Peng Gaodi noted that he used AI to create over 200 applications, including a homework submission platform. The school in Anhui utilizes developments from Z.AI, ByteDance, and Alibaba's Qwen models.

China currently lacks a unified standard for assessing AI literacy, leaving individual schools to experiment with their own methods. One study of nearly 27,000 teenagers linked AI use to an 18 percent increase in homework grades but a 20 percent drop in monthly exam results. A separate survey of over 320,000 students highlighted risks of dependency and a decline in independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower scores in creative, analytical, comprehension, and memory skills.

stories.Headline: Congressional report warns circular AI financing may expose economy to instability
stories.Summary:
A new Congressional Research Service report finds that circular financing arrangements among artificial intelligence companies could expose the broader economy to financial instability, according to Legis1. The practice has become increasingly prominent as technology companies pour billions of dollars into AI infrastructure, with analysts estimating U.S. AI-related infrastructure investment at approximately $500 billion this year and $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032. The report stops short of concluding that an AI investment bubble exists or that circular financing would necessarily trigger a broader financial crisis. Circular financing occurs when a company provides financial support to another business with the expectation that the recipient will purchase its products or services, and the arrangements have become increasingly common among AI developers, chipmakers and cloud computing providers.

The Bank for International Settlements found that 28.7% of investments made by AI companies between 2021 and 2025, measured by deal value, went to other AI companies, and that 55.2% of investment flowing into AI companies came from other AI businesses. The report identifies three types of arrangements: investor-supplier relationships, investor-purchaser relationships, and reciprocal arrangements involving financial commitments between companies. One prominent example involves Nvidia, which announced on Sept. 22, 2025, that it intended to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as the companies developed computing infrastructure powered by Nvidia technology, though Reuters reported in January, citing The Wall Street Journal, that the plan had stalled. Another example involves Amazon, which announced in April an additional $5 billion investment in Anthropic with the potential for another $20 billion, while Anthropic committed to spending $100 billion over 10 years on Amazon's chips and cloud computing services.

The report describes these arrangements as expanded forms of vendor financing, a longstanding practice in which suppliers help customers finance purchases, and notes that such deals can provide companies with capital they might otherwise struggle to obtain. The financing is particularly important for leading AI developers, many of which are startups spending more money than they generate in revenue and relying on outside investment to expand their operations. The report warns that complex financial agreements may obscure how much AI companies depend on one another, potentially understating their exposure to financial problems elsewhere in the industry, and compares these dynamics to circular financing relationships between telecommunications equipment suppliers and customers during the dot-com era, when investment dried up and some companies ultimately failed. The growing financial ties could let problems at one business spread to its suppliers, investors and customers, and if major banks or other financial institutions become heavily exposed, disruptions in the AI industry could also affect broader financial markets.

The International Monetary Fund's October Global Financial Stability Report identified a potential correction in AI-related investment as a major concern among financial market participants, though the extent of the risk depends partly on how companies finance their investments. When businesses fund AI investments through their own operating revenue rather than borrowing from banks or other financial institutions, the financial system's immediate exposure may be more limited. For Congress, the unresolved question is whether circular financing primarily helps companies build the infrastructure needed for AI development or creates financial dependencies that could deepen the consequences of an industry downturn.

stories.Headline: Trusteeship in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Building the Future Fiduciary
stories.Summary:

The authors examined how professional firms can rethink the way their people, controls, processes, and information function together. This analysis serves as the final installment of a three-part series focused on building the future fiduciary. The writers argued that embedding these technologies allows firms to reduce administrative burdens and improve the efficiency of their reporting.

Developing an AI-enabled operating model requires a strategic focus on information management, professional skills, governance, and internal controls. The authors stated that firms must align their overall AI strategy with their specific risk profiles, target markets, and existing operating models. This transition involves more than just automating current processes, as it requires maintaining human accountability and reliable data. The goal is to use automation to support decision-making and monitoring while preserving clear responsibility for execution and underlying expertise.

The authors from Teneo suggested that the primary challenge for boards and management teams is avoiding the adoption of individual tools in isolation. They emphasized that the correct approach strengthens oversight and increases capacity without sacrificing the necessary authority of the human fiduciary. These professionals noted that the integration of artificial intelligence provides a significant opportunity to redesign how professional services are delivered to clients. The report concludes that the future of the industry depends on balancing technological efficiency with professional accountability.

stories.Headline: Rabbi Sam Tygiel declines AI for sermon, citing frictionless answers and hidden authorship
stories.Summary:
Rabbi Sam Tygiel, the assistant rabbi at Congregation Sherith Israel in San Francisco, wrote an essay, delivered as a sermon at the congregation in October and published by J. on Nov. 17, 2026, about why he mostly chose not to use artificial intelligence while preparing it. In May, Pope Leo XIV released an encyclical, a written statement of church doctrine concerning current events, about artificial intelligence, and it opens with the story of the Tower of Babel as a cautionary tale about technology and human ambition. The essay says the encyclical and the pope’s use of that story raised questions for the rabbi about what a religious response to AI looks like and what a specifically Jewish one looks like. He then shared his own story of trying to write the sermon, how tempting it was to use AI and why he largely declined.

The dilemma began with research, when he wanted to learn more about the encyclical and was immediately tempted to use AI to get its main themes and key quotes. When he searched for resources about the encyclical, Google’s AI tool, Gemini, offered him a seemingly definitive summary of what the internet said about his query, which he described as making his attempt to learn “frictionless.” He wrote that there are many reasons not to use such a summary, including that chatbots are well known to be prone to “hallucinations,” or answers that satisfy a query but are partly or entirely false. The reason most meaningful to him was that the summary eliminates the direct encounter between the text’s author and the reader, and he cited the Hasidic master Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav, who writes that when we read another’s teachings our spirit becomes intertwined with the spirit of the teacher. Because he wanted that challenge and that fleeting but direct encounter, he decided to engage with the encyclical directly, even knowing he would miss important information given his necessarily limited capacity.

On another stop in preparing the sermon, he checked out a new chatbot for Jewish learning called Yochai, which also offered a library of Jewish texts, all translated, and one translation seemed strange and inhuman, with words and abbreviations rendered literally rather than according to their meaning in the received tradition. He asked the chatbot about the author of the translation and got a surprisingly evasive answer, in which Yochai said he was on the title page itself and that the translation was simply the straightforward rendering of those words into English. He asked again who wrote the translation, and the chatbot admitted it did not know, later saying the reader exposes no metadata about who produced the English renderings, with no translator credit, no publisher note and nothing attached at the passage level it could point to. He wrote that this is a common reality with AI programs known as large language models, or LLMs, which obscure authorship and the origin of ideas and thereby eliminate possible accountability, making it difficult to trace the lineage of human wisdom behind their responses. He also attempted to turn the chatbot into his study partner, aware throughout of the frictionless quality of the interactions, in which whatever prompt he gave, Yochai created something that mirrored and validated his input, and he likened it to the kind of parrot that leading AI thinker Dr. Timnit Gebru and her coauthors warned about in the 2020 article “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots.”

The essay cites an ancient story about Talmudic study partners in which Rabbi Yochanan celebrates the way his chevruta, Reish Lakish, pushes back on him, and it says that friction is the very quality that makes Reish Lakish a beloved partner in study, with spiritual growth coming from a relationship that involves friction. Ultimately, the rabbi wrote, it was the frictionlessness of his interactions with AI that made him turn away from using LLMs to help write the sermon, and he suggested that perhaps God scattered the ancestors who built the great tower as a way of saying that this is not what partnership looks like. He concluded that true partnership comes from the holy messiness of encountering the other and acknowledging and celebrating the distance between us even as we reach toward one another. The essay identifies Rabbi Tygiel as an alumnus of Hadar’s Rising Song Residency who was ordained at Hebrew College and composes original Jewish music, which can be heard on his website, samtygiel.com.

stories.Headline: AWS publishes a three-phase responsible AI roadmap for agentic systems
stories.Summary:
AWS published a roadmap on November 17, 2026, for responsible AI in agentic systems, aimed at the platform teams that govern agent infrastructure and the application teams that build agents on top of it. The post says companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use, and that the nondeterministic nature of generative AI models adds complexity earlier software practices did not anticipate. It gives examples of a real estate app that generates listings from retrieved data and a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases, asking whether each can be verified not to invent features or surface confidential information. It notes that responsible AI was until recently model-centric and scoped to the machine learning lifecycle of training, testing, and inference, when models did not reason, use tools, or take actions. Generative AI applications and agents now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, which the post says expands both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.

The roadmap maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars, which include security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance, to a three-phase maturity model of governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. An accompanying scorecard lets application and platform teams assess where they are today and iterate as applications mature, and the post says it covers key questions to ask at each phase while leaving out step-by-step implementation details and legal or compliance advice. It cites Robinhood, which built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance and achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. It also cites Wade and Wirtz in the Harvard Business Review on trust becoming a competitive differentiator, saying the same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate. The post defines an agentic AI platform as described in its AgentOps post on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale, and presents the pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline.

Four challenges surface consistently in conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, according to the post. Unpredictable runtime behavior covers nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures, and the post says a financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services. Data exposure and authority boundaries require scoping every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions, isolating session context, and granting privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions agents cannot modify themselves. Regulatory velocity names the EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation as creating requirements faster than governance can adapt, and the post says proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation on a predefined cadence such as daily, weekly, or monthly. Team collaboration covers the lack of a shared framework for who owns what across the agent lifecycle, and the post says a media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads.

In the first phase, application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric, while the platform team establishes the core landing zone infrastructure, including overarching monitoring and access control, and governs newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start. Teams evaluate access to the data and systems each agent needs and assess potential impact, which the post says lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy. They implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring. They build a map of data shared between agents, such as organizational knowledge bases, and subjective data such as context graphs individual agents might need, then establish access boundaries and assign read and write permissions accordingly. They define a risk classification rubric aligned to regulatory obligations such as EU AI Act risk tiers and financial services industry requirements, assign Low, Medium, High, or Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case, and document the control requirements each level triggers.
