stories.Headline: Lawfare article argues access to generative AI may become a derivative right
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a November 17, 2026, Lawfare article asking whether access to generative AI is a privilege or a right, and they trace how electricity, the telephone, and the internet moved from privilege to right. The article says use of generative AI rose sharply after ChatGPT launched in November 2022, and that by October 2026 OpenAI alone reported more than 1.2 billion monthly ChatGPT users. It reports that 24 percent of American adults use generative AI tools daily, and that a 2024 survey by Microsoft and LinkedIn found 66 percent of business leaders said they would not hire someone without AI skills. The article argues that access to generative AI may be on a path to becoming a right, following past technologies but at a quicker pace.

The article defines meaningful access to AI as requiring that the system be available, affordable, sufficiently reliable, accessible in different languages, and usable with reasonably accessible devices and connectivity, and not subject to arbitrary or discriminatory denial. It says this does not mean access to every model, frontier-level capabilities, unlimited compute, or uses that create substantial risks to others. It sets out three ways a technology may be conceived as a right: a freestanding human right, a derivative right necessary to exercise existing rights such as education, political participation, or access to information, or a statutory social entitlement like universal-service programs such as education. It cites the Universal Declaration of Human Rights Preamble, which establishes rights as "equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family," and lists rights to life and liberty, legal recognition and remedy, nationality, property ownership, and marriage, plus protection from slavery, torture, and arbitrary detention. It cites legal philosopher Joseph Raz's 1984 essay on derivative rights, and argues AI may become necessary to exercise already-recognized rights, making it best conceived as a derivative right.

The article says society and the AI industry should grapple with these questions now rather than waiting until necessity leaves no choice, and that developers should consider the degree to which generative AI is likely to evolve into a right and design systems and policies with that end state in mind. It says the development and deployment of generative AI has outpaced prior technologies. It says the practical implications concern the billion-plus daily users of generative AI tools today and the many billions who will use them or be impacted by their use in the near future. It says that if one accepts the premise that the public should take seriously the prospect that access to generative AI is on the path to becoming a right, critical considerations with regard to access need to be addressed.

The article says most technologies viewed as critical necessities today began as luxuries enjoyed by a wealthy and privileged elite, and that a technology's progression from privilege to right often involves an evolution in how it is perceived, regulated, and accessed. It says nonprofit organizations serving the basic needs of the unhoused previously provided food and shelter and now increasingly provide access to cheap mobile phones. It says internet access began several decades ago as a U.S. Department of Defense research experiment with highly limited access, and that the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals now include pursuing universal, affordable internet access in the least developed countries. It says that in the early 2020s access to generative AI was largely gated behind application programming interfaces and limited to wealthy corporations, select government agencies, and tech-forward early adopters. It says generative AI is being integrated into financial, health care, education, and other sectors, used by developers coding, doctors reviewing scans, and farmers determining ideal planting conditions.

The article says electricity began as a technology financed by private capital and available only to the wealthy, and that governments treated broad access as a public necessity only after society reorganized itself around electricity. It says more than a century passed from Benjamin Franklin's 1752 kite experiment showing lightning is an electrical phenomenon to Thomas Edison's commercially practical incandescent light bulb in 1879, and that electricity arrived in the homes of wealthy and urban American elites in the 1880s. It says urban electrification accelerated in the 1910s and 1920s, that indoor lighting allowed homes to dispense with dangerous gas- and kerosene-based lamps that emitted hazardous fumes, and that work days no longer needed to be oriented entirely around sunlight hours. It says that in 1936 nearly 90 percent of farms lacked electric power because serving rural areas was prohibitive for private utilities, and that the newly created Rural Electrification Administration responded by financing cooperatives and infrastructure expansion. It says President Franklin D. Roosevelt said at a 1938 celebration of the Rural Electrification Administration that "Electricity is a modern necessity of life," and that the UN's Sustainable Development Goal 7 calls for "universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services" by 2030.

The article says U.S. utility companies can shut down power to a home after repeated nonpayment, though many states have exemptions, and that a person moving to a rural location not yet connected to the electric grid typically bears some of the costs of extending the grid infrastructure, though the utility company cannot typically refuse their connection. It says that even where access to electricity is inhibited, such as when an electric power line no longer reaches a home, an inhabitant of that community can still get the benefit of electric power via devices, batteries, or local generators that do not require a connection to the grid. It says the first successful transmission of intelligible speech on a phone line occurred in 1876, and that early development was fractured, expensive, and heavily concentrated in commercial hubs. It says the article follows electricity, the telephone, and the internet from discovery to widespread adoption, from privilege to right, and that though unique in origin and velocity, each technology lands in a similar position. It says that should the trend continue, generative AI may gain a permanent foothold in economies and societies and may eventually become a necessity for full participation in the workforce and in civic life, though not all jobs will require it and a life without it will not be inherently poor.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Access to Generative AI: Privilege or Right?

stories.Headline: Justice department lawyers use Pangram AI detector to accuse defense attorneys of writing filings with AI
stories.Summary:
Lawyers for the Department of Justice used the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys were using AI to write legal arguments, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. In one filing the government attorneys told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT” and writing “AI slop” filings. The filings over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, trying to catch each other using AI and citing their opponents’ AI use in arguments to the court. The case centers on a high-profile voter fraud case against Khalwinder Bhengura, an Indian man who entered the United States on an immigrant visa in 2022. Bhengura registered to vote in Texas in 2024 after falsely stating on his driver’s license application that he was an American citizen, which his lawyers say was illegal and apparently accidental.

Bhengura was arrested in September on charges of lying about his citizenship status, illegally registering to vote, and illegally voting in the 2024 election. He was found guilty in October on two of the three counts. The case is taking place in federal court in the Northern District of Texas, which recently implemented a rule requiring attorneys to disclose generative AI use in filings. In some filings Bhengura’s attorneys wrote that “portions of this brief were prepared with the assistance of a generative artificial intelligence tool.” Government attorneys ran several of the filings through Pangram and filed the results as exhibits to one of its arguments, and the Pangram results were mixed, as they did not show the briefings were 100 percent AI-drafted.

The government’s attorneys wrote that they did not feel they should have to respond substantively to briefs that were partially AI-generated. The United States has “been trying to economize the amount of effort it puts into responding to Defendant’s meritless motions given that Defendant appears to be almost entirely using AI to generate them,” the DOJ attorneys wrote. They added that most of the non-AI generated text in the filings consists of statements from third parties other than Defense counsel, including statements from evidence or documents in the record or quotes from caselaw. In other words, virtually nothing of substance in these filings seems to have been drafted by a human on the Defense team, they added. The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.

The judge in the case, Mark Pittman, chastised the defense attorneys for their use of AI. He wrote that the Court is disturbed by counsel’s repeated filings which subtly bend the law by proffering superficially persuasive but fundamentally meritless arguments so clearly generated by artificial intelligence. Pittman wrote that Defendant is not a pro se litigant and has three counsel of record with decades of practice between them. He wrote that it is distressing to see how quickly the advent of artificial intelligence has undermined counsels’ ability to properly advocate for their client. Nicole Knox and Mario Herrera, two of Bhengura’s attorneys, told 404 Media that the story isn’t so simple.

Knox and Herrera said they felt they had to use AI because of a health emergency and in order to meet the court’s tight filing deadlines ahead of the election. Herrera said Knox experienced a medical emergency while they were at the U.S. Attorney's Office preparing the case with the prosecutors, and that he prepared a federal jury trial in four days with the lead attorney in the hospital. Herrera said he represented his client to the best of his abilities within this limited timeframe, utilized all available legal tools and did not violate any rules or laws in doing so. Herrera said the government's evidence consisted of output from Pangram, an AI-detection software that identifies patterns in writing styles based upon a document’s content and cannot determine who wrote a document, how it was written, or if the law applied within a document is correct. Herrera said the U.S. Attorney's Office did not identify any false citations.

Herrera said “Defense by ChatGPT” is a label the government placed in a court filing regarding the defense of a 70-year-old permanent resident facing prison and deportation, and that it is not a factual statement. Herrera said the attorneys who wrote it were present when Ms. Knox collapsed and knew precisely why he was standing alone with a new co-counsel in that courtroom four days later. Herrera said there was nothing requiring them to state what they stated. Pangram CEO Max Spero told 404 Media that anecdotally he has heard that law firms have begun to use his company’s software, but that most use cases he has seen have been from firms using the tool internally to check whether their junior attorneys and paralegals are using AI to draft legal briefs. Herrera said that the fact that Bhengura was found not guilty on one of the three counts he faced is evidence that Mr. Bhengura received the representation that he deserved.

Herrera said lawyers have been using templates, forms, and drafting software for decades and that this is merely a newer version of those very tools. Herrera said the arguments that the judge attacked were written by him, that some portions of the filings were written with the aid of AI but then reviewed and edited by him, and that all final work product was his and he stands behind the argument and logic of each and every document. Herrera said it was the use of AI during that week that allowed him to work on many tasks at once and produce so much work in four days. Knox said AI could have never come up with our argument, and said the new AI disclosure rule has made it such that if you obtain one sentence or phrase through the use of A.I., then you must disclose it, adding that we have nothing to hide. Herrera said Mr. Bhengura is 70 years old, a lawful permanent resident of this country, speaks Punjabi, and his English is limited.

Herrera said their defense on the one count of which the jury acquitted him was that he never knowingly claimed to be a U.S. citizen. Herrera said Bhengura has been in custody since the verdict, and in addition to whatever sentence he receives for the offenses of which he has been found guilty, he faces deportation from this country. Herrera said Bhengura is entitled to more compassion and humanity from everyone involved in this case than he has received so far. Bhengura has been in prison for months and is set to be deported. Bhengura’s case is one of a few dozen in which the Trump administration found disparate cases of voter fraud, which is exceedingly rare, and made big, public shows of the arrests it made.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Department of Justice Is Using AI Detector Pangram Against Defense Attorneys

stories.Headline: Sameer Mhaisekar leads a free TechGig masterclass on AI productivity on 4 December 2026
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig will hold a free live online masterclass on 4 December 2026 from 2:00 PM to 3:30 PM IST under the title "From 2 Days to 20 Minutes: How AI Is Transforming Workforce Productivity," according to a TechGig article published on 17 November 2026. The 90-minute session will be led by Sameer Mhaisekar, an AI consultant, technology evangelist and three-time Microsoft MVP with expertise in enterprise AI, intelligent agents, cloud technologies and enterprise software integrations. The article says the masterclass aims to help professionals understand how AI assistants and intelligent agents are changing workplace productivity and to explore practical ways to embrace AI-powered work. Registration is free, and the article urges readers to save a seat through its registration link.

The session is built around five stated topics, starting with the productivity revolution and the evolution from traditional software to generative AI and intelligent agents. A second segment on becoming a supercharged employee covers how AI can support research, writing, analysis, content creation and problem-solving while saving time and improving efficiency. A third looks at how businesses are adopting AI, transforming team responsibilities and redesigning workflows, and a fourth explains how AI agents differ from conventional assistants and how they execute multistep tasks alongside humans. The fifth is a practical demonstration of an illustrative AI-assisted workflow using Microsoft Copilot, followed by a live question and answer session.

The article says the masterclass is aimed at technology professionals, developers, business analysts, product managers, engineering managers, team leaders and digital transformation enthusiasts, and that no advanced AI or coding knowledge is required to take part. It frames the shift as one in which professionals must learn to collaborate with intelligent systems rather than use them for occasional tasks, delegating work to AI, evaluating its outputs and combining machine intelligence with human judgment. Mhaisekar will share perspectives on translating AI capabilities into practical workplace applications, according to the article. The article states that participants will gain insights into how professionals and organisations can approach AI adoption, improve everyday workflows and prepare for an increasingly AI-driven workplace.

The article presents the masterclass as a response to a workplace that is evolving faster than ever, arguing that professionals who understand how to leverage AI effectively will have new opportunities to improve productivity, strengthen their capabilities and adapt to changing business expectations. It says AI has moved beyond generating text, answering questions or creating presentations to assisting with research, analysing documents, supporting decision-making, automating repetitive activities and executing multistep workflows. The article does not say what happens after the session or whether any follow-up events are planned. It closes by inviting readers to join on 4 December 2026 and to turn hours of work into minutes of productivity.

Articles.Title: 2 Days of Work in 20 Minutes? Don't Miss This AI Productivity Masterclass

stories.headline_source: 2 Days of Work in 20 Minutes? Don't Miss This AI Productivity Masterclass

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public on Thursday in an offering estimated to raise about $64.35 billion
stories.Summary:
Capital Economics wrote on Monday that the AI stock boom is “in its final stages,” and Anthropic is going public on Thursday in a deal estimated to raise about $64.35 billion at the top of its range. That is nearly twice what every U.S. IPO raised together last quarter, according to Renaissance Capital. The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter while employers added an average of 48,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, before a 165,000 gain in October. AI spending drove more than half of business-investment growth in the first three quarters of the year, Goldman Sachs estimates. Bloomberg reported on Nov. 12 that the Anthropic deal was about six times oversubscribed, days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s David Kelly sees real GDP growth slowing to 1.6% over the next four quarters, with hiring stuck near 50,000 a month. Morgan Stanley’s research digest on Monday, summarizing chief U.S. economist Michael Gapen’s 2027 outlook, put the breakeven at about 50,000 jobs a month. Federal Reserve economists Seth Murray and Ivan Vidangos think labor force growth “could be near-zero starting this year,” which would put the breakeven near zero too. Goldman estimates AI investment will add 0.6 percentage points to “true” GDP growth in 2027 and only 0.2 points to the GDP that actually gets counted. Gapen sees hyperscalers spending $1.6 trillion on capex in 2027, adding 0.9 points to growth.

Capital Economics markets economist Joe Maher pointed to falling share issuance and “investors’ waning appetite for new shares of AI-firms at lofty valuations,” and wrote that Anthropic is “a key test.” Kelly said two years of 2.3% growth “should have led to a monthly gain of roughly 155,000 net new jobs,” and mainly blames “a lack of available workers due to a sharp reversal of immigration policy.” Gapen’s outlook says the AI money is mostly propping up upper-income households, while low- and middle-income consumers lead the slowdown, and he expects AI disruption and tighter Fed policy to keep hiring subdued. Goldman calls today’s job market “low-hire, low-fire,” a phrase made famous by former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. Goldman economists expect that job market to hold for about another year “before AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”

Morgan Stanley sees 2.5% growth in 2027 and Goldman 2.4%, against JPMAM’s 1.6% over the next four quarters. Nvidia is still buying about $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the offering, and Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the first two of 22 underwriters named on the cover of Anthropic’s prospectus. Employers hired at a 3.4% rate in September, according to the Labor Department’s JOLTS report, and the unemployment rate for 20- to 24-year-olds was 7.5% in October, against 4.1% overall. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found in August that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed work. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the 12 months through October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said, and JPMAM points out that “despite a tight labor market, real year-over-year wage growth has been negative for seven consecutive months.”

Productivity in the nonfarm business sector rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the third quarter, the BLS said Nov. 5, while labor’s share of output fell to 53.0%, the lowest since the series began in 1947. Indeed Hiring Lab’s Aubrey Woessner wrote that AI investment “appear[s] to be contributing” to the productivity gains, but that “increased labor productivity has not yet translated into higher real pay.” Apollo Global Management economists Sania Edlich and Torsten Slok sorted occupations by how heavily their tasks show up in Claude conversations, using Anthropic’s own Economic Index, and found that after 2023 real wage growth in the most-exposed occupations has run about 6.7 percentage points behind less-exposed jobs, with no statistically significant effect on employment. Workers in the lowest wage quartile of those jobs took the biggest hit, about 10.7 points, and the authors wrote that “the first measurable labor market effect of AI adoption has been wage compression rather than employment displacement.” Apollo estimates about 5.8 million workers are in the most-exposed occupations, and the authors caution that the period “may be partially confounded by post-pandemic labor market dynamics.”

Advertised salaries in the most AI-exposed occupations have risen 46% since 2021, against 25% for the least exposed, according to Indeed data reported in September. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index stood at 51.0 in its preliminary November reading, and survey director Joanne Hsu wrote that “about 57% spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices.” Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder and CEO, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai spoke to the press after a September 29 meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House. Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of the article, and the reporter independently reported and verified the factual claims, with a human editor reviewing it before publication. The article gives no date for when Anthropic’s shares begin trading beyond Thursday, and no figure for what the offering would raise below the top of its range.

stories.Headline: PM calls for considering disabling Wi-Fi at CSAT test sites to prevent AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook instructed government officials on Monday, November 16, 2026, to implement strict measures against artificial intelligence cheating. These urgent orders come just three days before the nationwide College Scholastic Ability Test, which is scheduled for this Thursday. The government is reacting to a shocking confession from the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam. This individual admitted on Sunday to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative AI to cheat on two rounds of that test. He further confessed to using these same sophisticated methods to cheat on a certified public accountant exam.

The new requirements involve the education ministry ensuring that all test takers turn in every smart device before the exam begins. Officials must conduct thorough checks to confirm that no smart devices are possessed by students during the testing period. Additionally, the science ministry has been asked to actively consider disabling all public Wi-Fi signals at the test sites. Prime Minister Han also announced the establishment of an interagency emergency response team for the 2027 CSAT to create comprehensive preventive measures. The government intends to investigate any abnormal signs that defy common sense after the exam using objective data.

Prime Minister Han stated that the government must concentrate all national capabilities to prepare against misconduct involving advanced AI technology. She explained that conventional exam management methods are now limited because AI technology is advancing so rapidly. The prime minister emphasized that upholding the fairness of examinations is a fundamental duty directly linked to public trust. She urged each government ministry to develop effective measures and ensure they are implemented thoroughly across all state-administered exams. Han called for the development of advanced detection technologies, including those leveraging AI, to counter ultra-small electronic devices and outside help.

The government is now scrambling to prevent similar AI-assisted cheating from occurring during the upcoming college entrance examinations. This concern follows reports of four separate cheating cases involving AI glasses at middle and high schools earlier this year. Authorities have indicated that they will pursue criminal punishment and a three-year exam ban for any CSAT cheaters using AI glasses. Officials are now tasked with creating a comprehensive government strategy to respond to increasingly diverse and sophisticated methods of cheating. They aim to create a fair testing environment that the public can trust through these new technical measures.

Articles.Title: PM calls for considering disabling Wi-Fi at CSAT test sites to prevent AI cheating

stories.Headline: South Korea and Philippines agree to deepen cooperation in AI and defense industry
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Philippine President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. held a summit on Monday, November 16, 2026, in Manila. This meeting occurred on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and marked the third time the two leaders have met. They previously held discussions in Gyeongju, South Korea, last year and again in the Philippine capital during March. The leaders focused on strengthening ties in traditional sectors and expanding their partnership into several emerging industries.

The agreement requires deeper cooperation in defense manufacturing, infrastructure, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence, nuclear power plants, aerospace, and disaster management. Bilateral trade between the two nations reached US$21.3 billion during the first nine months of this year, which already exceeds the previous annual record. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on science and technology to expand collaboration into smart farming. Additionally, they signed a grant aid agreement to help the Korea International Cooperation Agency implement various projects in the Philippines.

Spokesperson Kim Sung-wan stated that President Lee requested continued support from the Philippine government to help South Korean companies expand their operations. The spokesperson noted that both leaders pledged to foster mutually beneficial cooperation in areas where their bilateral ties are already strong. President Lee arrived in Manila on Monday for a four-day trip to engage with regional leaders. He is scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China, next to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Articles.Title: S. Korea's Lee, Philippines' Marcos agree to deepen cooperation in defense industry, AI
